News.title: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
News.content:
Young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support, the author of a major review of youth unemployment has told the BBC.

Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister whose proposals on welfare and young people will be unveiled on Tuesday, said those who refuse to take up the help could lose their benefits.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Milburn called for a radical shift in government spending away from benefits for young people to measures that support them into work.

He claims spending on benefits for young people is 25 times as much as spending on employment support, and believes the ratio should shift to two to one.

That would mean significant cuts to benefit spending and significant extra taxpayers' cash for training, education or other forms of support.

Milburn said "the pendulum's swung far too far from the one to the other - Â£25 to one, and we can take everything to Â£2 to one".

He added: "To do that, we've got to invest, less in benefits, so we've got to be paying out less in benefits."

The former MP acknowledged that would mean some young people losing out on benefits, arguing the system should focus on helping people into work rather than keeping them dependent on welfare.

News.title: King jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
News.content:
King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.

The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts.

"We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".

The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.

The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary.

"I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."

News.title: Widespread frost and freezing fog as cold health alerts continue
News.content:
Saturday began with temperatures widely below freezing in parts of England and Wales.

Temperatures in South Newington, England dropped to minus 7.2C, the lowest recorded temperature in the UK so far this autumn.

In Wales, readings bottomed out at minus 6.2C in Sennybridge.

Motorists should be alert for some patchy freezing fog which forms in air that is below freezing.

Super-cooled water droplets remain suspended in the air and it can be particularly dangerous as they can freeze on impact turning untreated pavements into instant ice rinks.

Yellow cold health alerts from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) are in force for the West Midlands and north-west England until 12:00 Saturday, external.

After the fog and frost clears, Saturday will largely become a bright and dry day.

By the afternoon, temperatures will rise across the UK - ranging from 7C in parts of the Highlands to a milder 12C in south-west England.

England and Wales are forecast to see long spells of sunshine, away from the odd shower early on in the far north-west.

Northern Ireland will have some bright spells in the morning, with thickening cloud in the afternoon and rain by evening.

A few showers are expected in parts of Scotland where is will also be a breezy day, and will feel colder due to the wind chill.

News.title: Brand, Walliams and Married at First Sight: Is this a reckoning for the entertainment industry?
News.content:
This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.

On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women.

By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him.

Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show.

These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry.

So why is this all happening now?

In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence.

All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago.

From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting.

"The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me.

In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court.

Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry.

It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him. The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations.

What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave".

News.title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
News.content:
After a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.

The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.

And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment.

"We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.

Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?

Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.

News.title: The search to find a friend for Jojo the gorilla after a lifetime of being alone
News.content:
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.

More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary â but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla â that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.

News.title: Eurovision is finally coming to Asia - meet the stars gearing up to take the stage
News.content:
On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.

Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year.

And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia.

It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts.

Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT).

Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region.

"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust.

"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer.

"It's all about popularity â fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly."

News.title: When to put up a real Christmas tree - according to an expert
News.content:
The appropriate time to put up your Christmas tree is a question almost as divisive as whether Yorkshire pudding has a place on the Christmas dinner plate.

Some might feel the best time is just after Bonfire Night, others may think Christmas Eve is more apt, and most will probably plump for somewhere in between.

Tesco started selling Christmas trees at half-price this week and said more than 90% of its trees had sold out by the end of November last year.

Lidl and some other retailers are also launching their ranges next week, while others including Dobbies Garden Centres are waiting until the last week of November.

But with Christmas Day still six weeks away, is it unwise to rush into buying a real tree so early? And do you risk spending your Christmas week cleaning up piles of pine needles?

Probably, says Mick Walker, from Bolton Christmas Trees, which grows trees in the Scottish Highlands before sending them to homes across the UK.

"It might last until the beginning of Christmas, but it won't last the full holiday," he warns. "Unless its a potted one, it's going to be sagging by Christmas Day - big time."

He calls Tesco's half-price deal "insane", adding that it's "sucking them into buying something now that isn't going to do the job".

So when would he suggest is the best time? "If it was me, I'd put it up a week before Christmas eve, [and it will] last straight through until New Year."

News.title: Family's two-year fight to bring killer driver back from Latvia
News.content:
Days after her 12-year-old son was killed by a BMW driver travelling at 70mph, Louise Slater sat outside the suspect's home, gathering the courage to plead with his family to hand him in.

She had been given the name and address of Aleksanders Dolars after her son Keaton was killed in a hit-and-run in Coventry.

Distraught, she was preparing to knock on the door when a neighbour approached and asked what she was doing.

When she explained, he told her the family, from Latvia, had packed up and left a day or two earlier.

Keaton's suspected killer had fled just hours after leaving him dying in the road.

What followed was a relentless two-year fight by his parents to track him down and bring him back to England to face justice.

He was finally jailed on Friday, for nine years and four months.

This article contains upsetting details

Dolars' name had been already circulating locally before police identified him as their main suspect on 18 June 2024, four days after Keaton was killed.

A family waiting at nearby traffic lights said their seven-seater "shook violently" as a BMW driver sped past at what appeared to be far more than the 30mph limit. Moments later, they saw something fly into the air behind them.

The car did not stop.

As it disappeared from view, the family noticed a black rucksack and a single shoe lying in Radford Road and realised a child may have been hit.

News.title: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".

It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".

When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".

"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.

Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."

Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.

Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.

"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

News.title: Burnham says Welsh Labour lost sight of devolution as review criticises ex-first minister
News.content:
Burnham spoke ahead of the publication of a review of what went wrong at the election.

Since he became prime minister he has been lobbying the Welsh government to devolve more powers to local councils.

"Somewhere along the way perhaps we lost sight of some of the principles that drove devolution in the first place.

"We probably stopped listening as much as we should have, and actually stopped driving power down into every Welsh postcode which is what the vision to me really should always have been about - about people and places."

He said the party would accept its defeat and "come back stronger" with a "vision for a stronger Wales in a fairer United Kingdom."

Burnham said he wanted to achieve the sense of a "one Labour team for Wales" where the party is "pulling in the same direction".

"Where I'm pulling with you and not creating problems for you or going against what Ken or colleagues want to achieve.

"We will put forward a vision for communities up and down Wales, as well as giving Wales a stronger national voice."

Addressing the event at Venue Cymru in Llandudno, Burnham said he loved "everything about Wales".

He said his last visit to Wales - to Aberfan - left the "biggest mark".

Referencing the fight for justice in the years after the disaster, Burnham said he wanted a "country where all people and all places are treated fairly and with dignity".

He said his vision for the country is a "reindustrialised nation with revitalised high streets".

Burnham said Labour should be "immensely proud" of the things it achieved in Wales - including free school meals, free prescription and the creation of Transport for Wales.

The prime minister said he wanted to show how "being in the UK is good for Wales because of the partnership that we can develop together".

Burnham said he had put the full devolution of employment support on the table with the Welsh government.

It was announced at the budget that standing charges for gas will come to an end. Burnham confirmed that the charges will be scrapped in the new year.

Menon's criticism of Red Welsh Way was one of several findings, including that the party suffered a long-term decline in support, laid bare as Labour took flak for dissatisfaction with public services.

It said "weaknesses in political communication" also left the party without "clear answers when voters wanted them.

The review says Labour should set itself against Plaid Cymru's "constitutional project", by seeking more powers based on what they would deliver rather than "debating powers in the abstract".

Labour has shared most of Plaid's constitutional demands, including the devolution of policing, the Crown Estate and rail devolution, with the exception of independence.

Plaid beat Welsh Labour in the May election, and was now running the Welsh government.

News.title: US Air Force says it responded to 'suspected drones' over RAF Lakenheath
News.content:
The US Air Force said it responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" over RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk on Friday evening.

No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a spokesperson for the US Air Force said.

It comes after unconfirmed reports that sirens were sounded at the base, which residents reported hearing from a nearby village.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson told the BBC it was "coordinating with all relevant parties", adding that US Air Force security personnel responded to the reports and the situation was resolved.

"We are working closely with them to establish the facts," they added.

West Suffolk MP Nick Timothy said he had been in touch with authorities at the base, and was told "there is no threat to the public, and the incident is now resolved".

"Given the raised threat level, I continue to encourage everyone to report anything suspicious or out of the ordinary to the authorities," he added in a social media post.

Earlier this week, at least 12 US Air Force aircraft departed the nearby RAF Mildenhall base.

They included two Boeing Stratotanker KC-135 refuelling aircraft, with one apparently headed towards Germany and another seen landing at Prestwick Airport near Glasgow.

News.title: Probation officers to take industrial action over pay and early release scheme
News.content:
Probation officers have voted to reject a 5% pay rise and take industrial action, citing growing pressure created by the government's prisoner early release scheme.

Members of Napo, the probation service union, voted to refuse overtime from 23 November - and could take strike action should the union "deem that option to be necessary".

Its general secretary Ian Lawrence said the service was "already in crisis" before the early release scheme came into force, which relies on probation staff monitoring freed prisoners in the community.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said the government had put forward a "strong offer" and was recruiting an extra "1,300 officers to significantly cut workloads".

They added that the government has "robust contingency plans in place" to ensure offenders "are still subject to the same rigorous supervision" in the event of industrial action.

Probation service unions have warned that officers have too many cases and the rate at which staff are leaving the profession has increased.

The service has come under renewed pressure in recent months as a result of the early release scheme, the union said, which the government introduced as prisons were dangerously close to capacity.

Seven-hundred eligible offenders originally sentenced to up to 19 months were released on 1 October, with another two groups of 650 prisoners released on 13 October and 10 November.

Another nine groups are expected to leave prison in the next seven months, with inmates who received longer sentences included in the later cohorts.

Some 250 prisoners serving more than 12 years are expected to be released on 9 June.

Napo's leader said staff had tried "desperately" to implement early release schemes introduced by the Labour government and previous Conservative government, but had been asked to do so with "inadequate staff and a lack of resources".

The government has said electronic tags and probation intervention will help to manage prisoners freed early.

The Probation Service uses electronic monitoring to track curfews and conditions of a court or prison order, with most of those eligible for early release now requiring tagging.

But a September report by His Majesty's Inspectorate of Probation (HMIP) found that almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders' movements were not fitted on time.

News.title: Fifteen taken to hospital after deliberate fire at Glasgow flats
News.content:
Police are treating a fire at a block of flats in Glasgow as deliberate.

Four fire engines were sent to the four-storey building on Copland Road, in the Ibrox area, just after 17:00 on Friday after reports of a fire on the ground floor.

Firefighters and paramedics initially said they were dealing with "multiple casualties" and police have now confirmed 15 people were taken to hospital as a precaution.

The fire was extinguished and crews left the scene by 22:00.

News.title: 'I'm lucky to be alive': Woman's warning over black market weight-loss jabs
News.content:
A woman has described how she could not speak or stand before being rushed to hospital after taking an unlicensed weight-loss jab.

Kay Roscoe, 38, from Birkenhead, said she had used a substance sold as retatrutide, or "reta", for two months before falling seriously ill.

The experimental drug is not approved for general use and is available only through clinical trials. Products claiming to contain it are widely sold online, but it is not known whether Kay took genuine retatrutide.

She is now warning others about the risks. "I am the luckiest person to be alive. Honestly I can't say it enough, get off the pens," she said.

On the day of her collapse, Kay had been due to go out for a roast dinner with a friend.

When she failed to answer her phone, her friend went to check on her at home and found her unable to speak or stand.

"I was frothing at the mouth, not responsive at all," she said, recounting what her friend later told her. "My eyes were moving around, but I couldn't speak or move or do anything."

Kay, who has no memory of the episode, said her friends rang an ambulance and told paramedics she had been taking "reta" before she was rushed to hospital.

She said it took more than an hour for her to regain consciousness.

News.title: Bluetongue virus confirmed on County Down farm
News.content:
The first case of Bluetongue in Northern Ireland this season has been confirmed on a farm in Kilkeel, County Down.

Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) said the virus had been detected in three sheep.

There will be no additional movement restrictions or disease control zones, because the virus has been present in Northern Ireland since November 2025.

It presents no risk to public health.

The minister, Andrew Muir, said the discovery of the virus was "disappointing but not unexpected", given the spread of the disease in Great Britain and Ireland.

The Chief Veterinary Officer, Brian Dooher, urged local farmers to be alert to any symptoms in their livestock.

News.title: Temperatures plunge to -6C in UK as new cold weather alert issued
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Yellow cold health alerts have been issued for large parts of the UK as temperatures drop below -6C in parts of the country.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued an alert for the North West of England, North East of England and Yorkshire from 9pm on Sunday.

The alerts will remain in place until Thursday morning, the agency said.

It is the second cold health alert this autumn, after a warning in the North West and West Midlands regions came into force on Thursday.

Paul Coleman, Consultant in Public Health at UKHSA, said: “This is the latest cold-health alert of the season, and we can expect more as we move further into winter. Cold weather can have a serious impact on the health of some people, including those aged 65 and over and those with pre-existing health conditions, so it is vital to check in on friends, family and neighbours who are most vulnerable.

“We’re also reminding people to take simple steps to stay warm and look after their health. If you can, try to heat the rooms you spend most of your time in, such as your living room or bedroom, and dress warmly to help you stay safe and well during colder weather.”

The UKHSA said the low temperatures could result in increased use of health care services by vulnerable people and an increased risk to health for those with pre-existing health conditions or over 65.

News.title: Wales v New Zealand LIVE: Hosts face daunting All Blacks test in Nations Championship
News.content:

Beauden Barrett captains New Zealand against Wales ( Getty )

Wales face up to the daunting challenge of New Zealand as they again seek to end their seven-decade wait for success against the All Blacks.

Steve Tandy’s side made a winning, if unconvincing, start to their November with Nations Championship success against Japan last week, but will know they must lift their level to stay with their vaunted visitors. Aaron Wainwright’s injury absence is a blow to the hosts, who have not beaten New Zealand since 1953.

This looks a touring team in increasingly fine fettle, too, though Dave Rennie takes the opportunity to look at the strength in the depth of his squad. Beauden Barrett captains the All Blacks for the first time as the full-back closes in on a century and a half of international caps, while Richie Mo’unga is a rather handy third-string fly half to bring in.

News.title: Andy Burnham accuses Tories of ‘burning bridges’ with EU over Brexit
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Andy Burnham accused the Tories of having “burned all of our bridges” in the aftermath of Brexit and said the country had “lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years”.

The prime minister’s remarks in recent weeks have fuelled questions about the prospect of the UK returning to the EU or adopting its freedom of movement rules, but Mr Burnham has insisted voters would ultimately be “the boss” of any changes.

At the 2016 EU referendum, 854,572 (52.5 per cent) voters in Wales chose to leave the EU, compared with 772,347 (47.5 per cent) supporting Remain.

Mr Burnham appeared at Welsh Labour conference in Llandudno as he acknowledged the party needs to “listen” and “take stock” following a major defeat in May’s Senedd election.

Defending his efforts to secure new deals with the EU, the Prime Minister told Welsh Labour conference: “We’ve got the Conservatives who are standing out against it, saying no change. Well, I don’t believe Brexit and the deal that they got has been good enough for Britain.

“I think we’ve lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years, and, actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016, because they burned all of our bridges in the aftermath, with the EU, and so I’m going to lead as Prime Minister on this issue, and I’m going to go and try and get the best deal I can for Wales, for those here who could benefit, Welsh farmers, exporters of Welsh shellfish and Welsh lamb.”

open image in gallery Andy Burnham accused the Tories of having 'burned all of our bridges' in the aftermath of Brexit and said the country had 'lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years' ( Getty )

Andy Burnham said working with the EU would mean “respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum result”.

He told the audience: “People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that’s what makes us who we are.

“And, yes, working with the European Union, as I said, but at the same time respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum, the referendum result. So, that’s the spirit, everybody, that I will take forward.

“Working with Wales as equal partners, and I know there is something that I can do to make a real difference.”

The prime minister is due to meet EU leaders in Brussels next week and sign agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4 per cent – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has reignited discussion regarding Britain’s future relationship with the EU ( AFP/Getty )

In an interview this week, Lord Cameron, who resigned from Downing Street in the wake of the UK vote to leave the EU, said that starting a conversation about rejoining the bloc would be “very long and painful”.

Lord Cameron told Bloomberg he was "desperately disappointed" when the UK voted to leave the EU 10 years ago, but he warned against attempting to reverse the decision.

"Instead of launching an argument about rejoining, which I think would be a very long and painful argument – and who knows where it would end up – instead of that, focus on how do we be the best friend, best neighbour, best partner," he said.

He said "flirting with rejoining" could hamper efforts to get a better deal, because EU countries might feel there is no point if the UK rejoins anyway.

"If you’re not going to, you know, commit to trying to make the partnership stronger because you’re flirting with rejoining, I think there’s some dangers there," he said.

News.title: Inside Sudan: The war the world ignored where ‘nowhere is safe’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Warning readers may find some of this content distressing

For the last six months Aisha*, 59, has been plagued by recurring visions of her murdered son talking to her.

She cannot sleep or think clearly, she says, stumbling to a halt. “Some days she is entirely mute,” a concerned friend continues, as Aisha stares into space.

The grandmother is one of around 100,000 displaced people who have limped into El Obeid in south-central Sudan after long marches along roads lined with corpses.

She has come here looking for shelter in this frontline town, which has only just survived a siege and is itself under regular drone fire and shelling.

El Obeid is the capital of North Kordofan state, which has become the epicentre of one of the deadliest, yet most forgotten, civil wars of the 21st century.

In the blistering heat of the day, Aisha describes how paramilitaries from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) slaughtered her son and extended family as they tried to flee their village in a tuk-tuk.

“They dragged them out, lined them up, and shot them. In front of me,” she says blankly.

open image in gallery Aisha has nightly visions of her son, who was shot dead in front of her ( Bel Trew )

Even though some of the wounded were still alive, she was forced to leave them behind, and that still haunts her. She describes watching from afar as the fighters looted the bodies, picking their way through the growing pools of blood.

“I grabbed my youngest daughter,” she continues. “There was no way to carry them all.”

Fighting erupted in Sudan in April 2023 between the paramilitary RSF and the Sudanese army, known as the SAF, after years of a bubbling power struggle in the wake of a 2019 uprising which unseated the country’s longtime autocrat, Omar al-Bashir.

Over the last three years, the internecine brutality has left at least 60,000 people dead, but the real figure is likely to be more than double that. An estimated 14 million people have been forced to flee their homes.

It has sparked the worst displacement crisis, and the largest humanitarian and hunger crisis, on the planet right now. Experts have accused the RSF of committing a likely genocide, the army and affiliates of atrocities, and the UN has declared famine in pockets of the country. That will have a devastating impact on generations to come, doctors tell us: in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) shrivelled newborns look otherworldly.

And so the people of Sudan see this less as a civil war than a war on them. And, for Aisha, she is tormented by her dead son talking to her.

“I am completely shattered, distraught. I don’t even know what I am doing. It is as if I am in a daze,” she says haltingly.

“When I remember him, I cannot hold myself together. In the middle of the night, I wake up crying. I ask God for forgiveness.”

In El Obeid, this is not really a camp. Families are living in mudbrick huts abandoned by residents who fled the area when the fighting came here. There is also very little aid. Everyone says they registered with UN agencies and NGOs but have received no support: Sudan remains one of the most underfunded conflict zones right now.

open image in gallery Sudanese aid workers with the Emergency Response Rooms attend to families who have fled to El Obeid ( Bel Trew )

And the stories are chilling: summary executions, starvation and mass rape. The UN has said conflict-related sexual violence in Sudan is unprecedented in terms of the scale, prevalence and brutality of its widespread use as a weapon of war, particularly by the RSF further west in El Fasher, Darfur.

There, the UN children’s agency has documented cases of rape of babies as young as one, and Sudanese officials in Khartoum tell The Independent the oldest rape survivor they have documented is 85. They worry the same will happen to El Obeid, home to half a million people, including tens of thousands of displaced.

Zaina*, 37, says she only just managed to rescue her daughter from being abducted by the RSF, who were taking women and girls from families who didn’t flee fast enough.

“I watched them abduct the women, screaming and begging, and take them to a ravine and rape them,” she says with a chilling calmness.

The problem was, the mother-of-seven continues, there was no one to stop them.

“There were no men to help. It was a matter of life and death.”

open image in gallery ‘Riham’ escaped slaughter on the front lines of North Kordofan to a makeshift displacement camp in El Obeid ( Bel Trew )

Riham*, a 30-year-old mother-of-eight, says her father and uncle were “shot to pieces” by RSF soldiers when they tried to stop them abducting female relatives.

“It was a bloodbath. Blood was splattered everywhere. Their brains were spilling out. It was a horrific scene.”

Until very recently, El Obeid was almost completely surrounded by RSF fighters, who had to tried to lay siege to and regularly bomb the strategic town, which has become a forward operating post for the Sudanese military and is crawling with soldiers. (The Independent visited SAF-controlled parts of the country and was obliged to conduct some interviews in the presence of a military minder).

Just a few hours after we visit the makeshift displacement camp, drone strikes pound the city centre and a neighbouring town, destroying a university and killing over a dozen people.

And so the families who flee the front line feel like it is chasing them, explains Abida*, who arrived after RSF soldiers shot dead her mother, laid siege to her village, looted everything “and burned the houses to the ground”.

“A few days ago I was almost killed by a drone here in El Obeid. The shock wave was so strong it threw me into the air. I was carrying my two-year-old daughter when it hit, the smell of gunpowder filled the air.”

open image in gallery Abida says she was nearly killed in a drone strike on the displacement camp ( Bel Trew )

Sudan’s most recent slaughterous war was sparked when tensions between the army, headed by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the powerful paramilitary RSF, led by General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, or “Hemedti”, exploded into open fighting across the country.

The two generals had initially joined forces and formed a joint military civilian government in 2019 after toppling al-Bashir. Two years later, the two men staged a coup. A vicious struggle between them reached breaking point in early 2023, mainly over plans to integrate the 100,000-strong RSF into the army.

Fighting initially erupted in the capital, Khartoum, and quickly engulfed the entire country. Conflict monitor Acled has been trying to keep track of the number of people killed, but aid groups say the death toll is likely to be close to 150,000.

That has since metastasised into an international conflict, with Human Rights Watch finding evidence that the UAE is bankrolling the RSF, which was accused of atrocities and crimes even before this war erupted. The Emirates denies this, and the RSF has, in turn, claimed the military is supported by Egypt and Iran.

open image in gallery General ‘Hemedti’ Dagalo, left, and General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, sign an agreement after staging a coup ( AFP/Getty )

The war has displaced a quarter of the population, and pushed parts of the country into famine.

Both sides, and their affiliated groups, have been accused of committing atrocities and war crimes, which both vehemently deny in statements to The Independent.

The UN and the US government have both accused the RSF and its allied militias of a systematic targeting of non-Arab communities that likely amounts to genocide in Darfur, during its 18-month siege of El Fasher. The RSF, again, has repeatedly denied this, but the fear is the same tactics will be used in North Kordofan.

In Dabbah refugee camp in the north of the country, families describe RSF slaughter but also coming under military fire.

One girl, Sara*, says she lost her entire family in an army mortar attack during fighting in Darfur, which left her gravely wounded as she hid in a shell hole.

open image in gallery Some families fled with nothing and are living in tents in El Obeid ( Bel Trew )

“It was a direct hit. The shock wave threw me to the ground. Many people were torn apart. My brother-in-law’s abdomen was torn open and his legs shredded by shrapnel,” she adds quietly.

“I was injured around 1pm and stayed like that until 5pm... They prevented people from coming to help me.”

“I was the only survivor,” she continues, breaking down in tears.

The next catastrophe on the horizon is famine. Families we spoke to talk of trying to survive on one meal a day or even resorting to eating animal feed.

This man-made food crisis, driven by sieges, is being made worse by the climate crisis. The Super El Niño has caused severe drought affecting more than half of Sudan, leading to crop failures, according to the IPC, the UN-backed global hunger monitor.

Carl Skau, then acting head of the World Food Programme (WFP), warns that Sudan is already “the largest hunger crisis in the world right now”.

But aid agencies are not equipped to respond: the UN’s humanitarian appeal for Sudan is 40 per cent unfunded.

“Twenty million people are acutely food insecure. Some 14 million people have been displaced, and there are still pockets of famine,” Skau tells The Independent from El Obeid. “And we’re struggling to meet these needs. We’re doing our best. There is access to many parts, but the funding is not there.”

open image in gallery A severely malnourished newborn is treated in a NICU unit in Omdurman, in Khartoum state ( Bel Trew )

That is most starkly seen in the maternity wards. At two NICUs in Omdurman, Khartoum state, severely malnourished babies are too weak to cry, their faces contorted in pain and their skin drawn tight across their skulls.

Dr Rehab Sid Ahmad, an obstetric anaesthetist who herself was nearly killed by RSF strikes and raids on the Omdurman maternity hospital, explains that this will impact Sudan for generations to come.

“The mothers have suffered from poor nutrition, so when they give birth, the children will face other issues – nutritional problems, developmental issues, and so on. They won’t develop properly – their growth will be affected,” she explains.

“This doesn’t end here but is impacting the generations being born now.”

Back in El Obeid, the scant humanitarian aid available is doing little to ease the nightmare.

Families still recovering from the massacre of their loved ones describe how they are surviving on grain.

And the front line is stalking them.

“People keep moving from place to place, but there’s no real safety anywhere,” Abida says quietly. “Nowhere is safe.”

*All names have been changed to protect interviewees.

This article has been produced as part of The Independent’s Rethinking Global Aid project

News.title: What to know about flights after the US nationwide ground stop
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A nationwide ground stop ended around 8:15 p.m. ET, and some domestic flights have now departed from U.S. airports.

However, normalizing air traffic after the longest flight stoppage in 25 years will be slow, authorities warned.

Officials say the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

Here’s what to know.

Flights have resumed but disruption continues

The Federal Aviation Administration said airplane departures could late Friday evening Eastern time. Passengers should contact their airlines for information about their flights, the FAA said.

The ripple effect from the stoppage could be felt for days, however.

More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. on Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned Americans traveling that getting air traffic back to normal won't be quick.

International flights are being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

San Francisco airport said that flights headed across the Pacific Ocean were cleared to leave the airport from Friday evening. That included flights destined for Hawaii and Asia.

Europe’s aviation agency suspended U.S.-bound departures at the request of the FAA from 5 p.m. Eastern on Friday until midnight.

Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers who want to continue their journey, or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.

The reason for the grounding

New technology being hooked up to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment, Trump administration officials said.

That caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, according to officials.

Duffy suggested more disruptions might occur.

“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said.

The air traffic control modernization began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.

The Microsoft outage and cyberattacks were unrelated to the stoppage

Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to the service disruption that took Outlook and other services offline Thursday, a spokesperson for the company said.

Mullin said there is no indication the failure was related to a cyberattack, either.

“There was never any lives at risk,” Mullin added. “There was no flights at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it."

The ground stop was enacted “out of an abundance of caution,” he said.

News.title: Watch in full: Sudan - The war the world ignored
News.content:
Warning readers may find this content distressing

Sudan is facing the word’s largest humanitarian, displacement and hunger crisis - yet its devastating civil war remains largely overlooked.

In this powerful new documentary, The Independent’s Chief International Correspondent Bel Trew and Field Producer Mohammed Amin report from the frontlines, witnessing the devastating impact of a conflict that has seen the United Nations warn of genocide.

As millions face unimaginable suffering, the film shines a light on a crisis that cannot be ignored, bringing viewers closer to the people caught up in one of the world’s most devastating humanitarian emergencies.

Watch the documentary in full.

Director, presenter: Bel Trew

Camera: Bel Trew, Sid Ahmed Ibrahim, Dan Faber

Field Producer: Mohammed Amin

Producer: Dan Faber

Editors: Todd Dalton, Vali Raza

News.title: What is happening in Sudan? The civil war the world forgot
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Since April 2023, Sudan has been in the grip of one of the deadliest civil wars in a generation. As many as 150,000 people are believed to have been killed and millions displaced.

Right now it is the largest humanitarian crisis, the largest displacement crisis and the largest hunger crisis in the world.

The UN has warned that attacks in Darfur bear the “hallmarks of genocide” and the brutality and widespread use of rape as a weapon of war is unprecedented.

There are no signs of an immediate ceasefire or an end to the conflict, which has been described by humanitarians and Sudanese families as a war on civilians.

How did the war start?

Sudan’s war broke out in April 2023. A vicious power struggle between Sudanese army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and General Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, or “Hemedti”, head of the powerful paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), exploded into open fighting across the country.

The two generals had once been uneasy allies. They joined forces after the 2019 popular uprising unseated the country’s longterm autocrat Omar al-Bashir, forming a joint government with a civilian prime minister.

At the time there were concerns about a deadly military crackdown on protesters and the involvement of the RSF, that with its precursor the Janjaweed – had already been accused of committing crimes, atrocities, and ethnic cleansing in Darfur, targeting non-Arab communities. (Both sides denied all accusations).

By 2021, the two generals staged a coup. But their power struggle reached breaking point in April 2023, mainly over plans to bring the 100,000-strong RSF under army command.

Fighting first erupted in the capital, Khartoum, and quickly spread across the country, morphing into an international proxy conflict.

Rights groups including Human Rights Watch have said there is mounting evidence that the UAE has bankrolled the RSF in breach of arms embargoes, which the Emirates denies. The RSF in turn accuses the army of being backed by Egypt and Iran.

open image in gallery The centre of destroyed Khartoum bears the scars of war between the Sudanese military and the RSF ( Bel Trew/The Independent )

Where is the fighting now?

The front lines have shifted dramatically. After losing control of Khartoum to the RSF, the army retook the capital in March 2025. But by October 2025, in the west, the RSF had captured El Fasher, the army’s last stronghold in Darfur, after an 18-month siege and slaughter.

This year, a UN independent fact-finding mission for Sudan said the RSF’s ethnically targeted killings, widespread sexual violence and enforced disappearances bore the “hallmarks of genocide”.

The SAF (Sudan Armed Forces) and its affiliated militias have also been accused of atrocities by UN investigators, which the SAF also denies.

Since then, the war’s centre of gravity has moved to the Kordofan region, which links Darfur to central Sudan.

open image in gallery North Kordofan has become the epicentre of the fighting in Sudan ( The Independent / Google Maps )

El Obeid: the new front line

El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, is now one of the most important battlegrounds of the war. Its position at a crossroads linking the country’s central and western regions makes it strategic. Until very recently, it was almost completely surrounded by RSF fighters and under partial siege.

The city of around half a million people is also now home to an estimated 100,000 displaced people. But it offers little safety. It has been under intense drone strikes. The UN has warned that the patterns of violence seen in El Fasher are now emerging in El Obeid.

open image in gallery Map of El Obeid showing RSF- and SAF-controlled territory around the strategic city and the Independent’s route in ( The Independent )

Key facts and figures

Death toll: There is no official death toll. Conflict monitor Acled says it has verified nearly 60,000 dead, although other estimates say as many as 150,000 have been killed

Humanitarian crisis: Nearly 34 million people across Sudan need aid, while 21 million lack health services; this has led to Sudan becoming the largest humanitarian crisis in the world, according to the WHO

Displacement: At least 14 million people have been forced from their homes, a quarter of the population, making it the world’s largest displacement crisis. Neighbouring countries host over 4.4 million Sudanese refugees

Sexual violence: Conflict-related sexual violence in Sudan is unprecedented in terms of the scale, prevalence and brutality of its widespread use as a weapon of war, according to the UN’s human rights office

Children: An estimated 825,000 children under five are expected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026. Unicef has documented the rape of children as young as one year old

Famine: Around 20 million people or 40 per cent of the population face high levels of acute food insecurity, according to the IPC, the UN-backed global hunger monitor. Famine was confirmed in El Fasher in 2024 and in Kadugli, South Kordofan, in September 2025. Sudan is also the world’s largest hunger crisis right now.

Drought: The IPC warned in October that Super El Niño-induced drought is compounding conflict and driving a growing risk of famine in Darfur and Kordofan. It also found that the drought now covers more than half of the country

Healthcare: The WHO has verified 217 attacks on healthcare since April 2023, resulting in thousands of deaths. In 2026, 37 per cent of health facilities were reported to be non-functional

Aid: As of 8 October, the UN’s $2.9bn appeal for Sudan is 40 per cent unfunded

Genocide: In February 2026, a UN fact-finding mission said RSF atrocities in El Fasher bore the “hallmarks of genocide” against non-Arab communities

This article has been produced as part of The Independent’s Rethinking Global Aid project

News.title: British Gas reveals minimum temperature to set heating when not home as Britons hit by freezing temperatures
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Britons have been told what to set their thermostats to if they are away from home as temperatures plummet and winter approaches in the UK.

British Gas has advised households to drop their heating to no lower than 5 to 7C in order to prevent damage to their homes, while not pushing up their energy bills too high.

It is urging the public to get their homes ready for winter with simple checks, including topping up boiler pressure, bleeding radiators, insulating pipes and clearing gutters ahead of the winter months.

The warning comes as wintry conditions kick in across the country and forecasters warn that Britain could face colder temperatures in late November when a collapsing polar vortex could push freezing Arctic air southwards.

Friday night was the coldest night of autumn for much of the UK, with temperatures dropping to lows of -6.5C, the Met Office said.

The NHS recommends that households are heated to at least 18C during winter months when people are home.

open image in gallery Household energy bills will rise by £276 a year from January ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

Peter Knowles, a British Gas service and repair engineer, said: “After the warmer summer months, it’s easy to put off some of those jobs around the home until the weather takes a turn.

“But getting ahead now can make all the difference. Checking your boiler and radiators are working as they should, protecting pipes and making sure your home is ready for wetter weather are all simple things you can do before winter sets in.”

The energy provider says households need to check their boiler pressure, which can drop over time and should usually sit between 1 and 1.5 bar.

It also advises people to make sure windows and doors are properly sealed to stop heat escaping when temperatures drop.

Households are also urged to insulate their pipes to prevent them from becoming frozen and causing serious damage.

open image in gallery Friday night was one of the coldest nights of autumn as temperatures dropped to -6.5C ( AFP/Getty )

Energy bills are forecast to rise by £276 a year from January, as the Iran war continues to push up gas prices. British Gas says one way to save money on energy bills is to use zonal heating and avoid heating rooms that aren’t regularly used.

The Met Office said a changeable and often rather unsettled period is most likely for the rest of November, with further areas of low pressure moving in from the Atlantic.

“Whilst all parts are likely to see some rain at times, it is southern areas which may turn out to be the wettest, relative to average conditions, through this period,” it said.

Next month, low pressure is expected to become slow-moving to the west, then south of the UK, whilst pressure builds to the north of the country.

“Further rain is probable across southern and perhaps central areas, but below average precipitation could occur in parts of the north, especially the northwest,” it said.

“With a blocked weather pattern signalled to develop, this increases the chance of colder conditions overall, with associated winter hazards, e.g. snow and ice, occurring; this most likely further to the north.”

News.title: France pull off one of their greatest wins as Erasmus mind games backfire
News.content:
Given Les Bleus’ injuries, only the 1999 World Cup semi-final victory over New Zealand can come close to this win over the back-to-back world champions, South Africa. The Nations Championship, with the Springboks previously unbeaten, has been blown wide open. Crikey, given these two could meet in a World Cup semi-final next year, rugby’s blue-riband event in Australia has been blown wide open.

And how lucky are we. France did not score a point in the second half and South Africa’s comeback befitted a champion side, but these audacious hosts regaled their Parisian audience with a rugby feast. Rassie Erasmus, the Springboks’ head coach, said that he was nervous before the game and so he should have been. Fabien Galthié, his counterpart, had promised some fun and games, but Erasmus could not help himself: not long before kick-off, he pulled the coup de théâtre, switching his starting and replacement front rows. Time will tell whether such a move was legal.

“We didn’t play well,” said Erasmus. “I can’t find a lot of excuses. They were on top of their game and we were a little bit off. It was one point here and there. They took their opportunities and we didn’t. We weren’t just outplayed, we were outsmarted.”

“I think we’ve killed our dreams for the Nations Championship with this result,” he added, suggesting he thinks New Zealand will beat England next week.

Demons were present for both sides, mainly France. South Africa lost Jasper Wiese to a 20-minute red card for a nasty ruck clear-out – just as Lood de Jager had received in the visitors’ win last year – and, at the end, there was a reverse of that utterly compelling World Cup quarter-final on the same turf. This time, it was South Africa desperately searching for victory, having dominated the scrum and scoring all three of their tries from close range or mauls.

News.title: England’s batting capitulates in defeat to lift Australia’s spirits
News.content:
“We weren’t quick enough to adapt to the conditions, we talked extensively leading into the game about the surface here at Optus,” Brendon McCullum, England’s coach, said. “It’s a bit like batting on a trampoline, there are certain shots that are very difficult to execute. We talked about trying to put those away.”

McCullum called for his team to scrap a bit more, and at least acknowledged this time that driving on the up was unwise.

“KP has got such a nice manner about him,” he said. “He sees his role to get the talent to perform on the world stage. His message will be measured but firm – adapting to conditions, what could we have done, trying to drive the ball on the up is not wise. Next time we hit a surface like this we have to try and work it better.”

After a quiet start, both openers fell tamely. Ben Duckett prodded Johnson to point, then Banton had a booming drive at Bartlett and was caught behind.

Enter Beardman. When he came on to bowl the 10th over of the innings, there was palpable excitement from his home crowd, who had watched another West Australian, Mike Hussey, present his ODI cap before the toss. Later in the day, Hussey was probably glad he rebuffed England’s recent approach to work with their Test batsmen.

Beardman, who is a mentee of Dennis Lillee and has a gorgeously rhythmical action that helped him touch 90mph, started with a maiden to Root, then found just another movement away from Brook to invite the edge. On the occasion of his 200th ODI, Root had been dropped badly on three off Bartlett, and his only boundary came when Beardman found his an inside edge and the ball flew past his stumps.

The pressure told, and Root edged a big drive behind, where Josh Inglis took the third of his five catches. That sparked a collapse of five for 10, with Jordan Cox edging behind prodding in defence, before Curran was caught on the fence hooking for nought. Beardman’s five-fer was completed when Liam Dawson – selected ahead of Adil Rashid again – skewed a flat-footed drive to backward point. Overton followed in the next over, leaving England 65 for eight, with their lowest ever ODI score, 86, inevitably recorded against Australia in 2001, appearing a distant possibility.

A stand of 37 from Will Jacks and Gus Atkinson averted that particular indignity, and the fear of being bowled out for double figures. But the total was never enough and, despite Atkinson bowling Head first ball, the chase was painfully routine thanks to Marsh’s early barrage.

News.title: Kane bends game to his will on record-breaking night
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of England vs Croatia in the Nations League, with the hosts’ captain Harry Kane set to become the country’s most-capped player.

The 33-year-old has enjoyed a memorable few weeks, becoming the first English Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years and following it up with a new Bayern Munich contract, and an appearance at Wembley tonight will take him clear of Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England caps.

Kane scored twice in his record-equalling appearance against Czech Republic at Wembley last month, extending his international tally to 91 goals – a total that is unrivalled for England.

“It’s not about me – it’s about the team,” Kane said before tonight’s landmark moment. “I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

The 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic left England on nine points after four Nations League group games, with a 2-0 win in the away contest and a 7-0 thumping of Croatia coming after a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

Thomas Tuchel will be hoping that his side can inflict another heavy defeat on Croatia this evening, but a draw will be enough to book their place in the quarter-finals, with the group’s top two teams progressing.

While Kane will collect plaudits for his 126th cap, attention will also be on a potential first, with Jude Bellingham’s younger brother, Jobe, included in a senior England squad for the first time.

The two Bellinghams appearing together in a senior match would be a new experience for them, while it would be the first time that brothers have taken to the field together for England in 19 years.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the Football Association’s England app. “It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great.”

News.title: Experts hail a “milestone” as TB deaths fall by more than a third in 10 years
News.content:
The number of people dying from tuberculosis has dropped by more than a third over the last 10 years but progress against the disease is still too slow, according to the World Health Organization.

Figures from WHO’s annual TB report showed that the lung disease took the lives of an estimated 1.13 million people in 2025, down from 1.7m in 2015, a drop of 35 per cent.

While WHO hailed this as a major milestone in achieving global targets - albeit five years too late - it said that progress in wiping out TB was still too slow.

Africa and Europe have made the greatest progress in reducing deaths, with numbers halving on both continents over the 10-year period. India and China - countries that have high burdens of the disease - also cut deaths by 35 per cent.

The report also showed that an estimated 10.6million people contracted the disease in 2025, a reduction of just 75,000 since 2024.

TB - still the world’s leading infectious disease killer - is preventable and curable, and is caused by the bacillus Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is spread when infected people cough or sneeze.

The disease has been around for centuries, and has been described as the quintessential disease of poverty as it spreads in areas of low quality housing, among people with poor nutrition and immunity. It is a particular risk to people who are HIV positive.

Treatment requires a six-month long regimen of medication, and while treatments have become less toxic in recent years, they still take a heavy toll on patients and have a range of side effects, including at the most extreme deafness. Adherence to medication is also a problem.

News.title: Low-cost parenting app halves rates of sexual violence amongst teenagers in Tanzania
News.content:
A low cost parenting intervention has more than halved rates of sexual violence among teenage girls in Tanzania, a study has shown.

The ParentApp digital parenting programme for families is aimed at reducing rates of violence experienced by teenagers of both sexes.

Researchers found the programme helped bolster family relationships and enabled mothers and fathers to better communicate with their children at what is often a tricky stage of their development.

The programme, led by Oxford University and the University of Cape Town in partnership with the Tanzanian government, the World Health Organization and Unicef, combines in-person and mobile parenting support.

Parents have an introductory session with a facilitator and then undertake 12 weekly sessions online. They also join a WhatsApp group with other parents where they can discuss problems and support one another.

The randomized controlled trial, published in The Lancet, included 2,396 children aged 10–17 and 2,396 parents and carers across 80 urban and rural areas.

Families were randomly assigned to receive either ParentApp or a comparison app focused on safe water and hygiene. Researchers analysing the results did not know which app each family received.

At the 14-month follow-up, girls in families participating in the ParentApp initiative reported a 67% reduction in sexual violence; a 54% reduction in sexual exploitation and an improvement in parent-child relationships. The successes were less marked in boys, however.

Violence against children is widespread globally: Unicef data shows that around one in five girls and women and one in seven boys and men globally have experienced sexual violence as children.

Lucie Cluver, professor of child and family social work at Oxford University and one of the authors of the study, said the intervention was aimed at helping parents and children talk to one another and discuss situations before they arise.

In Tanzania, for example, teenage girls might get a motorbike taxi late at night, potentially putting them in a dangerous situation.

“What you’re doing is making plans and problem solving ahead of these risky situations that teenagers end up in. And you’re building trust and the relationship so you can have these difficult conversations,” said Prof Cluver.

She said she was surprised at how big an impact the intervention had on sexual violence: teenage girls reported that because the app helped improve communication with their parents and carers they did not feel the need to go out as much.

The programme cost around $6 per family but researchers calculated that it goes up to around $10 per family if 20% are given smartphones. A traditional in-person parenting intervention generally costs around $120 per family.

Engagement in the sessions was high - around 70 per cent of participants completed the course - and some parents kept in touch with one another after the programme.

However, the authors of the study stressed that while the app focused on families there remains a need to prevent violence against children in other settings, such as schools and religious institutions. There also needs to be a broader societal push to address the scourge.

“The app isn’t the answer to everything - it’s just one part of the puzzle,” said Prof Cluver.

Prof Cluver said she hoped future versions of the programme would include greater focus on digital harms and test whether parents could take the lead themselves.

The programme is being rolled out in other countries, including Mexico, Panama and South Africa, and is easily adaptable for different contexts.

“Tanzania only has 20% smartphone use and we thought if it works in one of the hardest places to do a digital intervention it could work anywhere,” she said.

She said the study showed how parenting was a universal experience, with the majority focused on what is best for their children.

“Parents feel powerless. We live in a world where our kids are facing risks and parents just want to help,” added Prof Cluver.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: AI fuels fastest economic growth in two years
News.content:
The Prime Minister and the Chancellor should not claim credit for the AI-fuelled expansion of Britain’s economy in the third quarter, a think tank said.

Julian Jessop, economics fellow at the Institute of Economic Affairs, said the 0.7pc expansion in the economy was “a tribute to the resilience of the private sector in the face of the energy shock and policy headwinds”.

He said: “This resilience is despite rather than because of anything the Government has done. In particular, the persistent weakens of the construction sector underlines the failure of flagship policies to boost housebuilding and infrastructure spending.

“The Government’s clumsy interventions are also continuing to add to labour and housing costs, including rents. Instead, the key driver of growth and business optimism has been the rollout of AI. This is an area that the Government has not got round to messing up, though that may yet be coming.

“In the meantime, the Government is still borrowing more than expected and the labour market remains weak.

“The full impact of higher inflation and higher interest rates has also yet to be felt. Early surveys for the fourth quarter already show that consumer confidence, retail spending, private sector hiring and housing market activity are all starting to slide again.

“2026 will still be a year when the economy performed much better than expected – at least in terms of GDP. But the new year will start with further increases in energy bills and high levels of job insecurity, which will matter far more to most people.”

News.title: Bird flu viruses ‘gaining function’ through natural mixing, warn scientists
News.content:
The bird flu virus’ resurgence began with an 11-year-old. In February 2023, the schoolgirl was admitted to a hospital in Phnom Penh with severe pneumonia – within a day, she was dead.

Tests soon revealed that she had contracted avian influenza: Cambodia hadn’t reported a human case of bird flu since 2014, but the hiatus was over. Since then, 39 more people have been infected and 15 have died in the Southeast Asian country – a case fatality rate of roughly 40 per cent.

Researchers have been scratching their heads as to why, after nine years, this particular stain of H5N1 suddenly started jumping from birds to people again. The strain or clade called 2.3.2.1 had been circulating for almost a decade without spilling into humans. What changed?

Now, a paper in Emerging Infectious Diseases offers clues.

Scientists say the apparent rise in human cases has coincided with the virus gaining new genetic material and, potentially, new powers of infection, from a second flu virus via a process known as “reassortment”.

News.title: The country where diabetes is more feared than HIV
News.content:
Furthermore, even when antiretrovirals suppress the virus, the immune system can stay chronically activated, causing a low-grade inflammation that damages organs and blood vessels. The Lancet HIV Commission reported that, by one measure of biological ageing, people with HIV appeared about five years older on average than peers without the virus.

HIV also makes other infections more dangerous. For example, those living with the virus are more likely to contract human papillomavirus (HPV), the leading cause of cervical cancer, and they are less able to clear HPV from their bodies.

“With HIV, you don’t channel your mind into dying,” Ms Shongwe said. “But when I got to know that I have cervical cancer, I thought it was the end of the world.”

In 2018, Ms Ginindza moved from the Ministry of Health’s HIV programme to its NCD programme, but almost immediately, she asked to go back to her old job. “There is nothing here,” she recalled, “no tools, no data collection system, no guidelines”.

Even today, the ministry doesn’t have any dedicated NCD posts. While there are hundreds of people working on HIV, there are just 10 NCD staff, all borrowed from other programmes, Ms Ginindza said.

Although latest figures show that NCDs account for almost half of Eswatini’s deaths the government’s programme for NCDs, injuries and mental health received about one million emalangeni - roughly £45,000 - or 0.03 per cent of the health budget.

Foreign aid hasn’t filled the gap: international partners cover about five per cent of NCD spending, Ms Ginindza said, compared with 60 per cent of the HIV response. Donors “cannot give you money when they also need that money to address their own NCDs”, she added.

So, when it comes to these chronic diseases, patients struggle to get diagnosed, obtain their medicines or see a specialist for complications. In a 2024 government survey, fewer than 30 per cent of people with high blood pressure were on medication, and only 14 per cent had their hypertension under control.

The government’s own NCD report puts the stock-out rate for key medicines at 79 per cent, and the public system has no nephrologists, endocrinologists or cardiologists, Ms Ginindza said, relying instead on private specialists and Taiwanese medical missions to provide these services.

Faced with one of the worst HIV epidemics, Eswatini poured almost everything into fighting it. “The focus was HIV,” Ms Ginindza said, “so we forgot about the other conditions.”

Fighting on two fronts



Now, Eswatini is trying to turn its HIV machinery towards chronic diseases.

Since 2020, a government-led scheme has delivered NCD medication refills, blood pressure checks and glucose tests in hundreds of community settings, integrating this with existing HIV services. As it once did with antiretrovirals, the ministry is also shifting NCD care from hospitals to local clinics, Ms Ginindza said, aiming to train at least two nurses at each.

For Mr Mamba, that means he sees the same clinician for his HIV, diabetes and blood pressure. It saves time, he said, since he can get everything under one roof.

The challenge is not just extending HIV services to NCD patients but finding the money to sustain both. The Eswatini government aims to increase NCD funding to 20 million emalangeni, or £900,000, by 2028.

But last year, the Trump administration gutted the US President’s Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar), the backbone of Eswatini’s HIV response.

In December, Eswatini signed a five-year deal with the US to restore some HIV funding - on the condition that the government shoulders more of the cost itself. So, as the country scrambles to protect its HIV gains, NCDs risk remaining a secondary priority.

With his diabetes and blood pressure medicines so often out of stock, Mr Mamba has come to dread his check-ups, convinced each one will show his numbers have climbed again - and that his luck is running out.

Many of his neighbours have the same conditions and probably share these fears, he said, but much as people once kept quiet about HIV, they rarely discuss such things.

Over 30 years ago, Ms Gwebu contemplated suicide after being diagnosed with HIV. But today, she hopes Eswatini can sustain its hard-won progress against the virus without leaving those with other diseases behind. “What is going to kill our people,” she said, “is not going to be HIV.”

MANCHESTER UNITED have completed their first signing of the Mauricio Pochettino era after snapping up teenage striker Tyler Adjei.

The Red Devils have landed the highly-rated England youth international, 16, from League One side Reading.



Adjei can operate anywhere across the front three but has been recruited primarily as a No9 as United continue building for the future.

According to The Athletic, the youngster was registered with the club this week after attracting interest from several other teams.



Transfer guru Fabrizio Romano also confirmed an agreement was in place, with the remaining paperwork expected to be approved next week.

Adjei will initially link up with United’s Under-18s, managed by former Red Devils midfielder Darren Fletcher, rather than immediately joining Pochettino’s senior squad.



The promising forward has impressed scouts with his athleticism, movement and attitude, although he is still considered a work in progress.

A source told The Athletic: “He moves well; he has a good temperament, mentality and demeanour.”

The teenager will also be given time to build up his match fitness following his move to Old Trafford.

His arrival continues United’s aggressive approach to recruiting young talent, having already raided rivals Manchester City for Karim Cassim, 17, and David Eze, 16, during the summer.
