World.title: Ipetumodu Stool And Limit Of Obaship Affront
World.content:
By Mobolaji Sanusi

“Neither soldiers nor money can defend a king but only friends won by good deeds, merit, and honesty.” —Gaius Sallustius Crispus (86–35/34 BC)

In a faraway town of Ipetumodu in present-day Osun State, South-west Nigeria, an avoidable and antisocial traditional rulership behaviour is brewing, with grave consequences for the Obaship system across Yorubaland, if allowed to stand.

The world is watching as an otherwise straightforward resolution of an Obaship infraction is regrettably becoming legally intractable. Unless this avoidable but shameful standoff is checked, Ipetumodu might set a precedent that could haunt the traditional values and morals handed down through generations by Yoruba ancestors.

Oba Joseph Oloyede, the deposed Apetumodu of Ipetumodu who disappeared from his palace in March 2024, is the dramatis persona of this whole saga. Oloyede ascended the throne of his forefathers as the 27th Apetumodu in November 2019, following the death of Oba James Adedokun Adegoke in November 2017.

Sometime around May 2024, his coterie of high chiefs, presumably based on what he had told them, may well have believed that he had travelled to the United States on a routine visit, having been resident there until his coronation as an Oba. But his case changed when, upon arrival in the United States, he was arrested and taken into custody by the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). The now deposed monarch was subsequently charged with defrauding the United States government of $4.2 million in COVID-19 relief funds.

At that point, a hitherto respected traditional ruler from a prominent town in Yorubaland became an accused person who was treated like a common criminal. He was arraigned and tried in a court of law. On August 26, 2025, he was reportedly sentenced by Judge Christopher A. Boyko of the Northern District of Ohio to five years’ imprisonment. He was also ordered to repay more than $4.4 million to victims and to forfeit traceable assets acquired from the proceeds of the fraud.

Cumulatively, since March 2024 when Oloyede disappeared from the palace, the deposed monarch has been absent from his stool for an unexplained period of 32 months. More striking is the fact that it was not until May 7, 2026, about 26 months after his disappearance, that Governor Ademola Nurudeen Adeleke, after due diligence, firmly took the decision to depose him. The governor requested and received a Certified True Copy of the Ohio court judgment that convicted Oloyede.

This official decision is difficult to dismiss in view of the government’s rationale for his deposition, which it aptly describes as follows: “The fraudulent conduct of Oba Joseph Oloyede, as found by the U.S. court and to which he pleaded guilty, and his public trial and conviction have brought the institution of Obaship and the stool of Apetumodu of Ipetumodu into disrepute and public odium, hence the resort to deposition.”

Shockingly, and in wanton disregard for the decency expected of traditional rulership, the deposed monarch, acting in cahoots with some members of his kindred, threw the cherished Yoruba tradition of decorum to the winds by challenging his lawful and morally grounded deposition in court, seeking a judicial order to stop the process of filling the vacant stool by the governor. The suit, as reported in The Punch newspaper, was filed on September 16, 2026 by Oloyede alongside other claimants from his Latimogun Royal Family of the Arinola Ruling House of Ipetumodu. This suit is of public interest and should concern all Yoruba freeborn and lovers of tradition anywhere except those that are morally depraved.

Oloyede and fellow travellers also curiously allege that Governor Adeleke did not formally notify him of any infraction before commencing the process to replace him. This cannot be true and the question is: Do Yoruba traditional rulership customs and traditions allow an individual Oba to govern his domain from prison? If not, what is the legal basis for Oloyede and his supporters asking the court to halt the process of filling the stool of Apetumodu until the substantive suit is determined; a substantive suit which, in this particular instance, is nothing but a sheer waste of the court’s precious time and energy?

The issue going on in Ipetumodu should not be viewed as peculiar to that domain alone. It is an issue with dire consequences for Yoruba’s traditional rulership institution if not properly addressed by sons and daughters of Oodua anywhere in the world. The beaded crown on any Oba in any part of Yorubaland carries monumental significance that places on the shoulders of the wearer the custodial power over its history, culture and the traditional destiny of thousands of inhabitants of that domain and, by extension, that of Yorubaland in general.

Nigeria is a country where, until recently, history is untaught in schools, a situation that has saddled the Obaship traditional institution with ensuring the thoughtful preservation and nurturing of our heritage.

Following from the foregoing is that in any country like ours where history is for a long time not taught in any academic curriculum, it is the duty of the Obaship and traditional leaders, considered amongst others as “Kabiyesi”, one whose authority cannot be questioned, and “Alase Igbakeji Orisa”, second only to the gods, to ensure that our culture, morals and heritage are preserved and nurtured. To live up to this standard, such an Oba must be one of unimpeachable character and not a criminal that is not worthy of being called a true model for his subjects.

Yours sincerely believes that a true Oba occupying an ancestral stool must inspire reverence because he is expected to symbolise the Yoruba principle of Omoluabi, which places an undeniable premium on self and communal integrity, character, wisdom and respect. For any Yoruba Oba to be the moral compass of his domain, where he is expected to dispense justice in conflict situations and prevent moral decay, he must be above board. The deposed Oba Oloyede has failed this test of character.

Everyone with Yoruba DNA in his bloodline must rise against the trend of having dubious charlatans become Obas anywhere in the land of Oodua. As the first and last line of defence of our ancestral heritage, such morally depraved people masquerading as Oba cannot be respected custodians of our identity, land, ancestral wisdom, traditions, cultures, customs and values.

Nowhere in Yoruba land should a court affirmed criminal or someone devoid of ‘Omoluabi’ values be allowed to ascend our revered Obaship thrones. All leading Obas in the land of Oodua should rally round Governor Adeleke and ensure he’s not blackmailed for doing the right thing necessary to protect our ancient traditional Obaship values.

The kingmakers must also bear a significant share of the blame for the emergence of individuals of questionable character on the traditional thrones within their respective domains. In the days of old, Obas were traditionally chosen through Ifá divination, and upon their selection, they underwent a period of seclusion (Ipebi), during which they received extensive traditional orientation on the magnitude of their powers, the enormous responsibilities attached to their stools and the mystique surrounding their thrones. These sacred rites and time-honoured practices were not mere formalities; they were essential to preparing the chosen individuals for the spiritual, cultural and moral responsibilities of kingship.

Sadly, much of this has been abandoned, largely due to the pecuniary interests of some kingmakers and the reckless disposition of certain Obas who, in the name of modernisation, have disregarded the very traditions that confer dignity, respect and reverence upon their thrones and occupiers. They seem to forget that the majesty of a traditional throne lies not merely in the authority it commands but also in the mystique, sacredness and ancestral heritage surrounding both the throne and its occupant, who, in traditional Yoruba cosmology, is regarded as occupying a position next only to the gods of the land.

Equally disheartening is the growing tendency among some Yoruba Obas to ridicule or openly disparage the age-old customs, traditions and values of their respective domains. This is particularly troubling because, by virtue of the ancestral thrones they occupy, they are expected to be the foremost custodians, protectors and promoters of these cultural legacies. Were such Obas not reminded, before or during their ascension to the thrones of their forefathers, that one of their fundamental responsibilities was to preserve and uphold the customs, traditions and cultural identity of their people?

Yours sincerely strongly believe that the time has come for a more deliberate and uncompromising traditional approach to the selection and installation of traditional rulers. Princes ascending the thrones of their forebears should be required to swear an oath of fidelity to the customs, traditions and values of their respective domains. Such an oath should not be treated as a mere ceremonial ritual but as also as a solemn and binding commitment to preserve the ancestral heritage, cultural identity and traditional institutions entrusted to their care. After all, one cannot claim the honour, authority and privileges of an ancestral throne while simultaneously undermining the traditions that give it meaning and legitimacy under the guise of embracing modernity or any foreign religions. This is grossly unacceptable.

The gods of Yoruba land will inflict their wrath on any Oba who commits abominations capable of denigrating our cultural heritage and values. From the example of this deposed Oba Oloyede of Ipetumodu, it is clear that an Oba can only hide his misdeeds from his subjects but not from his ancestors/gods without incurring dire consequences for such abominable infractions. For those that have ears, let them hear.

I hereby rest my case for this week.

•Sanusi, former MD/CEO of the Lagos State Signage and  Agency, is currently Managing Partner at AMS RELIABLE SOLICITORS. (WhatsApp only: 07011117777)

World.title: Lagos Thugs, London Protesters and the Chaos Before the Ballot
World.content:
By Adeola Akinremi

On Thursday, November 12, two incidents with red flags for the 2027 elections emerged. In London, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan was detained in his car by a group of protesters. In Lagos, thugs invaded a meeting venue, where supporters of the National Democratic Party (NDC) gathered for a town hall.



The Lagos and London incidents are not the same, but together they portend an increasingly fraught electoral season. They are early indicators of where we are headed if nothing is done to arrest them. The grievance in London concerned duplicate entries, AI-generated photographs and fake polling units in INEC’s preliminary voters’ register. For this, the protesters circled Amupitan’s car and prevented him from leaving Chatham House, where he had gone to give a presentation. They got what they wanted: an election umpire embarrassed on a foreign stage.



The irony is that Amupitan had already conceded much of their case. On November 9, he disclosed that the commission had removed 1,608,660 invalid registrations and identified 54 people across ten states for possible disciplinary action or prosecution. At Chatham House, he also acknowledged that transmission glitches in the 2023 elections had eroded trust in the commission.



I’d say that Amupitan’s candour deserves applause. But a commission that discovers more than 1.6 million invalid entries in its own register has handed its critics a case, and the distrust that follows does not stay confined to demonstrations outside think tanks. The danger is that when citizens doubt the count will be fair, some will conclude that the contest must be settled by other means. That is where London ends and Lagos begins.



The kind of political violence Lagos witnessed on Thursday has happened so often that it has become a motif of our existence in this country: an enduring injury, a simmering sadness, an ambient terror. As supporters of the NDC gathered for their town hall, thugs descended on them, destroying property and hunting down those in attendance. As long as this continues, the Nigeria of our dreams will remain a mirage.



We have been here before. The 2011 general elections produced one of the deadliest outbreaks of post-election violence in the country’s history. After Goodluck Jonathan defeated Muhammadu Buhari, who would later become president, rioting erupted across major northern cities. Machetes and guns were freely used, and reports put the toll at more than 200 killed and 40,000 displaced. In February 2023, Oyibo Chukwu, the Labour Party’s senatorial candidate in Enugu East, was killed when his convoy was attacked days before the national election.



The catalogue is lengthening. The African Centre for Security, Governance and Development counts 70 election-related attacks and 27 deaths so far in 2026. The Nigeria Civil Society Situation Room, drawing on the CLEEN Foundation’s threat assessment, also reports 27 deaths in the first ten months of the year and names campaign rallies and party offices as principal targets. The counts differ in method, but they agree on direction.



Nigerians, to their credit, still want to vote. A September survey by Yiaga Africa found that while 84 per cent of Nigerians of voting age are keen to vote in 2027, about 61 per cent worry about their safety because of the risk of election violence. That gap between wanting to vote and fearing to is the first real cost of normalised violence, and it is paid before a single ballot is cast.



The course can still be reversed, but only if we stop treating the thug as a freelance nuisance. Researchers who have studied Nigeria’s thug networks link them to elected officials, political financiers and armed groups. Thugs, in other words, have backers, and backers have names.



First, the state’s response must be firm and even-handed. It must go beyond the tired quarrel over whether a party obtained a permit for its rally, meeting or town hall. When campaign events become dangerous, turnout on election day falls, because voters who fear the rally will also fear the polling unit.



Second, the police must act before the violence, not after it. Those who profit from violence learn that it works, and what works escalates. Political actors are already testing their strategies for 2027, thugs included, and the police must sharpen their intelligence to anticipate them rather than merely count the casualties.



Third, accountability must reach the sponsor, not stop at the implementers. Every election season, a handful of young men are paraded before cameras while the men who paid them return to their campaign councils untouched. The National Assembly has toyed for years with an electoral offences commission and has never found the urgency to establish one. Until those behind the violence answers in court for the mayhem the bankrolled, violence will remain what it has long been in our politics: a cheap and dependable campaign expense.



Fourth, INEC must win back the argument the London protesters won. Removing 1.6 million invalid entries is a beginning; publishing the cleaned register in a form that citizens and parties can audit, polling unit by polling unit, is the end. Trust does not return through press conferences. It returns when voters can check for themselves that the ghosts are gone and the phantom polling units have been struck off.



The two incidents of November 12 must be read together because they feed each other. A register that cannot be trusted makes violence look rational to the desperate; violence that goes unpunished makes a clean register irrelevant to the frightened. Break either link and the cycle weakens. Leave both intact, and 2027 may be settled by those other means, long before INEC announces a single result.



Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving global businesses and diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: adeola@hintells.com

World.title: Elumelu to Deliver Keynote at WOC Justice Summit on Rule of Law, Economic Growth
World.content:
Wale Igbintade

Renowned entrepreneur and investor, Mr Tony Elumelu, will deliver the keynote address at the 2026 edition of the WOC Justice Summit, where he is expected to examine the role of the rule of law in promoting private sector growth and economic transformation.

According to a statement by Wole Olanipekun & Co., Elumelu’s keynote address is titled, “The Rule of Law as a Catalyst for Private Sector Growth and Economic Transformation”.

Elumelu, a prominent investor and philanthropist, is the immediate past Chairman of United Bank for Africa Plc, Chairman of Heirs Holdings and Transcorp Hotels Plc, as well as Chairman-designate of Seplat Energy Plc. He is also a recipient of the national honour of Commander of the Order of the Federal Republic (CFR).

With investments spanning financial services, power, energy, hospitality, technology and healthcare, Elumelu is expected to examine the relationship between the administration of justice, the protection of economic rights, the prosperity of private enterprises and Nigeria’s broader economic development.

His address will form part of the summit’s broader examination of future possibilities against the backdrop of established legal precedents, as well as the role of lawyers and the justice sector in shaping the nation’s future.

The summit, scheduled for November 19, 2026, at the Body of Benchers’ Complex, Abuja, will also feature the unveiling of a six-volume publication titled Wole Olanipekun Through the Cases by President Bola Tinubu.

With the theme, “From Precedent to Possibility: The Lawyer’s Role in Shaping the Next Fifty Years of Justice, Democracy and Public Trust”, the summit will bring together eminent speakers to examine the evolving role of the legal profession in protecting commerce, strengthening democratic institutions, advancing justice and safeguarding the rule of law.

The event is expected to attract leading policymakers and decision-makers across the three arms of government at both federal and state levels.

An initiative of Wole Olanipekun & Co., the WOC Justice Summit is conceived as a platform for generating ideas and fostering discussions on ways to strengthen justice delivery.

The six-volume publication, Wole Olanipekun Through the Cases, features analyses and commentaries on landmark cases involving the firm’s founder, Chief Wole Olanipekun, CFR, SAN, spanning his 50-year legal career since his call to the Nigerian Bar in 1976.

World.title: Carte Blanche coming up: Arms race
World.content:
The Sunday, 15 November episode of Carte Blanche investigates allegations of a corruption syndicate operating within the Johannesburg Metro Police Department (JMPD), following explosive claims contained in an affidavit.

The programme examines questionable contracts, alleged kickbacks and claims that insiders have been benefiting from a scheme operating within the department’s armoury.

An insider reportedly reveals how the alleged syndicate works and who may have benefited, raising concerns about the management of public funds and the security of weapons, ammunition and protective equipment meant to safeguard officers policing Johannesburg’s streets.



The investigation asks who is protecting the public purse and holding those entrusted with public safety accountable.

Credibility among South African viewers

Carte Blanche is a South African investigative journalism television series that airs on M-Net every Sunday at 19:00.

Its first episode aired on 21 August 1988 and over the last 34-plus years has earned credibility among South African viewers for its investigation into corruption, consumer issues, and current events.

World.title: Benni McCarthy sends a big message to Bafana Bafana striker
World.content:
Benni McCarthy chats to the media before the Afcon 2027 qualifier against Bafana Bafana . Image: CAF media

Benni McCarthy is South Africa’s all-time leading goalscorer with 31 international goals. Foster’s tally is still 10 goals for his country. The record-holder McCarthy is counting on Foster to be his successor.

The Kenya head coach shared his thoughts after the 2-2 draw with Bafana in their CAF 2027 AFCON qualifier at the Orlando Amstel Arena in Soweto on Friday night.

BENNI MCCARTHY IDENTIFIES FOSTER’S BIGGEST CHALLENGE

According to McCarthy, Foster has a bit of a challenge on his hands. McCarthy says modern football’s tactical trends are making scoring a difficult task for strikers.



The Kenya coach pointed to the widespread use of inverted wingers, arguing that strikers are no longer receiving the same quality of crosses that benefited forwards during his playing days.

“Well, listen, it’s not just in South Africa, it’s a worldwide thing because when you look at modern-day football, now most teams play inverted wingers,” McCarthy told journalists.

“So you don’t get crosses anymore, putting it near post for strikers to make that near-post run. It’s difficult when you play a left-footer on the right, or a right-footer playing on the left.



“So where are the crosses going to come from? The strikers keep making movements. Back in my days, we had Delron Buckley, for example; he was a left-footer.

“Myself, Shaun Bartlett, and Sibusiso Zuma, we had to make sure, you know, when the ball is on the left foot, one goes near post, one goes second post. Wherever that ball lands, one of us is going to get it.”

BACKING FOR LYLE FOSTER

McCarthy believes Foster has the necessary quality, personality and presence to eventually take his name out of the South African record books.



However, he stressed that Bafana must build their attacking play around the strengths of their available strikers, including Mamelodi Sundowns forward Iqraam Rayners.

“But now it’s different, you make a run and then the wingers cut back onto their strong foot to bring it back, you know? So it’s difficult to breed strikers when you play inverted on the wings.

“But listen, Lyle [Foster], he’s finding his footing again. He’s top-notch. I said this a long time ago. I think if there’s a player that’s got the characteristics, that’s got the quality, that’s going to take my name off the record books there, it could be Lyle because he’s got the ability, and he’s got the aura.



“But he needs the service, he needs the team to play for him, you know? And Iqraam Rayners as well. You’ve got to play to the strengths of the strikers that you have; when you don’t play to the strength of your strikers, it becomes difficult for them to score goals,” he concluded.

World.title: Did they even shower?’ Bafana fans react to team’s surprise Kenya arrival
World.content:
Bafana Bafana supporters were left surprised on Saturday morning after discovering that the team had already arrived in Kenya, just 12 hours after their last match.

Pitso Mosimane’s men played out a 2-2 draw against the Harambee Stars at the Orlando Amstel Arena on Friday evening in an Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifier.

South Africa opened the scoring inside the first 10 minutes through an own goal before Kenya restored parity shortly before half-time.



Thabang Matuludi was adjudged to have handled the ball inside the penalty area, resulting in a spot-kick. Michael Olunga made no mistake, sending Ronwen Williams the wrong way to make it 1-1.

With just over 10 minutes remaining, Relebohile Mofokeng restored Bafana’s lead, putting the hosts on course for all three points.

However, a late goal from Ryan Ogam denied Mosimane’s men victory, leaving South Africa frustrated after twice surrendering their advantage.



Bagana fail to beat Kenya

The draw leaves Bafana Bafana top of their AFCON qualifying group with seven points, although their position could change depending on the results of the other teams.

South Africa will get another opportunity to collect maximum points when they travel to Kenya for the return fixture on Tuesday.

However, it was the team’s early arrival in Kenya that caught the attention of Bafana supporters on Saturday morning.



Mosimane and his squad touched down in the East African country just hours after Friday night’s encounter, prompting questions from fans about whether the players had enough time to shower, rest and recover following the match.

“They didn’t rest after playing? I mean they could’ve left this morning hle,” @Kedibone__ wrote on X.

@Dark_Secret247 also questioned the team’s quick departure, writing: “Did they even shower before leaving?”



What’s your take?

World.title: Velebayi makes a big Kaizer Chiefs promise
World.content:
Asanele Velebayi warms up for Kaizer Chiefs at the FNB Stadium. Image: Mazilitha

Velebayi became the matchwinner for Kaizer Chiefs against Siwelele FC. The 23-year-old winger scored the winning goal as Amakhosi came from behind to secure a 2-1 victory and reach the Carling Knockout Cup semi-finals.

Velebayi was delighted to make his first goal count, especially with Amakhosi progressing to the last four.

“Scoring my first goal means a lot, especially that it was a goal that won the match and takes us into the next round,” he said.



ASAVELA VELEBAYI TARGETS MORE GOALS FOR KAIZER CHIEFS

The former Cape Town Spurs attacker from Phillipi now wants to build on that breakthrough by improving his overall contribution whenever he gets an opportunity.

“I aim to help the team by improving my all-round game and scoring more goals when I get the chance,” he said.

The winger’s goal comes in what is his second season with the Soweto giants. He was signed from Spurs in the 2025/26 campaign.

He has made 21 appearances across all competitions, registering one goal and one assist. However, much of his involvement has come from the bench, making his latest contribution an important moment in his Chiefs career.

Velebayi also reflected on the contest against Siwelele, admitting that Amakhosi could have settled the tie much earlier.

“It was a game of transition. There were a lot of turnovers in possession. In truth, we should have wrapped up the game by half-time, and we are working hard to be more clinical in front of goal.”



His comments underline the areas Chiefs still want to improve as they chase silverware this season.

MAMELODI SUNDOWNS IN CARLING KNOCKOUt SEMI-FINALS

Velebayi and his teammates now have another major test waiting in the Carling Knockout Cup.

Chiefs will face Mamelodi Sundowns in the semi-finals, while Stellenbosch FC take on Orlando Pirates in the other last-four encounter. The dates and venues are yet to be confirmed.

World.title: World Rugby urged to punish Rassie Erasmus for late Springbok team changes
World.content:
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus is facing fresh scrutiny after making three late changes to South Africa’s starting line-up for Friday’s clash against France. Image: SA Rugby website

Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus is facing fresh scrutiny after making three late changes to South Africa’s starting line-up for Friday’s clash against France.

The changes, announced just an hour before kick-off on Friday, 13 November, involved the entire Springbok front row and have prompted calls for World Rugby to clarify its regulations.

According to Wales Online, some supporters and pundits have questioned whether the changes went against the spirit of the game, with suggestions that South Africa should face disciplinary action if the substitutions breached the rules.



Ultimately, the late changes didn’t help as the Springboks lost 21-19, their first defeat in Paris in 21 years.

RASSIE Erasmus changes entire Springbok front row

South Africa had initially on Monday named Ox Nche, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw as the starting front row for the match at the Stade de France.

Jan-Hendrik Wessels, Gerhard Steenekamp and Thomas du Toit were named among the replacements.



However, Rassie Erasmus subsequently promoted Wessels, Steenekamp and Du Toit into the starting XV, while Nche, Marx and Louw moved to the bench.

As per a SA Rugby statement, Erasmus have a vague reason for the swap, saying: “We waited until the captains run on Thursday to decide and even then, we were not sure if we should, but we decided shortly before the game, and it was mainly with testing that combination with the Rugby World Cup next year in mind”.

Erasmus used a similar tactic during South Africa’s Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series against New Zealand, when he also changed the entire front row shortly before kick-off.



At the time, the decision was reportedly influenced by the weather forecast, with the Springboks believing a different combination would be better suited to the conditions.

What do World Rugby’s rules say?

The controversy centres on World Rugby Regulation 15.1.2.

The regulation states that participating unions must announce and exchange their starting XV and up to eight replacements 48 hours before kick-off in an international match.



Major tournaments such as the Rugby World Cup also have strict procedures governing late team changes, with alterations generally restricted to specified circumstances, including genuine medical reasons.

However, questions remain about whether a player named among the replacements can be promoted into the starting XV shortly before kick-off, given that the player is already part of the matchday 23.

World Rugby has the power to impose fines where a coach breaches applicable regulations or agreements governing team announcements.



World Rugby clarification sought

Rassie Erasmus’s latest changes have renewed calls for World Rugby to explain precisely what is permitted under the regulations, particularly in the Nations Championship.

The issue is whether the late promotion of named replacements into the starting XV is allowed and, if so, under what conditions.

World Rugby had yet to issue a specific clarification on the latest incident at the time of publication.



Does Rassie Erasmus’ late changes to line-ups make a mockery of an official team announcement?

World.title: Body of missing Durban man found in Phuket
World.content:
The family of 65-year-old Durban man Devendren Naicker has confirmed his death after he went missing while on holiday in Phuket, Thailand. Image: Supplied

The family of 65-year-old Durban man Devendren Naicker has confirmed his death after he went missing while on holiday in Phuket, Thailand.

Naicker, from Yellowwood Park, was reported missing after losing contact with his family shortly after arriving in Thailand.

His body was found in an oil palm plantation in Patong on Friday afternoon, 13 November.



Collected evidence

Police, forensic officers and medical personnel attended the scene and collected evidence.

The clothing found on the body reportedly matched what Naicker was wearing when he disappeared.

The family has confirmed Naicker’s passing but has declined to comment further. The circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear.

Naicker arrived in Phuket on 6 November and checked into the Bel Aire Hotel on Rat-U-Thit 200 Pi Road.

He reportedly left his room that evening and never returned. He was reported missing on 9 November after his family became concerned when they could no longer reach him.

He had been scheduled to leave Thailand on 13 November.



His daughter, 35-year-old Lavanya Naicker, previously said her concerns grew when his cellphone remained switched off and attempts to contact him proved unsuccessful.

The family contacted the hotel, which provided CCTV footage showing Naicker leaving the premises and walking towards a nearby market.

However, the footage did not show him returning.

Hotel staff reportedly searched his room but could not find him.

Holiday years in the making

Naicker had looked forward to the trip for several years.

According to his daughter, he had originally planned the holiday to celebrate his 60th birthday but postponed it after his wife died in 2021, shortly before the planned celebration.

He eventually decided to travel to Thailand this year and had invited his daughter to accompany him, but she was unable to join him because of work commitments.

Lavanya was preparing to travel to Thailand to help with the search when she received the devastating news.

World.title: Muizenberg Beach visitors can expect these big changes from 16 December
World.content:
Visitors to Cape Town’s Muizenberg beachfront can expect a very different experience this festive season, with a major refurbishment project nearing completion ahead of the December holidays.

The City of Cape Town says the project is almost 90% complete, with most of the outstanding work expected to be finished by mid-December, when the builders’ break begins.

From 16 December, the entire beach is expected to be open to the public, along with all parking areas and bays.



The refurbishment, which began in February 2025, involves replacing ageing seawalls and upgrading public facilities along the beachfront.

What will be open at Muizenberg beach this festive season?

The City has outlined several facilities and improvements that visitors can expect to access from 16 December.

These include:

The entire beach, with additional access points to be confirmed closer to the festive season.

All parking areas and parking bays.

The new promenade and stepped seawall, running from Surfer’s Corner to the Muizenberg Pavilion side.

New showers at the central promenade and Surfer’s Corner.

The return of Muizenberg’s iconic beach huts.

Temporary ablution facilities on the western side of the beachfront.

The new central ablution facility may also be ready by then, although the City says this will be confirmed closer to the time.

Adequate signage will direct visitors to the available beach access points.

What has already been completed?

The project reached an important milestone last month with the opening of the St James Walkway, refurbished western parking area, promenade and seawall seating area.



Since 23 October, visitors have also been able to access the western side of the beach from Surfer’s Corner.

Work continues on the remaining sections of the promenade and stepped seawall, and around 95% of the precast steps and promenade units have already been installed.

These structures are designed to provide coastal protection while allowing beach access at different levels. Most of the steps will normally be covered by sand and will not be visible to visitors.

Other work currently under way includes the construction of the central ablution facility, refurbishment of the Shark Spotters and Adaptive Surfing buildings, and installation of overhead pergolas, planters and seating walls.

The playground area and its universal access facilities are also progressing, alongside the brick paving connecting the western and eastern parking areas.

Some finishing work will continue in 2027

Although most of the beachfront is expected to be ready for the festive season, the project will not be finished by December.

The contractor will return in the new year to complete outstanding work, including the installation of mosaic artwork, detailed paving on the central promenade, columns and overhead pergolas.

The eastern lawn area and some seating walls will also still need to be completed.

The City says the provisional festive-season arrangements will be updated and confirmed at the final community meeting before the builders’ break in mid-December.

World.title: Temba Bavuma set to extend remarkable Test captaincy record
World.content:
Temba Bavuma is set to extend one of Test cricket's most remarkable records when he captains South Africa in the first of two Tests against Bangladesh at the Wanderers on Sunday. Image: CSA supplied

Temba Bavuma is set to extend one of Test cricket’s most remarkable records when he captains South Africa in the first of two Tests against Bangladesh at the Wanderers on Sunday.

With 13 wins in his first 15 Tests as captain, Bavuma has had more success than anyone in the history of the game at an equivalent stage of their captaincy.

READ | Proteas vs Bangladesh Tests: Squad, dates, where to watch



Only Lindsay Hassett of Australia can match Bavuma’s record. They both had 13 wins, one draw and one loss in their first 15 matches in charge.

Hassett’s fortunes took a downturn in his 16th match at the helm, when they lost to South Africa in Melbourne in 1952/53 – and he had only one more win in his last nine matches as captain.

Shock

For South Africa to lose at home to Bangladesh would be similar in shock value to Australia’s loss against an unheralded South African team 74 years ago.

South Africa are the reigning World Test champions and their wins under Bavuma include three against Australia and three against India of which two were in India last year.

South Africa have won 14 of their 16 previous Tests against Bangladesh, with the other two matches having been rain-affected draws in Bangladesh in 2015.

But Bangladesh pulled off a surprise win against Australia in Darwin in August and as Bavuma noted in a recent interview, “the target is on our back and everyone wants to have a go at us.”



The tour schedule makes an already tough assignment for Bangladesh even more challenging. As recently as Monday, they were completing a drawn Test against West Indies in Sylhet. They arrived in Johannesburg on Wednesday, just four days before facing the world champions.

Lost all prior Test in SA

Bangladesh lost all eight of their previous Tests in South Africa. Five were by an innings and the closest of the other three defeats was by 220 runs in Durban in 2021/22.

A key player for Bangladesh could be Towhid Hridoy, who made 350 not out for Bangladesh ‘A’ against South Africa ‘A’ in a high-scoring draw in Potchefstroom in September and followed up with 242 not out and 82 in the second Test against the West Indies last week.

By Garrin Lambley © Agence France-Presse

World.title: No major incidents reported as matric exams near end
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Department of Basic Education is gearing up for the marking phase as the 2026 National Senior Certificate examinations near their end.

To date, the department's spokesperson, Terence Khala, said they have noted a few minor incidents reported, but none are serious enough to affect the integrity of the examinations.

READ | Senior teachers opt for early retirement as government trims wage bill

This is as he points to taxi violence in the Western Cape and scholar transport challenges in Gauteng as some of the issues experienced during the examination period.

But upon being notified of this, the department acted.

“The sector kicked in and was able to make sure that the requisite protocols were put in place. Learners in Gauteng were able to write adequately and equally in the Western Cape. “And I think it's only for us to commend the system and commend every individual that forms part of the system that assists us to make sure that we can really take this massive undertaking and make it a seamless one,” Khala said.

Markers, according to the department, will get to work on 1 December.

World.title: Six people killed in head-on collision on Eastern Cape N2
World.content:
At least six people have died in a horror crash on the N2 in the Eastern Cape.

The victims were travelling in a minibus taxi when it collided head-on with a truck on Saturday morning.

Provincial transport spokesperson Unathi Binqose said the minibus taxi was travelling from Alice towards Bizana while the truck was travelling from Kokstad towards Mzamba when the accident happened.

"Preliminary information suggests that the Toyota Quantum crossed into the path of the oncoming truck, resulting in a head-on collision. "There is also a suspicion that driver fatigue may have contributed to the crash. However, the exact circumstances surrounding the collision remain subject to police investigation," he said.

Three others were seriously injured, while three others sustained slight injuries.

"The injured were attended to by emergency services and transported for medical treatment".

The victims are believed to be university students travelling home to Bizana.

This comes just a day after seven people died in another crash on the N2 near Ndabakazi.

World.title: Madlanga Commission hears ex-JMPD top cop allegedly forced officers to take bribe
World.content:
PRETORIA - A major drug bust operation in Johannesburg has led to explosive testimony at the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry.

The commission heard on Friday how former JMPD superintendent Phineas Manyama allegedly instructed officers to release suspects and accept whatever money was offered in return.

READ | LIVE | JMPD corruption under the spotlight at Madlanga

Testifying at the commission Tactical Response Unit officer Michael Potsane said refusing the instruction came with threats of dismissal, arrest or even death.

He testified that he regarded the instruction as unlawful and did not comply with it.

World.title: Hot weather, dry taps, fuming Joburg residents
World.content:
SOWETO - Water shortages are worsening across various parts of Johannesburg, with residents reporting days without water supply amid the heatwave.

In Soweto, one resident detailed how the community has been without water since Tuesday, with supply returning briefly during the early hours of the morning.

“We've been having challenges with water in this community whereby each and every weekend we don't have water at all. It is becoming a new normal now,” the resident said.

The resident adds that the situation becomes more concerning during the current heatwave when residents need water the most.

“We are encouraged to drink more water because people are going to suffer because of dehydration, but at this particular moment, Joburg Water is not doing justice to us."

He said adding to the frustration is the lack of communication between Joburg Water and residents.

READ | Joburg residents urged to take precautions as heatwave continues

In a statement on Saturday, Joburg Water said bulk supply meters in the Roodepoort and Soweto regions, which were closed on Thursday to rescue and boost bulk supply levels, commenced reopening on Friday afternoon.

The water utility said it is worth noting that systems were not fully opened but taken back to their original curtailment before being fully closed on Thursday.

“While some bulk supplier systems have stabilised and recovered, there are still several systems which will take time to recover over the next few days. The recovery is also impacted by the demand for the system as they are integrated. “The affected Johannesburg Water reservoirs will first need to fill to acceptable levels before the system stabilises. Customers may experience low pressure or intermittent supply and, in some cases, no water until the system recovers,” the statement read.

In the meantime, Joburg Water said alternative water arrangements are being made and deployed through the central and regional coordination groups.

World.title: A grave clash: One family's search, many families' pain
World.content:
LICHTENBURG - A quest for closure for one family has thrown Boikhutso’s cemetery in Lichtenburg, North West and countless other families into chaos and heartache.

The families claim graves were disturbed and their dignity upended during an exhumation process conducted by the North West Department of Health after it got a court order in June 2023 to dig up graves, searching for a man missing from the old Thusong Hospital.

It was suspected that he had died and received a pauper’s burial at this cemetery.

However, families say the process has left the cemetery in disarray, with some unable to identify the graves of their relatives.

Mmakhumo Moja’s family is among those affected.

READ | Fort Jackson SAPS building turns into haven for criminals

She says both her parents’ graves have since vanished, lost in the shuffle. They found the graves disturbed, soil scattered and headstones missing.

"We want our graves, and we want to know exactly where they are located. After the exhumation, we were supposed to come and clean up, but we didn't know whose graves we were cleaning. When we're supposed to do some of our cultural rites at the grave, it's a problem. “When you carry out traditional rituals, you have to come to the ancestors and engage them. But the place is a mess; it's dug up, and there are holes everywhere,” Moja said.

The North West Health Department spokesperson Tebogo Lekgethwane insists it consulted some families ahead of the dig, and flat-out denies leaving the cemetery in shambles.

But three years on, the cemetery is still in a mess, and the family’s still waiting.

They’re holding out for answers, longing for restoration, and just a little respect for their dear departed.

eNCA Bafedile Moerane filed this report.

World.title: Fort Jackson SAPS building turns into haven for criminals
World.content:
MDANTSANE - Once a well-resourced police station where officers carried out their duties but today the Fort Jackson SAPS building in Mdantsane in the Eastern Cape has become a haven for criminal activity.

Criminals have taken over the building, vandalising offices that were meant to benefit the people of Mdantsane and surrounding areas.

This has left Mdantsane residents questioning how a government-owned building intended to strengthen policing could be allowed to deteriorate while crime escalates.

READ | Vandals savage Eastern Cape school

According to the community crime organisation, the Buffalo City Special Team Task Force, criminals have had easy access to the building since a taxi crashed into the perimeter fence earlier this year.

The full extend of the damage remains unclear, however police suspect opportunists trashed the premises after hours.

Eastern Cape police spokesperson Siphokazi Mawisa said following the incidents, cases were opened, and arrests were made.

"The cases are currently before court, and the suspects are out on bail,”she said.

Measures are being put in place to deploy police units that will utilise the building on a 24-hour basis to safeguard it.

eNCA's Ronald Masinda filed this report.

World.title: ANC to engage all parties in hung municipalities
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The ANC says it will engage all political parties, civic movements, and independent candidates as it seeks coalition partners following the local government elections.

The National Executive Committee is mandated to explore possible coalition arrangements in municipalities where no party secured an outright majority.

It says its priority is to establish stable councils capable of delivering basic services.

READ | No permanent enemies in coalition talks - MK Party

The ANC says any agreement must be based on a common programme with clear service delivery targets, accountability and decisive action against corruption.

The party says coalition talks are already under way and it will provide an update on their progress on Tuesday.

World.title: US says airspace now 'opened up,' no cyberattack
World.content:
WASHINGTON - The United States on Friday lifted an hours-long ground stop at the nation's airports, with top officials explaining that the disruption was due to old equipment and not a cyberattack or sweeping Microsoft outage.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told a late-night briefing at the White House that US airspace was now "opened up," while warning it would take time for the travel chaos to clear.

"At 8:15 tonight Eastern Time, we've opened up the airspace," Duffy said. "Now does that mean every flight is going to fly right now? It's going to be slow."

The breakdown came a day after Duffy and the White House had formally asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System.

"Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down," Duffy said. "It's the old hardware that went down, and I think the question for the American people is: Do you want your Congress to fund this?"

Duffy however insisted it was still safe for Americans to fly.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin dismissed speculation about a coordinated cyber assault on the United States, or any link to the Microsoft outage that affected services worldwide.

"Welcome to Friday the 13th, right? You know, I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft. I know a lot of people are making that jump," Mullin said.

Mullin added there was "actually no cyber attack."

"When we start looking at cyber threats, cyber attacks, typically some people are going to raise their hand up and say, 'Hey, we did that.' There's no chatter.' We haven't seen any footprints," he added.

But he said US security and law enforcement agencies were still checking and had ruled nothing out.

The two officials also defended President Donald Trump, who had yet to comment on the air stoppage some five hours after it began.

"President Trump immediately had people in his office," Mullin said. "We were communicating."

-AFP

World.title: IG Kanja, DCI boss ordered to produce missing Busia businessman, 292 days later
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

It is now 292 days after Busia businessman Ahmed Ibrahim Ali Mohamed went missing.

The High Court has ordered IG Douglas Kanja and DCI boss Mohamed Amin to produce missing Busia businessman Ahmed Ibrahim Ali Mohamed, dead or alive, within 48 hours and pay him Sh5.84 million in damages over his 292-day disappearance

Justice Samuel Mohochi issued an order like a writ of habeas corpus, compelling IG Douglas Kanja, DCI boss Mohamed Amin and the ATPU commander to produce Ahmed before the court within three days after declaring his nearly 10-month disappearance since January illegal, unconstitutional and a violation of his fundamental rights.

In a judgment delivered on Friday, November 13, 2026, the judge declared that Ahmed's unlawful arrest, incommunicado detention and continued enforced disappearance constituted a flagrant and ongoing violation of his fundamental rights under Articles 25(a), 28, 29 and 49 of the Constitution.

The court awarded him Sh5.84 million in general, aggravated and exemplary constitutional damages against the Inspector General, National Police Service, DCI, ATPU commander, Director-General of the National Intelligence Service, Interior Cabinet Secretary and Attorney General, jointly and severally.

The judge warned that the State could not escape accountability through blanket denials while a Kenyan citizen remained missing.

"Enforced disappearance is a continuous, agonising violation of Articles 25(a), 28, 29, and 49. The Constitution of Kenya does not permit citizens to vanish into thin air, nor does it tolerate unacknowledged, secret detentions," Justice Mohochi ruled.

The court rejected the State's argument that Ahmed could have been abducted by criminals posing as police officers, finding that the circumstances surrounding his disappearance raised serious questions about the involvement of security agencies.

Justice Mohochi noted that the abduction took place at the Korinda Main Prison area, a highly secured zone where armed prison officers were stationed.

The judge questioned how ordinary criminals could have stopped a passenger bus, switched on its interior lights, checked passengers' identification documents, removed Ahmed and ransacked his luggage in full view of a heavily guarded prison facility without intervention.

"Here, the abductors acted with the calm, unchallenged authority of state agents who knew they had absolute immunity and command over that specific geographical territory," the judge observed.

The court further found that police had failed to interview the bus driver, Peter Kimemia, despite his being at the front of the vehicle during the incident.

It also faulted investigators for failing to visit Korinda Main Prison or interview armed prison officers who were on duty when the businessman was seized.

Justice Mohochi said these omissions undermined the State's explanation that Ahmed had been taken by civilian criminals.

The judge consequently drew an adverse inference against the security agencies, noting that operational details surrounding the roadblock, including deployment rosters, vehicle logs, command structures and intelligence records, were exclusively within the State's knowledge.

"The executive cannot defeat the liberty of a citizen based on unsupported conjecture," the judge ruled.

In another significant order, the court directed the Inspector General and DCI director to convene a physical meeting with Ahmed's family within 14 days to tender an unreserved apology over what it described as institutional indolence, deliberate omissions and failure to conduct timely and effective investigations.

The two security chiefs must also publish a formal public apology within 21 days, including broadcasting it on at least two mainstream local radio stations within Busia County in Kiswahili and the predominant local dialect.

The court further ordered the Inspector General to institute a comprehensive internal administrative inquiry into possible involvement, collusion or gross negligence by officers from the National Police Service, DCI and ATPU who participated in joint operations in Busia County on January 25, 2026.

IPOA was ordered to immediately assume full, independent and exclusive investigative control over Ahmed's disappearance.

The authority must record statements from key witnesses who have not been interviewed, including the bus driver, booking clerk Ashraf and armed prison wardens stationed at Korinda Main Prison on the night of January 25, 2026.

It must also submit a comprehensive progress report to the court within 45 days.

The judge additionally directed the Interior Cabinet Secretary and the Attorney General to initiate the process of ratifying and domesticating the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance within the stipulated timelines.

The court noted that Kenya signed the international convention in February 2007 but had yet to ratify it.

Ahmed disappeared on the night of January 25, 2026, while travelling from Busia to Nairobi aboard a Buscar passenger bus, registration number KDM 252P.

According to evidence presented in court by petitioners led by Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah and Ahmed's uncle, the bus was intercepted near Korinda Main Prison by four men travelling in a black Volkswagen, who allegedly identified themselves as security officers.

The abductors reportedly checked passengers' identification documents before forcing Ahmed out of the bus following a physical confrontation and taking away his greenish luggage bag.

His phone subsequently went offline, with Safaricom data placing its last network signal at Korinda Main Prison Stage.

The State had denied having Ahmed in custody, arguing that he was abducted by unknown criminals impersonating security officers.

However, the court held that the State had failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for his disappearance.

The judge further ordered that any party that disobeys the judgment would be liable for contempt of court, including possible arrest, civil jail for up to six months and personal fines.

The court retained supervisory jurisdiction over the matter and directed that the case return for a compliance mention after the 45-day investigative reporting period.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Buxton estate tensions escalate after county officials attacked
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

A dispute over the multibillion-shilling Buxton Point housing project in Mombasa turned violent after county officials were allegedly attacked while enforcing a government order suspending construction over outstanding contractual obligations.

The confrontation came a day after County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Lands, Housing, and Urban Development Mohamed Hussein ordered GulfCap Real Estate to halt all construction activities pending the resolution of disputes involving the county government and hundreds of former Buxton Estate residents.

The officials were reportedly pelted with stones as they attempted to serve the developer with an enforcement notice, with allegations that individuals linked to businessman Suleiman Shahbal were involved in the confrontation.

Hussein condemned the incident, saying attempts to intimidate government officers would not derail efforts to enforce the law and protect public interests.

"Let them bring goons, machetes, and stones if they want. I am not intimidated. I will execute my duties, and nobody will threaten me. The law must be followed, regardless of who you are or how much money you have," he said.

"We are here for the people of Mombasa, and we will ensure their rights are protected. Nobody is above the law," he added.

The November 10 enforcement notice, issued by County Director of Physical Planning Qassim Ali, directed GulfCap Real Estate to stop further development activities and obtain valid construction permits.

The notice, issued under Section 72(1) of the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, cited construction under a varied development plan without county approval and an ongoing dispute involving the developer, former tenants, and the county government.

The notice was reportedly received by the project's manager, Billy Okendo.

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county government and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units and commercial spaces developed in the first and second phases.

An addendum to the agreement signed on January 15, 2020, outlines the county's entitlement, with the allocation expected to be transferred upon completion of the second phase.

In a letter dated April 30, 2025, the county demanded 10 per cent of the proposed 1,800 housing units, translating to 180 apartments. The demand was renewed in February 2026, with the county seeking details on how the allocation would be implemented.

However, in correspondence dated September 22, 2026, the Department of Lands, Urban Planning and Housing expressed concern over what it described as the developer's failure to provide substantive responses to previous demands.

The county also questioned whether GulfCap had provided performance security equivalent to 10 per cent of the total construction cost for each phase, as required under the agreement.

It further demanded proof of payment of the Project Development Fee, which is payable in instalments as the project progresses.

The county said it had also raised technical and planning concerns during a meeting with the developer on April 15, 2026, including the need to address outstanding issues and resubmit the masterplan application.

But the dispute goes beyond the county's financial and contractual entitlement, with more than 500 former residents accusing the developer of failing to honour promises made when they were displaced in 2019.

John Tsuma, Secretary-General of the Buxton Tenants Welfare Association, said former residents had waited for more than seven years to return to their homes despite assurances that they would be prioritised once construction was completed.

"We are very disappointed by what happened. We had a meeting with the CECM, and he made it clear that all construction activities should stop until the outstanding issues are resolved. We did not go there to fight anybody. We wanted the directive implemented," Tsuma said.

He accused the developer of benefiting from the project while former residents continued to struggle to secure the houses they were promised.

"The developer has benefited from A to Z. He was given land by the county government, and the houses were sold off-plan. Yet, when it comes to fulfilling the promises made to former residents, we are still being taken around in circles," he said.

Tsuma said residents were not demanding free houses but wanted the affordable tenant-purchase arrangement they were promised before leaving the estate.

"We are not asking for free houses. We want the tenant-purchase arrangement that was promised to us so that we can pay for the houses and return to our homes," he said.

He also questioned why the developer had allegedly failed to surrender the county government's 184 housing units under the joint venture arrangement.

Mohamed Mzee Rubea, chairman of the evicted Buxton residents, said the money paid to the families during their displacement was a relocation allowance and not compensation for their homes.

He said the former tenants were given Sh240,000, with assurances that they would rent alternative accommodation for 12 months and return once the houses were completed.

"What we received was relocation money, not compensation for our houses. We were told to take the money and rent houses for 12 months and that we would be the first people to return once construction was completed. But here we are, more than seven years later, still waiting," Rubea said.

He said the original agreement involved 522 former tenants who were promised priority access to houses under the redevelopment.

Rubea added that each household was also promised Sh60,000 as a deposit towards acquiring a house under the tenant-purchase scheme.

"We were promised Sh60,000 as a deposit for those who would take up the houses. The developer later said the money would only be given to those who actually acquired the units. We are still waiting, and many of us have not received anything," he said. At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Mudavadi urges Western Kenya to unite, says region cannot remain on sidelines
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi. [File, Standard]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has urged Western Kenya to unite ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying the region must strengthen its political representation to have a greater say in national decision-making.

Speaking during a UDA delegates' meeting in Shitoto village, Mumias East, Kakamega County, he said Western Kenya could not afford to remain on the sidelines while decisions affecting the country were being made.
