World.title: Liberia’s City Streets in Limbo
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — In Liberia’s county capitals, paved streets have been promised many times. This year, the money was finally set aside. The pavement has not followed.

By Rodney D. Sieh

By September 30, the government had recorded more than $10 million against 15 city street projects, in towns from Buchanan on the Atlantic coast to Zwedru near the Ivorian border. The figures appear in the Ministry of Public Works’ pages of the draft national budget for 2027. On Thursday, the ministry said not one contractor had been paid.



The money, it said, is caught in the paperwork of the Ministry of Finance, at the purchase-order stage, a step short of the vouchers that release cash. Contractors will not move equipment onto sites until advance payments arrive. The ministry expects the work to be substantially complete by March 2027.

In Liberia, public money passes several gates before it reaches a contractor.

The Legislature approves it. The PPCC, the procurement regulator, clears the contract. The Finance Ministry releases an allotment, a purchase order commits it to a named firm, and only a payment voucher releases cash. The ministry says most city streets money is stuck at the fourth gate.

The budget book suggests the money may run out before the asphalt arrives. Liberia’s fiscal year ends December 31. In the draft budget for 2027, every city streets line under Public Works is blank.

For a country of about 5.5 million people, where most roads outside the capital are unpaved and many turn to mud in the rainy season, city streets are among the most visible promises of President Joseph Boakai’s government. Public Works Minister Roland Layfette Giddings has called November and December critical months, as the dry season opens the best window to build.

A statement, and numbers that match

The ministry’s statement, headlined “MPW Sets the Record Straight,” followed local media reports that $10.1 million had been disbursed. It urged the public to do due diligence before publishing information about its work.

On its central claim, the government’s own figures support the ministry. Fourteen projects, it says, have cleared Liberia’s procurement watchdog, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC). All 14 show money recorded: $9.12 million of $13.2 million budgeted. The 11 projects still waiting for the commission’s sign-off, known as a “No Objection,” show nothing.

Most of the cleared projects sit close to 70 percent of their budgets.

That is the pattern of a fixed tranche set aside, not of bills paid for work done.

Where the account frays

Not every figure fits. Two projects are recorded in full: $300,000 for streets in Ganta, a trading hub near the Guinean border, and $200,000 for a road to the Duport Road/Soul Clinic community outside Monrovia. The ministry describes all of its allotments as partial. It did not explain the difference.

Then there is Kakata, a market town about 50 kilometres from the capital. The full $950,000 budgeted for its streets is recorded. The ministry says Kakata is a separate, older contract on which paving has begun, but did not say how much the contractor has received. In March, residents complained that work had stood still since November 2025.

Buchanan, the port city that carries the largest allocation at $2.5 million, raises a sharper question.

At a November 3 briefing, Giddings listed it among projects already underway. Nine days later, his ministry said the Buchanan contractor had not been paid and would mobilise only after an advance.

The delays are not new.

In October, Giddings acknowledged the programme was behind schedule. It had been drawn up with legislators, he said, so engineers had to gather data in the field before tendering could begin. He expected the contracts to be finalised with the Finance Ministry within about a month. Six weeks after the September tally, the money still had not moved.

A race against the calendar

The deeper problem is time. Roughly $4.1 million budgeted for the cleared projects has not been set aside at all. The 11 projects still awaiting clearance, worth $4.35 million, range from Greenville and Cestos, whose tenders closed only on October 23, to Sanniquellie, Yekepa, Tappita and the Gibi road in Margibi County. None has a line in the 2027 draft.

Unless unspent balances are carried over, or lawmakers restore the lines before passing the budget, towns could be left with signed contracts and no money to honour them. The same budget page raises wider questions about the ministry’s spending.

A programme to buy road-building “yellow machines” had recorded $8.57 million against a $5.97 million budget, $2.6 million over, and the 2027 draft proposes $14.2 million more. Street lights and two other lines show money recorded with nothing budgeted at all.

Larger projects fared better than the streets. The $26 million St. Paul Bridge and Bo-Waterside roads and the $5 million ELWA–RIA road are recorded in full. Across all its capital projects, the ministry had recorded $80.65 million of $115.4 million, or 70 percent, by September 30.

It is unclear whether the budget’s “year to date” figures record cash paid or money set aside, and whether unspent balances will carry into 2027. It also raises questions as to how much the Kakata contractor has received, and why Ganta and Duport Road are recorded in full.

The ministry closed its statement with a rebuke to its critics: the call for accountability, it said, must come from a position of transparency. In a dozen county capitals, residents will judge that by what is on their streets when the rains return.

World.title: What Benoni Urey’s Role on Dangote’s ECOWAS Business Council Means for Liberia
World.content:
MONROVIA – Three decades ago, Liberia needed West Africa’s soldiers to help end its civil war. Today, it has a chance to help shape the region’s economic future.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Benoni W. Urey, a Liberian businessman best known as a founding shareholder of the mobile network Lonestar Cell MTN, has been named Liberia’s representative on the ECOWAS Business Council. The council is a new advisory body chaired by Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, and is meant to give the private sector a direct line to the presidents of West Africa.



The appointment comes at a delicate moment. The regional bloc has lost three members, its trade ambitions have stalled, and its energy map is being redrawn by one giant Nigerian oil refinery.

Whether Liberia’s new seat delivers anything for ordinary people — cheaper fuel, easier border crossings, steadier electricity, a bigger market for Liberian goods — will depend on how the council works, whose interests it serves, and how hard Liberia’s representative fights for a small country in a room full of giants.

A Bloc Under Strain

The Economic Community of West African States, or ECOWAS, was founded in Lagos, Nigeria, in 1975. Liberia was one of its founding members.

For many Liberians, though, ECOWAS means peacekeeping more than trade. Its military force, ECOMOG, entered Liberia’s civil war in 1990, and ECOWAS mediators helped broker the 2003 peace agreement in Accra, Ghana, that ended 14 years of conflict.

Fifty years after its founding, the bloc’s economic promise remains largely unfulfilled.

It has also shrunk. In January 2025, the military-led governments of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger formally walked out and formed their own Alliance of Sahel States. That left ECOWAS with 12 members and cost it roughly a fifth of the levy revenue that funds its institutions. In October 2026 the two blocs agreed to set up working groups to manage their relationship, but there is no sign of a reunion.

Trade among members remains thin. Less than 15 percent of the region’s trade happens between ECOWAS countries, held back by tariffs, red tape, roadside checkpoints and poor roads. A long-promised single currency, the Eco, has been postponed again and again; leaders now say it will launch in 2027, starting with the countries that meet its economic targets.

The bloc also has new leadership. General Birame Diop of Senegal now heads the ECOWAS Commission, succeeding Dr. Omar Alieu Touray of The Gambia.

For Liberia, a country of about five million people, the stakes are practical. It trades heavily with neighbouring Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire, imports almost all of its fuel, and depends on regional power lines and road links that ECOWAS helps plan and fund.

Long Promised, Just Starting

The ECOWAS Business Council is not quite as new as it appears. ECOWAS ministers created it on paper in 2021, and its launch slipped from December 2024 to September 2025. Dangote was finally named its first chairman by the bloc’s foreign ministers in Abuja in December 2025, and West African heads of state later endorsed him.

The council’s job is to advise ECOWAS leaders on trade, investment and industrial policy, and to help clear the barriers that stop people, goods, services and money from moving freely across the region’s borders.

Each member state gets one representative, and Nigeria, the region’s largest economy, gets two more. Regional business associations also have a voice. Dangote’s team says his two-year term will focus on energy corridors to ease the power shortages that choke business, as well as ports and logistics, with funding to be sought from lenders such as the African Export-Import Bank and the Africa Finance Corporation.

The council is still finding its feet. By mid-2026 only a handful of national representatives had been confirmed, and its first meeting was planned for late October or early November, with further approvals due at a ministerial meeting in December.

The risk is familiar. Business councils across Africa have often become talking shops. This one will be judged on results — fewer roadblocks, faster customs clearance, power projects that actually get built — and on whether its members speak for market traders and young companies, not just the region’s biggest conglomerates.

Dangote at the Helm

Choosing Aliko Dangote sends a clear signal about how ECOWAS sees its future: industrial, energy-driven and led by large regional investors.

No single business has done more to change West Africa’s fuel market in recent years. Dangote’s refinery outside Lagos, built at a reported cost of about US$20 billion, reached its full design capacity of 650,000 barrels a day in February 2026 and is aiming for 700,000. It now supplies most of Nigeria’s fuel, and according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Nigeria’s fuel exports to other African countries rose to nearly 120,000 barrels a day in the second quarter of 2026. Analysts estimate the refinery has cut West Africa’s imports of refined fuel from outside the region by close to a quarter. When the conflict involving Iran disrupted supplies from the Gulf and Europe this year, Dangote stepped in with more gasoline exports across the continent.

The company markets its cleaner, European-standard fuel as an end to the days when West Africa served as a dumping ground for low-quality imports.

For Liberia, which imports nearly all its fuel and where pump prices have often run higher than in neighbouring countries, a major refinery a few days’ sail away could mean shorter supply chains, more reliable deliveries in a crisis, and cleaner fuel.

But there are real concerns.

The first is concentration. A region that trades its dependence on Europe and the Gulf for dependence on one private refinery gains proximity but may lose competition. And the council advising presidents on energy and trade policy will be chaired by that refinery’s owner.

The second is conflict of interest. Dangote’s empire spans cement, sugar, fertilizer and petroleum — all sectors shaped by tariffs, import rules and industrial policy. Dangote has long argued that Africa should produce what it consumes and has championed protection for local manufacturers. Regional protection can help West African industry grow, but small, import-dependent economies like Liberia can end up paying more for everyday goods.

The third is Nigeria’s weight. With three seats and the chairmanship, Nigerian business interests will carry outsized influence in the council’s decisions.

None of this means the council cannot serve the whole region. Dangote has publicly urged governments to protect private investment, back local investors and keep their policies consistent — messages that resonate with business owners in Monrovia. The real test is whether the council produces rules that open markets or rules that protect those already on top.

The Record Urey Brings

Urey’s career spans several of the sectors the council has made its priorities.His biggest business success is in telecommunications. Through his company PLC Investments, he was a founding shareholder of Lonestar Communications Corporation, which launched in 2001 in partnership with South Africa’s MTN Group. Lonestar grew into one of Liberia’s two main mobile networks and a major provider of mobile money. That experience matters: ECOWAS wants payment systems that work across borders, and cross-border mobile money may be the most direct way regional integration reaches traders and families who send money to relatives in neighbouring countries.

He also knows shipping. From 1996 to 2003, Urey headed Liberia’s Bureau of Maritime Affairs, which oversees the country’s international ship registry. Liberia, despite its size, flags one of the largest merchant fleets in the world, making the registry one of the country’s few globally significant economic assets. With ports and logistics high on Dangote’s agenda, that background could prove useful.

On energy, Urey once served as a deputy director general at the state-owned Liberia Electricity Corporation. Power is the council’s headline priority, and Liberia remains one of the least electrified countries in the region. Urey could press for faster completion of the regional power lines linking Liberia with Côte d’Ivoire, Sierra Leone and Guinea.

He also runs commercial farms in Konola and Careysburg, outside Monrovia, that supply the local market — relevant in a country that still imports much of its staple food, rice.

And he knows politics. Urey served as mayor of Careysburg and founded the All Liberian Party, running for president in 2017. That gives him a feel for how policy plays out on the ground, but it also raises a question: how will a political party leader keep party interests separate from a regional business role?

What Liberia Should Ask For

A well-connected representative could push hard on the issues that matter most to a small economy. Among them: ending harassment and illegal fees at busy border crossings such as Bo Waterside, on the Sierra Leone border, and Ganta, on the Guinea border; securing regional fuel supply on fair terms; speeding up power links; making mobile payments work across borders; and opening regional financing to Liberian small businesses.

Urey has said he wants Liberia’s entrepreneurs and young companies to have a clear voice in regional policy. That promise is the yardstick by which his tenure should be measured.

What to Watch

Three questions will shape how this appointment is judged.

Business interests. The council will advise on telecoms, digital finance, agriculture and trade — sectors in which Urey has commercial stakes. Lonestar’s competition with rival Orange Liberia is one example. The council should publish a clear conflict-of-interest policy for all its members.

Selection. The press statement announcing the appointment says Urey was chosen after consultations across the region and that membership is by invitation. It is not clear whether Liberia’s government, its Chamber of Commerce or its business associations had a say.

Accountability. Liberian businesses will need a way to bring their concerns to their representative, and a way to hear back from him.

The Bottom Line

Liberia has gained a voice in a body that, if it works, could influence how fuel, power, money and goods move across West Africa. Dangote’s chairmanship gives the council financial muscle and direct access to presidents. It also concentrates influence in the hands of the region’s most dominant industrialist.

For a small country with limited bargaining power, the value of Urey’s seat will be measured in concrete results: lower costs at the border, reliable fuel and electricity, and real opportunities for Liberian entrepreneurs. Anything less, and the appointment will be just another title.

World.title: DPP Says 90 Days in Detention Not Unreasonable as Treason Accused Cite 45-Day Legal Limit
World.content:
Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) Gilbert Phiri told the High Court that holding opposition leader Mr Brian Mundubile, Mr Makebi Zulu and 16 others for 60 or even 90 days could not automatically be considered unreasonable. Their lawyers countered that the Anti-Terrorism Act sets a maximum detention period of 45 days. The panel must now weigh one position against the other.

The 18 accused have petitioned the court against Attorney-General Mulilo Kabesha and the DPP, alleging that their continued detention violates their constitutional rights. Their application for constitutional bail is before Justices Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga, who began hearing the matter on Friday.

Opening the State’s case, Mr Phiri and Mr Kabesha submitted that the seriousness of the charges and the complexity of the investigations justified the time taken to bring the accused before court. Given the nature of the alleged offences, they said, detention periods of 60 or 90 days could not be judged unreasonable on their own.

To support that position, the DPP reached back into Zambia’s treason history. He cited The People v Njapau of 1967 and The People v Edward Jack Shamwana and 12 others, telling the court that constitutional bail had not been granted in either matter. He urged the judges not to depart from that position, maintaining that there had been no unreasonable delay in bringing the accused before court.

The defence team of Mr Milner Katolo, Mr Sakwiba Sikota and Mr Chifumu Banda answered with a statute rather than a precedent. Their clients, they said, had not been brought before court within the legally prescribed period, in violation of their constitutional rights.

The lawyers relied on Section 55 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, which requires suspects arrested under that law to be brought before court within 48 hours. Any extension is subject to judicial approval, and detention may not exceed 45 days.

Mr Katolo then set out the detention count for each group of applicants. Three of them, arrested on August 1, 2026, had spent 72 days in custody by October 12, when the petition was filed. Business executive Mr Harry Findlay, arrested on August 4, had been held for more than 68 days.

Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu, arrested on August 27, had spent more than 47 days in detention by October 13. The seriousness of the charges and the need for further investigation, Mr Katolo said, could not override the constitutional right to be brought before court within a reasonable time.

Before either side could fully test those arguments, the panel ruled on what evidence would remain on the record. The State had asked for parts of the applicants’ affidavit to be struck out as extraneous and inadmissible, and the judges granted part of that request.

They expunged paragraph six of the affidavit for introducing a new issue at the reply stage. That paragraph concerned a claim that law enforcement officers had confiscated certificates for training in Russia on August 1, 2026, material linked to three applicants facing terrorism-related charges. Paragraph 21 was also struck out after the court found it went beyond the issues raised by the DPP.

On other points, the State lost ground. The court declined to expunge material about Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu’s stay at a United Nations facility, an episode the State had cited to portray the two as flight risks who emerged only after negotiations.

The applicants said they sought refuge there because they feared for their lives following an alleged incident involving gunfire. The court held that the allegation was relevant, and ruled that the two should explain the circumstances surrounding their decision.

The judges also retained video allegedly showing State agents breaking into Mr Mundubile’s Kabulonga residence. They relied on Section 9 of the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act No. 4 of 2021, which recognises electronic evidence. Mr Katolo said the court found the footage relevant to the State’s allegations about the United Nations refuge.

The hearing stalled before the core submissions were concluded, after Mr Phiri raised concerns about security arrangements and lock-up times for the applicants at the correctional facility where they are held.

The panel adjourned the matter to Monday for continued submissions. When it resumes, the judges will weigh the DPP’s treason precedents against the 45-day limit written into the Anti-Terrorism Act.

World.title: Never Trade Your Values for Organisational Gain, ZICA Tells New Chartered Accountants
World.content:
Zambia Institute of Chartered Accountants (ZICA) president Mr Joseph Matimba has warned the country’s newest chartered accountants never to compromise their professional values for personal or organisational gain. Their judgement, he told them, would now shape public resources and the livelihoods of many people.

He delivered the warning at the second CA Zambia convocation ceremony, held at the Golden Peacock Hotel in Lusaka on Thursday night. The designation, he said, marked the start of a heavier responsibility rather than the end of the designates’ professional journey.

Mr Matimba spelt out how far that responsibility would reach once they took up their posts.

“As Chartered Accountants, you will occupy positions in which your judgement and actions can influence organisations, investment decisions, public resources and the livelihoods of many people,” he said.

That reach, he said, was why they had to remain steadfast in upholding professional ethics, exercising independent judgement and making the public interest the core of their work. The values attached to the title would be measured by conduct, not by certificates.

“The CA Zambia designation represents competence, integrity, accountability and public trust. These are not merely values to be stated in professional documents; they must be reflected in the decisions you make, the advice you provide and the manner in which you conduct yourselves,” the ZICA president said.

He then drew a clear line between what the qualification could do for its holders and what only they could do for themselves.

“Your qualification will open doors, but your integrity, competence and commitment to excellence will determine the lasting contribution you make,” Mr Matimba said.

He urged the new professionals to carry the designation with pride while exercising their responsibilities with humility.

Turning to the institute’s own role, Mr Matimba reminded the gathering that ZICA is the statutory body established under the Accountants Act No. 13 of 2008 to regulate and develop the profession. That mandate, he said, went beyond qualifying accountants to maintaining standards, promoting ethical conduct and supporting continuing professional development.

The CA Zambia qualification, introduced in 2017, sits at the core of that mandate. Its purpose, he said, was to produce competent, ethical and adaptable professionals whose capabilities matched international standards and the needs of the economy.

He was clear that the institute was not chasing numbers for their own sake.

“Our ambition is not simply to increase the number of Chartered Accountants in Zambia. It is to develop professionals whose competence, integrity and leadership inspire confidence and create lasting value wherever they serve,” he said.

The ZICA president acknowledged that technology was reshaping the profession and pledged that the institute would keep strengthening professional education to keep pace. Emerging risks and increasingly complex decision-making, he said, now required accountants to pair technical foundations with analytical thinking, digital competence and leadership.

Some things, however, would not change with the tools.

“Technology may change how accounting work is performed, but integrity, professional judgement and accountability will remain indispensable,” Mr Matimba said.

He linked the profession directly to the country’s economic goals. Higher productivity, investment, job creation and sustainable growth, he said, depended on strong institutions, responsible stewardship of resources and confidence in financial information.

The Grow Zambia Agenda, he added, underlined the need for national resources and opportunities to translate into tangible benefits for citizens. ZICA stood ready to work with the Government, the private sector, professional bodies and academic institutions on initiatives that strengthened accountability and improved governance.

The guest of honour, Technology and Science Minister Felix Mutati, is himself a fellow of both ZICA and the Association of Chartered Certified Accountants (ACCA). Mr Matimba congratulated him on his appointment and cited his experience in the profession and in leadership across the public and private sectors.

Mr Mutati gave the new accountants an economic assignment of his own. He said the profession should take a leading role in the national quest to more than double gross domestic product by 2030, moving beyond traditional financial reporting to become a strategic partner in economic transformation.

“You must use your professional expertise, technical knowledge and ethical judgement to support the implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda,” the minister said.

Before closing, Mr Matimba thanked the ZICA Council, the Education and Training Committee, management, employers, mentors, training partners and sponsors for supporting the qualification. The ceremony followed the institute’s inaugural convocation last year.

His final words were addressed directly to the designates.

“Let your qualification be recognised not only by the letters you place after your names, but by the quality of your work, the integrity of your conduct and the positive difference you make in society,” he said.

The newly designated chartered accountants now take the title into public institutions and private firms. Their regulator has given them one measure to work by: the true value of a chartered accountant lies in the trust earned and the contribution made.

World.title: Mwiimbu Won’t Say If Hichilema Would Back End to Term Limit
World.content:
Mwiimbu Declines to Say Where Hichilema Stands as Rival Petition Quotes President’s Own “Third Term” Words

Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu declined to say whether President Hakainde Hichilema would support scrapping the presidential term limit if Parliament approved it. Rival petitions on Article 106(3) of the Constitution are now before the National Assembly, and one of them uses the President’s own words against a third term.

Asked at a media briefing in Lusaka whether the Head of State would back such an amendment, Mr Mwiimbu said he could not speak on the President’s behalf and described the question as speculative. Only moments earlier, he had insisted that neither the President, the United Party for National Development (UPND) nor the Government was behind the three petitions seeking to remove the clause.

The minister was emphatic that the push came from citizens rather than from the Executive.

“I want to repeat, President Hakainde Hichilema has not and does not intend to influence anyone to amend Article 106. It is the people of Zambia who are making those submissions,” Mr Mwiimbu said.

His answers settled one question, who is behind the petitions, and left the other open: what the President would do with the result.

The campaign to remove the limit began with the Zambia Youth Organisations Consortium (ZYOC). The group handed its petition to nominated Member of Parliament Mr Francis Kope, seeking an end to the term limit and the removal of the Grade 12 certificate requirement for parliamentary and council candidates. Mr Kope pledged to personally initiate the process of taking it before the House.

ZYOC chairperson Mr Jacob Longwe said the organisations believed term limits restricted citizens’ freedom to keep voting for leaders of their choice.

A counter-petition dated November 12 now sits beside that submission. Its authors, Mr Xhuzwayo Phiri, Mr Chabota Mweetwa, Mr Danson Lungu, Mr Joseph Kambele and Mr Changala Siame, addressed it to Speaker of the National Assembly Nelly Mutti through Feira MP Emmanuel Tembo.

The five asked the House to reject the ZYOC initiative and to decline any motion aimed at weakening the two-term limit. They also asked the Clerk of the National Assembly to formally acknowledge their submission and bring it before the Speaker and Members.

Their strongest exhibit was the President’s own record. The petitioners recalled what Mr Hichilema said on August 17, 2021, shortly after taking office.

“Third term is not part of our language. It should not be anyone’s language and Zambians have spoken about it,” the President said at the time.

They also cited his September 2021 address at the United States Institute of Peace in Washington, where he cautioned against special favours that allowed office-holders to stay in power longer.

The petitioners went on to invoke the 2025 Electoral Reform Technical Committee, which they said recommended keeping the two five-year limit after finding that most submitters wanted it upheld. They traced the same position through the Mvunga, Mwanakatwe and Mung’omba constitutional review commissions.

History formed the final plank of their case. They pointed to the 2001 third-term bid by supporters of former President Frederick Chiluba, which collapsed under pressure from civil society, churches, lawyers and members of the then ruling party.

The five closed with a direct appeal to the House.

“The Constitution must remain supreme. No individual is indispensable, no political party is bigger than the Republic, and no political ambition should take precedence over the democratic aspirations of the Zambian people,” they wrote.

Mr Mwiimbu said both camps were entitled to a hearing. Article 88(1) of the Constitution, he said, gave citizens the right to petition the National Assembly to initiate, amend or repeal legislation. Those opposed to removing the limit enjoyed the same right, provided they acted within the law.

The Executive, he added, would stay out of a process that fell within the jurisdiction of the legislature. Any attempt to influence the House’s procedures would be unconstitutional.

He reserved his firmest message for politicians whom he accused of fuelling speculation about the petitions.

“We will not be diverted by political speculation. We call upon all politicians to exercise responsible leadership and avoid misleading the nation and respect the democratic rights of the Zambian people,” the minister said.

Outside Parliament, opposition to the proposal is already organised. A coalition of Chapter One Foundation, Transparency International Zambia, Caritas Zambia, the Council of Churches in Zambia, the LCK Foundation and the NGO Coordinating Council has notified the Zambia Police Service of a peaceful procession and public assembly on November 25 in defence of the limit.

Information and Media Minister Elvis Nkandu said earlier that neither President Hichilema nor members of the UPND supreme organ had expressed any intention to extend presidential term limits.

Both petitions now rest with the National Assembly, and the procession is set for November 25. The President has yet to state his own position on the outcome.

World.title: TECH Global University, leader in employability, sets the standard for professional insertion
World.content:
TECH Global University, leader in employability, sets the standard for professional insertion

With a 99% employability rate, the institution ensures the professional growth of its graduates

Amid the growing demand for highly educated professionals in the labor market, TECH Global University has responded by launching an extensive catalog of degrees designed to boost the employability of its students. Thanks to the skills and competencies developed through these programs, 99% of its graduates secure a position matching their level of qualification within less than a year.

The university has found that specialists with superior capabilities and competencies have more opportunities to access high-level jobs, offering better economic returns and professional prestige. To foster this, its programs focus on practical application, ensuring that the most refined theory is paired with simulated cases and real examples, helping professionals contextualize and apply all acquired knowledge.

These degrees are created by the best experts in each field, carefully selected by the university for both their professional and academic merits. As a result, thousands of students complete their academic experiences each year with increased opportunities for professional growth, backed by innovative knowledge in their field.

This also presents an opportunity for professionals in fields such as Medicine, Nursing, Physiotherapy, or Business, who need to stay updated to maintain professional relevance.

This continuous pursuit of academic excellence has propelled TECH Global University to achieve a 4.9 out of 5 rating on opinion platforms such as Trustpilot and Google Maps, making it the highest-rated university in the world by its students.

TECH Global University, the largest digital university in the world

TECH Global University offers a wide range of professional development and training programs. Its degrees include Doctorates, Bachelor’s degrees, Master’s degrees, Diplomas, University Experts, and Language Courses in fields such as Sports Science, Health Sciences, Business, Computer Science, and Engineering, among others.

Given that pedagogical innovation is essential in the ever-evolving educational landscape, the university has refined and perfected the Relearning methodology for its degrees. This allows students to avoid investing extensive hours acquiring all the knowledge offered; instead, key concepts are naturally reinforced throughout the academic process. Furthermore, it eliminates the need for in-person classes and fixed schedules, adapting the coursework to individual responsibilities.

TECH Global University, “the best online university in the world” according to Forbes

TECH is the world’s largest online university. With an impressive catalog of more than 14,000 educational programs available in 11 languages, it is positioned as a leader in employability, with a 99% job placement rate.

It is officially recognized in America, such as TECH Universidad (Mexico). It also has a strong presence in Africa, with TECH RUCU University (Tanzania) and TECH Euromed University (Morocco), and in Europe through TECH Global University (Andorra) and TECH Universidad (Spain).

Thanks to its international scope, TECH has a presence in more than 150 countries and has twice been recognized by the Financial Times as one of the 250 fastest-growing companies in Europe in recent years.

Furthermore, the prestigious Forbes magazine has distinguished it as the “world’s best online university,” highlighting its innovative learning methodology, Relearning, as well as the implementation of the Harvard Case Method.

In addition, it boasts an Ivy League faculty, at the level of Harvard or Stanford. Its more than 6,000 professors work in the best companies, organizations and institutions in the world. The largest multinationals (Amazon, Apple, Google, Nike…), the best hospitals (Mayo Clinic, MD Anderson Cancer Center…) and the best sports institutions (Boston Celtics, Dallas Cowboys…) collaborate with their best professionals to lead TECH’s academic programs.

The quality of its digital infrastructure and its high educational standards have been recognized by Google with Google Premier Partner status, a distinction reserved only for the top 3% of online institutions.

TECH is also considered the top-rated university by its students, with an average rating of 4.9 out of 5 in more than 25,000 public ratings on leading international portals.

World.title: PRESIDENT HICHILEMA ENGAGES SOUTHERN PROVINCE TRADITIONAL LEADERS ON DEVELOPMENT
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has called on traditional leaders in Southern Province to encourage their subjects to reserve adequate maize stocks ahead of the 2026/2027 farming season, which is projected to be affected by El Niño weather conditions.

‎And the Head of State has reaffirmed the government’s commitment to sustaining development gains achieved during his first term, including investments in free education.

‎Mr Hichilema was speaking in Choma today when he addressed traditional leaders during a celebratory community engagement following his re- election in the August 13 general elections.

‎ President Hichilema assured traditional leaders that the government will work closely with them to ensure the successful implementation of various development programmes.

” We are grateful that the public trusted us by ensuring UPND emerged victorious. They elected us into office to serve the Zambian people therefore we pledge to ensure that we deliver on our developmental promises,” He explained.

President Hichilema also called on traditional leaders to help fight early marriages and keep young girls in school so they can benefit from the Free Education Policy.

He implored traditional leaders to engage headmen and other community leaders to heighten public awareness against the vice.

“As a government we have invested in the free education policy that ensures all children have an opportunity to go to school. I implore you all to sensitize your subjects about the need to ensure all children go to school. Education is one-way girls can be safeguard from early marriages” He added.

Meanwhile, Southern Province Council of Chiefs Chairperson, Chief Nalubamba, has pledged the traditional leadership’s continued support for Government programmes aimed at advancing national development.

World.title: MINISTRY OF INFORMATION AND MEDIA PS ANNOUNCES LAUNCH OF THE 2027 SADC MEDIA AWARDS COMPETITION
World.content:
Ministry of Information and Media Permanent Secretary Thabo Kawana has announced the launch of the 2027 Southern African Development Community (SADC) Media Awards competition.

The competition is open to journalists in four categories: Photojournalism, Print Journalism, Television Journalism and Radio Journalism.

To be eligible for the competition, entries must comprise journalistic works that were published or broadcast between 1st January and 31st December 2026 and only works published or broadcast within this eligibility period will be considered for the 2027 Awards.

Mr Kawana said the competition underscores the important role of the media in informing citizens about SADC’s activities and achievements, while providing a platform for journalists to bring regional issues closer to communities across the region.

The Permanent Secretary noted that through quality, accurate and impactful journalism, media practitioners play a critical role in strengthening public awareness, enhancing the visibility of SADC and promoting greater citizen participation in the regional integration process.

“Under the 2027 competition, the first-prize winner in each of the four categories will receive US$2,500, while the runner-up in each category will receive US$1,000. The winners will be announced during the Opening Ceremony of the 47th SADC Summit of Heads of State and Government, scheduled to be held in Zambia,” Mr Kawana revealed.

He has since encouraged journalists across the country to participate in the competition and take advantage of the opportunity to showcase their journalistic talent, creativity and professionalism while contributing to greater public awareness and understanding of SADC’s regional integration agenda.

Established in 1996, the SADC Media Awards recognise outstanding journalistic work that contributes to the dissemination of information about SADC and promotes greater public understanding of the regional integration agenda.

The Awards seek to recognise journalists who demonstrate excellence, originality, accuracy, depth of research and impact in reporting on SADC programmes, policies, initiatives and matters relating to regional cooperation and integration.

Interested journalists can obtain further information and entry forms from the SADC National Media Coordinator at the Ministry of Information and Media or through the Ministry’s website: www.mim.gov.zm.

Completed entry forms, with all required information duly typed, must be submitted to the SADC National Media Coordinator at the Ministry of Information and Media no later than 28th February 2027.

World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) has continued to gain popularity across the country, with its growing support reflected in the over three million votes he secured in the August 13 general elections and the party’s performance in the recently held 14 by-elections.

Speaking during a UPND thanksgiving community engagement at Choma Sports Club in Southern Province, President Hichilema called on party members to remain united, protect the party and continue expanding its support base to make it the party of choice across all ten provinces.

He challenged councillors and party officials to intensify mobilisation, urging them to reach out to communities and strengthen party structures down to polling station level.

“Councillors, let us go out there and mobilise our people. Let us start from our constituencies, our wards and right down to every polling station. We must make sure that our people are mobilised,” Mr Hichilema said.

The President said party mobilisation was important in sustaining the development programmes being implemented by his administration.

“If we want to continue enjoying the different developments we are enjoying, let us mobilise for the party because it is the party that delivers,” he said.

Mr Hichilema thanked the people of Southern Province for giving him a second mandate, assuring them that his administration remained committed to delivering development and improving the lives of citizens.

He reaffirmed his government’s commitment to free education, saying the policy remained central to expanding access to education for children across the country.

The President also directed teachers who had deserted their rural stations to immediately return to their original places of deployment or risk being replaced.

Meanwhile, UPND alliance partner Highvie Hamududu and former Minister of Transport and Logistics Frank Tayali called on the people of Southern Province to continue supporting President Hichilema and his development agenda.

The thanksgiving community engagement attracted thousands of people from across Southern Province, including party supporters, alliance partners, local leaders and residents who gathered at Choma Sports Club to interact with the Head of State.

World.title: Harare lawyer takes Zifa, PSL matter to parliament
World.content:
Press Release

Donald Nyandoro · November 13, 2026

A Harare lawyer, Lonias Rozvi Majoni, has petitioned Parliament over reported integrity concerns in Zimbabwean football after the Zimbabwe Football Association (ZIFA) and Premier Soccer League (PSL) allegedly failed to acknowledge his formal complaints within the stipulated seven-day period.

Majoni, who lodged reports with ZIFA and the PSL on November 2, 2026, said the two football governing bodies had not formally acknowledged receipt of his petition, despite the expiry of the seven-day response window on November 9.

He has since approached Parliament, seeking legislative and oversight intervention on matters he argues fall within the State’s jurisdiction, while maintaining that football’s internal disciplinary and governance processes must remain independent.

“Although the 30-day action window has not yet closed, the seven-day period for ZIFA and PSL to acknowledge and respond to our petition has lapsed without reply,” Majoni said.

“Consequently, we have engaged Parliament on the aspects of this matter within its jurisdiction, without interfering in ZIFA’s internal processes or breaching FIFA statutes.

“In a petition submitted to the Clerk of Parliament on November 12, Majoni is seeking the involvement of the Portfolio Committee on Youth, Sport, Arts and Recreation, with relevant legal affairs committees also expected to consider aspects within their mandate.

The petition follows a series of reported controversies in domestic football, including an alleged approach to CAPS United goalkeeper Washington Arubi to influence teammates, disputes surrounding player registrations and questions over the ownership and control of football clubs.

The lawyer, however, emphasised that the allegations remain unverified and that no individual or club should be presumed guilty.Among other issues, he wants Parliament to examine possible gaps in Zimbabwe’s laws relating to sports manipulation, corruption, beneficial ownership transparency and protection of individuals who report suspected wrongdoing.

He also called for greater accountability from State institutions, including the Sports and Recreation Commission, the Zimbabwe Anti-Corruption Commission and the police.

Majoni stressed that his approach was not intended to trigger FIFA intervention or undermine football’s autonomy.

“We have taken these steps in good faith and in the public interest to exhaust all local remedies before escalating the matter internationally, which could carry adverse consequences,” he said.

The 30-day response period granted to ZIFA and the PSL expires on December 2, 2026. Majoni indicated that he would consider approaching FIFA and the Confederation of African Football (CAF) through their established channels if the internal remedies fail.

He said he would not support any suspension of ZIFA or freezing of football development funds, arguing that such measures would ultimately hurt players and clubs.

The petition calls for constructive engagement and legislative reforms to strengthen accountability and restore public confidence in Zimbabwean football without compromising the autonomy of its governing institutions.

World.title: Minister orders ZIMDEF to deliver results, not just collect money
World.content:
Local News

Valentine Maya · November 12, 2026

HIGHER and Tertiary Education minister Frederick Shava has reminded the Zimbabwe Manpower Development Fund (ZIMDEF) that its success will be measured by the skills it imparts on students and the jobs it supports, not by the money it collects or disburses.

Officially opening the 2026 ZIMDEF strategic planning workshop in Mutare this Thursday, Shava said, “ZIMDEF must remain focused on interventions that deliver tangible value to the economy, within its statutory mandate and the Ministry’s policy priorities.”

Shava said the retreat must produce a comprehensive assessment of 2026 performance against the strategic plan; clearly defined corrective measures for outstanding commitments and implementation challenges; and a realistic, costed and prioritised 2027 annual work programme and budget aligned with the government’s long-term plans.

He also said the workshop’s outcomes must be an evidence-based assessment that demonstrates what has been achieved, what remains outstanding and what must be done differently to improve delivery.

“Last year, ZIMDEF developed its 2026–2030 strategic plan, aligned with the Second National Development Strategy (NDS2). Our task today is to take stock of implementation during 2026, identify areas requiring improvement and agree on strategic priorities for 2027,” he said.

He urged delegates to approach the exercise with openness, objectivity and a clear focus on results.

The Minister of Higher and Tertiary Education, Innovation, Science and Technology Development, ambassador Frederick Shava, receives a token of appreciation from ZIMDEF vice chairperson colonel Siwinile Tauya at the ZIMDEF 2026 Strategic Planning Review Workshop in Mutare.

Pictures: MHTEISTD Communications and Advocacy Officer Kudakwashe Hunda

On the 2027 budget, Shava said resource allocation must be guided by strategic priorities, available resources, demonstrated needs and the readiness of proposed projects for implementation.

“Particular attention must be given to completing ongoing projects and ensuring that previous investments generate their intended benefits,” he said.

Shava also called for tighter revenue collection.

“I wish to emphasise the importance of strengthening revenue mobilisation and compliance and ZIMDEF must sustain engagement with contributing employers, improve the efficiency of collections and pursue outstanding obligations consistently and professionally, within the applicable legal framework,” he said.

The minister also tied the fund’s work to the ministry’s heritage-based education 5.0 philosophy.

“Within this framework, ZIMDEF has a critical responsibility to support the development of a skilled, competent and productive workforce that responds to the needs of our economy,” he said.

He acknowledged the ZIMDEF board and management’s continued commitment to strengthening the fund’s contribution to skills development and human capital formation in Zimbabwe.

World.title: Africa: Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games - After The Historic Achievement, The Challenge of a Lasting Legacy for Africa
World.content:
The first Youth Olympic Games held on the African continent, the Dakar 2026 YOG, concluded on November 13th with a record praised by leaders of the Olympic movement. Beyond the organizational success and popular enthusiasm, Senegal and its partners now face a major challenge: transforming this historic first into an engine of sporting, economic, and social development. Youth training, job creation, infrastructure development, and the emergence of new talent are the main priorities for the post-Games period.

Senegal is preparing to close a historic chapter in world sport. For two weeks, from October 31 to November 13, 2026, Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly hosted the first Youth Olympic Games (YOG) organized in Africa, placing the continent at the center of attention of the international Olympic movement.

With approximately 2,700 young athletes representing 204 National Olympic Committees, 25 competitive sports, ten engagement sports and 153 medal-winning events, this fourth edition of the Summer Youth Olympic Games was an exceptional showcase for Senegal and, beyond, for the entire African continent.

But behind the sporting performances, the ceremonies and the popular mobilization, a question now arises: how to make Dakar 2026 more than just a successful event and ensure its lasting impact on the development of Africa?

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

This question was a major theme of the joint press conference of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and the Organising Committee of the Youth Olympic Games (COJOJ), held on November 12 in Diamniadio.

IOC President Kirsty Coventry hailed the event as a "100% organizational success," stating that expectations had been exceeded. She particularly encouraged the continent to build on this experience.

"My wish is that Africa and the continent become fully aware of their potential. It is now up to us to make it a reality," she said.

A message that sums up the challenge of the post-Dakar 2026 era: to transform the international recognition acquired during the Games into concrete prospects for new African generations.

An Olympic first that changes the way we see Africa

By hosting an Olympic event of this magnitude, Senegal has taken a symbolic step in the history of African sport. Long absent from the map of host countries for Olympic competitions, the continent has demonstrated its ability to mobilize infrastructure, skills, and human resources around a major international event.

For the IOC's executive director of the Olympic Games, Christophe Dubi, one of the most striking elements of this edition will remain the welcome given to foreign delegations and the enthusiasm of the Senegalese people.

From Dakar to Saly, via Diamniadio, the mobilization of the public helped to give these Games a popular dimension, beyond just the competition venues.

This success also sends a signal to other African countries that aspire to host major international sporting events.

However, this does not mean that all organizational and financial obstacles have been removed. The Senegalese experience will need to be analyzed to identify financing, governance, and infrastructure management models that could be replicated elsewhere on the continent.

The stakes thus go beyond mere symbolic recognition: it is about making Dakar 2026 a reference for the organization of future sporting events in Africa.

New talents and disciplines to develop

From a sporting perspective, the Youth Olympic Games provided an international platform for a new generation of African athletes, while also allowing the Senegalese public to discover disciplines that are still underdeveloped in the country.

The chairman of the IOC Coordination Commission for Dakar 2026, Humphrey Kayange, particularly emphasized the interest generated by the sporting activities organized on the Corniche of Dakar.

These discovery spaces have allowed many young people to try out different sports and consider new opportunities for involvement.

But this enthusiasm will need to be maintained.

For Humphrey Kayange, national sports federations now have an essential role to play in order to extend this momentum, structure emerging disciplines and facilitate their access for young people.

The issue of talent identification and support is another major challenge. Kirsty Coventry pointed out that approximately 15% of participants in the Youth Olympic Games go on to compete in the Olympic Games.

This proportion highlights the role that the Youth Olympic Games can play in preparing future generations of elite athletes.

For Africa, where many young athletes still face difficulties accessing equipment, qualified coaches and funding, the continuity of training programs will be crucial.

The true sporting success of Dakar 2026 will therefore not be measured solely by the number of medals won, but also by the ability of African countries to support the talents revealed during the Games.

Training and employment: the economic legacy takes shape

Beyond sport, one of the most promising achievements of Dakar 2026 concerns the development of professional skills.

The Dakar 2026 Learning Academy, set up to prepare young professionals for jobs related to the organization of major events, has trained more than 300 participants, from 21 African nationalities, according to information provided by the IOC.

This program is a concrete example of how an international sporting competition can contribute to strengthening human capital.

Event management, operational coordination, communication, logistics and sports organization represent all areas in which the skills acquired could be valued after the Games.

The challenge now is to transform these training programs into sustainable career opportunities.

The president of the COJOJ, Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye, notably mentioned discussions with the World Bank regarding employment prospects and integration of young people.

Presented in Washington before the Games, the Learning Academy reportedly attracted the interest of the international financial institution, particularly for its potential in terms of training and employability.

In this context, closer ties have been envisaged with the World Bank's regional SIRA program, dedicated to skills development and access to employment.

These discussions, however, have yet to be finalized. No definitive funding has been announced at this stage.

For Senegal, the sustainability of this type of program could contribute to developing a pool of African professionals capable of intervening in the organization of sporting, cultural and institutional events on an international scale.

Infrastructure to be valued beyond the Games

Another central question of the Olympic legacy: the future of the sports facilities mobilized or modernized for Dakar 2026.

Organizing the Youth Olympic Games required investments in infrastructure and reception facilities, particularly in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly.

While this equipment has met the requirements of the competition, its future use will represent a real test for public authorities and sports federations.

International experience shows that the legacy of major sporting events largely depends on the ability of host countries to ensure the maintenance, financing and accessibility of facilities after the competitions.

For Senegal, several perspectives could be explored: development of training centers, organization of regional competitions, hosting of international internships and opening of infrastructure to schools and sports associations.

The development of these facilities could also contribute to the development of a local sports economy, by promoting training activities, event services, sports tourism and related jobs.

These potential benefits will, however, need to be accompanied by appropriate management mechanisms and a long-term financing strategy.

Sport as a response to the social challenges facing youth

Beyond infrastructure and performance, Senegalese officials also want to inscribe the legacy of the YOG in a social perspective.

Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye thus mentioned a project to create sports academies in several coastal localities, including Saint-Louis, Kayar and Rufisque.

This initiative aims to offer young people new opportunities for training, guidance and integration through sport.

It takes on a particular dimension in areas facing youth unemployment, economic insecurity and perilous departures by sea.

The ambition would be to make sport a tool for support and opening up towards professional prospects, possibly involving public actors, federations and development partners.

The project remains at a design stage and will need to specify its financing arrangements, its operating model and the target audiences.

Its success will also depend on its ability to combine sports practice with education, vocational training and access to employment.

Because while sport can play an important role in social inclusion, it cannot, on its own, address the structural difficulties faced by African youth.

A legacy to be built on a continental scale

The organization of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games finally raises the question of African sports cooperation.

Close 

By bringing together athletes, coaches, officials and professionals from different countries, the Games have created opportunities for exchange and collaboration that can continue after the competition.

This dynamic could promote the sharing of expertise between federations, the implementation of regional training programs and the development of partnerships around emerging sports disciplines.

The participation of young professionals of several African nationalities in the Learning Academy already illustrates this continental dimension.

But to produce lasting effects, these initiatives will need to be part of coordinated sports policies, supported by long-term institutional funding and commitments.

Africa has significant demographic and sporting potential. However, its development requires regular investments in local infrastructure, coach training, athlete support, and the professionalization of sports-related jobs.

Dakar 2026 could thus serve as a starting point for a broader reflection on the place of sport in African development strategies.

After the celebration, the test of the results

As the first Youth Olympic Games held in Africa come to a close, Senegal can boast of international recognition and popular mobilization that have marked this edition.

But the Olympic legacy is not decreed at the end of a closing ceremony. It is built over time, through public policies, sustained investments and programs capable of producing measurable results.

How many young people trained by the Learning Academy will find employment? How will the sports facilities be used? Will the disciplines discovered during the Games find a place in national federations? Will the sports academy projects actually come to fruition?

These are all questions that the coming years will need to answer.

Dakar 2026 will have demonstrated that Africa can host a major international Olympic event. The next challenge will be to prove that such an event can also contribute sustainably to the economic, social, and sporting transformation of the continent.

Only under this condition will the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games be able to transcend its status as a historic first and become a true legacy for future generations.

This article was originally published in French
