World.title: South Africa: Africa's Waste Pickers Demand Recognition in Climate Action
World.content:
As COP31 puts zero waste on the climate agenda, waste pickers across Africa say the continent's circular-economy transition cannot succeed without the people who already recover and recycle much of what it throws away.

Waste is the third-largest source of human-caused methane emissions, accounting for nearly 20% of the global total, yet the sector remains underfunded and inadequately monitored.

The UN Environment Programme estimated that municipal solid waste reached 2.1 billion tonnes in 2023 and will be at 3.8 billion tonnes by 2050. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), improved waste management, through a circular economy and better treatment technologies, has the potential to make a substantial contribution to reductions in national GHG emissions.



Under its Global Climate Action Agenda, COP31 is championing the Zero Waste initiative, which seeks to unlock the climate potential of waste management through scalable circular economy solutions. The initiative is focused on preventing food waste, moving towards circular economy solutions that turn waste into resources, and encouraging countries to include waste-related methane reductions in their updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). The aim is to prevent emissions at source and make waste management an integral part of national climate strategies.

The need is greatest in low-income countries, where 97% of waste is openly dumped or burned. Uncontrolled dumpsites and open burning threaten communities, contaminate water and release climate pollutants, and without knowing where these sites are, how much waste they receive and what they emit, effective intervention is extremely difficult. As COP31 pushes countries to include waste methane in their climate plans, some African investors say the continent has a chance to turn waste into an economic resource.

Waste pickers say they must be part of that shift.

Across Africa, waste pickers and reclaimers collect, sort and recover recyclable materials that would otherwise end up in landfills, rivers or the environment. Many still work with limited formal recognition, social protection, and decent working conditions. Their inclusion is therefore emerging as a key question in discussions about Africa's zero-waste future. A transition to more sustainable waste management systems, advocates argue, must build on the knowledge and contribution of existing waste workers rather than exclude them.

For the International Alliance of Waste Pickers (IAWP), the success of such initiatives will depend in part on whether the people already driving recycling and resource recovery are recognised as essential partners in their implementation.

In an interview, Eva Mokoena of South Africa's African Reclaimers Organisation (ARO) discusses the role of waste pickers in climate action, the opportunities presented by the Zero Waste Districts initiative, and the changes needed to secure their place in Africa's transition to a circular economy.

Waste is often seen as an environmental and sanitation problem, but it is increasingly recognised as a major climate challenge. Why does tackling waste matter for the fight against climate change, and what role can zero waste play in reducing emissions?

Waste is a climate issue because what we throw away does not disappear. Organic waste buried in landfills and dumpsites rots without oxygen and releases methane, a gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide in the short term. Open burning of waste adds black carbon and toxic smoke to the air our communities breathe. Every item that is landfilled or burnt also means new materials must be extracted, manufactured, and transported to replace it.

Zero waste addresses all of these at once. When materials are separated at source, recovered, reused and recycled, and when organic waste is composted or turned into biogas, methane from landfills falls and the demand for virgin materials drops. This is one of the fastest and most affordable ways to reduce emissions.

The key to making it work is already on the ground. Waste pickers and reclaimers are the people removing waste from landfills, rivers, and streams every day. With proper recognition, equipment, and collaboration from governments, municipalities, and residents, they can multiply the climate impact they already deliver.

Waste is often overlooked in climate talks, yet food waste and landfills are major sources of greenhouse-gas emissions, especially methane. What practical policies and local actions would most effectively reduce food waste and keep organic waste out of landfills?

The most effective policies are the ones that recognise and include waste pickers and reclaimers. They are the frontline educators of their communities: they already teach residents to separate and recycle what they buy and eat. Governments and policymakers should write waste pickers into waste and climate legislation, so that this work is formally recognised, supported and paid for.

In practice, this means separation at source, in households, markets and businesses before it reaches the landfill, with waste pickers leading door-to-door awareness and collection.

In logistics, waste picker organisations need access to land, storage facilities and transport, so that organic material can be collected, stored and processed close to where it is generated. Local processing of food waste should be turned into compost, manure and biogas through community-run facilities, creating useful products and income instead of methane.

Investment in people is also important. Incubating reclaimer cooperatives, with full access to logistics and infrastructure, is what turns good policy into results.

If we continue to ignore the people on the ground, we will keep struggling. If we invest in them, organic waste can become a resource for our communities.

How can African governments make waste reduction and the circular economy a more central part of their national climate policies?

Governments can start by recognising who already runs Africa's circular economy. Waste pickers and reclaimers are unrecognised heroes: many spend their own time and resources recovering materials and cleaning public spaces without pay or protection. Bringing them into national climate policy means three things.

First, recognition in law. National climate plans, including Nationally Determined Contributions, and waste management legislation should name waste pickers as essential service providers and set out their rights, their role and how they will be paid.

Second, a seat at the table. Waste picker organisations should take part in designing, implementing and monitoring these policies. When waste pickers help shape the rules, the rules work on the ground, and waste pickers gain the recognition and confidence to expand their work.

Third, real support. Recognition has to come with resources: equipment, infrastructure, social protection and fair payment for the services waste pickers provide to cities and to the climate.

Looking at initiatives such as Zero Waste Districts and the 1x100 campaign, how can these programmes translate into tangible benefits for African communities, from cleaner cities and reduced landfill waste to decent jobs and better livelihoods for waste pickers?

These programmes deliver real benefits when everybody works together: governments, municipalities, residents, the private sector and waste picker organisations. Waste pickers are already on the ground, in every neighbourhood and in every landfill. What makes the difference is giving them space, resources and a central role.

Education is the most important key. With educational tools, training and empowerment, waste pickers can lead awareness campaigns, help households separate their waste, and recover a much wider range of materials at once. The result is cleaner streets, less waste reaching landfills and rivers, and recycling that actually works.

For waste pickers, the benefit must be decent work: formal contracts, fair payment for collection and recovery services, safe working conditions and social protection. When district programmes are built around existing waste picker cooperatives, the jobs and income they create stay in the community.

Two African nations that have joined the Zero Waste Districts programme are Ghana and Kenya. What are the biggest waste management challenges these countries are hoping to address, and what makes the district-level approach different from previous efforts?

What makes the district-level approach different is that it starts from the community and from the organisations that already exist, rather than from large, centralised projects designed far away from the people who manage waste every day. Our affiliates in both countries describe it in these terms.

In Ghana, the Green Waste Pickers Cooperative Society Limited and the Kpone Landfill Waste Pickers Association are supporting community-led circular initiatives that build on existing cooperatives. These cooperatives drive the process of diverting waste at source, adopt measures to pre-process materials, and lead environmental campaigns in their communities.

In Kenya, the Nakuru County Waste Pickers Association is advancing zero waste through waste reduction, reuse, recycling and waste picking, alongside community-led initiatives, progressive policies and the promotion of a circular economy.

In both cases, the district becomes the unit where waste pickers, residents and local authorities can work side by side, and where results can be seen and measured.

Many African cities are still grappling with poor waste collection, overflowing landfills, and very limited recycling. What kind of investment and what kind of partnerships are required to build effective waste management and recycling systems across the continent?

Close 

The investment that works is investment in the people already doing the job. Instead of expensive systems that bypass or displace waste pickers, African cities should incubate reclaimer and waste picker cooperatives and give them full access to what they need.

In infrastructure, sorting centres, storage space and land can help make the work safer. In logistics, vehicles and equipment to collect and move materials efficiently are needed. Processing capacity with facilities to recycle materials and to turn food waste into compost, manure and biogas is necessary. Fair contracts are also a key issue to provide payments from municipalities for the collection and recovery services waste pickers provide.

The partnerships that work are inclusive ones. Municipalities, national governments, producers, funders and residents should partner directly with waste picker organisations, as equals and from the design stage. If we keep ignoring the people on the ground, cities will keep struggling with the same problems. If we invest in them, Africa can build recycling systems that are effective, fair and locally owned.

Given that COP31 is placing such a strong emphasis on zero waste, what specific commitments should African countries be demanding in order to ensure that waste reduction actually becomes a measurable element of climate action rather than just another one of the international promises?

African countries should demand commitments that reach the ground, not only the negotiating rooms. In particular, direct funding for equipment and machinery that allows waste pickers and reclaimers to recover and recycle more materials, including food waste.

Educational tools must also be designed with waste pickers and be easy to use for both reclaimers and residents, so that separation at source becomes everyday practice in every household.

Formal recognition of waste pickers in national climate plans and waste policies, with a guaranteed role in their implementation and measurable targets for diverting organic and recyclable waste from landfills, monitored with the participation of waste picker organisations, are commitments that promote long-term climate solutions.

Waste pickers are good at what we do, and we make sure that everyone we work with understands our livelihoods on the streets and in the landfills, and the important role we play. Climate commitments on waste will only become real when they are built with us.

World.title: Nigeria: Index Ebola Case - Swiss Diplomat's Wife Recovers, Discharged From Hospital
World.content:
Nigeriaâs Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) issued a public health advisory following the countryâs confirmed Ebola case.

Abuja — Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has said that the Nigeria's Ebola index case- Swiss diplomat's wife has recovered and discharged from hospital in Switzerland.

The disease intervention centre had confirmed the infection on October 20, 2026 after the patient's blood samples tested positive at the Abuja Reference Laboratory.

After receiving preliminary treatment at an undisclosed private hospital in Abuja, she and her husband were subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland with an air ambulance on October 26, 2026.

Addressing journalists in his office in Abuja on Friday, NCDC Director General, Dr. Jide Idris, said the Swiss authorities had announced the recovery and discharge of the woman after testing negative.

He said index case tested negative after receiving treatment in an isolation facility in Switzerland.

More details later...

World.title: South Africa: Joburg Turns Up the Heat As Residents Wait for Relief
World.content:
Outdoor workers should take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

Cooler weather and thunderstorms are expected over the weekend, offering some relief from the heat.

Johannesburg residents face another scorching day on Friday, with emergency services urging people to drink water, take breaks and stay out of the midday sun.

The City of Johannesburg's Emergency Management Services says extremely hot conditions are expected to continue across much of the city. Outdoor workers have been urged to take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

The South African Weather Service's heatwave advisory issued earlier this week included southern Gauteng, with persistently high temperatures expected until Friday, 13 November.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

But some relief could arrive over the weekend.

Weather service senior forecaster Tokelo Chiloane said cooler conditions, accompanied by thunderstorms and thundershowers, are expected over the weekend.

Until then, residents have been urged to protect themselves from the heat.

"Residents are urged to stay hydrated, drink lots of water, avoid direct sunlight especially between 11h00 and 15h00 in the afternoon," Johannesburg emergency services spokesperson Robert Mulaudzi said earlier this week.

For street traders, gardeners, construction workers and others spending hours outside, regular breaks in a cool or shaded place are especially important.

The World Health Organization says older people, babies, outdoor workers and people with existing medical conditions face greater risks during hot weather. Residents should also check on relatives and neighbours who live alone.

Keeping cool does not have to mean switching on an air conditioner. The organisation recommends loose, light clothing, cool showers and wetting the skin with a damp cloth. Drink water regularly and avoid alcohol.

Never leave children, dependent adults or pets alone in a parked vehicle, even while running a quick errand.

Parents have also been warned to watch children seeking somewhere to cool off.

Mulaudzi urged families to keep young children away from dams and river streams to prevent drownings.

Heat illness needs prompt attention. Dizziness, weakness, intense thirst and headaches are signs to move into a cool place and drink water.

Confusion, seizures or a loss of consciousness require urgent medical help. Move the person into shade or a cool room and use cold, wet cloths to help cool them while waiting for assistance.

Close 

For life-threatening emergencies in Johannesburg, call 011 375 5911. The city says this number connects residents to emergency assistance, including ambulance and fire services.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: DR Congo Ebola Outbreak - Armed Groups Unrest Hold Back Response
World.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to spread amid repeated and ongoing deadly attacks on civilians and frontline health workers by armed groups that are obstructing efforts to stop transmission, UN responders said on Friday.

In an update, the UN Senior Ebola Response Coordinator, Julien Harneis, stressed that more people are being killed by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters than by Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in recent days.

And yet the attacks on "tens of villages all across the south of Ituri and North Kivu (provinces) goes unnoticed", Mr. Harneis maintained. "People are scared, people are furious at the lack of action on this."

Up to 500 infections per week

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Echoing that message, the UN World Health Organization (WHO)'s Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu, Executive Director of WHO's Health Emergencies Programme, said that despite much progress in containing transmission within eastern DRC, about 400 to 500 cases of infection are still being identified every week.

This trend is linked to the emergence of cases in rural and hard-to-reach areas.

In more positive developments, the WHO official noted that prevention efforts have led to "a significant reduction" in transmission in previous hotspots, in particular Bunia, Mongbwalu, Rampara and Nizi, all in Ituri province in eastern DRC.

Nonetheless, the violent unrest across the vast area impacted by Ebola creates huge challenges for responders.

"We've seen so many attacks on healthcare, attacks on communities as well, attacks on people providing care, and people losing their lives, nurses in burials," Dr Ihekweazu explained. "So, we need to keep working with the community, and this is very important. And working with the specific groups instigating these attacks."

Disease threats in addition to attacks

Communities are already facing outbreaks of diseases, malnutrition and displacement driven by decades of violent unrest fuelled by dozens of armed

groups that remain active in the resource-rich region.

Earlier this week, WHO condemned attacks against frontline healthcare workers and community awareness officers, including in Cantine-Aloya in North Kivu that killed 66 civilians including three health workers. Three health facilities were also looted.

Two weeks ago, a nurse was also killed and another health worker badly injured when they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in Tshopo province.

Tedros appeal

Other attacks have included an arson attempt on a treatment centre and stones thrown at a vehicle used for conducting safe and dignified burials, an indication of the need to continue to build trust with extremely vulnerable communities.

"We cannot focus only on Ebola. Some people in the affected communities have said told me personally that Ebola is a lesser evil compared to some of the other threats they face," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus stressed earlier this week.

A massive humanitarian emergency

The DRC Ebola outbreak was declared in May and has since become the largest yet as it continues to spread faster than any previous outbreak in the vast country's east and northeast provinces.

To date, more than 11,000 cases have been confirmed and more than 5,000 people have died.

In a related development, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned that nearly 29 million people in the DRC face acute food insecurity, with most in the conflict and Ebola-affected eastern and northeastern provinces. That number is likely to continue to increase, said Jean-Martin Bauer, WFP Director of Food Security and Nutrition Analysis.

Briefing journalists via video in Geneva, Mr. Bauer stressed that conflict is driving the hunger crisis, in addition to the Ebola outbreak.

Close 

"What we need right now is access, and we need resources to avoid the situation becoming more difficult in the DRC," he said.

Hunger emergency

Latest UN-backed food insecurity expert assessments indicate that between January and June 2027, 30.3 million people will be in crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse, with 4.2 million of this number experiencing "emergency levels" of hunger and the most acute needs in North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri provinces "driven by persistent conflict and large-scale displacement".

Mr. Bauer noted that Ebola is just one of many disease outbreaks in DRC, but that it is compounding the hunger crisis for communities already struggling to eat.

"Families are being displaced, they're being cut off from their farms, from their livelihoods," he explained. "Food prices are rising, making affording a meal quite complicated for too many households."

World.title: Ethiopia: Mekelle Residents Call for Sustained Federal Govt Efforts to Advance Reforms in Tigray
World.content:
Addis Ababa — Residents of Mekelle have urged the Federal Government to sustain and accelerate reform, reconstruction and development efforts in Tigray region.

The inhabitants further emphasized the need for consolidating progress toward lasting peace, stability and prosperity in the region.

The call was made during a consultative forum of Mekelle residents, presided over by Chief of Staff of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), Field Marshal Birhanu Jula.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Speaking at the gathering, Field Marshal Birhanu said the defunct TPLF faction had aligned itself with the so-called "Tsimdo" group, an alliance orchestrated by Ethiopia's historical adversaries to wage war against the country.

He said his engagement with residents was aimed at fostering dialogue, strengthening cooperation and encouraging collective efforts to ensure lasting peace and stability in Tigray region.

During the discussions, residents underscored their strong desire to see an end to conflict, identifying peace, security and sustainable development as their foremost priorities.

They called for the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure, expanded employment opportunities for young people and the restoration of security to enable communities to resume normal life without fear.

"Our foremost priorities are the reconstruction of critical infrastructure, the creation of meaningful employment opportunities for our youth, and the restoration of security so that citizens can go about their daily lives in peace," participants said.

Residents also welcomed the resumption of salary payments for civil servants and ongoing infrastructure rehabilitation efforts, describing them as important steps toward restoring normalcy and accelerating the region's recovery.

Concluding the forum, participants called on the Federal Government to maintain its commitment to Tigray, sustain ongoing interventions and accelerate reform, reconstruction and development initiatives to secure lasting peace and improve the livelihoods of communities across the region.

World.title: Africa: How African Women's Rugby Teams Broke The Glass Ceiling At Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics
World.content:
An emotional moment for Team Kenya as they received their gold medals at Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics.

Kenya's all-women coaching staff turned a squad full of wingers into a team that could come from behind to win Olympic gold. As Madagascar's players balanced school and training to earn a historic bronze, both teams showed what it took to reach the rugby sevens podium.

Before heading to the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, every player on Kenya's girls' rugby sevens team wrote down what she wanted to achieve. They all had the same goal.

"Before heading to Dakar, every player had written down their goal and it was to win gold," Kenya coach Knight Otuoma said in Dakar.

"In our first game, despite being a former player, I tensed, but they were so relaxed and this made everything easy."



The Rising Lionesses delivered on that ambition with a 17–12 extra-time win over Australia, one of the tournament favourites. They became the first African team to win rugby sevens gold at either the Olympic Games or the Youth Olympic Games. It was Kenya's first medal in Dakar, the country's first Olympic gold in a team sport and the first time a Kenyan rugby team had won gold at a major global championship.

The final was a nerve-wracking affair for Otuoma and her players. Darci Mackay opened the scoring for Australia before Kenya captain Zain Hido crossed the line to make it 5–5 at half-time. Grace Buchanan scored after the break, and Billie Backus converted to put Australia 12–5 ahead.

"When we were down in that final, I reminded everyone where most of us came from and the difficulties we have faced in our lives," said captain Hido. "We did not need any motivation from the coach because we knew this could be a potentially life-changing moment."

With time up, Josphine Kerubo crossed for Kenya and Diana Wanjiku added the conversion to level the score at 12–12 and force sudden death. Two minutes into extra time, Mitchelle Chemtai scored in the corner to seal a dramatic 17–12 victory.

"It is still hard to believe," said Chemtai, who only took up rugby three years ago, when she joined high school. "This win made my parents emotional because they have seen my struggles. They never doubted me and I believe now, there is a chance to land further scholarships and contracts that could change our lives."

Kenya opened their campaign with a 12–5 win over China, then beat hosts Senegal 19–0 to reach the semi-finals with a pool match to spare. They lost their final pool match 17–5 to Australia, then beat Madagascar 15–5 in the semi-finals to earn another shot at the Australians.

Getting the Rising Lionesses ready for Dakar meant finding out what each player could do beyond the position she usually played.

"Ninety per cent of those girls came in as wingers and as a coach, I had to identify other attributes and strength to see which other positions they could fit. We trained them until everything went well," Otuoma said.

She said understanding her players' backgrounds and working with an all-women coaching staff were just as important. The squad was made up of students aged 16 and 17. Many came from families with limited means and relied on rugby scholarships to stay in school.

Kenya went into camp in the second week of September. With nearly two months together before the Games, Otuoma wanted the players to feel comfortable asking for what they needed.

"As a female coach and having an all-female technical coaching team, they could share personal stuff like if they needed soap, sanitary pads, or if they wanted to eat something different, things they would ordinarily not share if it was a male coach," she said.

Those conversations helped the team grow closer. Otuoma went a step further, handing out sticky notes every day so the players could raise anything they felt uncomfortable discussing in person.

"Most of the girls could not open up to me directly but they were comfortable writing down their issues. So every morning, I would read and address them," said the former Kenya international.

Chemtai, whose try won Kenya gold, said the trust she and her teammates built with the coaching staff gave them confidence.

"It was so easy sharing our issues with the coach… she made us feel very important. That gave us confidence and we did not want to let her down," said the 16-year-old.

Otuoma also discovered what some of her quietest players could do on the pitch.

"We have two shy girls who rarely talk but when they stepped onto the pitch, they were the fastest and the most fearless when tackling," she said.

One of them was Elizabeth Naliaka. The 17-year-old came from Dakar, eager to finish school, play rugby professionally, and earn a place in Kenya's senior team.

"I hope to make the senior team soon and help them qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics," she said.

In Kenya, the men's rugby teams get most of the funding and the biggest contracts while women lag behind but the triumphant Youth Olympics team feel they have earned the right for a change in fortunes.

"We want to be treated equally, if not better, because we are the first Kenyan team to win an Olympic gold medal," affirmed Diana Wanjiku.

"If they invest in us fully, we will deliver more. Most of us are finishing high school soon and we do not want to get lost after that. There must be a structured pathway so that we make that transition to the senior team and help them qualify for the LA 2028 Olympics and World Cup."

Close 

Madagascar had a milestone of its own to celebrate. The team's only defeat in Dakar came against Kenya in the semi-finals. They went on to beat Czechia 26–10 to win bronze, Madagascar's first medal at either the Olympic Games or the Youth Olympic Games.

For Madagascar captain Tracy Ftiavananomenjanahary, 17, the bronze medal rewarded the time she and her teammates had put into rugby while keeping up with school.

"It is incredible," said the 17-year-old. "This medal is for the country. We put in a lot of effort as we had to balance rugby training and our studies."

"None of us came to Dakar thinking that we could win a medal. We grew in strength with every win and now back home, our families are happy," stated Princia Ranaivoson.

At Nanjing 2014 and Buenos Aires 2018, the two previous editions to feature rugby sevens, Tunisia were Africa's only representatives in the girls' competition and finished sixth both times.

At the first Youth Olympic Games held on African soil, Kenya and Madagascar took two of the three places on the girls' rugby sevens podium. Their results offered a glimpse of how the balance of power in the sport could shift as this generation moves into senior rugby.

World.title: Africa: Tuggar Calls for Stronger African Unity, Condemns Xenophobia
World.content:
Former Minister of Foreign Affairs, Yusuf Maitama Tuggar, has called for stronger African unity and greater tolerance among citizens of the continent, condemning discrimination against fellow Africans as a betrayal of the ideals of Pan-Africanism.

Tuggar made the call yesterday at the 2026 end-of-year event of The Bridge Club in Lagos, which focused on the theme, 'Xenophobia Contradicts Pan-Africanism'.

The event featured renowned Kenyan scholar and Pan-African advocate, Professor P.L.O. Lumumba, as the keynote speaker.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Speaking as chairman of the occasion, Tuggar commended the club for providing a platform for experienced public office holders to continue contributing to national and continental development after leaving government.

He lamented that African societies often failed to utilise the wealth of experience of former public officials, noting that other countries had developed institutional frameworks through which former office holders contributed to policy development and implementation.

He also described the theme of the event as timely and critical to Africa's political, economic and social future.

Recalling Nigeria's historical contributions to the liberation of Southern Africa, particularly its support for victims of apartheid and liberation movements in South Africa, Namibia and Angola, Tuggar condemned the targeting of Nigerians and other black Africans in South Africa.

He described the development as Afrophobia, arguing that the term better captured the discrimination against black Africans.

"Call it Afrophobia, which may be a better description than xenophobia, as non-black Africans appear to be exempted, or the more euphemistic framing of anti-migration protests, it is wrong and must be condemned," he said.

The former minister maintained that Africa's unity would remain incomplete without economic integration, industrial development and the free movement of people across national borders.

He identified the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as a critical instrument for advancing Pan-Africanism, urging African countries to strengthen manufacturing and regional economic cooperation.

Tuggar also called for stronger relations between Nigeria and South Africa, describing the partnership as essential to the continent's future.

He warned against allowing historical divisions and external influences to undermine African solidarity.

In his remarks, President of The Bridge Club, Abdulhakeem Mustapha (SAN), said the theme was particularly relevant at a time when Africa continued to pursue continental integration, economic cooperation and regional solidarity despite persistent incidents of hostility against fellow Africans.

Mustapha said the continent must move beyond political declarations and diplomatic agreements to demonstrate genuine commitment to African unity through the treatment of its citizens.

"Pan-Africanism must mean more than political declarations, diplomatic conferences and economic treaties. It must be reflected in our attitudes, our conduct, our institutions and, above all, in how we treat one another," he said.

The senior lawyer questioned the rationale behind the mistreatment of Africans in other African countries on account of their nationality, ethnicity or place of origin.

He argued that the prosperity, security and dignity of one African nation could not be sustainably achieved at the expense of another.

Describing The Bridge Club as more than a social association, Mustapha said it had evolved into a community of accomplished individuals from diverse professional, cultural and social backgrounds, united by friendship, fellowship and a shared commitment to societal development.

He explained that the club's name reflected its philosophy of building bridges across differences, connecting people and creating opportunities for meaningful engagement.

"Our diversity is our strength. Our friendships are our bonds. Our collective aspirations are what give us purpose," he said.

Reflecting on his nine-year tenure as president, Mustapha expressed gratitude to members, officers and committees whose contributions had helped strengthen the organisation.

He said leadership should not be measured by the length of one's tenure or positions occupied, but by the relationships built, institutions strengthened, values preserved and opportunities created for others.

Close 

"Leadership, I have come to appreciate, is not measured merely by the length of one's tenure or the positions one occupies. It is measured by the relationships one builds, the institutions one strengthens, the values one preserves and the opportunities one creates for others to carry the vision forward," he said.

Mustapha expressed satisfaction that the club had grown beyond an association into a family bound by shared values and mutual support.

He urged members to preserve the spirit of camaraderie, tolerance, generosity and mutual respect that had defined the organisation.

"The greatest legacy we can leave behind is not simply an association that has endured, but a family that remains united, a community that continues to grow, and a platform that makes a meaningful contribution to society," he added.

The event attracted members of the diplomatic community, captains of industry, legal practitioners, public servants, professionals and other friends of the club.

World.title: The 2028 presidential race is already full of surprises, prediction markets say
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The 2028 presidential election seems far away. Or is it already here?

The midterm ballots are barely counted, and a long list of would-be candidates is already elbowing for a lane in a campaign that, by Election Day, will feel like it started during the Truman administration.

Outside the Super Bowl, few things are as popular on prediction markets as a presidential race. Two years before anyone casts a ballot, Kalshi's 2028 markets have already drawn nearly half a billion dollars in trading.

While prediction markets have an excellent long-term record of accuracy, this far from an election, you can't expect surgical precision.

STU BURGUIERE: PUT YOUR MONEY WHERE YOUR MOUTH IS: PREDICTION MARKETS WON THE MIDTERMS

What the markets can show us is who's trading like a blue chip, who's stuck in the middle, and whose campaign feels like a penny stock that needs a miracle rally to be competitive. So let's look ahead with a way-too-early presidential market report, starting at the top.

The blue chips

What if I told you the Democratic front-runner for 2028 is a man a third of Democrats have never heard of? That's what a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found when it comes to Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, and plenty of other Americans are drawing a blank too.

Still, a Democrat who wins Georgia by 18 points, in a state President Trump carried in 2024, doesn’t stay anonymous for long. Kalshi gives him a 26% chance of winning the Democratic nomination, the best in the field. Not bad for a guy much of his own party couldn't pick out of a lineup.

NEW POLL COMPLICATES VANCE’S STATUS AS TRUMP’S LIKELY 2028 HEIR APPARENT

On the Republican side, Vice President J.D. Vance leads the pack, with a 33% chance of winning the nomination but only a 12% chance of winning the presidency. That gap fits what election analyst Nate Silver calls the VP curse. Vice presidents whose bosses are underwater in the polls tend to win their party’s nomination, then lose in November. Then again, Vance has been underestimated before, and he seems to be at his best in high-leverage situations.

Both men have also hinted they might not run at all. Coming from politicians, that promise has roughly the credibility of a vow of celibacy from Jensen Huang.

The mid-caps

California Gov. Gavin Newsom looked like a blue chip a year ago. His chance of winning the Democratic nomination has since cratered from 37% to about 12%. He leaves office in January, which frees him up for a full-time campaign and gives even more airtime to a man who has never been accused of camera shyness. Whether voters want that is another question.

AOC TAPS POWER PLAYER WHO HELPED BERNIE SANDERS DEFY THE ODDS AS MAJOR 2028 DECISION LOOMS

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez sits around 13% to win the Democratic nomination. The bigger question is which race she's running in. Traders actually think she's more likely to run for the Senate than for president. Either way, somebody is going to claim the democratic socialist lane. If it's not her, maybe Bernie Sanders takes a third crack at it. He'll only be 87.

Like Ocasio-Cortez, Secretary of State Marco Rubio faces a which-job question. He's at 18% to win the Republican nomination, and the market sees him as just as likely to be the running mate as the nominee.

VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ran in 2024 and also leaves office in January, has been the biggest riser in the Republican market since the midterms. He was under 5% to win the nomination before the votes were counted and is now at 17%, nipping at Rubio's heels.

The penny stocks

Then come the penny stocks. On the Democratic side, that's a crowd in the single digits for the nomination: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. Former Vice President Kamala Harris lands here too, a somewhat embarrassing showing for the woman at the top of the ticket two years ago.

If you're shopping the bargain bin, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore at 2.2% and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at 0.7% might be in your wheelhouse.

(In dead last, at 0.0%: Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz.)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

On the Republican side, the penny stocks include Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley could be value plays. And somewhere in that mix is President Donald Trump, who I wouldn't put past publicly flirting with a constitutionally prohibited third run just to annoy the media.

The long-term outlook

Many of these names won’t make it to the first primary. Today’s penny stock could be next summer’s blue chip. That’s the fun of watching these markets this early: prices will move with every speech, stumble and suspiciously timed book tour between now and then.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Check back in a year. A few of these stocks will have soared, and plenty will have been quietly delisted.

World.title: Restaurant chain may rethink controversial 20% service charge in some venues after customer pushback
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Ford's Garage may be reconsidering a controversial policy that automatically adds a 20% service charge to customers' checks at select Florida restaurants, with the chain's president acknowledging that some diners are unhappy with the mandatory fee.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Billy Downs said the policy, which is being tested by one franchisee at five Florida locations, remains under review.

"I think that we need to listen to the consumer on those things, to be honest with you," Downs said. "So, we are, and we may be encouraging a change to that program."

RESTAURANT 'ADMIN' FEES SPARK BACKLASH AS DINERS QUESTION WHAT THEY'RE PAYING FOR

Marc Brown, president of franchisee 23 Restaurant Services, told Fox News Digital the program has been largely successful, resulting in higher wages for employees without alienating most customers.

"Our servers in the locations that run our service charge program are making significantly higher average hourly pay than our servers and bartenders in locations that do not have it," Brown said.

The policy is part of a team service model introduced by 23 Restaurant Services, which operates Ford's Garage restaurants throughout Florida.

Rather than relying on traditional tipping, the model automatically adds a 20% service charge to each check to support a commission-based compensation structure.

Servers and bartenders earn commissions based on sales, while the model is also designed to provide more equitable compensation for kitchen and support staff, according to the franchisee's website.

EX-WAITRESS REVEALS RESTAURANT TIPPING SECRET MOST CUSTOMERS DON'T REALIZE — EXPERT CALLS IT 'BAD HOSPITALITY'

Additional tips are optional.

Downs said the experiment was intended to explore whether a different compensation model could help control costs while rewarding employees for their service.

"It certainly was a test to see if this can help keep the cost down to the consumer, as well as reward the server," he said.

The Ford's Garage location in Plantation near Fort Lauderdale is among the restaurants that have implemented the policy "in lieu of a traditional gratuity," according to its website. That location also adds a separate 1% entertainment fee assessed by the shopping center.

"This fee is passed directly to the retail center, is not a gratuity and is not retained by Ford's Garage or distributed to employees," the website states.

APPLEBEE'S CUSTOMER PUSHES BACK ON SUGGESTED TIP AFTER CHECKING THE MATH

Brown said the service charge is disclosed to customers multiple times verbally and in writing before they order, giving them the choice of whether to dine there.

"So, to us, it's no different than just charging a higher price on the menu," he said.

Most guests aren't bothered by the fee, Brown said, "because they like the Ford's Garage experience."

But Downs acknowledged the policy has produced some controversy.

"There's been some big wins, and there's been consumers that just do not want to pay a service charge," he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

The experiment comes as restaurant operators grapple with rising labor costs and changes to tipped minimum wages.

"But the biggest pushback is people don't want to have a mandated service charge, and I get it," Downs said. "You know, I'm not sure I want it either in certain times."

"We have not made any decisions, but we talk about it regularly."

Brown, however, said the criticism appears to come from a relatively small percentage of diners, noting that most participating restaurants have experienced year-over-year growth after operating under the model for multiple years.

CLICK HERE TO 

He also rejected the notion that an automatic service charge diminishes a server or bartender's incentive to provide quality hospitality, saying employees are expected to "provide great service to every guest regardless of what they expect to get in terms of additional tip."

Founded in Fort Myers in 2012, Ford's Garage has grown to 36 restaurants across nine states. Downs said the chain has prioritized affordability, with an average customer check of about $26 and weekday value meals starting at $10.99.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Downs, who previously spoke to Fox News Digital about the chain's emphasis on old-fashioned hospitality, said providing consistently good service can help address customer concerns.

"If you give great service all the time, that can help to eliminate problems," Downs said.

As for whether the service-charge policy could change, Brown said discussions are ongoing.

World.title: Prince William, Kate Middleton get unexpected help enforcing strict rule for George at elite school: experts
World.content:

Prince William and Kate Middleton are reportedly giving Eton College's smartphone ban the royal thumbs-up — especially for their eldest son, Prince George.

The 13-year-old began his studies at the prestigious boarding school in September, where first-year Etonians are banned from using smartphones, according to The Telegraph. Instead, Year 9 students like George are issued basic "brick phones" with no internet access, limiting communication with their parents to calls and texts outside school hours.

Eton College said the decision to ban smartphones for first-year students is intended "to balance the benefits and challenges that technology brings to schools." Eton reportedly tightened restrictions on first-year students' school-issued iPads in September 2026, following parental concerns about gaming and internet browsing.

PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON COULD SEEK 'GENTLEMAN'S AGREEMENT' TO PROTECT PRINCE GEORGE AT ETON: EXPERTS

Fox News Digital reached out to Eton College and Kensington Palace for comment.

In 2025, William told actor Eugene Levy on the Apple TV+ series "The Reluctant Traveler" that "none of our children have any phones, which we’re very strict about."

That same year, William told Brazilian TV host Luciano Huck during the 2025 Earthshot Prize events in Brazil that it had been "really hard" to protect his children from the harms of social media.

WATCH: PRINCE GEORGE'S FUTURE AT ETON COLLEGE COULD LOOK VERY DIFFERENT: EXPERT

"Our children don't have phones," he explained at the time. "I think when George moves on to secondary school, then maybe he might have a phone that has no internet access. And to be honest, it's getting to a point where it's become a little bit of a, like, tense issue."

"But I think he understands why," William continued. "We communicate why we don't think it's right. And again, I think it's the internet access I have a problem with. I think children can access too much stuff they don't need to see online, and so having a phone and text message, the old sort of 'brick phone' as they call them, I think that's fine."

"It has been rumored that William and Kate were having battles with George over having a smartphone with internet access," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital. "Usage could get him into trouble but also allow him access to views on the royal family, good and bad, which may worry him."

"It is now becoming more common practice for schools to ban smartphone usage during school days, and parents want age-appropriate locks on internet technology," Turner added.

British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that Eton's smartphone policy is "music to Prince William and Princess Catherine's ears."

"Prince William and Princess Catherine restrict smart devices to protect their children from internet safety risks," she explained. "A healthy rule of accessing only 'brick phones' at Eton only enables essential communication and calls and texts at home. The couple take great comfort in knowing that Prince George will not be wasting his time gaming, 'doom-scrolling,' or accessing inappropriate online content."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"Prince George has never owned a smartphone," Chard continued. "He will be more than happy with a brick phone. As Princess Catherine has shared, smartphones can create an emotional disconnection. Prince George has years of smartphone access ahead of him and certainly will not go without!"

Eton College, a world-renowned all-boys boarding school, was founded in 1440 by King Henry VI. It serves students between the ages of 13 and 18. About 1,350 students attend Eton, where they live in 25 boarding houses, each housing approximately 55 pupils, according to the school's website. People magazine reported that tuition was about $80,000 for the 2025-26 academic year.

William and his younger brother, Prince Harry, attended Eton, making them both "Old Etonians." Princess Diana's father, John Spencer, and brother, Charles Spencer, also attended the school, as did Queen Elizabeth II's cousins, the Duke of Kent, the Duke of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent.

Hugo Vickers, author of "Behind Closed Doors" and a fellow "Old Etonian," told Fox News Digital that Eton College's use of "brick phones" is "sensible." Vickers has written several books about the British royal family.

"In my day, most of our communication was by writing a letter home," he said with a smile.

"And there was about, if I remember rightly, about four telephone boxes planted at different places around the school. On a Sunday morning, if you wanted to ring your parents, you had to get there, and then you'd have to queue up while other people were in there. It sounds very archaic now. And sometimes you never got into the telephone box because it's time to go to chapel or something."

"So I think the whole thing about communicating with parents is a whole new concept," Vickers continued. "Basic communication with parents is a good thing, but of course, to get the full advantage of the school, it's probably better not to be linking to things all over the world via internet."

Melanie Sanderson, managing editor of The Good Schools Guide, told People magazine that Eton College's phone decision "was very much welcomed by parents."

"And the boys are so busy, they don't have time to be sat on their beds scrolling TikTok," she said.

George was recently on Eton's "Long Leave," a 16-day break that ended Nov. 8. The royal family lives at Forest Lodge in Windsor. World.title: Inside the House GOP strategy to capitalize on Democrats' warring factions in the new Congress
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

EXCLUSIVE: House Republicans are heading into the next Congress ready to brawl.

Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., who is set to go from the No. 3 most powerful House Republican to No. 2 next year, told Fox News Digital that the GOP will hold the new Democrat majority "accountable" for their far-left faction's ideas over the next two years, even if they cannot control what bills get a vote.

Emmer, who has served as House majority whip for the past four years, was elected Tuesday to serve as minority whip alongside incoming House Minority Leader Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. The Speaker of the House position turns over to Democrats, and will likely be won by current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.

And despite Jeffries poised to take control of what legislation gets to the House floor, Emmer signaled House Republicans would find ways to push their agenda as well.

JIM JORDAN BECOMES NEW HOUSE GOP LEADER AFTER CLOSED-DOOR VOTE, DEFEATING STEVE SCALISE

"What's their answer to dealing with costs and wages? We're going to investigate Trump," Emmer said in reference to Democrats. "That's not going to solve the problems that they created. So that's going to be the job of the whip, is to make sure that we have a coordinated process — committee hearings, floor votes — to expose and define exactly who these people really are."

PROGRESSIVE GROUP'S 182-PAGE BLUEPRINT MAPS OUT POTENTIAL DEM INVESTIGATIONS INTO TRUMP, CORPORATE ALLIES

Emmer, in his first print interview since winning the House minority whip job, would not go into detail about how Republicans would utilize floor votes, however.

"There's a toolbox with a bunch of different tools, and you're going to have to build that strategy as you go from week to week," he said.

The Minnesota Republican also signaled there would be little appetite for bipartisanship over the next two years, a sentiment he suggested would come from the other side of the aisle.

"Well look, they're not going to work with us, that's pretty clear, and I don't even know if they're going to be able to work with each other," Emmer said.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES FACES PROGRESSIVE HOLDOUTS BUT NO RIVAL AS HOUSE SPEAKER RACE TAKES SHAPE

He repeated a short time later, "I see nowhere where they're going to work with Republicans. And Republicans who think they are should think again, because they will tell you nice things, and then they will just go do what they do."

Meanwhile other House Republicans are already coming up with ideas on how to put Democrats on the spot on the House floor in the new Congress.

"We'll file amendments," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "And I think that'll be where having good debaters and communicators would be important."

Holding amendment votes is commonplace before large pieces of legislation like the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which Congress has enacted annually for decades to update and reauthorize critical national security policies.

Rep. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., suggested an emphasis on a parliamentary procedure called the "motion to recommit," which allows the minority party to get a vote on altering or even killing a bill in its tracks.

"I expect we'll use that smartly," LaLota said. "But as well, a Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will be wise to work these problems backwards, to know that anything he puts on the floor that he wants to become law or budget needs President Trump's signature and probably 60 votes in the Senate."

Rep. Mark Harris, R-N.C., said "there's been a lot of conversation about going on offense."

"We want to make sure that they know when they come to the floor, they're gonna dread it, I hope," Harris said.

DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY

But there's another mechanism for forcing a House vote that's been used more and more often in recent years — often by their fellow Republicans.

Privileged resolutions allow lawmakers on either side to get a vote on a given bill within two days of its introduction. It generally begins with a procedural vote on whether to "table" the bill or refer it to committee in order to stop it, before a vote on the measure itself.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., most recently invoked it to force the House to consider impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. But that was defeated when the rest of the House GOP banded together to refer the bill to committee.

The GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital, however, signaled little appetite for using it.

"I think either party would be wise to build consensus around things that help actually deliver for the American people," LaLota said. "The privileged resolutions have been abused in my time here, and there's a better way to do business."

And Emmer said his main goal for the next two years would be winning back the House majority in 2028 — which he insisted was a realistic goal.

He said at least 38 seats flipped by Democrats would be "ready to return to Republican hands," and could see some old faces return.

Asked whether he wanted to see some of those losing GOP incumbents run for their seats again, Emmer said, "I absolutely hope so, I've talked to several already."

World.title: Trump keeps signaling an end to Iran war, but expert warns a crucial piece of his strategy is missing
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump declared Thursday that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran, abruptly shifting his diplomatic message just three days after expressing optimism about negotiations and directing Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic issues instead.

"We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

Trump's latest declaration came just one day after he proclaimed victory over Iran during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery, while acknowledging that the conflict had not yet formally ended.

"We won," Trump said Wednesday. "It’s just a question of when we end it. I want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93 percent victory."

TRUMP DEFENDS IRAN WAR DURING VETERANS DAY ADDRESS, SAYS HE IS MAKING THE WORLD 'SAFER'

The president also thanked veterans "working to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of state terrorism, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never have a nuclear weapon."

An administration official defended Trump's strategy, arguing that the United States has substantial leverage over Iran through its naval blockade and continued military pressure, even as questions remain about how the conflict will end.

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. The President has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Operation Iron Gate will continue with full effect," a U.S. official told Fox News Digital.

"President Trump holds all the cards, will do what is best for the United States, and will make sure that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," the official added.

Trump's latest words follow months of predictions that an agreement could be reached soon, including comments earlier this week that Tehran "would love to make a deal."

Trump's declaration raises questions about the future of U.S.-Iran negotiations, including whether diplomatic efforts will continue through other administration officials as Washington maintains its military and economic pressure on Tehran.

AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

Trump has suggested on at least a dozen occasions since February that Iran wanted to negotiate or that an agreement could be reached soon, according to a preliminary review of his public remarks.

Ludovic Hood, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said the administration's combination of economic coercion, military force and regional partnerships is sensible, but warned that a crucial diplomatic component remains underdeveloped.

"What’s lacking is disciplined diplomacy to complement the economic squeeze and possible airstrikes," Hood told Fox News Digital. "Our Gulf partners are singing from different hymn sheets and we need to draw European partners in more meaningfully."

Trump's optimistic assessments began before U.S. military operations against Iran commenced. On Feb. 13, he suggested Tehran could avoid an attack by accepting Washington's terms. After military operations began, he increasingly emphasized Iran's weakened capabilities and the prospect of ending the conflict.

IRANIAN NEGOTIATORS KICKED OUT OF US AS TALKS STALL, TRUMP LAYS OUT 'POSSIBLE' TIMELINE FOR MORE STRIKES

On March 20, Trump said the United States was "getting very close" to achieving its military objectives.

The administration agreed to a ceasefire in April and continued pursuing a diplomatic settlement, but subsequent military actions and disagreements over Iran's nuclear program and regional shipping have left the broader conflict unresolved.

Trump continued expressing confidence that Iran wanted an agreement, including in May, when he suggested Tehran was eager to negotiate because of the damage inflicted on its military.

During an unscheduled appearance in the White House briefing room Monday, Trump said, "Iran, militarily, is effectively over," while warning that U.S. forces remained "locked and loaded" should circumstances change.

Hood said Trump's seemingly contradictory messages could be part of a deliberate negotiating strategy.

"The administration is pursuing a sensible hybrid strategy of economic coercion, selective use of force, and reliance on capable regional allies," Hood said.

TRUMP SAYS IRAN IS 'NEGOTIATING ON FUMES,' BELIEVES REGIME THOUGHT THEY COULD OUTWAIT HIM

"Trump’s messaging seems designed to both signal his preference for a diplomatic solution while preserving the option of force," he added.

Hood defended the president's willingness to maintain military pressure.

"Bluster, bluffing and brinkmanship are inherent in the public dimension of negotiations like this; Trump does it, Rubio does it, and senior figures in Tehran do it," he said.

"Strategic patience is essential in this standoff, which has essentially been 40 years in the making."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

But Hood also suggested that securing meaningful nuclear concessions or a more cooperative government in Tehran would require coordination with regional partners.

World.title: NYC woman allegedly struck by LGBTQ+ activist after questioning trans youth treatments: 'Never have answers'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A woman says she was assaulted by a prominent LGBTQ+ activist at a recent New York City protest as she was questioning his push for transgender medical procedures for children, according to video of the incident provided by the alleged victim.

Christiane Torello was a counter-protester at the rally outside Mount Sinai Hospital in Manhattan on Nov. 5 when she was allegedly elbowed in the chest by Jay Walker, the president of Gays Against Guns who also served as a 2026 NYC Pride Grand Marshal.

Walker was part of a group rallying against the hospital's decision in September to end transgender treatments for minors to resolve a Department of Justice investigation into youth gender transition procedures.

"The hospital is no longer providing any type of gender-affirming care for minors, including surgeries, puberty blockers and hormones," Torello told Fox News Digital. "There’s always a group of individuals who go to these protests to show their discomfort and displeasure with the hospital stopping these procedures because they want the children to transition. I usually go there in opposition to them. I support the hospital’s decision to stop providing that care. I always go by myself and ask questions."

MAJOR BLUE STATE HOSPITAL PULLS PLUG ON CONTROVERSIAL CHILD TRANSGENDER TREATMENTS AFTER DOJ INTERVENTION

In the video she captured of the incident, Torello questioned Walker why he wanted to "have penises in the locker room" as he was yelling and walking away from her on a sidewalk. Walker then stopped, wound his elbow up and allegedly struck her in the chest before repeatedly shouting at her to "get away from me."

She said demonstrators often attempt to obstruct her path and shove their signs in her face, but that this incident was more violent than most of the rallies she has been to.

"I'm usually followed around the protest by two or three people. They block me and put signs in my face, which is fine because they’re allowed to do that. But this time, it became particularly violent," Torello said.

"When I asked the organizer of the protest, Jay Walker, what size dongs he’d like in the girls’ locker room, he didn’t have an answer. They never have answers to those questions. They don’t like to talk about it," she continued.

Torello said Walker was shouting slurs at her as he was walking away from the protest and she followed him to question him more about what he was saying.

She then accused Walker of hitting her in the chest with his elbow, adding that she thinks he intended to strike her in the face but had "pretty bad aim."

"As we were walking, he stopped in front of me, wound up his elbow and blasted me in the chest," she said. "He’s about 6'5" and I’m 5'5", so I’m pretty sure he intended to hit me in the face but had pretty bad aim and hit me in the chest."

After the alleged assault, Torello continued following Walker down the street.

UTAH STUDENT CITED AFTER PHYSICAL ALTERCATION WITH COLLEGE REPUBLICAN CAUGHT ON CAMERA

The video shows both Torello and Walker yelling and cursing at one another as they were walking.

Walker was heard calling her "psychotic," "scumbag," a "garbage person" and a "stalker," while she accused him of being a "woman abuser." At one point, he was allegedly seen lunging at Torello, to which she dared him to "do it again" and said she would post the video on social media.

"I'm so glad I got it on camera," she shouted at Walker.

Torello told Fox News Digital that she reported the incident to the New York City Police Department, but she is not confident any charges will be filed.

"I want to press charges because I feel like New York doesn’t do anything when it comes to a lot of violence," she said. "But this is a different type of violence. I have a First Amendment right to be there and peacefully protest. I wasn’t hitting anybody. Do I ask questions that may be annoying or triggering? Sure. But that’s the extent of what I do. That doesn’t warrant me getting hit, elbowed or punched."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"This is actually the second time a man has put his hands on me at a protest," she continued. "The first happened about a month and a half ago. There were two NYPD detectives in front of that other protest who watched me get hit, and they didn’t even talk to me. I asked them if they could direct me somewhere, and they wouldn’t say one word to me. I had to figure it out on my own. I filed a report, and nothing happened to that man either."

It is unclear if police plan to make any arrests in connection with the alleged assault.

The NYPD and Walker's group, Gays Against Guns NY, did not respond to Fox News Digital's multiple requests for comment.

"I just really hope this brings some awareness and puts pressure on the NYPD to do something, because they don’t do anything at all," Torello said.

World.title: SEN BERNIE SANDERS: Democrats won big. Deliver real change now, or pay a terrible price
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

On Election Day, the American people, all across the country, sent a very powerful message to our country’s ruling class. In a loud and surprisingly unified voice, they said NO to Trump’s pathological lying, his contempt for the Constitution and the rule of law, his narcissism, his corruption and his disastrous policies. But they also said something more.

At a time when 60% of our people are living paycheck to paycheck, when we have unprecedented income and wealth inequality, when we have the highest rate of childhood poverty of any industrialized nation, when millions of seniors are unable to retire with dignity, and when our younger generation may end up having a lower standard of living than their parents, working families voted for change, REAL change. Despite billions of dollars in ugly and dishonest TV ads, Americans made it clear. They want an end to status quo politics and status quo policies that prop up a rigged economy and a corrupt campaign finance system.

And it wasn't just the election results. According to a recent AP poll, 80% of registered voters want either "complete and total upheaval" or "substantial change" in how this country is run, including 97% of Democrats, 90% of independents and 58% of Republicans.

BERNIE SANDERS WARNS DEMOCRATS NOT TO SPEND ALL THEIR TIME INVESTIGATING TRUMP

On Election Day, Democrats won a massive victory. When the new Congress convenes, Democrats will have more than 250 members in the House and at least 55 members in the Senate.

Democrats now have the votes to pass legislation that will greatly improve the lives of millions of working families. And that’s exactly what they must do. No more empty rhetoric and poll-driven messaging. No more telling people, over and over again, how terrible Donald Trump and the Republicans are. No more excuses. The new Democratic majority must deliver for a long-neglected working class.

Will Trump veto that legislation? Maybe, maybe not. If he signs the bills, the American people will benefit and be grateful. If he doesn’t, Republicans will pay a terrible political price.

In my view, here is some of what the new Democratic Congress must focus on:

HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY'

HEALTH CARE: Our health care system is broken and wildly expensive. We spend twice as much per person as other major countries, yet more than 90 million Americans are uninsured or underinsured, over half a million go bankrupt each year because of medical debt and more than 60,000 die unnecessarily because they cannot afford care.

Health care must be a human right, not a privilege. Democrats must pass Medicare for All, now supported by 66% of Americans. As a first step in a four-year transition, we must lower Medicare eligibility to 55, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing, and guarantee health care for every child from birth through age 19.

INCOME AND WEALTH INEQUALITY: We have more income and wealth inequality in America today than at any time in our history. The top 1% now owns more wealth than the bottom 93%. Elon Musk alone owns more wealth than the bottom 53% of American households.

Democrats must pass a 5% wealth tax on billionaires, supported by 61% of Americans. The new funds raised would provide working-class families of four with a $12,000 direct payment, build 7 million affordable housing units, make public colleges and universities tuition-free, establish free child care for 13 million children and improve public education.

RAISE THE MINIMUM WAGE: While the rich get richer, 60% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck. The federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour is a starvation wage. We must raise it to at least $20 an hour and pass the PRO Act to make it easier for workers to organize unions. A job must lift people out of poverty, not keep them in it.

At this extraordinary moment in our history, we must restore faith in democracy. One way we do that is by delivering tangible benefits for working families.
