World.title: What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop
World.content:
What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop

The Federal Aviation Administration took an extraordinary step Friday afternoon by issuing a nationwide ground stop. No planes are taking off at any airport and millions of passengers are stranded.

Transcript

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

The U.S. air travel system is slowly getting back off the ground. The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the rare nationwide ground stop it issued earlier today, citing telecommunications failure. That grounded thousands of planes at airports across the country, stranding millions of passengers. NPR's transportation correspondent Joel Rose is here. We've been talking all afternoon and evening trying to sort this out. Joel, now we have a little bit of a resolution, but not really. What's the latest?

JOEL ROSE, BYLINE: Yeah. We just heard from the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, that, as you said, the airspace has reopened. The ground stop is lifted. But it's going to take some time to get this hourslong - to get through the backlog of canceled and delayed flights. And it's going to take even longer to figure out, apparently, what happened here.

During the news conference, Duffy said that investigators are still trying to understand exactly what the problem was. Duffy blamed the - Duffy cited intermittent communications, intermittent radar and blamed this on outdated air traffic control equipment that was overloaded with data. We have old switches, old routers, he said. It's an old system that went down. It got overloaded. Here's more of what Duffy said.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: We're getting very little information. Our pilot's been great and has been giving us updates every 15 minutes, which has been really helpful and reassuring.

DETROW: I think we had the wrong tape there, Joel. But...

ROSE: That's the wrong cut. Well, you got...

DETROW: Yeah, yeah, keep going.

ROSE: I'll tell you more about Secretary Duffy.

DETROW: Sure.

ROSE: So he spent a lot of this press conference blaming old gear that failed. But when reporters pushed and asked for clarity on exactly what went wrong today, he wasn't able to give them a whole lot of specifics. He pivoted again and again to pushing for more money to rebuild the nation's air traffic control system, which has been a big priority for this administration but was - we just don't - we still have only Duffy's word that this was the old gear that failed. We don't have a lot of detail on what it was.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was at this press conference too. He said, there's no indication that this was a cyber attack, but he could not rule that out entirely - also started the press conference by saying that this outage is not related to the Microsoft outage that knocked out Outlook and some other services yesterday.

DETROW: Yeah, I feel like I had a lot of questions watching that briefing, as did many other people. And meanwhile, there's people all over the country trying to get home. Our reporter at Washington National Airport, Ava Berger, says she is hearing announcements that the hold's has been lifted, but the announcements are saying - urging people to please be patient. About half the board there is red with canceled flights. But she said people are now starting to optimistically slowly go back to their gates to see if their plane's ever going to leave. I mean, Joel, what is the situation like on the ground at other airports around the country?

ROSE: This is a mess, and it's going to be a mess for days. I mean, we've canceled - airlines have canceled thousands of flights. Thousands more are delayed. Planes are out of position. Crews are out of position. This is, you know, imagine if you had a giant blizzard at every airport in the country all at once.

DETROW: Ooh.

ROSE: You know, it's like the whole system is scrambled, and it's going to take days, optimistically...

DETROW: Yeah.

ROSE: ...Before we are back to normal in the U.S. aviation system.

DETROW: We've got about 10 seconds left. Remind us how rare something like this is.

ROSE: Very unusual. This is the second nationwide groundstop since September 11. The most recent was in 2023, and that one only lasted less than 2 hours. So this now appears to be the longest nationwide groundstop since September 11 of 2001.

DETROW: NPR's Joel Rose, thanks so much.

ROSE: You bet.

World.title: GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election
World.content:
GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election

toggle caption i Lynne Sladky/AP

Voting for this year's midterm elections just concluded, but Republican officials in a number of states are already looking to shape how votes are cast in 2028.

Twelve GOP state attorneys general are pushing to revive the president's bid for mail-in voting restrictions in time for the 2028 election.

On Thursday, they started the process of appealing a September order by U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, one of the two judges who blocked the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan released in response to an executive order by President Trump.

The Republican state attorneys general represent Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas. It's not clear, however, how long some of these states will continue this case, given that Democrats won up and down the ballot in the midterms. In Texas and Kansas, Democratic candidates are set to take control of their states' attorney general's offices in January.

Sponsor Message

In September, the Supreme Court refused to pause a similar ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who is based in Boston. That order stopped USPS from working on its revised rule for federal ballot mail, but it only applied to this year's midterm elections.

Nichols' preliminary injunction blocks USPS from implementing the plan for all federal elections, including the 2028 race.

In a court filing, Justice Department attorneys confirmed the Trump administration is not appealing Nichols' ruling. The appeal deadline was Thursday.

The blocked rule — which the Postal Service released in late August — would require states to turn over lists of voters' names and addresses in order to have them delivered by USPS.

Nichols, a Washington, D.C.-based judge who was nominated by Trump, found that the mailing agency likely has no power to impose that requirement on states.

"As the Government concedes, the Postal Service could issue (and enforce) the Rule only if Congress gave it the authority to do so, but here no statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule," Nichols wrote.

The administration's earlier push to put these new restrictions in place for the midterms alarmed many election officials, who were concerned about last-minute changes causing major disruptions to the tens of millions who regularly vote by mail. Some voters with disabilities and those in places without polling sites, they feared, could have lost the ability to exercise their right to cast a ballot.

Sponsor Message

A whistleblower report claimed the online system officials would need to use to follow USPS' revised ballot requirements had not been properly tested and could have resulted in many eligible voters not getting their mail-in ballots in time or at all.

While the Supreme Court ultimately stopped implementation of the USPS rule for the midterms, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from that ruling.

Fellow conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said in a concurring opinion that he believed state and local election officials did not have enough time to "reasonably implement the rule" this time. But Kavanaugh noted that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority."

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

World.title: Can the Carney government end homelessness? (Not on its own)
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mark Carney is not the first prime minister to embrace an ambitious commitment about homelessness. He is not even the first prime minister to do so in the last 10 years.

In 2017, Justin Trudeau's government released its national housing strategy. As part of a broader plan for housing, the Trudeau government set a goal of reducing "chronic" homelessness by half over the subsequent decade — at the time, an estimated 25,000 people were said to be chronically homeless.

Three years later, in a speech from the throne , the Trudeau government went further, stating that it was now focused on "entirely eliminating chronic homelessness in Canada."

However worthy the goal, and whatever efforts the Trudeau government put toward achieving that goal, it was not met. A progress report released by the federal government last December acknowledged that there had been a 34 per cent increase in chronic homelessness among shelter users between 2016 and 2024.

Carney has committed himself to a more ambitious target — putting Canada on a path to end all homelessness within 10 years.

"There's no simple answer. This is a hard problem," Carney said in Winnipeg last week. "And hard problems demand the humility to learn from previous well-intentioned efforts that have fallen short. And it demands the resolve to build on what's succeeded."

Homelessness is hardly a new problem, but it was in the wake of the pandemic that homelessness came to the fore as a visible and salient concern in communities across Canada — exemplified by the issue of encampments in public places .

A national homelessness enumeration in 2025 found that more than 65,000 people were homeless on a given night in Canada, a 59 per cent increase over five years. The share of unhoused people living in unsheltered locations, including encampments, had also increased from 23 per cent to 27 per cent.

The underlying factors that might have contributed to the current situation are numerous and thorny: a longstanding lack of government funding for new social housing, an insufficient supply of rental housing, the disruption of the pandemic, the post-pandemic spike in inflation and the increasing cost of living, the opioid epidemic.

"It was on a rapid but slow burn from 1995 and then it hit 2018, 2019 and the housing crisis, pandemic, affordability crisis, toxic drug supply — all came together to create the problem we're seeing today," said Tim Richter, president and CEO of the Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness.

In the face of a problem that was driven by overlapping crises and challenges, the Trudeau government's actions obviously weren't enough to solve the problem.

Nick Falvo, a researcher and consultant who focuses on homelessness, said the national housing strategy lacked an emphasis on supportive housing — "deeply subsidized housing with a lot of social work support."

Richter says the Trudeau-era plan failed to create enough deeply affordable housing of the sort that people on income-support programs could afford.

Carney's homelessness agenda

The Carney plan maintains two pieces of the Trudeau strategy.

As laid out in this month's budget, the Carney government plans to renew funding for the Canada Housing Benefit, a rent supplement for low-income Canadians. Both the Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness and Falvo have argued that an expanded and better-targeted CHB could do even more to reduce homelessness. The Carney government is also maintaining a program — Reaching Home — that provides direct funding to communities to support efforts to reduce homelessness.

On top of that the government is adding three capital funds: $10 billion for supportive and transitional housing, $5 billion for "integrated supports" projects and $2 billion for new health-care infrastructure. The government is also directing new funding to Build Canada Homes in hopes of boosting the construction of non-market housing.

WATCH | Carney's mission to end homelessness starts in Manitoba: Carney's mission to end homelessness kicks off with joint effort in Manitoba | Duration closed caption 2:05 A day after his budget laid out billions to end homelessness in Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney joined Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew to announce a joint effort to build homes and a new mental health and addictions centre in Winnipeg.

More broadly, the Carney government is talking about a "renewed partnership" with the provinces, one in which the federal government would provide funding for capital (i.e. building things), while the provinces would fund operations and services.

"The Carney government's announcement is different in a couple of ways. One is they've set themselves a much bigger target," Richter said. "But they've also led with a major capital infusion.… And this conversation with the provinces. So their first steps are different than the Trudeau steps, which I think is important from a first-step point of view."

The challenge that Falvo sees is operational funding — the ongoing expenses that provincial governments will have to be willing to cover.

"I would say [the Carney government's plan] was a very impressive down payment. It showed great leadership," Falvo said. "I'll be very interested to see what happens with the provinces."

The federal government has at least already found one province that was eager for a renewed partnership. In Manitoba, the Carney government committed $800 million toward the construction of 2,000 supportive and transitional homes and $200 million toward a new centre for mental health and addictions. The province will provide funding for the operation of both and cover half of the cost of constructing the centre.

'Canadians want to do something'

In Winnipeg, Carney acknowledged that governments have spent "decades" trying to address homelessness. But, he said, "too often those efforts have been inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated and not sustained."

Richter co-authored a proposal earlier this year for a new national accord on housing , which would align all levels of government on solving the larger crisis of housing availability and affordability. On homelessness, Richter says the conversation between federal and provincial governments should focus not just on dollars, but on approaches, priorities and desired outcomes.

Absolutely eliminating the phenomenon of homelessness is unrealistic, Richter says. But he and the CAEH talk about achieving " functional zero ," whereby a community is able to house more people than will become homeless in a given month — a situation in which homelessness is rare, brief and not recurring.

If it was somewhat surprising to see the Carney government — a government that has seemed resolutely focused on large macroeconomic issues — use its second budget to make such a headline-grabbing commitment to reduce homelessness, it's perhaps not a surprise that governments are feeling some pressure to do something.

"My theory is that his government started to realize that voters were growing quite unhappy with visible manifestations of poverty, homelessness and social disorder," Falvo said.

WATCH | How does the federal government plan to end homelessness? How do the feds plan to end homelessness in Canada? | Duration closed caption 8:56 As part of a nationwide 10-year strategy to eliminate homelessness, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew announced a $1-billion federal initiative in Winnipeg on Friday to build 2,000 supportive housing units and a new mental health and addictions treatment campus. Power & Politics hears from Housing Minister Gregor Robertson.

A survey commissioned by the CAEH earlier this year found that 66 per cent of Canadians encountered homelessness at least once per week, 39 per cent considered it a "very" or "extremely" serious problem and 60 per cent believe the problem has gotten worse in their community in the last few years.

(Earlier this year, Carney also told the Globe and Mail that he was reading Encampment by Maggie Helwig, which won this year's Shaughnessy Cohen Prize for political writing.)

But if the problem has become very visible, governments could also think not only about the long term, but also about what they can do to show visible progress in the near term, Richter suggests.

"If you look at the polling, it says like Canadians want to do something. They want to do the right thing," he said. "They feel compassion. They understand a lot of it is housing. It's also mental health and addiction. But they want to see a difference."

If the years since the last ambitious goal to reduce homelessness have unfortunately seen the problem get worse, that has perhaps at least created an even greater impetus for governments to finally solve the problem.

World.title: Is a cure on the horizon for hepatitis B? New drug offers hope, but there's a 'long way to go'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This is an excerpt from Second Opinion, a weekly analysis of health and medical science news emailed to subscribers Saturday mornings. If you haven't subscribed yet, you can do that by clicking here .

Despite decades of efforts to wipe out hepatitis B, the viral liver infection remains a quiet threat — and one that's long lacked a cure.

While rates have dropped dramatically since the rise of childhood vaccination programs, an estimated 260,000 Canadians are still living with the virus, including roughly half who don't know they're infected . Over time, many of those silently carrying the virus go on to develop a range of life-threatening issues, including cancer or sudden liver failure.

Could a long-awaited cure finally be in sight?

In early November, Health Canada approved a breakthrough drug offering the first "functional cure" for a portion of chronic hepatitis B patients, which drugmaker GSK expect to roll out in early 2027 .

Dr. Carla Coffin, a hepatologist and professor at the University of Calgary's Cumming School of Medicine, calls it a "major step forward."

At the same time, she warned it's only effective in a relatively small proportion of people with hepatitis B — and questions remain around cost, access and just how long the impacts of the powerful new treatment last.

Virus can lead to chronic liver infection

The hepatitis B virus spreads through infected bodily fluids, including blood, semen and vaginal fluids, making it both a sexually-transmitted infection and one that passes from mother-to-child, or via contaminated drug-injection equipment like needles.

Most healthy adults who contract the virus clear it on their own and develop lifelong immunity.

But when someone contracts hepatitis B as an infant or during childhood, it can become a chronic infection that causes long-term damage and inflammation to the liver, leading to serious complications or death.

The burden of these infections is disproportionately carried by certain populations. There are higher rates among Indigenous communities, illicit drug users, individuals engaging in high-risk sexual activity and immigrants from countries where hepatitis B is more common.

Up until now, patients have required long-term antiviral therapy to surpress the virus, explained Dr. Curtis Cooper, who leads the Ottawa Hospital's viral hepatitis program.

"This new treatment, it completely clears all of the viral markers for hepatitis B out of the blood," he said, noting it offers "quite a bit of hope" for patients aiming to discontinue other treatments.

LISTEN | Health Canada approves first 'functional cure' for hepatitis B: Ottawa Morning 7:02 Health Canada approves first "functional cure" for Chronic Hepatitis B Dr. Curtis Cooper, the head of Infectious Diseases at the Ottawa Hospital, explains how the treatment would work and what it means for patients.

Drug may replace long-term antiviral treatment

The drug, called bepirovirsen, is a short-term course of injections which can lead to undetectable levels of virus DNA in some patients.

"From the data that we have now, if it works, then we can reassure [patients] that they have a functional cure and they won't need to take any further hepatitis B treatments in the future," said Coffin, from the University of Calgary.

The data is based on clinical trials comparing the drug to a placebo, which showed around one-fifth of patients still had the virus under control 24 weeks after stopping all other hepatitis B treatments, with undetectable levels in their blood.

The drug works only for a minority of patients, Coffin stressed, and "clinicians have to very carefully decide on which patients would be eligible and which would benefit from the treatment."

For instance, individuals with a history of cirrhosis — where healthy liver tissue is permanently scarred, blocking normal blood flow — don't qualify, Coffin noted. She added there can be more side effects from the shot, including a rash, compared to taking a daily anti-viral medication.

It's also not clear just how durable the treatment will be. Coffin says data is still emerging as more time passes since the clinical trials, with the latest figures showing the drug has a lasting impact of at least 96 weeks.

"Our expectation is that it will last," Coffin said. "But of course, we won't know that until we do the long-term follow-up in these patients."

WATCH | CDC panel vote to stop universal hep B shot for babies called 'irresponsible': CDC panel vote to stop hep B vaccine for babies called 'irresponsible' | Duration closed caption 2:05 U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s hand-picked panel of advisers at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has voted to remove the long-standing recommendation to universally vaccinate infants against hepatitis B.

Questions around cost, access

Dr. Eric Yoshida, a professor of medicine in the division of gastroenterology at the University of British Columbia, is skeptical of where the drug fits into the broader landscape for hepatitis B treatments.

While he agreed bepirovirsen offers a major scientific leap forward, he says access and cost could be barriers to uptake — meaning the drug may not reach many Canadians.

In Japan, where the drug was approved earlier, Yoshida says a course of therapy costs roughly $84,000 Cdn. Though actual pricing for Canada isn't yet clear, he questioned whether private drug plans and the provinces will end up covering it.

"Looking into the future, well, this is the first generation. The next generation is probably going to be even better and even less expensive, so I think the future is looking bright," Yoshida said.

"But I think for the average Canadian patient with hepatitis B, it's probably not going to mean a heck of a lot."

WATCH | N.W.T. dentist's patients possibly exposed to HIV, hepatitis: N.W.T. dental patients possibly exposed to HIV and hepatitis want to see improved care | Duration 1:45 It seemed like a regular dental visit for an Ulukhaktok patient's family, until they got a notice telling them to get tested for HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C. For those who may have been exposed, this is just the latest in a string of concerns over dental care in region.

Canada calls for universal infant vaccination

Treatment possibilities aside, both Coffin and Yoshida stressed the need for more awareness of hepatitis B vaccination as a way to stamp out the virus for good. Yet global immunization programs for this virus remain fraught.

In November, Canada's vaccine advisors issued a new recommendation for all Canadian infants to receive the hepatitis B shot , which may — in time — align provinces that offer the shot at a mix of ages, from infancy to children in grades six or seven.

"If every country in the world vaccinated their newborns," said Yoshida, "I think hepatitis B would be basically on the way out."

But Canada's recent move is a stark contrast from the U.S., where the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) removed its longstanding universal hepatitis B vaccination recommendation for newborns in late 2025.

Many countries also struggle with hepatitis B immunization, leading to significantly higher rates of chronic infection in certain regions. In 2024, 75 per cent of all global hepatitis B-related deaths were across Africa and the Western Pacific, World Health Organization data shows .

"We still have a long way to go," Coffin said.

World.title: 4 decades ago, Robert Munsch attended Moira Green's birthday. Her story became a children's classic
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On Moira Green’s 10th birthday, she put on a giant paper bag and a homemade crown and headed down to Hay River’s public library, where a surprising number of residents from the remote Northwest Territories town were waiting.

There were 200 pizzas and 200 little cakes. She ran into a dragon, Prince Ronald and other valiant attempts by her Grade 5 classmates to bring the beloved characters from Robert Munsch’s earliest works to life.

Technically, Green could have come dressed as herself: the inspiration behind Moira’s Birthday.

“After we did our little performances and stuff, they got Robert Munsch on the line,” Green said in a recent interview. “I don't know how they did it back in the day, but everyone in the library could hear him. And then, he read the story [to] all of us."

It was November 1987.

Six months earlier, Toronto-based Annick Press had published Moira’s Birthday. And exactly four years previous, the Guelph, Ont., children’s author had visited the Northwest Territories for the first time, leaving behind a trail of memories for many in the community of roughly 3,500 people living there at the time, and, as Green recalls, whenever anyone new turned up, her parents insisted they come for supper.

That small-town friendliness was how Munsch, known for billeting with families during his tours, came to stay with Bruce and Marilyn Green and their five children, all of whom would make an appearance in the first of three books he would dream up during the trip.

Green, shown wearing the Paper Bag Princess costume, is seen here at her 10th birthday party in Hay River, N.W.T., in November 1987. She and other kids performed skits based on Munsch's books. (Submitted by Moira Green)

Those connections Munsch forged with kids, living in big cities and tiny hamlets, became the fabric of the nearly 100 books he has written in his career. In an interview with CBC News last year , his “last hurrah,” the author revealed that another 50 books will likely be published after his death.

As first reported in the New York Times in September 2025, Munsch has been approved for medical assistance in dying (MAID), when he chooses. He has been living with Parkinson’s disease and dementia.

“Nobody lives forever," he told CBC in December. “But I will at least have a couple of years, as many years as I’ve already had [after I’m gone], and that will be nice," he said, of his hope to publish a book per year after his death.

Munsch and his wife, Ann, who have been married for more than five decades, are shown here at their home in November 2025. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)

The breadth of his travels helped him capture what it was like to be a kid in a country as vast as Canada.

Even in a place as remote as Hay River.

Moira’s 6th birthday

On the morning of her sixth birthday party in November 1983, Green and her siblings went to see Munsch perform at the library. He captivated his audience, she said, despite having just flown in hours before from Yellowknife.

Her party had already been planned for that afternoon before news of Munsch’s visit came out.

It was not quite as raucous as the story suggests — a handful of friends, not the whole school, showed up. And during a quiet moment, her dad walked over.

“He said ‘You should ask Mr. Munsch if he could tell you a story.’ And I was like, ‘Mmmm, I'm not going to do that. I'm way too shy.’”

Green, left, shown in her Grade 1 photo, which helped artist Michael Martchenko illustrate the book, shown right. (Submitted by Moira Green/Annick Press)

But a friend did it for her, she said. The author recalls that he couldn’t refuse.

“Sometimes when a kid asks me to make up a story, I get this strange feeling that something is going to happen,” Munsch wrote of the experience . “I look out at a group of kids and get this firm conviction that I can tell a new story about a particular kid.

“Usually, it’s not true, but I do always try a new story when I get the feeling.”

Green was just as surprised, as she had assumed he would retell a previous story.

“But he came over … sat down and then he just sort of started telling — making up — the story on the spot: Moira’s Birthday.

Anyone who has heard Munsch perform knows how he revs up a crowd, along with his own volume, asking questions and weaving the answers into his words.

“Lots of interactions, stopping to talk about the local bakery and, you know, other things from around town and kind of integrate that into the story."

Even before he finished, Munsch said, he knew he had a winner.

He added Green to his “Story Kids file" and asked if he could stay in touch, both recalled. Illustrator Michael Martchenko followed up, looking for pictures of the family, their green house and even the dog.

The Green family's home, shown here in the 1980s, in Hay River, N.W.T. It became part of the iconic story. (Submitted by Moira Green)

“We heard later that he had continued to tell that story,” Green said, “kind of fine-tuning it and shaping it as he does by telling it to the kids and gauging their reaction."

When Munsch sent her an early draft, Green saw the story had evolved.

In the first rendition, she had received money in all of her presents. And she said she used the money to either pay for the massive order of pizza and cake — or paid her guests to help clean up.

"There was a little bit of a difference in how the story kind of tied up.”

In the published version, Moira’s beleaguered parents look at the destruction of their home. Then, the birthday girl announces that anyone who helps clean up will get one of her (many, many) presents. Within minutes, the house is spotless.

WATCH | New stories will live on after him: Robert Munsch has a lot more stories to tell | Duration 0:56 In an exclusive interview with CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, bestselling Canadian author Robert Munsch revealed he's written dozens of unreleased stories and there are plans to publish them after his death.

Reconnecting as an adult

Green and the author stayed in touch, exchanging Christmas cards, letters and signed copies of new books.

“Sometimes, he would even send manuscripts of a potential story, asking for feedback,” she said. “It was kind of a neat world to be a part of at that point — you sort of joined the Robert Munsch family."

Each of Munsch’s books — which have sold more than 90 million copies in North America alone — is dedicated to the child who inspired it. Several feature his own children: Tyya, Andrew and Julie. In fact, Julie’s decision to invite far more kids than she was allowed to contributed to the narrative behind Moira’s Birthday, the author writes.

Others, like Green, continued corresponding with Munsch — like Gah-Ning Tang, the protagonist in Where is Gah-Ning, whose letters spanned more than 30 years, leading her to eventually refer to the author and his wife as uncle and aunt, she told CBC’s Day 6 in a 2025 interview.

LISTEN | How a Hearst, Ont., girl came to call Munsch her uncle: Day 6 14:06 Gah-Ning Tang reflects on a lifetime of correspondence with Robert Munsch and his book that bears her name

Green lost touch shortly after university, she said.

Then, as a young mother in Saskatoon, she saw that Munsch was coming into town for a performance. She brought her daughter and reconnected with him afterward.

“He spent some time with us and was thrilled,” Green said. They exchanged contact information and he got in touch before his next trip to the city.

Green loved reading her copies of Munsch’s books to her four children, though “mine wasn’t necessarily their favourite,” she said, laughing.

WATCH | Munsch performs The Paper Bag Princess: Watch world-renowned storyteller Robert Munsch perform The Paper Bag Princess | Duration 4:11 Forty years ago, the story of Princess Elizabeth and the dragon launched Munsch's career and changed the face of children's literature in Canada.

As she celebrates her 49th birthday this month, she recalls being a shy kid who didn’t always appreciate the attention.

Now, though, she said she “can recognize the cool factor” in all of it.

“It’s my go-to icebreaker.”

World.title: Minimum wage hasn't kept pace with the cost of living across Canada, new reports show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Minimum wage hasn't kept pace with the cost of living across Canada amid high food prices, rents and other everyday necessities, according to a series of new reports.

Of the 59 cities and regions in the reports for every province reviewed by CBC News, none had a provincial minimum wage equal to the calculated living wage — the amount a full-time worker needs to meet their basic needs.

A gap between the two wages means a person working full-time at minimum wage would not be able to cover their basic expenses. Some of the widest gaps were found in Alberta, which has the lowest minimum wage in the country, and in parts of Nova Scotia, where living wages were driven up in some areas by significant rises in rental costs.

Brandon, Man., had just a $1 gap between its estimated $17.40 living wage and $16.40 provincial minimum wage, according to data published by the Manitoba Federation of Labour on Sept. 28. But o n the other end of the spectrum, Montreal; Halifax; the northern peninsula of Labrador; Banff, Alta.; and Whitehorse had some of the widest gaps, each between $12 and $14.

Taken as a whole, the data suggests the wage floor has been permitted to "lag considerably" behind the cost of providing for the basic necessities of life, says Tom McDowell, a lecturer in politics and public administration at Toronto Metropolitan University.

"T he minimum wage is a political measure that is largely disconnected from the actual costs of living," McDowell, who researchers living wage and basic income, told CBC News.

"The failure of the minimum wage to keep up with the rising costs of essentials can help to explain why so many households today are falling short on basic needs."

WATCH | You need $30/hour to live in Halifax, report says: Halifax living wage $30 an hour: report | Duration closed caption 5:20 Melissa Marsman, president of the Nova Scotia Federation of Labour, says the province's current minimum wage rate of $17 an hour isn't enough.

What's a living wage?

A living wage represents the hourly income required to cover basic expenses like shelter, food, transportation and child care, with enough buffer to avoid chronic financial stress and manage unexpected expenses, and to participate meaningfully in society — all based on the actual costs in that person's community.

It assumes each adult is working 35 hours per week, and considers government transfers and tax deductions, according to the Alberta Living Wage Report, released last week.

"It is also a conservative, bare-bones budget without the extras many of us take for granted," said the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives in its recent living wage update for Regina and Saskatoon.

CBC News reviewed data from nine separate provincial and regional reports compiled by different organizations, though they didn't all use the exact same methodologies to calculate living wage. Montreal's, for instance, is based on a single-person household, while the reports for Ontario, Alberta and B.C. use a weighted average of different household types.

In addition, some reports looked at specific cities, while others looked more broadly at regions. There was also no current data available for Nunavut or the Northwest Territories. So the city comparisons shouldn't be interpreted as a definitive ranking between provinces or territories.

Still, the fact remains that in all the data that's available from coast to coast, the living wage surpasses the minimum wage — and the living wage is climbing in most areas.

WATCH | Why minimum wage doesn't cover the cost of living: Struggling to get by? Here’s why minimum wage doesn’t cover the cost of living | Duration closed caption 2:26 Ontario’s minimum wage just went up by 35 cents to $17.95 an hour. Meanwhile, workers' advocates say a living wage in Toronto would actually hover around $27. So what accounts for the gap? As CBC's Kate McGillivray reports, it's the latest chapter in a debate has been raging in the province for decades over how to address poverty and balance the interests of businesses and workers.

For instance, in Whitehorse, the living wage jumped 13.3 per cent from 2025, according to the Yukon Anti-Poverty Coalition. And provincial average living wages increased just under four per cent in Nova Scotia, 5.75 per cent in P.E.I., and and 7.39 per cent in Newfoundland and Labrador compared to 2025, according to a new report from the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives.

Who isn't earning a living wage in Canada?

All told, it means there's a significant proportion of Canadians unable to raise themselves out of poverty even if they're working full time, says Molly McCracken, the Manitoba director at the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives.

"These are more likely to be women, immigrants and racialized people because that's just how the labour force is stratified," McCracken said.

In Metro Vancouver, for instance, 35 per cent of all employees earn less than the region’s living wage of $27.85 per hour, according to Living Wage B.C. The majority of them are women, and three-quarters are racialized. N early half of all racialized women working in Metro Vancouver earn less than the living wage, notes Living Wage B.C.'s May report.

On the other side of Canada, h alf of women workers in Newfoundland and Labrador do not receive a living wage, according to the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives. This includes many home-care workers and early childhood educators, the centre says.

Shelves at the North York Harvest Food Bank in Toronto on Oct. 20. A new report from the Salvation Army says nearly one in three Canadians is skipping or reducing meals because they can't afford groceries. (Frank Gunn/The Canadian Press)

In downtown St. John's, demand at the Bridges to Hope food bank is up this year by 20 per cent over last year, executive director Lesley Burgess said earlier this week, and she says inadequate incomes and high costs are driving the need.

"Food banks are designed to [provide] a few days of food to get you through an emergency until your next cheque comes," she said.

"The problem that we're seeing now is that the cheque coming is not enough to cover even the basics."

Canadian food bank usage hit record highs this year, and a new report from the Salvation Army says nearly one in three Canadians is skipping or reducing meals because they can't afford groceries.

So what needs to change?

The failure to provide an adequate living wage leaves workers chronically stretched to afford the basics of life, says McDowell, the lecturer at Toronto Metropolitan University. Some have to work additional hours or take on extra jobs to make ends meet.

The reality for those making about minimum wage may be even more dire than the data suggests, adds McCracken, because a living wage assumes someone is working full time. When more often, someone making a lower wage might be working part time or have precarious work with shifting schedules and no sick days.

So, what's the answer? The Canadian Federation of Independent Business told CBC News earlier this week that it isn't very realistic for many small- and medium-sized businesses to offer a living wage while lower profits and trade and tariff pressures are dampening bottom lines.

McDowell says the minimum wage should be formally indexed to the local living-wage benchmark and to the actual costs of living, "rather than being left to the discretion of politicians and policymakers."

"The underlying principle, however, is that full-time work should be sufficient to cover the essentials of life," he said.

There are a lot of potential benefits to increasing provincial minimum wages, McCracken added, like less employee turnover and fewer costs to the public sector for resources like employment insurance. But there also needs to be better low-income supports, like tax breaks, rent control and stronger employment standards, she says.

Manitoba's minimum wage increased to $16.40 on Oct. 1. But even then, it falls about $4 short of the living wage in Winnipeg, which, as McCracken points out, was the site of the famous 1919 general strike.

"The fight for a living wage was one of the main asks of that movement and still to this day we're fighting for it," she said.

World.title: Experts warn about risks of AI-generated content in child sexual abuse material
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains disturbing descriptions of child sex abuse. Resources and supports for anyone who has experienced sexual violence can be found at the bottom of this story.

Prince Edward Island RCMP say there has been a "notable increase" in child sex abuse material made using artificial intelligence across parts of the province. Online exploitation specialists say this surge in illegal AI-generated content could be growing the demand for real-world child abuse.

Internet watchdog reports indicate a trending global rise in AI-generated child sex abuse content, previously known as child pornography.

In an email, P.E.I. RCMP senior communications adviser Scott Ferris said it’s a "safe estimate" that one third of Island RCMP online child abuse investigations now involve AI-generated material.

That estimate considers only areas under RCMP jurisdiction, which excludes Charlottetown, Summerside and Kensington.

LISTEN | How criminals are using AI to abuse children: This is PEI 23:45 How criminals are using AI to abuse children Police on P.E.I. say the use of artificial intelligence to create child exploitation sex abuse material is on the rise — and the offenders don't even need to make contact with kids to commit a crime. CBC's Joseph Watt reports on the cases in our region, and how police are trying to stem the tide. If you or someone you know has experienced sexual violence, here’s where to get help:Victim Services P.E.I.: Queens and Kings County: 902-368-4582; Prince County: 902-888-8218.Rise P.E.I.: Phone or text: 902-218-6143.P.E.I. Rape & Sexual Assault Centre: 902-368-8055 or 1-888-368-8055.Report Child Abuse: daytime 1-877-341-3101; after hours 1-800-341-6868.You can check out a list of support services, programs, and other information on the 211 website or call 211 to be directed to the help you need.Kids Help Phone (national): 1-800-668-6868.

AI child exploitation cases are surfacing across the Atlantic region.

In St. John’s, N.L., this summer, a 17-year-old boy was charged with nearly 60 counts related to the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse material. Police allege he used AI tools to alter images of 19 minors and make them explicit.

Const. Stephanie Myers with the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary told CBC News On the Go host Krissy Holmes the case is "probably one of our first if not the first" specifically involving AI being used to create child sexual exploitation material.

A 17-year-old in St John's, N.L., faces 58 charges related to his alleged use of AI to alter images of teenagers. Const. Stephanie Myers with the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary (RNC) says this is likely one of the RNC's first AI-specific child abuse cases. (Danny Arsenault/CBC)

What is AI-generated child sexual abuse material?

Technological developments have dramatically changed how child sex abuse crimes are committed. With AI, criminals no longer need to make direct contact with an underage victim to create new abusive content.

But that doesn’t mean these are victimless crimes.

"In many of the cases … AI-generated content is either produced to create material of a child that’s in the family or the neighbourhood of that offender," said Mauranne Ste-Marie, senior research analyst with the national RCMP’s sensitive and specialized investigative services unit.

"It increases the demand for the material, it normalizes the abuse."

Certain generative AI models — which are ultimately trained on images of real people — can create abusive images or videos either in the likeness of a specific person or by generating a non-existent, synthetic child from scratch.

Some offenders also use AI-powered "nudify" tools to create explicit "deepfakes" — realistic fake images or videos of a victim.

WATCH | 'Nudify' apps and AI-generated child sex abuse material are on the rise. Here’s what you can do about it: 'Nudify' apps and AI-generated child sex abuse material are on the rise. Here’s what you can do about it | Duration closed caption 2:48 P.E.I. RCMP are investigating more child sex abuse cases that involve AI- generated images. CBC’s Gwyneth Egan has the story.

"Anyone can take pictures that are posted online ... take the face of your children and create very graphic sexual abuse material with it," Ste-Marie told CBC News.

“There are virtually no limits to what can be produced.... If their sexual preferences are for young girls with blond hair, blue eyes, they don’t need to spend time searching for that preference online anymore. They can simply create it."

Mainstream generative AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude have strict safeguards in place that are designed to block the generation of any child abuse material. Confirmed violations are supposedly then reported to law enforcement.

To circumvent these controls, offenders often rely on freely available open-source software to generate abusive media offline, where is it far harder to detect.

Since these models are typically used without an internet connection, any exploitative content they produce can be incredibly difficult for police to track.

Ste-Marie warned using generative AI models this way could lead to more real-world abuse.

"It is a stepping stone, it is one step closer to sexually abusing a child," she said.

"After viewing material for a certain number of weeks or months, it may not meet their needs anymore."

Sextortion

In an email, Summerside police reported at least one instance where a suspect used AI-generated child sex abuse material in a "sextortion" attempt this year.

Sextortion is a form of online blackmail where offenders coerce victims into sending money or explicit media by threatening to release sensitive images or videos.

In April 2023, 17-year-old Harry Burke from Fortune Bridge, P.E.I., tragically took his own life hours after telling his parents he had been victimized by a sextortion scam.

Carl Burke and Barbie Lavers hold up a photo of their son, Harry Burke. He took his own life after being victimized by a sextortion attempt. (Laura Meader/CBC)

Jacques Marcoux, director of research for the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, said AI-generated or manipulated material is increasingly used in sextortion attempts. His organization operates Cybertip.ca, Canada’s national tip line for reporting online child abuse.

"In lieu of being able to trick the child into giving them an intimate image, they’ll simply create one using AI," Marcoux said, noting that offenders then threaten to release images online, claiming that they're real.

P.E.I. RCMP media relations officer Gavin Moore said there were 26 reported instances of sextortion last year in Island areas under RCMP jurisdiction.

Moore didn’t specifically reference AI-generated material in any of these cases, but he did note reporting rates are typically "very low" for this type of crime.

"This is a type of crime that victims are extremely embarrassed [about]," Moore told CBC News.

"[It] can have very devastating and significant effects on its victims."

As AI tools become more sophisticated, it’s getting harder to tell what’s real and what’s not, said Marcoux.

Jacques Marcoux, director of research and analytics at the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, says its getting more and more difficult to tell what's AI and what's not. (Jeff Stapleton/CBC)

"Unlike three years ago … you can’t discern whether or not it’s real in many cases. It’s almost a coin flip," Marcoux said.

But, from a legal standpoint, it doesn’t matter.

Under the criminal code, AI-generated child abuse is treated the same as authentic abuse material. Altering or generating explicit media with AI through written prompts can constitute making child sexual abuse material.

Police in St. John’s, N.L., applied that standard this summer.

The 17-year-old boy, who was hit with 58 criminal charges, faces 19 counts of making child sexual exploitation material after allegedly using AI to digitally alter photos of teenage girls.

What can you do?

Since offenders can now use AI tools to create abusive material based on any image, Ste-Marie warns there is always a risk involved when posting children online.

"Every time you post a picture or a video of yourself or your children, there is a risk that it could be used by someone with bad intentions," she said, noting that one recommendation is to take precautions like covering a child's face in photos.

"The more images and information that are publicly available about a person, the easier it is for that model to create very convincing fake or manipulated content," Ste-Marie said.

"So, as soon as you reduce that availability, it makes it more difficult to create that type of content."

Although she said people can reduce the risk of being victimized, she stressed that online child abuse is never the victim’s fault.

"Your child is never responsible for the creation of that type of content, even if they posted images online and they feel like it was their fault, it never is," Ste-Marie said.

"They have the right to post and to share without thinking that someone will use it against them."
