He also expressed his opposition to the possibility of being transferred to an African country, given the difficulties he already faced in adapting to a new life after several years of imprisonment.

His concern is compounded by the revocation of his Nicaraguan citizenship, a measure that has affected numerous opponents and critics of the Ortega-Murillo regime.

The existence of a deportation order does not necessarily mean that his expulsion has already been carried out or that the transfer will be immediate. The situation will depend on pending legal proceedings and the appeal decisions of immigration authorities.

In this case, Javier’s defense team will seek to overturn the court’s decision while he remains in custody in Georgia. He is currently seeking support from human rights organizations and bodies that could help resolve his situation.

Centeno’s situation raises questions about the legal options available to people who were expelled from their country, lost their nationality, and now face deportation proceedings in the United States. It also raises questions about whether convictions handed down by governments accused of political persecution should be considered valid evidence in immigration proceedings.

In Javier Centeno’s case, there is a United Nations ruling documenting the arbitrary nature of his imprisonment, but it is not yet publicly known whether that information was fully considered in the U.S. immigration decision.

The Nicaraguan reiterates that he did not arrive in the United States on his own initiative, but rather as part of a group of political prisoners transferred from Nicaragua in February 2023.

The fear of returning to Nicaragua, the uncertainty surrounding his immigration status, and concern for his four children are all part of a situation that, as he told LA PRENSA, has deeply affected him.

The outcome of his appeal will determine whether he can continue to seek protection in the United States or whether he will face new deportation proceedings.

Seven of the 222 Nicaraguan ex-prisoners revictimized by ICE

According to a September 18th article in the Nicaraguan news site Confidencial, seven of the group of 222 have been newly detained by ICE. One was released, one has been ordered deported to Ecuador, and – at the time of the article – the others, including Centeno, were awaiting resolution of their cases.

First published in Spanish by 100% Noticias and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Nicaragua here on Havana Times.

World.title: US resumes flights after a four-and-a-half-hour shutdown caused by obsolete equipment
World.content:
US resumes flights after a four-and-a-half-hour shutdown caused by obsolete equipment

14th Saturday, November 2026 - 05:24 UTC Full article

Photo: AP / Ross Franklin

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday night lifted the nationwide ground stop it had ordered in the afternoon, after some four and a half hours of airspace closure that left thousands of flights cancelled. Donald Trump’s administration blamed the failure on overloaded, outdated analogue telecommunications equipment at air traffic control centres, ruled out a cyberattack for now and warned that the return to normal would be slow.

Airspace reopened at 8.15 p.m. Eastern time (10.15 p.m. in Montevideo), according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. According to his account at a White House press conference, at 3.36 p.m. radar and communications at control centres began giving inconsistent data, and shortly before 4 p.m. the FAA ordered that no aircraft take off. Duffy said the switches and routers of the old analogue telecommunications system became overloaded with data and began giving erroneous information. At that moment more than 3,500 aircraft were in the air, and they landed normally.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the failure was unrelated to Thursday’s global Microsoft outage and that, “as far as we have seen”, there was no cyberattack, although the investigation remains open.

More than 6,000 flights were cancelled and more than 25,000 delayed, according to FlightAware. Duffy spoke of “tens of thousands” of people stranded at airports, and the federal emergency agency, FEMA, activated its centres to ensure no passenger went without medication. Recovery will depend on the availability of pilots and crews, and flights that did not leave on Friday will be rescheduled from Saturday, less than two weeks before Thanksgiving.

Duffy used the briefing to ask Congress, which Democrats will control from January, for US$50 billion in emergency funding to build a new air traffic control system, on top of the US$12.5 billion already approved. According to the secretary, previous administrations received US$15 billion over 25 years and “barely anything was done”.

It was the third nationwide ground stop in US history, after the September 11, 2001 attacks and January 2023, when the pilot notification system failed.

World.title: US grounds all departing flights over an air traffic control communications failure
World.content:
US grounds all departing flights over an air traffic control communications failure

14th Saturday, November 2026 - 00:53 UTC Full article

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the failure affects the 22 regional centres that guide aircraft en route between airports and that FAA technicians are investigating

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday ordered a halt to all flights departing from the country’s airports “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”, following a communications failure affecting air traffic control centres. Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed and hundreds of thousands of passengers were stranded. The government has so far ruled out an attack.

The order took effect at around 4 p.m. US Eastern time (6 p.m. in Montevideo) and was extended until at least 11.30 p.m. Eastern time, according to TheStreet. “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis,” the FAA said, attributing the problem to a “temporary telecommunications outage” and saying it halted flights out of an abundance of caution. Aircraft already airborne continued to their destinations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the failure affects the 22 regional centres that guide aircraft en route between airports and that FAA technicians are investigating. According to an internal Alaska Airlines message cited by CNBC, the problems affect communications and radar.

“There was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House, though he said all possibilities were being examined. Mullin rejected comparisons with the 2001 attacks — “This is not the same as 9/11” — and warned that the problem “is not going to be resolved in an hour”.

The most affected airports were Atlanta, Chicago O’Hare and New York’s airports, according to FlightAware. Just over two million passengers fly domestically in the US each day, and the disruption comes less than two weeks before Thanksgiving, the busiest travel period of the year. United and American Airlines said international departures were also being handled case by case.

It is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a failure of the pilot notification system halted take-offs for hours, and before that since the September 11, 2001 attacks.

World.title: Microsoft restores services after a global outage hit Outlook and Teams in more than 70 countries
World.content:
Microsoft restores services after a global outage hit Outlook and Teams in more than 70 countries

13th Friday, November 2026 - 17:09 UTC Full article

In Australia, the outage affected the tax office, some courts, the Federal Police, the ASIO intelligence agency and the New South Wales state services platform

Microsoft said on Friday its services were recovering after a global outage that began on Thursday afternoon, European time, and for hours affected millions of users in more than 70 countries, including public bodies in Australia and Japan. The company ruled out a cyberattack.

The disruption hit Outlook email, the Teams work platform, SharePoint Online, the Copilot artificial intelligence assistant, the OneDrive and OneNote cloud services and the Microsoft 365 suite, widely used by businesses and governments. “We’re seeing continued progress in recovery across affected regions,” the company said, warning that some users could still experience intermittent problems. “We know our customers rely on our services to do important work every day, and we’re sorry for the impact these outages had,” it added.

“At this time, I can confirm there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platforms, wrote on X. According to the company, several servers unexpectedly became unavailable and their load shifted to the remaining ones, in a domino effect that overwhelmed systems linked to Exchange Online, its email service. There is still no definitive analysis of what happened.

In Australia, the outage affected the tax office, some courts, the Federal Police, the ASIO intelligence agency and the New South Wales state services platform. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke activated a clause in the digital resilience agreement signed with Microsoft in June so that the country would receive priority in restoring services. In Japan, government spokesman Minoru Kihara confirmed that the government’s IT infrastructure was also disrupted, with no incidents at health facilities. Problems were reported in public services in Singapore and the Philippines, and in Thailand four major banks temporarily suspended email-dependent services.

Complaints on the Downdetector platform peaked first on Thursday afternoon, European time, and a second wave came on Friday morning, before returning to normal levels in the afternoon. According to the company, Microsoft 365 has more than 450 million corporate users and 95 million consumers, and Teams more than 320 million.

World.title: Chile tells Argentina “countries do not ask permission” for its ship bound for the Falklands
World.content:
Chile tells Argentina “countries do not ask permission” for its ship bound for the Falklands

13th Friday, November 2026 - 17:06 UTC Full article

The Chilean-flagged Danstar aims to restore a route suspended for some 15 years, carrying food, machinery and building materials as an alternative to supplies from Montevideo

Chile’s Foreign Minister Francisco Pérez Mackenna has ruled out asking Argentina for authorisation for the voyage of the Chilean vessel Danstar, which plans to reopen the commercial route between Punta Arenas and the Falklands in December, invoking the right of innocent passage recognised by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. “Countries do not ask permission,” he said, according to Argentina’s La Nación.

“Chile believes in the right to free navigation, which is guaranteed, the right of free passage, innocent passage, as it is called in UNCLOS maritime law. And we trust that right will be respected,” Pérez Mackenna said. He was responding to his Argentine counterpart, Pablo Quirno, who said on Monday on the A24 channel that the vessel must request permission to cross Argentine jurisdictional waters. “Thousands of ships pass through the Strait of Magellan every year. There are thousands of ships that ask for authorisation to cross when they leave for the Malvinas,” Quirno said. Since 2010, Argentina has required by decree prior authorisation for ships sailing between the mainland and the islands or crossing Argentine waters towards them.

The Danstar, a 72-metre Chilean-flagged cargo ship operated by Easter Island shipping company, aims to restore a route suspended for some 15 years with a cargo of food, machinery and construction materials, as an alternative to the supplies that arrive regularly from Montevideo. The private-sector initiative is promoted by the Falkland Islands Development Corporation and backed by Punta Arenas. “We want to be the islands’ big supermarket,” said its mayor, Claudio Radonich.

The Argentine government fears the route could provide logistical support to the Sea Lion oil project. Quirno recalled “the Chilean government’s commitment that this will not contribute logistically to the exploitation of natural resources” in the islands. According to La Nación, Chilean diplomats privately expressed “indignation” that Argentina has tolerated regular trade between the islands and Uruguay for years but concentrates its pressure on Chilean vessels. Argentina’s Foreign Ministry denies seeking to provoke an incident.

The exchange comes during a key week in the dispute over the islands. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will announce on November 28 its decision on Argentina’s request to halt Sea Lion, after the hearings in Hamburg, and Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies is debating the sovereignty defence bill, which toughens sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation in the archipelago. In October, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham raised with Chilean President José Antonio Kast London’s interest in the islanders’ right to self-determination.

World.title: Leo XIV to 52,000 young people in Lima: “Be passionate about everything worthwhile”
World.content:
Leo XIV to 52,000 young people in Lima: “Be passionate about everything worthwhile”

13th Friday, November 2026 - 02:58 UTC Full article

Photo: REUTERS/Yara Nardi

Pope Leo XIV met some 52,000 young people at Lima’s National Stadium on Thursday, according to El País, in the last event of his stay in the Peruvian capital before travelling to Chiclayo, the diocese he led as bishop. “Someone told me that Peru needs hope. You are the sign of hope,” he told them, to applause.

The young people came from the coast, the highlands and the jungle, many with parish groups and others on their own, and alongside Peruvian flags there were also Venezuelan and Chilean ones. The Pope entered the stadium track in the popemobile at around six in the evening, as the stands displayed signs asking for his blessing. The vigil included testimonies, a theatrical performance in which Peruvian saints came to the rescue of young people in crisis, music and scissor dancers, an Andean ritual.

At around half past seven, Leo XIV spoke with a message of comfort and encouragement. “Dear young people, when you suffer, turn to Jesus. Do not be afraid to speak to him sincerely. He knows our tears,” he said. “Be passionate about everything worthwhile. Cultivate your talents. Discover the richness of your culture. Do not settle for living according to what others expect of you.” He ended with an invitation to those who believe they are beyond redemption: “It is not too late to begin again.”

The Archbishop of Lima, Cardinal Carlos Castillo, recalled during the event Inti Sotelo and Bryan Pintado, the two young men of around twenty who were shot dead during the November 2020 protests. “In the recent history we have lived through in our country, young people often took to the streets to protest and in some cases several were shot. There are two martyrs: Inti and Bryan,” he said. Castillo said that after the crackdown many young people found in dance a form of expression that eventually reached the parishes. The testimonies included that of a young woman who lost a dozen relatives and of a nun who suffered abuse by a member of the Church.

Leo XIV, 71, who is recovering from lung cancer surgery, celebrates Mass on Friday at the Pampas de Pimentel, near Chiclayo, where nearly a million faithful are expected. On Saturday he will visit Cajamarca and Zaña, and on Sunday Cusco and Pucallpa, before returning to Rome on Monday, November 16.

World.title: British veteran returns to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took in 1982
World.content:
British veteran returns to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took in 1982

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:01 UTC Full article

Aged 18, Andy Gatrick found two wounded Argentine soldiers, later captured, at Mount Harriet in June 1982 and kept one’s helmet, which bore a name: Hector. Photo: Mick Dawson

A former Royal Marine has travelled to Argentina to return to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took during the Battle of Mount Harriet in the 1982 Falklands War, in a reunion filmed for a documentary, BBC Sussex reported.

Andy Gatrick, who was 18 at the time of the war, came across two injured Argentine soldiers during the Battle of Mount Harriet, fought on June 11 and 12, 1982. Both were captured by the Marines. Gatrick kept the helmet of one of them, which bore a name: Hector. Now 63, he managed to track him down and on October 23 flew to Gualeguaychú, in Entre Ríos province, to return it in person to Héctor Pereyra.

“I put my weapon down and as I bent down to put the strap over my shoulders, I saw movement and a cloth which looked like a white handkerchief. My eyes adjusted and there was two Argentinians, I didn’t know they were badly injured. I dived to the floor, weapon up. There was lots of shouting and swearing, bedlam,” Gatrick, from Bolton in northern England, said in footage sent to the BBC.

He was joined by another Royal Marine veteran, Mick Dawson, 62, who filmed the meeting for a documentary called Hector’s Helmet. According to Dawson, the British kit was poor and the Marines fought in berets, while the Argentines had American helmets, so Gatrick “borrowed” Pereyra’s. “In a very emotional day, he handed the helmet back in person to the guy he could have just as easily killed that night,” Dawson told BBC Radio Sussex. The two veterans “embraced like long lost brothers”, he said.

Dawson interviewed Pereyra about the moment when, wounded, he saw Gatrick emerge from the darkness. “He said, ‘I knew this man had the power of life or death over me and he chose life’,” Dawson recounted. “He then showed me a picture of his nine grandchildren and four children that wouldn’t have existed if Andy made a different decision that night. It was just the most amazing thing to witness.”

Dawson hopes to release the documentary next year. The 74-day war in 1982 left 907 dead: 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British personnel and three civilian islanders.

World.title: Lula to visit Madrid on Monday to meet Sánchez, two weeks before Spain’s election
World.content:
Lula to visit Madrid on Monday to meet Sánchez, two weeks before Spain’s election

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 18:02 UTC Full article

The visit will also include a political event at which Lula will expressly back the Socialist candidate, and Sánchez’s team had spent two weeks trying to arrange it

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will visit Madrid on Monday, November 16, to meet Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, less than two weeks before the snap general election on November 29, in which Sánchez is seeking re-election. It will be Lula’s first visit to Spain since he won Brazil’s election on October 25.

According to the Spanish government’s official statement, the two will hold a bilateral meeting at the Moncloa Palace to discuss relations between the two countries and coordination of initiatives such as Democracy Always and the Global Alliance against Hunger and Poverty. Lula will stop in Madrid on his way back from the UN climate summit, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, where he will also make a state visit to the Philippines.

According to the Spanish press, the visit will also include a political event at which Lula will expressly back the Socialist candidate, and Sánchez’s team had spent two weeks trying to arrange it. Sánchez has presented Lula’s re-election and the Democratic victory in the US midterms as proof that the advance of the radical right can be halted.

CNN Brasil reported that Lula will be accompanied by congressman André Janones, the architect of the digital strategy that helped his electoral comeback. The Spanish government and the Socialist Party insist that Janones is not advising Sánchez’s campaign and there are no plans for him to do so.

Polls show a slight recovery for the Socialists, so far insufficient to govern. A survey by 40dB for El País and Cadena SER shows the Socialist Party up almost two points, but the People’s Party and Vox would together win a comfortable absolute majority of more than 190 seats; 176 are needed to govern. The state-run Centre for Sociological Research shows a stronger Socialist recovery.

Neither Lula nor Sánchez attended the Ibero-American Summit held in Madrid last week. According to El País, Lula needed to rest and recover his voice after the campaign. Sánchez spoke by phone on Thursday with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum about bilateral relations and the outcome of the summit.

World.title: Paraguay’s banking superintendent arrested in the Ueno Bank investigation
World.content:
Paraguay’s banking superintendent arrested in the Ueno Bank investigation

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 11:20 UTC Full article

Insfrán was named in a criminal complaint expanded by opposition lawmakers last week, alongside the economy minister and other officials

Paraguay’s Superintendent of Banks, Holger Insfrán, was arrested on Thursday as part of the investigation into the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has already led to the pre-trial detention of former President Santiago Peña and former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, according to prosecution sources cited by the EFE news agency. The charges against him have not been disclosed.

The Superintendency of Banks, part of the Central Bank, is responsible for supervising and regulating Paraguay’s financial institutions, including Ueno. Insfrán was named in a criminal complaint expanded by opposition lawmakers last week, alongside the economy minister and other officials.

According to prosecutors, Ueno received large amounts of public funds during Peña’s term, including from five pension funds, while granting allegedly irregular loans to companies owned by its owners, the Vázquez Group. The bank had 2.94 million customers.

Peña, removed by the Senate on November 6, is charged with alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator, and could face a maximum sentence of 15 years, according to prosecutors. He says he is innocent. Carvallo, who headed the finance company from which the bank emerged before Peña appointed him to lead the Central Bank in 2023, is accused of breach of trust, producing false public documents and self-serving administration.

The Central Bank said on Wednesday that 100% of customers covered by the state guarantee have received an advance of up to 40 minimum wages, about 121.8 million guaraníes or roughly US$19,600, under the emergency law passed by Congress. It has until Monday to complete repayments up to the guarantee ceiling of 75 minimum wages, about 228.3 million guaraníes or roughly US$36,600.

World.title: Ready to host another World Cup? Mexico-US-Costa Rica-Jamaica joint bid for 2031 women’s tournament likely
World.content:
Mexico appears set to host another World Cup in less than five years after FIFA green lighted a joint hosting bid of which the Mexican Soccer Federation is a part.

FIFA, soccer’s international governing body, announced on Wednesday that the bid to host the 2031 Women’s World Cup submitted jointly by Mexico, the United States, Jamaica and Costa Rica “has a strong foundation” and will be voted on at the Extraordinary FIFA Congress on Nov. 23.

If approved (as the lone bid, it is expected to pass with little difficulty), it would mark the second FWWC to be hosted jointly after Australia and New Zealand co-hosted the 2023 tournament.

The Congress will also be considering the joint bid to host the 2035 FIFA Women’s World Cup (FWWC) submitted by England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Next year’s FWWC is to be hosted by Brazil and will feature 32 teams and 64 matches. The 2031 tournament will be expanded to include 48 teams and 104 games.

The joint 2031 bid proposes 20 host stadiums across the four countries, with 14 in the United States, four in Mexico and one each in Jamaica and Costa Rica. Mexico’s proposed host cities are Mexico City (Estadio Azteca), Guadalajara (Estadio Akron), Monterrey (Estadio BBVA-Bancomer) and Torreón, Coahuila (Estadio Corona).

Following a thorough assessment of the proposal, including inspection visits to the prospective host countries, FIFA published an evaluation report indicating that the bid exceeded its minimum requirements.

“While certain commitments require further engagement, there is a sound basis for confidence that continued dialogue and collaboration with the relevant government agencies should support the successful organization and delivery of the tournament,” FIFA said.

In endorsing the bid, FIFA acknowledged the success of this year’s men’s World Cup which Mexico and the U.S. co-hosted alongside Canada.

FIFA also praised Mexico’s “longstanding record as a FIFA host, having staged the FIFA World Cup in 1970 and 1986, the FIFA Confederations Cup in 1999 and multiple youth competitions, including the FIFA U-20 World Cup 1983 and FIFA U-17 World Cup 2011.”

The technical evaluation focused on “defined priority areas, including the event vision, infrastructure, services and commercial considerations” as well as FIFA Fan Festival sites, while the risk assessment considered “safety and security, sustainability, human rights and environmental protection.”

As co-host, Mexico’s women’s team would be participating in its fourth FWWC after qualifying for the 1999, 2011 and 2015 tournaments. The El Tri Femenil also participated in the unofficial 1971 Women’s World Cup hosted by Mexico. The first FWWC was held in 1991.

With reports from Reuters, Fox Sports, FIFA and ESPN

World.title: New faces and old favorites: Mexico’s 2026 Latin Grammy wins
World.content:
Mexican and Mexican American artists won in at least 10 categories at the Latin Grammys in Las Vegas on Thursday — from 22-year-old Xavi collecting his first two trophies to hitmaker Edgar Barrera becoming the awards’ most decorated winner ever.

Nominated in six categories, Silvana Estrada won one award with her song “Dime,” while Texan Bobby Pulido followed his election to Congress last week with his third Latin Grammy — then announced his retirement from music.

The 27th annual ceremony at Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena also featured a first win for Guadalajara-born mariachi singer Camila Fernández and a big centennial tribute to the late Mexican singer-songwriter and ranchera legend José Alfredo Jiménez.

Barrera, born in McAllen, Texas, to a Mexican family, converted a leading 10 nominations into two awards: producer of the year and best regional song for “No Capea.” The two wins brought his career total to 31, breaking the all-time Latin Grammy record he had shared with Puerto Rican rapper Residente.

Xavi, Grupo Frontera – No Capea (Official Video)

Watch this video on YouTube

Barrera, 36, shared the songwriting award with five co-writers, including Xavi and Grupo Frontera singer Adelaido “Payo” Solís III. The prize recognizes the writers, not every member of the performing group.

Xavi won both his nominations, also taking best contemporary Mexican music album for “Dosis.” Born Joshua Xavier Gutiérrez Alonso in Arizona, Xavi was raised largely by his grandparents in Nogales, Sonora, before moving to Phoenix at age 15 with his father.

Grupo Frontera, a Mexican-American band that formed in Texas in 2022, won best norteño album for “Lo Que Me Falta Por Llorar.”

Fernández won best ranchero/mariachi album for “La Fernández.” The 28-year-old is the daughter of ranchero star Alejandro Fernández and the granddaughter of the late Vicente Fernández, one of Mexico’s most famous entertainers of all time.

Edén Muñoz, 36, the former Calibre 50 frontman from Los Mochis, Sinaloa, won best banda album for “Piedras a la Luna.” He was also nominated for best regional song as the writer of “Osadía,” his duet with Cristian Castro.

Estrada, 29, recently named the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s first creative chair for Latin music, received six nominations, including album of the year for “Vendrán Suaves Lluvias” and record and song of the year for “Dime.”

Silvana Estrada — Dime (Video Oficial)

Watch this video on YouTube

The ballad about heartbreak and the liberating power of anger didn’t win in those two categories, but it did garner best singer-songwriter song. The native of Coatepec, Veracruz, now has two Latin Grammys, following her best new artist award in 2022.

Alejandra, Daniela and Paulina Villarreal — three sisters from Monterrey, Nuevo León, who make up the hard-rock trio The Warning — shared best rock song honors for “Ego” with three co-writers.

Mexico City singer Marco Barrientos shared best Spanish-language Christian album for “Eterno” with two others.

Pulido, who has Mexican heritage, won his third Latin Grammy, taking best Tejano album for “Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol.2/En Vivo).”

“I want to tell you that I’m retiring from music, and I’m leaving with so much gratitude,” Pulido said in Spanish while accepting the award. He missed the traditional group photo for incoming House members while traveling to Las Vegas, according to The Hill.

Afterward, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries congratulated his fellow Democrat in a social media post: “Felicidades and what a month for Congressman-Elect Pulido.”

¡Felicidades! @bobbypulido425 Mejor Álbum de Música Tejana 🎶👏👏👏 #LatinGRAMMY https://t.co/e39HDhTISH — The Latin Recording Academy / Latin GRAMMYs (@LatinGRAMMYs) November 12, 2026

Chilean Mexican singer Mon Laferte, who has a house in Tepoztlán, Morelos, performed “Femme Fatale” — a week after a concertgoer threw a cellphone that struck her in the face — but went winless in six categories.

Carín León lost both his nominations, for record and album of the year.

Arath Herce from the city of Veracruz went winless in four categories: best new artist, singer-songwriter album, singer-songwriter song and pop/rock song.

Spanish singer Rosalía won five awards, including album of the year for “LUX (Complete Works)” and song of the year for “La Perla.” Argentine singer Milo J took four, including record of the year for “Niño.”

Colombian singer Aria Vega won best new artist, besting a field that included Mexicans Herce, former street sweeper Macario Martínez and Sofía Monroy.

In all, Mexican and Mexican American artists won across all six regional Mexican categories, an umbrella grouping for styles including mariachi, banda and norteño. For the full list of winners, see Billboard.

With reports from Billboard, Uno TV, Infobae and Hola!

World.title: Mexico sets a new record for tourist arrivals and spending, even as growth slows
World.content:
Listen to this article

Despite increased travel costs, a decline in air arrivals and a lack of promotion, Mexico registered record figures in international tourist arrivals and spending during the first nine months of 2026.

Data compiled by national statistics agency INEGI through September indicates that foreign currency spending by travelers grew 1.4% year-on-year to nearly US $26.1 billion and the number of international tourists rose 3.8% to 35.97 million people.

However, rising travel costs are blamed for a drop in the segment of tourists arriving by air which experts link to the lower dynamism observed since these travelers represent 80% of tourism foreign exchange.

The INEGI report, released on Thursday, reveals that the 1.4% increase in tourism revenue is lower than the 6.1% growth recorded during the first three quarters of 2025.

Additionally, the International Travelers Survey (EVI) found that the 3.8% increase in international tourist arrivals (by air and by land) came in below the 6.4% rise registered during the same period last year.

After the release of the EVI and INEGI data, the Tourism Ministry on Friday lauded “the historic records both in the arrival of international travelers and in their spending.”

The private sector does not share this enthusiasm.

Humberto Molina, tourism analyst at Grupo Empresarial Estrategia, told El Economista newspaper that although the accumulated results are good, it’s clear that tourism “isn’t taking off,” lamenting the lack of a public policy to provide certainty of sustained growth in the short term.

“In addition to the lack of promotional campaigns, next year will be impacted by the 17.8% increase in the Non-Resident Tax paid by foreign tourists (1,158 pesos starting in January),” he said.

The private sector has also criticized the government’s lack of attention to the tourism sector, describing the 20 million pesos dedicated to tourism in the 2027 budget proposal as “clearly insufficient to promote the different destinations and segments of tourism in the source markets and in the national market.”

The decline in air arrivals is seen as the biggest challenge.

The INEGI figures reflect a cumulative decrease for two consecutive years in that indicator, unseen since records began, impacting the country’s three primary sun and beach destinations: Cancún, Los Cabos and Puerto Vallarta.

The Center for Advanced Research in Sustainable Tourism (STARC) at Anáhuac University Cancún reported that, through October, the airports that service these three locations have seen a cumulative reduction of 1.9 million international passengers compared to 2025.

Still, spending by tourists arriving by air increased by 7.1% in September.

One reason cited for the September boost is the gradual recovery of business tourism, which had contracted due to this summer’s World Cup.

This could be good news for the tourism sector since the second half of the year is popular for Mexico’s meetings industry, with an increase in congresses, exhibitions and conventions.

With reports from El Economista, UnoTV and La Jornada

World.title: Mexico has delivered less than 1% of the water it owes to the US as border dams run low
World.content:
Despite recent agreements to resolve the situation, Mexico continues to have problems meeting its water-delivery commitments to the United States, having covered only 0.36% of the deficit it accumulated during the 2020–2025 water-sharing period.

According to the U.S. section of the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC), as of Oct. 24, Mexico this year had delivered only 3,159 acre-feet of the 865,139 acre-feet it owes from coming up short in the previous five-year period. It has until 2030 to pay off the rest, during which period it is also obligated to send north 350,000 acre-feet per year to meet its current obligations for the 2025-2030 period, which will total 1,750,000 acre-feet.

Mexico and the U.S. share water from the Río Bravo under the terms set out in a 1944 water treaty that establishes that Mexico must deliver to the U.S. a minimum of 350,000 acre-feet of water every year. But Mexico concluded the five-year cycle spanning Oct. 25, 2020 – Oct. 24, 2025, delivering only 884,861 acre-feet, resulting in a deficit of 865,139 acre-feet owed to the U.S.

In October, the two countries signed onto a plan that was meant to ease repayment with both agreeing to use less water from the Río Bravo (called the Rio Grande in the U.S). But compliance continues to drag.

A major factor hampering Mexico’s water delivery commitments has to do with reduced reserves, as international border dams La Amistad and Falcon remain at less than 30% capacity.

According to data from the Mexico section of the IBWC, as of Oct. 26, La Amistad dam, located on the Río Bravo along the border of Coahuila with Texas, stood at 28% of its capacity. Meanwhile, Falcon, located along the border of Tamaulipas and Texas, was at 17%.

Water deliveries from Mexico are stored in those dams.

Roberto Constantino, a researcher at the Metropolitan Autonomous University (UAM), told the newspaper El Economista that reduced availability in the Río Bravo and Colorado River basins threatens both compliance with binational agreements and the water supply on both sides of the border.

The expert suggested that the 1944 Water Treaty should be revised to better reflect current environmental conditions. However, he noted that bilateral tensions and the trade agenda make this an inopportune time to initiate such negotiations.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: El Jalapeño: Disgruntled Quetzalcóatl not recognized on his long-awaited return to Mexico
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

VERACRUZ — Quetzalcóatl, the Feathered Serpent, Lord of the Dawn and Creator of Mankind, expressed profound frustration Friday after making his long-prophesied cosmic return to the shores of Veracruz, only to discover that no one seemed to recognize him.

The deity, who descended upon the port city in a blaze of iridescent plumage, windstorms and celestial lightning, reported that despite checking every traditional physical requirement of the Mesoamerican return myth, locals merely asked if he had a reservation for the port tour or if he was part of a promotional campaign for a local craft brewery or something.

“I manifested on the exact promised date, riding a raft of interwoven serpents, wielding the wind of the four cardinal directions, and people just kept walking past me to get iced coffee,” said Quetzalcóatl, speaking to reporters while attempting to parse a laminated city map. “From time immemorial, it has been written that when a bearded figure arrives from the east, he’s coming to reclaim his throne. But apparently times have changed.”

According to municipal officials, the god’s arrival caused minor traffic delays along the malecón, but failed to trigger the existential awe documented in ancient texts.

“We had a gentleman in full ceremonial feathers claiming to control the cycle of Venus and the rebirth of the sun,” said Veracruz transit officer Roberto Morales. “He seemed very surprised when we asked him to move his serpent-raft out of the commercial loading zone. I told him that while we respect cosmic creators, the dock permit guidelines apply universally.”

Sources close to the deity confirmed he attempted several standard divine demonstrations, including summoning localized squalls and speaking in ancient Nahuatl verse, but was repeatedly directed toward the municipal cultural center’s administrative desk.

World.title: Sheinbaum denies ‘friction’ in bilateral ties after US reportedly shelters a wanted Mexican official: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🔎 Sheinbaum asks Security Cabinet for information on Zuany: Responding to a Thursday New York Times report that former Chihuahua special prosecutor Guillermo Zuany Portillo has fled to the U.S. and is under U.S. government protection, Sheinbaum said “the story about this character is long” and that she didn’t want to discuss it. However, she said his alleged collaboration with U.S. authorities is “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship” and that she will ask the Security Cabinet for all the information it has on him, including his whereabouts.

Responding to a Thursday New York Times report that former Chihuahua special prosecutor Guillermo Zuany Portillo has fled to the U.S. and is under U.S. government protection, Sheinbaum said “the story about this character is long” and that she didn’t want to discuss it. However, she said his alleged collaboration with U.S. authorities is “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship” and that she will ask the Security Cabinet for all the information it has on him, including his whereabouts. 🇲🇽 🇺🇸 No friction expected with U.S.: Asked whether the Zuany situation could strain bilateral ties, Sheinbaum said it wouldn’t.

Asked whether the Zuany situation could strain bilateral ties, Sheinbaum said it wouldn’t. 📊 Gap between INEGI and SESNSP homicide data under review: Sheinbaum said a working group is looking into why INEGI’s 2025 homicide total (29,488) is well above the SESNSP’s (24,348), a difference of 5,140. She noted that the monthly figures presented at her press conference come from state Attorney General’s Offices, while INEGI uses death certificates and other records. INEGI data shows a 12.1% drop in homicides in 2025, compared to 21.2% per the SESNSP’s numbers.

Sheinbaum said a working group is looking into why INEGI’s 2025 homicide total (29,488) is well above the SESNSP’s (24,348), a difference of 5,140. She noted that the monthly figures presented at her press conference come from state Attorney General’s Offices, while INEGI uses death certificates and other records. INEGI data shows a 12.1% drop in homicides in 2025, compared to 21.2% per the SESNSP’s numbers. 🏍️ Drug lord’s motorbikes fetch 71 million pesos: INDEP director Mónica Fernández said the auction of Ryan Wedding’s luxury motorcycles raised 70.91 million pesos (US $3.8 million), about 11 million pesos above expectations. Fifty-seven of the 62 motorcycles were sold, and the remaining five will go up for auction in late November. Proceeds will go to the Office of the Presidency to fund social justice projects, including for the widows of the 2006 Pasta de Conchos mine disaster and for Indigenous Raramuri and Amuzgo communities.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The New York Times’ reporting on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, was once again a topic of discussion at President Sheinbaum’s morning press conference.

The Times reported on Tuesday that Zuany had facilitated the operation of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency in Chihuahua and, in exchange, his U.S. visa — reportedly revoked “because of his suspected ties to the very cartels the C.I.A. wanted to root out” — was reinstated. At her Wednesday morning press conference, Sheinbaum described the report as “very interesting,” and said that it was “worth learning about” who Zuany is “and how he collaborated with one of the U.S. agencies.”

On Thursday, the Times reported that Zuany — who is wanted by Mexican authorities — had fled to the United States.

The former prosecutor’s alleged cooperation with the CIA is part of a larger story that has remained in the headlines in Mexico for much of 2026. In April, CIA officers allegedly participated in a drug lab raid alongside Chihuahua state forces without the authorization or knowledge of the federal government. Two CIA agents and two Chihuahua police officials were killed in a car accident after the raid.

The CIA’s alleged participation in the operation has strained relations between the federal government and the Chihuahua government, which is led by Governor Maru Campos of the National Action Party, Mexico’s main opposition party. It also led Sheinbaum to accuse the U.S. government of interference in Mexico. The former attorney general of Chihuahua, César Jáuregui, was taken into federal custody last month on a charge of treason related to the CIA’s alleged involvement in the drug lab raid.

Beyond the case involving Zuany and the CIA, another notable topic at today’s mañanera was homicide statistics.

A range of experts have expressed skepticism about the accuracy of the Sheinbaum administration’s homicide statistics, with claims that state-based Attorney General’s offices — which provide homicide data to the federal government — are fudging the numbers. There has been renewed focus on the accuracy of the data this week after the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) reported over 5,000 more homicides in 2025 than the federal government’s Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System (SESNSP), the largest gap in more than a decade.

Sheinbaum: US collaboration with former Chihuahua prosecutor won’t cause friction in bilateral ties

A reporter asked the president about a report published by The New York Times on Thursday that states that Zuany “has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.”

“The story about this character is long,” Sheinbaum said.

“I don’t want to talk about it here at this time,” she added.

Sheinbaum said that Zuany’s collaboration with U.S. authorities is “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship” between Mexico and the United States.

She said she would ask the federal government’s Security Cabinet to provide all the information it has about Zuany, including anything it knows about his current whereabouts.

🚨Claudia Sheinbaum considera que el caso de Guillermo Zuany, exvicefiscal de Chihuahua señalado por presunta corrupción y vínculos con el crimen organizado, es relevante para la relación entre México y Estados Unidos. La presidenta pidió al Gabinete de Seguridad informar sobre el caso de Zuany, quien se encuentra en territorio estadounidense. 🗞️Israel Aldave | @Radio_Formula — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) November 13, 2026

“Hopefully the federal Attorney General’s Office or the Security Cabinet can provide information,” Sheinbaum said.

Asked whether “the situation” with Zuany could create “friction” between Mexico and the United States, the president responded:

“No, because it’s been spoken about with the U.S. government.”

Sheinbaum said in April that the U.S. government had agreed to comply with the Mexican Constitution and Mexican laws in bilateral security cooperation. She also expressed confidence that U.S. participation in a security operation on Mexican soil wouldn’t be repeated.

Sheinbaum says government is reviewing discrepancy between INEGI and SESNSP homicide numbers

A reporter asked the president about the discrepancy between INEGI’s 2025 homicide statistics and those of the SESNSP.

Sheinbaum said that the gap between INEGI’s 2025 homicide total (29,488) and that of the SESNSP (24,348) is “something we’re reviewing with INEGI.”

She stressed that the homicide statistics presented at her press conference on a monthly basis come from the country’s Attorney General’s Offices. Sheinbaum noted that INEGI looks at death certificates and records (among other information) when classifying deaths as homicides. She also noted that INEGI publishes preliminary and final data on homicides. Sheinbaum said that the upward revision in INEGI’s 2025 homicide count between its preliminary and final figures was larger than in previous years.

“We have a working group to look at why this situation occurred,” she said.

“And we’re also looking at the difference in each state between what the Attorney General’s Offices reported and what the civil registry later reported. This revision is done with INEGI,” Sheinbaum said.

The Security Ministry said in August that the difference between INEGI’s homicide numbers and those of the SESNSP is “expected” as “each institution performs different functions, uses different [data] integration procedures, has different collection, validation, and publication periods, and generates information for specific purposes.”

However, “both sources show the same trend with respect to the evolution of intentional homicide,” the ministry said.

INEGI’s final data shows that homicides declined 12.1% in 2025 compared to the previous year, whereas the SESNSP reported a significantly larger reduction of 21.2%.

Auction of drug trafficker’s motorbikes raises 71 million pesos

Mónica Fernández, director of the Institute to Return Stolen Goods to the People (INDEP), reported early in the press conference that the auction this week of a collection of luxury motorcycles formerly owned by Canadian drug lord Ryan Wedding raised 70.91 million pesos (US $3.8 million). That amount was around 11 million pesos above expectations.

“We sold 57 of 62 motorcycles,” Fernández said, noting that the motorbikes were seized by authorities and subsequently handed over to INDEP in July.

Wedding’s motorcycles were seized last December after authorities raided four properties in Mexico City and México state linked to the former Olympic athlete known as The King of Cocaine. Wedding turned himself into Mexican authorities in January after more than a decade on the run.

Fernández noted that there was a large turnout at the auction of the drug trafficker’s motorbikes, which was held in Mexico City.

She said that the five motorcycles that weren’t sold will be put on the block at another INDEP auction to be held in late November.

The resources obtained from this week’s sale of Wedding’s motorbikes and other seized assets will be allocated to the Office of the Presidency, and will be used to finance social justice projects, including actions benefiting the widows of the 2006 Pasta de Conchos mine disaster and communities of the Indigenous Raramuri and Amuzgo peoples.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: El Tri is back in action Saturday in its first official match of the Rafa Márquez era
World.content:
After a winless start to the Rafa Márquez era, Mexico’s national soccer team has an opportunity to right the ship on Saturday evening in Kingston, Jamaica.

El Tri will take the field at Independence Park against underdog Jamaica in the first leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, making it Márquez’s first official match as Mexico manager.

Márquez, who succeeded Javier Aguirre after serving as his top assistant during the 2026 World Cup, has yet to win a match as Mexico’s top man. El Tri is 0-2-2 since he took over, including an embarrassing 3-0 loss to Team USA.

For this two-game stretch (the second leg will be played in Monterrey on Tuesday), Márquez summoned a more experienced squad than he did for the four friendlies during the September-October window.

Back with the team is forward Julián Quiñones, who was Mexico’s leading scorer during the World Cup. Also returning are winger Jesús Corona (a 33-year-old with experience in Europe) and fullback Rodrigo Huescas, who missed the World Cup after suffering a knee injury 13 months ago.

However, the team will be without top striker Raúl Jiménez, who underwent surgery to repair his medial collateral ligament last month.

Teen midfielder Gilberto Mora will be expected to direct the El Tri attack, while captain Johan Vásquez and Erik Lira form the backbone of the defense. All eyes will be on goalie Raúl Rangel whose two howlers against Team USA won’t soon be forgotten.

As humiliating as it was to lose to the U.S. in the manner they did, Mexico’s players realize that, as heavy favorites to advance to the semifinals, a loss to Jamaica would be even more devastating.

The defending Nations League champions are ranked 59 spots above Jamaica in the FIFA World Rankings (Mexico is No. 10, Jamaica No. 69), losing just three of 29 matches against The Reggae Boyz, while winning 21 and drawing five. And El Tri has outscored Jamaica 72-15 overall.

However, Mexico is only 3-3-1 in its last seven official matches against Jamaica, including a 1-0 loss in the 2017 Copa Oro semifinals.

Jamaica’s other two victories over Mexico were by identical 1-0 scores: in an Oct. 11, 2008, World Cup qualifier and in a Nov. 17, 1996, World Cup qualifier.

Still, The Reggae Boyz failed to qualify for this summer’s World Cup even though Concacaf had six slots in the tournament. Jamaica finished second to an upstart Curaçao side in the regional final group stage, then lost to DR Congo in an interconfederation playoff.

With reports from SBNation, ESPN and Soy Fútbol

World.title: MND Local CDMX: Pilgrimage preparations, ancient remains and delivery protests
World.content:
From preparations for one of Mexico’s largest annual religious gatherings to archaeological discoveries and transportation projects, Mexico City has plenty happening this November.

Authorities are gearing up to welcome millions of pilgrims to the Basilica of Guadalupe, while construction of a major passenger rail connection revealed an unexpected discovery. Meanwhile, a proposed licensing overhaul for motorcycle delivery workers hit a roadblock following protests.

Let’s get into it.

Authorities outline priorities for ‘Operation Basílica 2026’

Mexico City authorities have begun organizing a major security and public services operation ahead of Día de la Virgen de Guadalupe, the annual December celebrations honoring the Virgin of Guadalupe. Approximately 13 million pilgrims are expected to visit the Basilica of Guadalupe this year, which is on par with last year’s figures.

The Gustavo A. Madero borough, home to the religious complex, held its first interagency planning meeting earlier this month to coordinate the “2026 Operativo Basílica.” More than 30 federal and local government institutions are expected to participate in the effort.

The operation will cover public security, traffic management, emergency medical assistance, civil protection, sanitation and more. Participating agencies include the National Guard, Mexico City’s Citizen Security Ministry, the Navy, the National Defense Ministry, the Red Cross, the fire department and the city’s Metro and Metrobús systems.

Planning and coordination

Gustavo A. Madero Mayor Janecarlo Lozano said early coordination is necessary to manage crowds and ensure authorities can respond quickly to emergencies.

“Our responsibility begins with the planning stage and continues until the pilgrims begin their journey home,” Lozano said, according to Excelsior. “We want them to find guidance when they need it, assistance when they require it, and dignified treatment at all times.”

The holiday and pilgrimage honor an event in 1531, when an apparition of the Virgin of Guadalupe is said to have appeared to an Indigenous peasant named Juan Diego on a mountain above the holy site.

Last year’s operation provides a starting point for this year’s preparations. In 2025, the borough deployed 10,600 city workers, 250 law enforcement officers and 110 law enforcement vehicles. Authorities also installed 450 portable toilets, 26 hydration stations and two bike parking structures capable of housing 12,000 bicycles.

“We have years of experience and the opportunity to improve,” Lozano said, according to Milenio. “Let’s make each meeting a source of clear agreements and use all our institutional capacity to provide a timely response to the people. Because governing is about caring, we work together to live up to the trust of millions of people.”

INAH discovers possible pre-Hispanic ossuary during Mexico-Querétaro train works

Meanwhile, archaeologists have uncovered what may be an ancient ossuary containing human remains and artifacts at Mexico City’s Buenavista railway terminal, according to a news release from Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH). The discovery was made Sept. 17 during construction work on the Mexico City-Querétaro train line.

Researchers have so far identified nine human skeletons, five mandibles and several other bones, including ribs, femurs and pelvic fragments.

According to Secretary of Culture Claudia Curiel de Icaza, the discovery reveals new dimensions to the region’s pre-Hispanic funerary practices and how they honored their dead.

1 of 3

“A possible ossuary speaks not only of death: it raises questions about how the ancient communities of this territory treated and remembered their dead during a time of profound change,” Icaza said in a statement.

The burial deposit may date to the Late Postclassic period (1200-1519) or the early years of Spanish contact (1519-1535). Associated artifacts include domestic pottery, miniature spindle whorls, figurines and stone tools. Several obsidian blades may have originated in Hidalgo’s Sierra de las Navajas region.

“Taken together — bone fragments and ceramics — they could correspond to the final years of the pre-Hispanic period and the colonial era (1535-1821),” said José Manuel Cervantes Pérez, head of the Physical Anthropology Laboratory.

The recovered materials have been transferred to laboratories in Hidalgo for cleaning, restoration and further study.

“The associated materials offer clues to this encounter between different historical moments; it will be up to the INAH to study them rigorously and explain what they reveal,” Icaza said. “In this way, a history that lay hidden beneath the city can be incorporated into the knowledge of everyone.”

Mexico City-Querétaro train line construction is now 32% complete

Speaking of the Mexico City-Querétaro train line, construction has reached 32% completion, President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Oct. 31 during a visit to a portion of the project in Polotitlán, State of Mexico.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Expansion (@expansionmx)

Additionally, Sheinbaum said 90% of the land rights needed for the project have been secured and that construction is progressing according to schedule.

At a cost of roughly 700 billion pesos, the approximately 230-kilometer railway will connect Mexico City with Querétaro, passing through the State of Mexico and Hidalgo. The journey is expected to take approximately two hours, with trains averaging 130 kilometers per hour.

The route will feature six stations: Buenavista in Mexico City, Huehuetoca and Teoloyucan in the State of Mexico, Tula de Allende in Hidalgo, and two stops in Querétaro.

Sheinbaum described the project as part of a broader effort to revive passenger rail services across the country, which in turn would offer an alternative to increasingly congested highways.

According to officials, 47 trains have been contracted and are currently being manufactured.

Mexico City suspends special license and commercial plate plan for delivery drivers

And now a win for the thousands of men and women who keep this city humming via Rappi, Uber Eats and countless other delivery services …

Mexico City authorities have suspended a pilot program that would have required motorcycle delivery workers operating through digital platforms to obtain special licenses and commercial plates, following protests over the proposed regulations.

The city’s Mobility Ministry (Semovi) reached the agreement Nov. 9 after Secretary Héctor Ulises García Nieto met with representatives of several groups to discuss their concerns. Both sides also agreed to establish additional working groups to review any revised proposals and develop an alternative regulatory framework.

The announcement followed several hours of demonstrations in western Mexico City, where app-based delivery workers blocked major roads in the Santa Fe area, causing traffic delays.

‘Unnecessary administrative hurdles’

Protesters argued that the proposed requirements would impose unnecessary administrative hurdles and additional expenses on workers who already hold motorcycle licenses. Some also complained about frequent police enforcement operations targeting delivery riders during their shifts, as well as unsafe working conditions.

“I mean, we already had a license, first the regular one, then they made us get another one for a motorcycle, and now a special one. It’s tough,” a delivery driver who did not give their name told La Gazzetta DF. “Besides, the police are around all the time on this side; there are operations, they keep driving their trucks around us, and now the National Guard is involved, they show up and everything. It’s like we’re criminals, and we’re not.”

Semovi said the initiative was intended to organize motorcycle-based delivery services and improve protections for workers in a sector that has historically faced precarious working conditions.

The program’s suspension leaves the proposed licensing and registration requirements under review, with further discussions expected between authorities and motorcycle delivery groups.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Bolivia to Repay Banks US$438M in Dollars
World.content:
BOLIVIA · DOLLAR LIQUIDITY

The central bank will release dollar cash held by banks and credit unions in stages, with small rural lenders paid first and most money due next year.

Bolivia’s central bank will hand back US$438 million in dollar cash to the country’s financial institutions by the end of September 2027. The Banco Central de Bolivia (BCB), the state monetary authority, announced the plan in press note NP 27/2026 on Friday 13 November 2026.

The same decision lets all new dollar operations run without restrictions, after years in which some of them were limited. It builds on earlier steps in our report on dollar withdrawal limits in Bolivia.

Key Facts Who Banco Central de Bolivia (BCB), the central bank, returns dollar cash that lenders hold with it.

Amount US$438 million in total, paid out from 13 November 2026 to 30 September 2027.

Next date US$43 million is due on Friday 18 December 2026 for 18 institutions.

Biggest part US$384 million, about 88% of the total, is due in 2027 for 8 institutions.

New rule New dollar operations run “without any restriction” through special accounts, under Resolution 162/2026, announced 13 November 2026.

What the Central Bank Decided

Board Resolution No. 162/2026 contains two measures, the BCB said in its note of Friday 13 November 2026. The first creates “Auxiliary Liquidity Accounts” (Cuentas Auxiliares de Liquidez) for all financial intermediation entities, meaning banks, credit unions and similar lenders.

New dollar operations through these accounts cover transfers abroad, cash movements and transfers between institutions. The BCB said they run “without any restriction”, something that “had been restricted in recent years”.

From 13 November the BCB publishes the combined balances of these accounts on its website. The central bank said this gives “full certainty” that the money is available at the BCB.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 13th of 14 with 27.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: economic weight (11). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.6%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The BCB describes the package as a move toward the “full normalisation of foreign-currency operations in the whole financial system”. It also reaffirmed its commitment to “transparency and price stability” in the same note.

The snow-capped Illimani mountain above La Paz, Bolivia. File photo: Hernan Payrumani via Wikimedia Commons.

Who Gets Paid and When

The second measure is a schedule for the US$438 million that institutions held in their current and reserve accounts at the BCB as of Tuesday 10 November 2026, the BCB said. Reserve accounts hold the legal reserve (encaje legal) that lenders must keep with the central bank.

On Friday 13 November 2026 the BCB credited US$11 million to 35 institutions that held up to US$1 million there. The note says these lenders mainly serve people in rural areas and on the edges of cities.

On Friday 18 December 2026 the BCB will credit US$43 million to 18 more institutions that held less than US$5 million. The last US$384 million goes to the 8 remaining institutions on Friday 30 April 2027 and Thursday 30 September 2027.

By our arithmetic, about 12% of the total returns in 2026 and about 88% in 2027. The note does not give the split of the US$384 million between the two 2027 dates.

Why the Timing Matters

The mechanism is simple: dollar cash that lenders deposited at the BCB comes back to them in instalments, smallest holders first. The 8 remaining institutions wait until 2027 for US$384 million, about 88% of the total, according to the BCB schedule in its note of 13 November.

Small rural lenders therefore regain their cash first, while the 8 institutions that held the rest of the money are paid last. That order comes from the BCB’s own schedule, and the note does not explain the reasoning.

The step follows press note NP 26/2026 of Friday 30 October 2026. In it, the BCB moved the return of US$333 million to households with deposits between US$10,001 and US$50,000 forward to Thursday 5 November 2026, up to 130 days earlier than planned.

From Monday 9 November 2026, institutions manage the legal reserve on new foreign-currency deposits themselves, so the money stays available for withdrawals. The BCB said this should avoid repeating the “corralito” (a freeze on access to dollar savings) that people faced “since February 2023”.

What It Means for Savers and Firms

Directly affected are Bolivian banks, credit unions and their clients. The new accounts cover transfers abroad, so businesses that pay foreign suppliers in dollars may also feel the change, though the note does not say so.

The BCB note names no consequence for the United States or for US investors. The note itself is silent on any wider effect.

Four dates are fixed in the BCB note. Friday 18 December 2026 brings US$43 million for 18 institutions, and Friday 30 April and Thursday 30 September 2027 together bring US$384 million.

According to its note of Friday 30 October 2026, the BCB’s remaining household returns continue on the schedule it set in May 2026. The same note moved the US$333 million for mid-sized household deposits forward to Thursday 5 November.

From 13 November the BCB publishes the aggregate balances of the new accounts on its website. Readers can compare those figures with the dated instalments above.

What Is Not Known

The BCB note names no institution, so it is not known which lender receives which amount. It also does not say how the US$384 million splits between 30 April 2027 and 30 September 2027.

The note does not say whether the new Auxiliary Liquidity Accounts earn interest. We found no published reaction from ASOBAN, the association of Bolivian private banks, or from economists as of Saturday 14 November 2026.

No named critic has challenged the schedule, so we cannot cite an opposing view. The schedule itself shows that most of the money, about 88%, comes back only in 2027.

The BCB note gives no US figure or consequence, so none is claimed here. Its stated aim is the normalisation of dollar operations across the whole financial system.

In Plain English BCB: Banco Central de Bolivia, the country’s central bank, which sets monetary policy and holds banks’ reserves.

Banco Central de Bolivia, the country’s central bank, which sets monetary policy and holds banks’ reserves. Financial intermediation entities: Banks, credit unions and similar lenders that take deposits and make loans.

Banks, credit unions and similar lenders that take deposits and make loans. Reserve account (encaje): Money that lenders must keep at the central bank as a legal reserve.

Money that lenders must keep at the central bank as a legal reserve. Corralito: A freeze on access to dollar savings, which the BCB says people faced since February 2023.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much dollar cash is Bolivia’s central bank returning?

The BCB will return US$438 million in dollar cash to financial institutions, from 13 November 2026 to the end of September 2027.

When do Bolivian lenders get their money back?

US$11 million was credited on 13 November 2026 and US$43 million follows on 18 December 2026. The remaining US$384 million is due on 30 April and 30 September 2027.

What are the Auxiliary Liquidity Accounts?

They are new BCB accounts for banks, credit unions and similar lenders. New dollar operations through them run without restriction, and the BCB publishes their combined balances online.

Which institutions get which amounts?

The BCB note does not name any institution. It only says 35 small lenders, 18 more and 8 remaining ones are paid in that order.

Sources: Banco Central de Bolivia, press note NP 27/2026, 13 November 2026; Banco Central de Bolivia, press note NP 26/2026, 30 October 2026.

World.title: Argentina Lose 2-1 to Uruguay Without Messi
World.content:
ARGENTINA · FOOTBALL

Argentina lost a friendly to Uruguay with two early second-half goals against them, in the first match since Lionel Messi retired from the national team.

Argentina lost 2-1 to Uruguay in Buenos Aires on Friday 13 November, in their first match since Lionel Messi, who now plays club football for Inter Miami in the United States, retired from the national team in early October. The friendly was played at La Bombonera, the Boca Juniors stadium, the Argentine Football Association (AFA) said in its match report of 13 November.

Uruguay scored twice early in the second half, through an own goal by Argentina defender Leonardo Balerdi in the 48th minute and a goal by forward Maximiliano Araújo in the 53rd. Argentina forward Julián Álvarez pulled one back for Argentina in the 73rd minute, and our preview of the friendly has the kick-off details.

Key Facts Result Uruguay beat Argentina 2-1 at La Bombonera in Buenos Aires on Friday 13 November.

Goals Argentina defender Balerdi own goal (48th) and Uruguay forward Maximiliano Araújo (53rd); Argentina forward Álvarez (73rd).

Context A friendly, so no points or qualification at stake; the first match since Messi retired.

Next Argentina play Costa Rica in Córdoba on Tuesday 17 November, 20:00 local time.

Number 10 Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni has left the No. 10 shirt unassigned.

How Uruguay Won at La Bombonera

The match was 0-0 at half-time, according to Montevideo Portal, a Uruguayan news site, in a report published on Friday 13 November. It wrote that Argentina controlled the first half, and that the clearest chance was a shot by Álvarez that Uruguay’s goalkeeper Cristopher Fiermarín saved in the 7th minute.

The first goal came when Uruguay midfielder Giorgian De Arrascaeta crossed and defender Ronald Araújo flicked the ball on, Montevideo Portal wrote. Argentina defender Lisandro Martínez headed it clear, but it hit Balerdi and went into the net.

Maximiliano Araújo made it 2-0 five minutes later with a header at the near post from a De Arrascaeta corner, according to the same report. Álvarez pulled one back in the 73rd minute, but Argentina did not find an equaliser, the AFA match report shows.

The referee was Flavio Rodrigues de Souza of Brazil, the AFA said. Lionel Scaloni coached Argentina and Diego Forlán coached Uruguay.

Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes in Córdoba at night during a league match in 2016, the venue of Argentina’s next match. File photo: Alepizarro32, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

A Team Without Its Number 10

This was Argentina’s first match since Messi retired from international football in early October, the Associated Press (AP, a US news agency) reported on 13 November. Scaloni left the No. 10 shirt unassigned, AP said, and he has not picked a successor and says it is not mandatory.

AP judged that Argentina kept its polished possession but “lacked the explosive, incisive spark that Messi typically delivered in the final third”. It added that neither Argentina players Nicolás Paz nor Thiago Almada filled that void.

Scaloni took a different view at his press conference on 13 November, saying the team played well in general, as the AFA recorded. The two judgments differ: AP saw a missing spark, while the coach saw good things to analyse.

What Scaloni Said After the Match

Scaloni said at the press conference on 13 November, in remarks we have translated from Spanish, that “beyond the final result, the match leaves good things to analyse”. He added that Argentina knew Uruguay would be a difficult rival and must keep working, according to the AFA transcript.

He said Uruguay deserved congratulations and called them “a good team” that gives the powers a game. On Tuesday, he said, he will surely make some changes, but some players should repeat to gain rhythm.

He also said he has “no doubt the fans will support us” and that the team must repay that trust. Scaloni extended his contract through 2030 earlier this week, AP reported on 13 November.

The same report said La Bombonera fell short of a sellout.

What This Means for Argentina Followers

Nothing in a league table or in qualification was at stake, because the AFA described the match as a friendly in the November FIFA window, the period reserved for international games. The result therefore matters for mood and for the debate on how Argentina plays after Messi, not for points.

For US readers, this was a first look at Argentina after Messi’s international retirement, which AP dated to early October. Messi still plays club football for Inter Miami in the United States, according to our earlier reporting.

Argentina play Costa Rica on Tuesday 17 November at 20:00 local time at the Mario Alberto Kempes stadium in Córdoba, the AFA said. It is the second and last match of the window.

Uruguay host the Dominican Republic on the same day, Tuesday 17 November, AP reported. Our Argentina news page will carry the Costa Rica match.

What Is Not Known

Scaloni has not named a successor to the No. 10 shirt, and he said it is not mandatory to pick one, AP reported on 13 November. It is not known who, if anyone, will wear that shirt against Costa Rica on Tuesday.

AP gave no attendance figure, only that the stadium fell short of a sellout. Scaloni did not name the changes he plans for Tuesday, he said at the press conference on 13 November.

It is not yet clear how the 2-1 defeat will change his view of the squad. He said the team played well in general, but he gave no further detail on what he would adjust.

The Argentine Football Association, the body that runs Argentina’s national team. Friendly: A match that counts for no league table and no qualification.

A match that counts for no league table and no qualification. FIFA window: A period set aside for national teams to play, which pulls players away from their clubs.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the score between Argentina and Uruguay?

Uruguay won 2-1 at La Bombonera in Buenos Aires on Friday 13 November, the AFA said. Álvarez scored Argentina’s goal in the 73rd minute.

Did Lionel Messi play against Uruguay?

No. It was Argentina’s first match since Messi retired from international football in early October, AP reported, and the AFA line-up does not list him.

Who scored the goals in Argentina against Uruguay?

Leonardo Balerdi’s own goal (48th minute) and Maximiliano Araújo (53rd) scored for Uruguay. Julián Álvarez (73rd) scored for Argentina, the AFA said.

When does Argentina play next?

Argentina play Costa Rica on Tuesday 17 November at 20:00 local time in Córdoba, the AFA said. It is the last match of the November window.

Cosan, a Brazilian holding company listed in São Paulo, is replacing its chief executive after about two years in the job. It has named an interim leader but no permanent successor.

What Cosan Announced

Cosan, a Brazilian holding company listed on the B3 stock exchange in São Paulo under the ticker CSAN3, said in a statement on Friday 13 November 2026 that it has started a succession process for its chief executive, Marcelo Eduardo Martins. Martins will leave the post on Monday 4 January 2027, about seven weeks after the announcement.

Cosan owns stakes in Rumo, a rail operator, Compass, a gas distributor and pipeline group, and Moove, a lubricants maker. Raízen, a fuel and sugar-ethanol company, was set up as a joint venture of Cosan and Shell, the global energy company, and went through an out-of-court restructuring this year.
