WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Martins has spent 20 years in the group and has been chief executive since 2024. He stays on the boards of Cosan, Rumo, Compass and Moove and will support shareholders and his successor, especially on strategy and mergers and acquisitions.

Cosan said the transition will be run with planning and transparency, in line with its governance practices. The stated aim is continuity of strategy and value for shareholders.

File photo of a building carrying the logo of Raízen, the fuel and sugar-ethanol joint venture of Cosan and Shell. Photo: Raphael Henrique Figueira, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Rumo (Brazil) Email address Follow

Who Takes Over

The board elected Guilherme Penin, now vice president of Strategy, Communications and Institutional Relations, to take over as interim chief executive when Martins leaves on 4 January 2027. Interim means temporary, so Penin holds the job until a permanent chief executive is chosen.

Penin has more than 20 years in the infrastructure sector and about a decade in the Cosan group. The company says he already takes part in the portfolio’s strategic decisions.

The company lists two milestones from the Martins years. They are the 2025 capital raise by Cosan with new shareholders, including BTG Pactual, a Brazilian investment bank, and Perfin, a Brazilian investment manager, and leading, together with Raízen’s team and Shell, the out-of-court restructuring of Raízen, known in Brazil as an extrajudicial recovery.

Live Company Intelligence Cosan S.A — the full investor dossier Company overview and the latest Rio Times coverage.

What It Means for You

For a reader in the United States, the change matters mainly to people who follow Cosan’s American depositary receipts (ADRs), certificates that represent Brazilian shares. In a material fact (a formal disclosure to the market) dated 18 August 2026, Cosan told the market that it would delist them from the New York Stock Exchange, with 18 September 2026 as the expected last trading day there, as we reported in our coverage of the delisting.

From 4 January 2027, the group’s strategy sits with Penin as interim leader until a permanent chief executive is chosen. The company has not said whether its plans will change under him or under a permanent successor.

A leadership change at a group this size can move its shares, but we have no price reaction to report. This article is not investment advice.

For the background on the company’s move away from Wall Street, see how Cosan quit Wall Street. Our Brazil news page collects the latest business stories from the country.

What to Watch

Cosan’s investor-relations page lists a conference call for Monday 16 November 2026 at 09:00 Brasília time (12:00 UTC), after the third-quarter earnings release listed for Friday 13 November after the market close. Investors may listen for any word on the succession process.

The second date is Monday 4 January 2027, the day Martins leaves the chief executive post. Cosan has not said whether a permanent successor will be named by then.

What Is Not Known

Cosan has not named a permanent successor and has not said why Martins is leaving beyond calling it a succession process. We also do not know how the shares will react.

Cosan’s calendar lists its third-quarter results for release after the market close on Friday 13 November 2026, and this article does not cover them. Nor has the company said whether Penin is a candidate for the permanent role.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is leaving Cosan?

Marcelo Eduardo Martins, chief executive since 2024 and a 20-year veteran of the group, will leave the post on Monday 4 January 2027. He stays on the boards of Cosan, Rumo, Compass and Moove.

Who runs Cosan in the meantime?

Martins stays in the job until 4 January 2027. The board elected Guilherme Penin, vice president of Strategy, Communications and Institutional Relations, to take over as interim chief executive from that date, and he has more than 20 years in infrastructure and about a decade in the group.

Has Cosan named a permanent chief executive?

No. The company said it started a succession process and gave no name or timetable for a permanent successor, and no reason beyond that wording.

Does this affect US investors?

Cosan told the market in August 2026 that its American depositary receipts would leave the New York Stock Exchange, with 18 September 2026 as the expected last trading day, and its shares stay on B3 in São Paulo. Holders of either face a leadership change; this is not investment advice.

Chief executive José Ignacio Jiménez backs opt-out enrolment: workers join unless they decline. Afore Inbursa, the pension manager of Grupo Financiero Inbursa, a Mexican financial group, wants Mexican workers enrolled in voluntary retirement saving unless they opt out. Its chief executive says no pension system can rest on mandatory contributions alone.

What the Afore Chief Said

Afore Inbursa, one of Mexico’s Afores (private firms that manage workers’ retirement savings), belongs to Grupo Financiero Inbursa. Its chief executive, José Ignacio Jiménez, said in a recent interview that no modern pension system can rest only on mandatory contributions.

He spoke ahead of the Amafore 2026 meeting, Amafore being the association of Mexico’s Afores. Voluntary saving, he said, should be pushed as early as possible.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 70.8 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Jiménez said the industry should push automatic enrolment with a “negative option”, an opt-out design in which workers join unless they decline. He said it should cover workers already registered in the system, the Sistema de Ahorro para el Retiro (SAR), Mexico’s retirement-savings scheme.

Such strategies “have been very successful in several countries”, he said. They built large savings in European countries and raised replacement rates, the share of pre-retirement pay that a pension covers.

The longer people wait, he said, the greater the effort needed to reach a better pension. He called rising life expectancy a main structural challenge in Mexico and worldwide, since savings must fund an ever longer retirement.

Education should start early, even in schools, Jiménez said. Retirement, he added, should be seen as a life stage that can last two or three decades.

Office towers in Mexico City. File photo.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Mexico Email address Follow

Why Informality Matters

Jiménez said independent workers must be brought into the SAR on a recurring basis. He put labour informality, meaning work outside formal employment, at about 55% of employed people.

That, he said, means low contribution density, because workers pay in for only part of the time. He called Mexico’s mixed system, contributory Afores plus the Universal Pension for Older Adults (a state pension needing no contributions), “not only convenient but necessary”.

The core challenge, he said, is not only about pensions but also about labour and productivity. Voluntary saving is no longer a complement but strategic, he said, because it can offset informal periods or interruptions in work.

Small flexible amounts can build habits without high incomes, he said. Technology, digital contributions, schemes for the self-employed and simplified enrolment can help close the gap.

What It Means for You

Treat this as an industry idea, not policy, because nothing in the interview points to a rule change. Afores hold Mexican workers’ retirement savings and invest in Mexican assets, so investors and families with ties to Mexico follow the system closely.

For background, see how Mexico’s pension funds recovered from a record loss in the first half of 2026. Also read why Mexico wants its pension pool to build the country.

Our Mexico news page tracks the pension story as it develops. Nothing here is investment advice.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the government or CONSAR, the pension regulator, plans any enrolment reform, and we found no current rule or announced plan from either. We also lack Afore Inbursa’s size and returns, and the date of the Amafore 2026 meeting.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Afore Inbursa chief propose?

José Ignacio Jiménez said Afores should push automatic opt-out enrolment into voluntary saving for workers already in the SAR. It is an industry proposal, not a government plan.

What does opt-out enrolment mean?

Workers are enrolled in voluntary saving automatically unless they decline. Jiménez said such strategies have been very successful in several countries.

Why does informality matter for pensions?

Jiménez put informality at about 55% of employed people, which he said means workers contribute only part of the time. He called voluntary saving strategic to offset those gaps.

Sources Interview with Afore Inbursa chief executive José Ignacio Jiménez ahead of the Amafore 2026 meeting, published in November 2026.

KENYA · POLITICS

Key Facts The country Kenya votes in a general election on Tuesday 10 August 2027, the electoral commission has set.

What happened Gachagua, a former Deputy President, buried his 77-year-old sister in Nyeri County on Saturday 14 November 2026.

Who came Kalonzo Musyoka of the Wiper party and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna joined the mourners.

The family Eunice Nyangari Gachagua died in Naro Moru, and her brother announced the death on 6 November.

Kenya's opposition leaders attended the burial of Rigathi Gachagua's sister in Nyeri County on Saturday 14 November 2026. Gachagua is a former Deputy President who now opposes President William Ruto, and Kalonzo Musyoka and Edwin Sifuna joined the family and other mourners.

For US readers, the day matters because Kenya votes in 2027 and the opposition has not yet named its one candidate. Who attends such events shows which rivals stand together in public.

What Happened

The burial took place in Nyeri County, in the central highlands where Gachagua comes from. His 77-year-old sister, Eunice Nyangari Gachagua, died in Naro Moru, a place in Nyeri County, and he announced her death on 6 November.

Gachagua described her as a mother figure who helped hold the family together after their mother died seven years ago. The family remembered her for her warmth and wise counsel.

Kalonzo Musyoka, a former Vice President who leads the Wiper party, and Edwin Sifuna, a Nairobi senator who leads the Linda Mwananchi movement, were among those who joined the mourners. Both joined the family and other mourners at the ceremony.

Who Is Who

Rigathi Gachagua was Kenya's Deputy President from 2022 until the Senate removed him from office in October 2024, in a process called impeachment. He now leads his own opposition party and criticises President William Ruto.

Kalonzo Musyoka served as Vice President from 2008 to 2013 and has sought the presidency before. Edwin Sifuna represents Nairobi in the Senate, the upper house of Parliament.

Our guide to Kalonzo Musyoka's presidential bid explains his record. It also sets out what he plans for the 2027 vote.

In Plain English

Nyeri County lies in the central highlands north of Nairobi and is Gachagua's home area. The Wiper party and the Linda Mwananchi movement are two of the groups opposed to President Ruto.

The electoral commission, known as the IEBC, runs Kenya's elections. It has set Tuesday 10 August 2027 as the date of the next general election.

Why It Matters

Seeing Gachagua, Kalonzo and Sifuna in one place raises the question of who the opposition will put forward against Ruto. The vote is set for Tuesday 10 August 2027.

The opposition has said it will back one candidate against Ruto, but it has not named who that will be. Gatherings like this are signals, not decisions.

What It Means for You

Travellers to Nyeri or Nairobi need not change plans because of the burial. Political gatherings in Kenya can draw large crowds, so visitors should avoid them and follow local advice.

Investors in Kenyan bonds and companies follow the election closely, since the result will set the government's direction. US firms with Kenyan operations should watch whether the opposition forms one alliance.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the leaders moved closer on naming a joint candidate. Nobody has publicly named one.

Reports differ on the exact village of the burial, and the speeches of Kalonzo and Sifuna could not be confirmed. Nothing in the public record shows what the leaders said to each other.

Whose Burial Did Kenyan Opposition Leaders Attend?

They attended the burial of the 77-year-old sister of former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua. It took place in Nyeri County on Saturday 14 November 2026.

Who Attended the Burial in Nyeri?

Kalonzo Musyoka, leader of the Wiper party, and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna joined the family. Gachagua, her brother, announced her death on 6 November.

Why Does the Burial Matter Politically?

Public gatherings show who stands with whom ahead of the vote. The opposition has said it will back one candidate but has not named who.

When Is Kenya's Next General Election?

The electoral commission set Tuesday 10 August 2027 as the date. Candidates have not yet been named.

PANAMA · SECURITY

Key Facts The country Panama, home of the Canal, runs its economy on the US dollar.

What happened A court sentenced 18 people on Friday 13 November 2026 for selling drugs in San Miguelito.

The sentences Terms run from 80 to 120 months, or about 6.7 to 10 years in prison.

The case Prosecutors say the group sold drugs near schools, shops, sports courts and a mall.

Panama learned on Friday night that 18 people will spend between about 6.7 and 10 years in prison for selling drugs in San Miguelito, a district north of Panama City. The Attorney General's Office announced the sentences on Friday 13 November 2026 in a case it calls Operation Shield.

For US readers, the case shows how Panama, a US dollar economy, fights drug sales at street level and not only at its ports. Operation Shield is the name prosecutors gave to the investigation, not a military action.

What Happened

Panama's Attorney General's Office, which leads criminal prosecutions in the country, announced the convictions on the night of Friday 13 November 2026. A Tribunal de Garantías, a Panamanian court that supervises criminal cases before trial, imposed the sentences after the accused accepted responsibility.

The prosecutors built the case through the Specialised Drug Crimes Prosecutor's Office of San Miguelito, working with the National Anti-Drug Directorate, the drug unit of the National Police. They say the investigation began in July 2026.

The charges were selling and trading illegal substances, and in some cases simple possession. The court set the sentences after the accused accepted responsibility.

Who Got What

The Attorney General's breakdown by area, the corregimientos or sub-districts of San Miguelito, shows terms of 80, 82, 84, 86 and 120 months. Five people arrested in the José Domingo Espinar area each received 86 months, and four arrested in Belisario Frías received 84 or 86 months.

In Omar Torrijos Herrera and in Arnulfo Arias, one person each received the longest term of 120 months. The other groups were arrested in Amelia Denis de Icaza, Belisario Porras and Mateo Iturralde.

The Attorney General's Office puts the number at 18, and its area-by-area breakdown adds up to 18. Some outlets reported 20 people, and one reported two others still in process.

How the Group Operated

Prosecutors say the accused sold drugs near shops, schools, sports courts and a shopping centre in the district. They say some drugs were hidden in sweets.

Officers seized synthetic drugs, cocaine, marijuana, cash and mobile phones. The announcement does not say how much of each drug was found.

The neighbourhoods named include El Poderoso, Santa Marta, Torrijos Carter, Cerro Batea, Samaria, Mano de Piedra, Cerro Viento, El Crisol and Villa Lucre. The list continues with other places, which the announcement does not name.

In Plain English

Operation Shield is the name prosecutors gave to this drug-sales investigation. San Miguelito is a densely populated district north of Panama City.

Tribunal de Garantías means a guarantees court: the judge who checks that arrests were legal and approves plea deals. Simple possession means holding drugs without selling them.

Why It Matters

Our report on a seizure of 914 suspected drug packages showed enforcement at the border end of the trade. That case and the San Miguelito case are separate investigations.

Recently a court also jailed nine alleged gang members. The announcement does not say whether the accused are linked to any larger network.

What It Means for You

Travellers to Panama City will not notice a change, since the case concerns local drug sales in one district. Anyone visiting should still follow local police advice.

Investors in Panama's banks and logistics firms should treat this as a law-enforcement story, not a market event. It names no company and no shipment.

What Is Not Known

It is not known who supplied the drugs or whether the group belongs to a larger network. The announcement gives no amounts, street values or names of those sentenced.

Some reports say 20 people were convicted, and one outlet says two others are still being processed. The announcement does not say whether any of the accused will appeal.

More: Panama news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is Operation Shield in Panama?

It is a drug-sales investigation run by prosecutors and the National Police in San Miguelito since July 2026. A court has now sentenced 18 people to 80 to 120 months in prison.

How Long Are the Sentences?

They range from 80 to 120 months, or about 6.7 to 10 years. The court set the sentences after the accused accepted responsibility.

Where Is San Miguelito?

It is a densely populated district just north of Panama City. The case covers neighbourhoods such as El Poderoso, Santa Marta and Cerro Viento.

What Drugs Were Found?

Officers seized cocaine, marijuana, synthetic drugs, cash and phones, with some drugs hidden in sweets. The announcement gives no quantities.

Sources: Attorney General's Office of Panama (Procuraduría General de la Nación, part of the Ministerio Público), announcement on the convictions in Operation Shield, 13 November 2026; Specialised Drug Crimes Prosecutor's Office of San Miguelito.

World.title: Tanzania Urges Bank to Fund Carbon Projects
World.content:
The Dar es Salaam skyline seen from a high point, in an undated photo. Tanzania's ministries sit in Dodoma, and the photo does not show Parliament. Photo: Ali Damji / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

TANZANIA · CLIMATE FINANCE

On Friday 13 November 2026, Tanzania’s National Carbon Monitoring Centre (NCMC), the government body that coordinates carbon trading, and CRDB Bank signed a memorandum of understanding, a type of cooperation agreement. CRDB is a Tanzanian commercial bank.

The signing took place that Friday in Antalya, Türkiye, on the sidelines of COP31, the United Nations climate conference. It matters because Tanzanian carbon project developers, and the buyers of their carbon credits, need finance to build projects.

Key Facts Deal NCMC, Tanzania’s carbon monitoring body, and CRDB Bank signed a cooperation agreement.

Where Antalya, Türkiye, at COP31, the UN climate conference, on Friday 13 November 2026.

Aim Support the development, financing and expansion of carbon trading projects in Tanzania.

Government ask The minister urged CRDB to design loans, guarantees and other investment instruments.

Open No financing amount or project list has been announced.

Tanzania’s government wants a large bank to finance carbon projects. Money, projects and timing have not been published.

What Happened

NCMC and CRDB Bank signed the memorandum at a CRDB side event in Antalya. The event was held on the sidelines of COP31.

Hamad Yussuf Masauni, Minister of State in the Vice-President’s Office (Union and Environment), the ministry that handles environment and Union affairs between the mainland and Zanzibar, spoke at the signing. He urged CRDB to design innovative financial products, such as loans, guarantees and other investment instruments.

The minister said these products should help carbon project developers get capital, subject to the bank’s assessments and legal requirements. He also stressed that projects must comply with the Environmental Management Act, Tanzania’s main environmental law.

Projects must also follow the Environmental Management (Control and Management of Carbon Trading) Regulations, 2022, as amended in 2023. These regulations govern carbon trading in Tanzania.

File photo. A container ship leaves the harbour of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, 2018. Photo: Rasheedhrasheed / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Tanzania Email address Follow

Who Was in the Room

Richard Muyungi, Permanent Secretary in the Vice-President’s Office (Union and Environment), attended the signing. So did Ngenda Kathryn Kigaraba, Executive Director of NCMC.

Abdulmajid Mussa Nsekela, CRDB Bank’s Chief Executive Officer, also attended. He said the partnership would open investment opportunities and attract capital.

Nsekela added that it would help carry out carbon projects with economic and social benefits. NCMC brings experience in coordinating and overseeing carbon trading, while CRDB brings financial services and investment capacity.

In Plain English

Carbon credits are certificates for emission cuts or removals that can be sold. A memorandum of understanding is a cooperation agreement that sets out how two sides plan to work together.

Background

NCMC was launched in 2016 at Sokoine University of Agriculture in Morogoro, with NIBIO, a Norwegian research institute, as technical partner. It is the coordinator of Tanzania’s national system for measuring and reporting emissions.

Tanzania’s carbon trading regulations took effect on 28 October 2022 under Government Notice 636 of 2022, the official gazette number of the regulations. The 2026 agreement builds on that legal framework.

Why It Matters

Carbon project developers need capital, and that is what the minister asked CRDB to help supply. Buyers of Tanzanian carbon credits are also affected, because the deal aims to expand the projects that create the credits.

No financing figure has been published, so no number yet shows the scale of the support. The effect on developers will depend on the products CRDB designs.

What Is Not Known

No financing amount, number of projects to be funded or first products has been announced. We could not confirm any CRDB or NCMC press release on the memorandum.

It is also not known whether the memorandum is legally binding. Both sides have yet to say how the cooperation will be run.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Tanzania and CRDB Bank sign?

Tanzania’s National Carbon Monitoring Centre and CRDB Bank signed a memorandum of understanding on Friday 13 November 2026. It aims to support the development, financing and expansion of carbon trading projects.

What did the minister ask CRDB to do?

Minister Hamad Yussuf Masauni urged CRDB to design innovative financial products, such as loans, guarantees and other investment instruments. They would help carbon project developers get capital, subject to the bank’s assessments and legal requirements.

Who is affected by the deal?

Tanzanian carbon project developers could gain access to capital. Buyers of Tanzanian carbon credits are also affected, because the deal aims to expand the projects that supply them.

How much money is involved?

No financing amount has been announced. The number of projects and the first products are also not known.

Sources: Environmental Management (Control and Management of Carbon Trading) Regulations, 2022 (Government Notice 636 of 2022, as amended in 2023); statements made at the signing in Antalya, Türkiye, on 13 November 2026.

World.title: Edo Gives State Oil Firm Refinery Land
World.content:
File photo. A dredger and workers at the Dangote refinery site in Lagos, March 2020. Photo: GodwinPaya, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

NIGERIA · ENERGY

On Friday 13 November 2026, Edo State Governor Monday Okpebholo handed NNPC Ltd, Nigeria’s state oil company, the land title for a proposed refinery. The ceremony took place at the Edo State Government House in Benin City.

The Certificate of Occupancy, the legal document that grants the right to use land, was presented on Friday 13 November 2026 for a plant named Oredo Refinery and Petrochemical Company Limited. It matters most to Edo State and to Nigerian fuel users, who depend on whether the plant is built.

What A Certificate of Occupancy (land title) for the proposed Oredo Refinery and Petrochemical Company Limited.

Where and when Edo State Government House, Benin City, on Friday 13 November 2026.

Earlier plan February 2026 agreement for a 10,000 barrels-per-day refinery for condensate, a light oil from gas fields; November reports give no capacity.

Open Construction cost, site size and start date are not confirmed.

Edo State has given NNPC Ltd the land title for a proposed refinery, but the cost, the capacity and the start date are still unconfirmed.

What Happened

Governor Okpebholo presented the Certificate of Occupancy during a courtesy visit by NNPC Ltd to the Edo State Government House. Alhaji Mumuni Dagazau, NNPC Ltd’s Executive Vice President for Downstream (refining and fuel supply), received it.

The NNPC Ltd delegation also included Ikedichi Dick-Nwoke, the company’s Chief Downstream Investment Officer. The document names the project Oredo Refinery and Petrochemical Company Limited.

Dagazau said the plant fits the federal government’s Renewed Hope Agenda, its national policy programme. He said it would support energy security, reduce dependence on imports and add local value.

Dagazau also said the refinery would create jobs, transfer technology and support industry in Edo. Okpebholo said providing land is meant to attract investors, raise revenue and create jobs.

File photo. A waterfront on Nigeria's coast with a small boat in the foreground, undated. Photo: XEON / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0).

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Edo State (Nigeria) Email address Follow

The February Agreement

The Edo government said on 5 February 2026, and the Federal Ministry of Information, Nigeria’s federal information ministry, repeated on 6 February, that the state and NNPC Ltd had agreed to build a 10,000 barrels-per-day condensate refinery. Condensate is a light oil that comes from gas fields.

Completion was targeted within 24 to 36 months, across the Oredo and Orhionmwon local government areas (districts of Edo State). The state pledged land, certificates of occupancy, security and logistics.

Output was projected at about 20 truckloads of petrol and 10 of diesel a day. The November reports give no capacity, so the 10,000 figure comes from February.

In Plain English

A Certificate of Occupancy is the document that gives its holder the legal right to use a piece of land. “Downstream” means refining crude oil and condensate and supplying fuel to users.

Why It Matters

The story has no direct US consequence. Edo State and Nigerian fuel users depend on whether the plant is built.

No sourced number ties this project to a wider market, so we draw no such link. For scale, Dangote, Nigeria’s large privately owned refinery in Lagos, said on 11 February 2026 that its crude distillation unit and motor spirit (petrol) block reached 650,000 barrels per day, a company claim.

What Is Not Known

Reports do not give the size of the site in hectares or its exact location. They also do not say what construction will cost or who will pay.

No start date for construction has been confirmed. It is also unclear whether the title covers both local government areas, how many barrels the plant will process and what the final project name will be.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Edo State give NNPC Ltd?

Governor Monday Okpebholo presented NNPC Ltd with a Certificate of Occupancy, the land title, on Friday 13 November 2026. It covers a proposed refinery named Oredo Refinery and Petrochemical Company Limited.

How big will the Edo refinery be?

The November reports give no capacity. A February 2026 agreement spoke of a 10,000 barrels-per-day condensate refinery.

Who benefits if the plant is built?

Edo State and Nigerian fuel users depend on whether the plant is built. Officials say it would create jobs, transfer technology and support local industry.

Does this affect readers in the United States?

The story has no direct US consequence. It matters mainly to Edo State and to Nigerian fuel users.

We will report any confirmed cost or start date as it emerges. For wider coverage, see our Nigeria news.

World.title: Dollar Falls to a Record Low of 446 Colones in Costa Rica
World.content:
The U.S. dollar closed at its weakest level on record against the Costa Rican colón on Friday, falling to a weighted average of 446.10 colones on the country’s wholesale foreign-exchange market. The Monex close came in 0.72 colones below Thursday’s average of 446.82 and beat the previous low of 446.80, set on Sept. 17, according to Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) trading data. On Thursday, the rate had sat just 0.02 colones above that record.

Friday marked the eighth consecutive session of decline, a slide that began on Nov. 4, when the average stood at 452.01 colones. Trades ranged between 445.80 and 446.30 colones per dollar, with $49.3 million changing hands in 228 operations. The BCCR’s reference rate for Friday stood at 442.74 colones for buying dollars and 448.37 for selling. The currency had already fallen to around 448 colones earlier this week.

The dollar has now lost 50.97 colones, or 10.3%, since the first trading session of 2026 on Jan. 2, when it opened the year at 497.07. After the September low, it recovered to 460.45 on Oct. 1, then fell 3.1% in a little over six weeks. Measured against its peak of 696.76 colones on June 21, 2022, the dollar has lost 36% of its value in Costa Rica.

In practical terms, every $1,000 converted at the Monex average now yields about 446,100 colones, roughly 51,000 fewer than at the start of the year. Bank and exchange-house rates sit on either side of the wholesale average, but they have moved in the same direction. The shift cuts both ways. Households and businesses that earn in dollars and pay their bills in colones receive less local currency for each dollar, while anyone who needs dollars, whether to pay a dollar-denominated loan or to import goods, needs fewer colones to buy them.

For people living on income from abroad, the squeeze comes as lawmakers weigh a bill that would tax residents’ foreign income at 15%. Dollar debt is a significant part of the picture. Data from the General Superintendency of Financial Entities (Sugef) through August show that 62% of foreign-currency loans in the financial system go to borrowers exposed to exchange-rate risk, meaning their income is not in dollars.

A strong colón lowers those payments for now. Sugef has warned, however, that if the exchange rate rises, the ability of a significant share of those borrowers to pay could be affected. Foreign-currency lending has also been growing faster than lending in colones. Sugef figures for September show dollar loans grew 6%, compared with 2.7% for colón loans.

The Central Bank has been buying dollars as the rate falls. Through Nov. 12, it had purchased $94.9 million this month in stabilization operations, bringing its 2026 total to $1.36 billion.

On Thursday alone, the BCCR bought $13.7 million for stabilization and another $11 million to cover the currency needs of the non-bank public sector. Stabilization purchases are meant to smooth sharp swings in the rate rather than to defend a specific level. Costa Rica has operated under a managed float since February 2015. Monex began operating in November 2006, which makes Friday’s close the lowest in the platform’s two-decade history.

Trading has been heavy in recent weeks. On Oct. 27, Monex recorded $153.4 million in transactions, the largest volume since its creation. Monex trading resumes on Monday, Nov. 16, when the market will show whether the slide extends to a ninth session.

World.title: Costa Rica Flights Caught in Only the Third Nationwide US Ground Stop Ever
World.content:
If you’re flying between the United States and Costa Rica this afternoon or tonight, expect delays and possible cancellations. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) stopped every departing flight across the United States on Friday, citing “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety.”

The order took effect shortly before 4 p.m. Eastern time, just before 3 p.m. in Costa Rica. It stays in place until further notice. Any flight scheduled to leave a U.S. airport for San José or Liberia is grounded for now. That includes flights from the Florida hubs that carry much of Costa Rica’s U.S. traffic, such as Miami, Fort Lauderdale and Orlando, as well as other major gateways.

Planes already in the air are being allowed to continue to their destinations. Flights from Costa Rica to the United States are less clear. The FAA said inbound international flights will be handled case by case. Even if your flight is cleared, it may still be late. Many U.S. airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same aircraft back, so a jet stuck on the ground in Miami or Houston means a late or canceled departure here.

The FAA hasn’t officially said what caused the stop. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communications issue is affecting all of the country’s Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle planes flying between airports. Outages on radio frequencies used by controllers had been reported in parts of the country before the order was issued.

There’s no confirmed time for flights to restart. Some flight-tracking services listed 5 p.m. Eastern time, or 4 p.m. in Costa Rica, as the first point the order would be reviewed, but it could be extended. Delays will likely last well past the end of the stop, because planes and crews will be out of position. In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop of about 90 minutes, triggered by the failure of a computer system that sends safety notices to pilots, led to more than 11,000 delays and cancellations.

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare. The January 2023 one was the most recent. Before that, the only other was ordered after the September 11, 2001, attacks. Check your flight with your airline before you head to the airport. Airline apps and text alerts usually update before airport departure boards do.

Look for a travel waiver on your airline’s website. During large disruptions, airlines often let you change your flight without a fee, which can be easier than waiting for a rebooking. If your flight is canceled and you decide not to travel, U.S. rules entitle you to a cash refund, even when the cause is out of the airline’s control. Airlines aren’t required to pay for hotels or meals when the disruption isn’t their fault, so keep your receipts if you have travel insurance that covers delays.

If you’re connecting through a U.S. hub, you may miss your connection even after flights restart. Rebook through the airline that issued your ticket rather than each carrier separately. Updates on local flights are posted on the official social media channels of Juan Santamaría International Airport and Guanacaste Airport.

This is a developing story and will be updated as the FAA and airlines release more information.

World.title: Banks and Businesses in Costa Rica Must Accept Digital ID Starting January
World.content:
Starting January 1, 2027, banks, government agencies, businesses and other institutions in Costa Rica will be required to accept the Costa Rican Digital Identity (IDC), the smartphone version of the national ID card, for any transaction or procedure that requires identification. The Supreme Electoral Tribunal (TSE) said the digital credential carries the same legal validity as the traditional plastic ID card. From that date, institutions will no longer be able to turn it away simply because it is presented on a phone.

The digital ID has been available since September 9, 2025, but until now institutions could decide whether to accept it. According to the TSE, 107,243 people had requested one as of November 1, 2026. The change could make everyday procedures simpler, from banking to administrative paperwork and any service that requires proof of identity. It does not replace the physical card, which will continue to be issued and accepted throughout the country.

Unlike the physical ID, which is free for most applicants, the digital version costs 2,600 colones (about $5.80) and is valid for four years. Senior citizens are exempt from the fee. The service is available only to Costa Rican citizens. Applicants need a valid physical ID card, a smartphone with an active phone line running iOS or Android, and no identity document waiting to be collected at the TSE.

People applying for their first Costa Rican ID must get the physical card before they can request the digital version. Applications are handled online through the TSE website at tse.go.cr/idc. Applicants enter their ID number, complete an identity verification step, provide a valid email address and pay with a Visa or Mastercard credit or debit card.

Once the application is approved, the credential is activated through the official IDC-Ciudadano app, available on Apple’s App Store and Google Play. It is protected by a personal PIN and facial recognition, which the TSE checks against the biometric data collected during the holder’s most recent physical ID procedure.

Citizens can still obtain or renew their physical IDs free of charge at the TSE’s headquarters in San José or at any of its 32 regional offices. A fee applies only when a person exceeds the annual limit on duplicate replacements. The January requirement applies to the institutions that must accept the credential, not to citizens. Getting a digital ID remains optional, and anyone who prefers the plastic card can keep using it.

World.title: Heavy Storms Could Drop Nearly 3 Inches of Rain on Costa Rica Today
World.content:
The rest of this Friday afternoon could bring short, heavy downpours and thunderstorms to the Central Valley, the northern zone and the Caribbean. If you still have to get somewhere today, plan your trip around them. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) expects intense storms lasting one to three hours, with 20 to 40 millimeters (0.8 to 1.6 inches) of rain in most affected areas. In the Central Valley, the Caribbean and the northern zone, totals could reach 70 millimeters (2.8 inches).

That much rain in a short window can overwhelm city drains and push creeks over their banks, especially in the Central Valley. If you live or park near a stream or on a street that floods, move your car early and don’t drive through standing water. Wind is the other risk. Isolated gusts could reach 80 kilometers per hour (50 mph), strong enough to bring down branches and power lines. When a storm hits, get indoors and keep away from trees and fallen cables.

The mountains and the eastern and northeastern parts of the Central Valley have the highest chance of storms. Rain could also spread to the northern lowlands and the northern Caribbean. On the Pacific side, expect storms in the mountains of the Central and South Pacific. The Nicoya Peninsula and the southeast of the North Pacific should see less activity.

The storms come in bursts rather than as an all-day rain. If one hits while you’re on the road or about to drive home, it is usually safer to wait it out than to push through it. The reason for the change is the trade winds. They usually keep the Pacific side dry at this time of year, and earlier this week they were bringing strong gusts across the country. Now they have weakened, which lets sea breezes and westerly winds carry moist Pacific air inland. Warm temperatures then build storm clouds over the mountains by afternoon.

This back-and-forth is typical of the transition from the rainy season to the dry season, which has already begun in Guanacaste and the Central Valley. Unsettled weather continues into Saturday, with more chances of afternoon rain. From Tuesday, the IMN expects rising pressure over the Caribbean Sea to strengthen the trade winds again.

If you’re driving between the Central Valley and the Caribbean coast, keep an eye on Route 32. Heavy rain in the mountains is what brings rock and mud down onto the highway through Braulio Carrillo National Park, which has closed repeatedly this year. If Route 32 closes, the usual alternatives are Route 10 through Turrialba and Route 126 through Vara Blanca. Both are narrower and slower, so leave extra time.

Check the IMN’s website and social media for updated warnings before you head out this afternoon or on Saturday.

World.title: Salvadoran Troops Turn Haiti National Stadium Into Base After Retaking It From Gangs
World.content:
El Salvador will turn Haiti’s national soccer stadium into a forward base for its troops after Salvadoran and Haitian forces retook the Sylvio Cator stadium in Port-au-Prince from armed gangs on Thursday, President Nayib Bukele announced. The joint operation took place in the early hours yesterday and involved the Haitian National Police, the Armed Forces of Haiti, a government-contracted security unit known as the Task Force, and Salvadoran special forces, according to Bukele and Haitian police. Bukele said it was carried out under a bilateral agreement between the two governments.

The Haitian National Police said in a statement that its officers had taken full control of the stadium and its surroundings before handing security of the complex to the Salvadoran armed forces. More than 20 armored vehicles and trucks carrying Salvadoran military personnel were stationed inside the stadium after the operation, according to local media reports.

Bukele said troops found several human skulls inside the facility. Authorities have not announced any identification of the remains or said whether they will be examined. The Salvadoran president said his forces would use the stadium as a base to advance deeper into territory held by gangs, and that the allied forces now hold the advantage on the ground.

In a message addressed directly to gang members, he told them to leave the area before the next phase of operations begins and warned that those who stay to fight Salvadoran and Haitian forces will face the consequences. He did not give a start date. The stadium, home ground of Haiti’s national soccer team, had been held by gangs since early 2024. Its loss forced Haiti to play every one of its home qualifiers for the 2026 World Cup outside the country.

The recovery is the latest step in a rapidly expanding Salvadoran military presence in Haiti. El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 troops since October 18, when gangs ambushed an armored vehicle carrying four Salvadoran Air Force aviation technicians in Croix-des-Bouquets, northeast of Port-au-Prince. The Salvadoran military said the vehicle was struck by gunfire and explosives and caught fire, and that the four men got out before going missing.

The technicians were serving with the Gang Suppression Force, a multinational mission authorized by the United Nations Security Council to support Haitian police against armed groups that control large parts of the capital and other areas. Salvadoran officials have described them as non-combat personnel whose main job was carrying out medical evacuations.

The Salvadoran government maintains that the four are alive, but their whereabouts remained unknown as of now. Bukele has previously offered to withdraw all Salvadoran forces from Haiti if the technicians are released unharmed. The Gang Suppression Force has distanced itself from the actions of the Salvadoran troops sent in after the ambush, which operate under the separate bilateral arrangement with the Haitian government. Bukele has said the contingent is focused on confronting the gangs responsible for the October attack and related violence.

The stadium operation came two days after Bukele said Salvadoran troops had destroyed the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo gang, an operation for which Haiti’s prime minister publicly praised the Salvadoran leader. Gang violence in Haiti has forced nearly 1.5 million people from their homes, and the international force sent to help contain it has so far deployed only a fraction of the 5,550 personnel the Security Council authorized.

World.title: Shakira Returns to Costa Rica in 2027 After More Than 15 Years
World.content:
Shakira’s world tour has added Costa Rica to its 2027 Latin American leg. It’s the strongest sign yet that the Colombian superstar will perform at the National Stadium in La Sabana on Sunday, January 31. It would be her first concert in the country since April 2011. The tour’s official accounts posted a graphic this week listing six countries for the new leg: Brazil, Venezuela, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Puerto Rico and Panama. The post gave no dates or venues for any of the stops.

The January 31 date comes from the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Commerce (MEIC). In October it authorized a presale plan for the show. The authorization lists an 8 p.m. start at the National Stadium and lets the production company, Two Shows Ltda., sell 53,114 tickets through eticket.cr.

Ticket prices and the on-sale date have not been announced. The ministry requires a presale authorization before any large event goes on sale, to protect buyers, but it doesn’t mean tickets are available. Wait for an official announcement and buy only through the authorized seller.

There is a reason for caution. In September 2024, the ministry approved a presale of 51,446 tickets for a Shakira concert at the same stadium on March 27, 2025. That show never happened bug the difference this time is that the tour itself has named Costa Rica as a stop.

The show is part of the Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour, named after her 2024 album, her first studio record in seven years. The tour opened in Rio de Janeiro in February 2025. Her production team says the tour has grossed more than $534 million and sold over four million tickets worldwide. Shakira recently closed a 13-show residency in Madrid that drew more than 700,000 people.

She has played Costa Rica twice before. She brought her Pies Descalzos tour to the Palacio de los Deportes in Heredia in 1995. She then performed at the National Stadium on April 3, 2011, shortly after the stadium opened. A full stadium on the last Sunday of January would also land in the middle of high season, when flights and hotels around San José are already busy.

Prices, seating sections and the sale date are expected once the producers make a formal announcement.

World.title: Finish Your Government Paperwork by Dec. 21 as Costa Rica Offices Close
World.content:
The government has ordered seven days of collective vacation for public employees: Dec. 22, 23, 24, 28, 29, 30 and 31. With Christmas, New Year’s Day and two weekends in between, offices that work Monday to Friday will be closed from Tuesday, Dec. 22, through Sunday, Jan. 3. Staff return on Monday, Jan. 4, 2027.

President Laura Fernández signed the directive with Planning Minister Carla Morales Rojas and Labor Minister Mercedes Flores Badilla. The government announced it on Thursday, Nov. 12. It takes legal effect once it’s published in the official gazette La Gaceta. The tricky part is that not every public office follows the same calendar. If you assume everything closes, or that everything stays open, you could be caught out.

The directive covers the central and decentralized public administration, meaning the ministries and the agencies under them. Five groups set their own dates instead: the Education Ministry (MEP), the Office of the Attorney General (Procuraduría General de la República), the National Registry, police forces and emergency institutions. The leaders of each will decide based on what their services need.

Other branches of government don’t have to follow the order. The Legislative Assembly has already approved its own recess, from Dec. 21 to 31. The judiciary sets its own year-end closure under its 2026 vacation plan. In June it ruled that a similar government directive was not binding on the courts.

Autonomous institutions and municipalities also decide for themselves. When the government ordered a collective vacation week in July, the Social Security System (CCSS), the Comptroller General’s Office, the public universities and the judiciary all chose to keep working. Some services keep running no matter what. Every institution must keep essential services open and have staff ready for emergencies. Health care and public security must not be interrupted.

Each institution must also publish its holiday hours and say which service channels stay open. Most had not done so as of Nov. 13. Check the schedule for the office you need before you make the trip. Immigration is where an unplanned gap hurts most. If you have a residency application, a DIMEX renewal or another filing with the General Directorate of Migration and Immigration, finish it well before Dec. 21 and expect appointments to be in high demand. In past years, Migración has partly closed its main office in La Uruca over the holidays. In 2023 it also stopped accepting new filings on its digital platform until offices reopened.

Immigration control at airports and border crossings continues through the holidays because it is a security function. Some land border posts have changed their hours over the holidays in past years. If you plan to cross by land, check the hours first. If you’re buying property, registering a company or transferring a vehicle, the National Registry’s dates matter. The Registry will set its own schedule, so ask your lawyer or notary when it will stop receiving documents. A sale signed in late December may not be recorded until January.

One deadline does not move: the 2027 marchamo, the annual vehicle circulation fee, is due by Dec. 31. It’s collected by the National Insurance Institute (INS), not a ministry. You can pay it online, in banking apps or at authorized payment points. From Jan. 1, unpaid vehicles face fines, surcharges and possible removal of their plates.

If you need a Costa Rican criminal record certificate (hoja de delincuencia), request it early. The Judicial Registry issues these certificates. During last year’s judicial closure it shut for the first week and reopened with shorter hours in the second. Tax filings with the Finance Ministry are made online, but the ministry has not announced its holiday schedule. If a filing or payment deadline falls between Dec. 22 and Jan. 3, ask your accountant whether it moves. If you have a court case or a legal deadline, the judiciary’s calendar applies, not the government’s.

The state-owned banks compete with private banks, and in the past the government has only invited companies like them to join its collective vacations. Online banking normally runs through the holidays, but check branch hours before you go. The government says the closure will reduce the large backlog of unused vacation days in the public sector. It also expects savings on electricity, water, telecommunications and fuel. The seven days come out of each employee’s own vacation balance.

The directive also allows the Ministry of the Interior and Police to give public employees in central San José the day off on Dec. 31 for the city’s year-end civic festivities. The simplest plan: if a task needs a government stamp, signature or appointment, finish it by Dec. 21. Then check the published schedule of the specific office before heading out in late December.

If you have paperwork pending with a Costa Rican government office, plan to finish it by Monday, Dec. 21. The government has ordered seven days of collective vacation for public employees: Dec. 22, 23, 24, 28, 29, 30 and 31. With Christmas, New Year’s Day and two weekends in between, offices that work Monday to Friday will be closed from Tuesday, Dec. 22, through Sunday, Jan. 3. Staff return on Monday, Jan. 4, 2027.

President Laura Fernández signed the directive with Planning Minister Carla Morales Rojas and Labor Minister Mercedes Flores Badilla. The government announced it on Thursday, Nov. 12. It takes legal effect once it’s published in the official gazette La Gaceta. The tricky part is that not every public office follows the same calendar. If you assume everything closes, or that everything stays open, you could be caught out.

The directive covers the central and decentralized public administration, meaning the ministries and the agencies under them. Five groups set their own dates instead: the Education Ministry (MEP), the Office of the Attorney General (Procuraduría General de la República), the National Registry, police forces and emergency institutions. The leaders of each will decide based on what their services need.

Other branches of government don’t have to follow the order. The Legislative Assembly has already approved its own recess, from Dec. 21 to 31. The judiciary sets its own year-end closure under its 2026 vacation plan. In June it ruled that a similar government directive was not binding on the courts.

Autonomous institutions and municipalities also decide for themselves. When the government ordered a collective vacation week in July, the Social Security System (CCSS), the Comptroller General’s Office, the public universities and the judiciary all chose to keep working. Some services keep running no matter what. Every institution must keep essential services open and have staff ready for emergencies. Health care and public security must not be interrupted.

Each institution must also publish its holiday hours and say which service channels stay open. Most had not done so as of Nov. 13. Check the schedule for the office you need before you make the trip. Immigration is where an unplanned gap hurts most. If you have a residency application, a DIMEX renewal or another filing with the General Directorate of Migration and Immigration, finish it well before Dec. 21 and expect appointments to be in high demand.

In past years, Migración has partly closed its main office in La Uruca over the holidays. In 2023 it also stopped accepting new filings on its digital platform until offices reopened. Immigration control at airports and border crossings continues through the holidays because it is a security function. Some land border posts have changed their hours over the holidays in past years. If you plan to cross by land, check the hours first.

If you’re buying property, registering a company or transferring a vehicle, the National Registry’s dates matter. The Registry will set its own schedule, so ask your lawyer or notary when it will stop receiving documents. A sale signed in late December may not be recorded until January.

One deadline does not move: the 2027 marchamo, the annual vehicle circulation fee, is due by Dec. 31. It’s collected by the National Insurance Institute (INS), not a ministry. You can pay it online, in banking apps or at authorized payment points. From Jan. 1, unpaid vehicles face fines, surcharges and possible removal of their plates.

If you need a Costa Rican criminal record certificate (hoja de delincuencia), request it early. The Judicial Registry issues these certificates. During last year’s judicial closure it shut for the first week and reopened with shorter hours in the second. Tax filings with the Finance Ministry are made online, but the ministry has not announced its holiday schedule. If a filing or payment deadline falls between Dec. 22 and Jan. 3, ask your accountant whether it moves. If you have a court case or a legal deadline, the judiciary’s calendar applies, not the government’s.

The state-owned banks compete with private banks, and in the past the government has only invited companies like them to join its collective vacations. Online banking normally runs through the holidays, but check branch hours before you go. The government says the closure will reduce the large backlog of unused vacation days in the public sector. It also expects savings on electricity, water, telecommunications and fuel. The seven days come out of each employee’s own vacation balance.

The directive also allows the Ministry of the Interior and Police to give public employees in central San José the day off on Dec. 31 for the city’s year-end civic festivities. Bottom line is if a task needs a government stamp, signature or appointment, finish it by Dec. 21. Then check the published schedule of the specific office before heading out in late December.

World.title: Microsoft Global Outage Disrupts Outlook, Teams and Health Services Worldwide
World.content:
Microsoft’s global outage ran into a second day Friday. Outlook email is still failing for many users, and parts of Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 tools only partly work. If your work or school email runs through Microsoft, this is what’s happening and what you can do.

The problems began late Thursday morning, Costa Rica time, when Microsoft opened an incident for users who couldn’t reach their Exchange Online mailboxes. At first the company said the problem was concentrated in the Americas. It later confirmed that users in any region could lose their connection to Microsoft 365.

Downdetector, which tracks outages, logged problems in 74 countries and territories. At Thursday’s peak it had more than 130,000 reports about Outlook alone, most of them from the United States. On Friday morning Microsoft said traffic was gradually coming back. The biggest improvements were in North America, with steady progress in much of Europe. The company still hasn’t said when everything will be fully restored.

Microsoft says Teams messaging, calls and meetings are mostly working. Teams calendars, meeting invitations and scheduling are still affected because they rely on the same email system. Some Outlook users still can’t sign in, and many messages are arriving hours late. Copilot users may get errors when they load a chat or ask for an answer. Planner, To Do and some SharePoint sharing features have also had problems.

Microsoft hasn’t named a root cause. It first blamed heavy load on part of its infrastructure in several regions. Later it said many servers had unexpectedly gone offline, which pushed their traffic onto the machines still running. Engineers stopped all deployments, moved traffic away from the affected systems and restarted servers. They’re also reviewing recent network configuration changes. Some servers brought back overnight failed again once traffic returned, and Microsoft said its early fixes had only marginal success.

Microsoft said it isn’t aware of any malicious activity. Executive vice president Charles Lamanna said the outage doesn’t appear to be a cyberattack. Many Costa Ricans remember the 2022 ransomware attacks that took down Finance Ministry systems and the Social Security System (CCSS). This is different: people can’t get into their accounts, but nothing Microsoft has said suggests customer data was exposed.

Health services abroad have been hit hard. In the United Kingdom, the National Health Service rescheduled some procedures after Teams went down, because it’s a key link between managers and health workers. The NHS also warned that some patients may struggle to get prescriptions, since pharmacies can’t reach doctors’ offices by email.

A UK union, the GMB, said ambulance services and medical centers saw a serious impact, although urgent care appeared unaffected. Japanese economy minister Ryosei Akazawa warned the impact was significant. New Zealand’s foreign ministry had trouble receiving email at its embassies and consulates.

In Australia, schools, courts and government offices began Friday without Outlook. The Euronext stock exchange told listed companies to use the phone, and Workhorse Group, a US company, postponed its quarterly results. No count of affected users in Costa Rica has been published, and no national institution has announced disruptions so far.

Still, Microsoft 365 is part of daily public life here. The Ministry of Public Education gives public school students and teachers institutional email and Microsoft Teams accounts. The Judiciary has made Teams its official platform for virtual hearings. If your email is down, check Microsoft’s official service page at status.cloud.microsoft before you assume the problem is on your end. Resetting your password or reinstalling Outlook won’t fix this.

A message that hasn’t arrived isn’t necessarily lost. Microsoft extended its delivery window to 48 hours, so delayed email is held and delivered instead of bounced back. If you’ve sent anything urgent since Thursday, call or use another channel to make sure it arrived. For urgent coordination, use Teams chat and calls, which mostly work. Double-check meeting times, though, because calendars may be out of sync.

Watch for scama since outages bring a wave of fake “support” emails and texts asking you to log in or reset your password. Don’t click links in those messages. Go to the status page directly. Microsoft said it will keep posting updates on its service status page until everything is restored. It’s the latest of several large cloud outages this year, and it shows how much work, school and public services depend on a few technology providers.

World.title: Pletts Electronics opens new branch in Punta Gorda
World.content:
Pletts Electronics opens new branch in Punta Gorda

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Pletts Electronics has officially opened its newest branch in Punta Gorda Town.

The store, located on George Price Street, opened its doors today, giving residents of the Toledo District local access to phones, speakers, accessories and more.

The company says it is excited to serve the people of Punta Gorda, who can now shop for electronics without the hassle of driving long distances or shipping items in.

To celebrate the opening, customers who visit on Friday and Saturday can enjoy special deals at the new branch.

The store is open from 8:00am to 5:00pm.

For more information, call 671-8900 or visit www.plettselectronics.com.

World.title: Website honoring Garifuna Settlement Day founder Thomas Vincent Ramos launches in Dangriga
World.content:
Website honoring Garifuna Settlement Day founder Thomas Vincent Ramos launches in Dangriga

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A new website documenting the life and work of Thomas Vincent Ramos, the Garifuna civil rights advocate who founded Garifuna Settlement Day, was launched in Dangriga on Friday, November 13, to mark the 71st annual tribute to Ramos.

His granddaughter, Adele Olva Ramos, developed the Thomas Vincent Ramos Memorial Website to make his story more accessible. The site brings together biographical accounts, historical material and information on honors he received after his death on November 13, 1955. She said more multimedia content will be added over time.

National Garifuna Council President Alex Nolberto welcomed the launch, saying it would help pass Garifuna history on to younger generations. He also credited Adele Ramos for her earlier book, Thomas Vincent Ramos: The Man and His Writings, published by the council in 2000.

Ramos helped organize the first November 19 celebration in Dangriga in 1941 and pressed colonial authorities to recognize it as a public holiday. The observance, originally known as Carib Disembarkment Day, became a nationwide public holiday in 1977. Belize later honored Ramos by renaming the Southern Highway after him.

World.title: Major US flight shutdown threatens widespread delays for Belize travellers
World.content:
Major US flight shutdown threatens widespread delays for Belize travellers

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Flights have been grounded across the United States because of an air traffic control “communication issue,” and travellers heading to or from Belize should prepare for delays.

According to the BBC, US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem hit air traffic control centres and that technicians from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) are investigating.

US aviation officials earlier ordered all flights grounded, citing “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

Several major US airports have confirmed the ground stop. There is currently no indication of when the order will be lifted.

Duffy said updates will be provided as soon as they are available.

For Belize, the impact could be significant. Most international flights into the Philip S. W. Goldson International Airport come from US cities, including Miami, Houston, Dallas, Atlanta and Fort Lauderdale.

Passengers travelling today are advised to contact their airline directly or check flight status online before heading to the airport.

This is a developing story.

World.title: National Police Leadership workshop strengthens youth diversion efforts
World.content:
National Police Leadership workshop strengthens youth diversion efforts

The Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, through its Community Rehabilitation Department (CRD), in collaboration with the Belize Police Department (BPD) and with support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) through the European Union-funded PACE Justice Project, today hosted the National Police Leadership Diversion Workshop at Hidden Hall by Oasis in Belmopan.

The workshop brought together senior police officers, including the Commissioner of Police, Superintendents, and Officers Commanding various police formations, to strengthen their understanding of youth diversion and its application at the police station level.

Youth diversion allows eligible young people under the age of 18 who come into conflict with the law to be referred to the Community Rehabilitation Department for structured rehabilitation and support programmes instead of being formally charged. These programmes, typically lasting three to six months, may include counselling, life skills development, mentorship, and referrals to community-based organizations, depending on the young person’s needs and the nature of the offence.

The workshop featured welcome remarks by Mrs. Ganesha Smith, Acting Director of CRD; special remarks by Mr. Michael Lund, UNDP Deputy Resident Representative; and a keynote address by Commissioner of Police Dr. Richard Rosado.

Facilitated by Attorney-at-Law Diana Shaw, the workshop examined the legal framework for diversion, institutional responsibilities, and proposed updates to police and court diversion protocols. Participants also engaged in discussions and group activities to review and validate procedures aimed at strengthening the consistent application of diversion.

The workshop forms part of the ongoing Police Diversion Training Campaign under the National Diversion Program and follows consultations on the 2026 Revised National Diversion Protocol. The initiative seeks to strengthen coordination between the CRD and the Belize Police Department while reinforcing the important role of police leadership in ensuring that eligible young people are appropriately considered for diversion.

Youth diversion is not about removing accountability. It is about providing young people with the guidance, support, and opportunity to learn from their mistakes and make better choices.

Through continued collaboration with the Belize Police Department and development partners, the Ministry remains committed to strengthening a child-centered justice system that prioritizes rehabilitation, accountability, and second chances.

World.title: EntreCon 2026 brings entrepreneurs together in Belize City
World.content:
EntreCon 2026 brings entrepreneurs together in Belize City

By Zoila Palma: Small business owners and entrepreneurs from across Belize have gathered at the Biltmore Plaza Hotel in Belize City for the 2026 National Entrepreneurship Convention (Belize EntreCon), hosted by BELTRAIDE and the Government of Belize.

Organized by SBDCBelize, a unit of BELTRAIDE, the convention aims to promote the growth and development of micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) through networking, knowledge-sharing, and business development opportunities.

Prime Minister John Briceño delivered the keynote address, sharing his own journey in business and highlighting his Government’s efforts to create an enabling environment for entrepreneurs.

Belizean businesswoman Kalila Enriquez-Reynolds, founder and CEO of Jamaica-based Money Media Limited, also shared insights into the strategies and experiences that helped grow her company from a start-up into a successful business.

World.title: International News: ALL flights grounded across U.S. following communications outage
World.content:
International News: ALL flights grounded across U.S. following communications outage

By Zoila Palma: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a rare nationwide ground stop, temporarily halting all flights across the United States due to a telecommunications outage affecting aviation operations, CNN reports.

The agency said the decision was made “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” with no immediate timeline provided for when normal operations would resume.

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the disruption was not caused by a threat to national security and was not connected to the recent Microsoft outage. Preliminary reports also indicate that the incident was not a cyberattack. President Donald Trump has been briefed on the situation.

The ground stop has triggered delays and cancellations at major airports across the country, leaving thousands of travelers uncertain about their travel plans.

United Airlines notified passengers that all new domestic departures would be suspended while the FAA restriction remains in effect, although aircraft already in the air would be allowed to continue their flights. The airline said it would work with affected customers to get them to their destinations once the issue is resolved.

Passengers at airports including New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport and Chicago O’Hare International Airport reported receiving limited information about the disruption. Some travelers were informed shortly before departure, while others learned about the nationwide ground stop through news reports.

Pilots and air traffic controllers also reported significant communication difficulties, with outages affecting air traffic control radar systems and radio frequencies.

Aviation officials have yet to establish the precise cause of the telecommunications failure, and authorities have warned that resolving the disruption could take time.

World.title: ‘$500 Is No Kind Of Money To Me’: Roy Earl Jones ordered to repay runman $501 and pay $1,435 in fines and court costs
World.content:
‘$500 Is No Kind Of Money To Me’: Roy Earl Jones ordered to repay runman $501 and pay $1,435 in fines and court costs

By Breaking Belize News Staff: “$500 is no kind of money to me,” Roy Earl Jones said in an interview Friday after spending a night at the Belize Central Prison. The 24-year-old Belize City man walked free after sentencing, but the senior magistrate ordered him to repay a deliveryman $501 before paying another $1,435 in fines and court costs.

Jones pleaded guilty Thursday to seven counts of obtaining property by deception and was remanded overnight pending sentencing. He apologized in court and said he needed time to get a loan to clear his debts.

On Friday, the senior magistrate fined Jones $200 on each count and added $5 per count in court costs. He has until February 26, 2027, to pay the court, with a default sentence of two months on each count if he fails to pay. The magistrate told him the deliveryman must be repaid first.

According to the facts presented in court, the deliveryman agreed to use his own money to buy items and deliver cash to Jones’ mother on the understanding that Jones would pay him back. On September 29, he said he dropped off $100 in cash, then returned later that day with a $100 bag of dog food and another $40. The next day, he said he spent $50 on cereal and condensed milk and delivered another $50 in cash.

The requests continued into October. The deliveryman said he paid $20 for fried chicken from Benny’s Restaurant on October 6 and $29 for two orders of rice and beans with pork and two Cokes the next day. When he asked Jones on October 8 when he would get his money, Jones replied on WhatsApp, “Thank you for your patience.” The deliveryman said he still dropped off another $70 that evening, followed by $22 in barbecue meals on October 10 and another $20 in chicken on October 12.

The deliveryman told police he never got his money back. After repeated attempts to collect, he made his own inquiries and learned that the man he knew as “Rayjaughn” was Roy Jones. He reported the matter to police on November 9, and officers detained Jones two days later.

In handing down the sentence, the magistrate cited the seriousness and prevalence of the offence, the financial loss and the breach of trust. She also weighed Jones’ early guilty plea, his remorse, his lack of previous convictions and the night he had already spent in custody. She noted that although the transactions took place on different days, the seven counts arose from the same course of conduct.

In Friday’s interview, Jones called the deliveryman a friend and said their agreement gave him until that day to repay the money. He said he had not expected the deliveryman to go to police.

World.title: American tourist says San Pedro vendor cursed him after he refused to buy carving
World.content:
American tourist says San Pedro vendor cursed him after he refused to buy carving

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An American visitor to San Pedro says he and his wife were verbally abused by a street vendor on Friday after they declined to buy a wood carving.

In a social media post tagged in downtown San Pedro, the tourist said the couple was walking peacefully down the street when a man asked if they wanted to buy one of his carvings.

The visitor said he told the vendor the carvings were beautiful but that he had no cash on him. According to the post, the vendor responded with an insult laced with profanity, calling him an “American” in a derogatory way.

“I was pretty shocked because this isn’t our first time in Belize and we’ve never been treated so unkindly,” the tourist wrote.

He said he was wearing camera equipped smart glasses and told the vendor he was being recorded. At that point, he said, the man apologized, quickly packed up and left.

The visitor said he shared the post so others could be careful, but stressed that he sees it as a one off.

“I realize this was an isolated event,” he wrote.

The vendor’s side of the story is not known.

World.title: Finally!
World.content:
The entrance to Cornwall Regional Hospital’s newly opened Accident and Emergency department (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

MOUNT SALEM, St James — The opening of the refurbished Accident and Emergency (A&E) department at Cornwall Regional Hospital (CRH) on Friday was accompanied by an apology from Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness to the people of western Jamaica for the prolonged delay in completing the facility’s $23.5-billion rehabilitation.

Holness acknowledged that the near-decade-long undertaking to rehabilitate the 52-year-old, 10-storey hospital might have been completed more quickly had the Government opted to demolish the structure and build a new facility from the ground up.

“In retrospect, it may have been a quicker operation to have torn down the building and just built it anew. But politically, we’re not certain whether or not the public would have appreciated that. But I can tell you, going forward, the economics is that it is better to just tear down those old buildings and build brand new,” said Holness.

The hospital officially opened on May 10, 1974, following the start of construction in 1968 at a cost of approximately US$12 million and another US$5 million to equip it, through a grant from Canada. Holness argued that in today’s terms, that type of work, plus land acquisition and other expenses, would cost approximately $40 billion.

He said the 25.9-acre campus on which the upgraded CRH and the under-construction Western Child and Adolescent Hospital (WCAH) sit will be renamed in honour of former chairman of the Jamaica Labour Party and Minister of Health Dr Herbert Eldemire. He also reiterated that the WCAH will bear the name of former Prime Minister Portia Simpson Miller, who was instrumental in securing funds from the Chinese for that project.

During his address, the prime minister acknowledge the hardship faced by residents in western Jamaica as the work on CRH dragged on.

“I must, first of all, apologise to the people of the region who have been without their hospital, and for the suffering that it has caused. No doubt, the absence of the hospital would have caused suffering, particularly during COVID. I toured during COVID and I saw the difficulties being experienced both by the service providers and the patients in cramped quarters, in difficult circumstances,” stated Holness.

Pointing out that a large percentage of the 24 hospitals across Jamaica were built before the country’s Independence from Britain in 1962, Holness said he views the Government of Jamaica’s ability to execute major projects like the CRH upgrade as a symbol of the country’s independence.

According to him, all the other sections of CRH will be open to the public by March 2027.

“I leaned over to Minister Tufton to inquire, ‘When will we finally open this hospital fully?’ And he was hesitant in committing to me. But he did say to me that by the end of the fiscal year they would be in a good position to open,” said the prime minister.

Clinical coordinator for the Western Regional Health Authority Dr Delroy Fray expressed delight at the completion and opening of the A&E department.

“Look at what stands before you now: A first-class accident and emergency department. We are handing over a state-of-the-art facility designed for dignity, speed, and comfort. From the moment you present with an emergency, you are seamlessly triaged in a high-efficiency environment,” stated Dr Fray.

The newly renovated facility boasts advanced diagnostic stations and cutting-edge operating theatres for immediate surgical intervention.

“This is not just health care; this is First-World medicine at the absolute highest level — the first of its kind in Jamaica and the entire English-speaking Caribbean,” Dr Fray said.

World.title: 1,446 new homes for St James
World.content:
