World.title: Croatia Will Need 100,000 New Hotel Beds Over the Next Decade
World.content:
November the 13th, 2026 – Croatia is going to need anywhere between 80,000 and 100,000 new hotel beds over the next decade, according to hotelier reps warn.

Croatia will need between 80,000 and 100,000 new hotel beds over the next ten years, hoteliers’ representatives warned at a recently held congress in Poreč. There’s an issue, however, as building new hotels is becoming increasingly difficult due to high land prices, expensive construction work, slow administration and shrinking opportunities for profit. Index reports that in Croatia currently, hotels currently account for only 9.2 percent of total accommodation capacity in Croatia, yet generate approximately a quarter of all tourist overnight stays. Hoteliers are therefore calling for the continuation of state incentives, better conditions for investment and measures that would attract more tourists outside the summer months.

croatia’s accommodation capacity poses an issue

Veljko Ostojić, president of the Association of Entrepreneurs in Croatian Hospitality and director of the Croatian Tourism Association, said that the hotel sector achieved good results this year, but that Croatia must change the structure of its tourist accommodation. “Croatian hospitality is the winner of this tourist year, not only according to physical indicators but also according to everything it does to raise the quality of Croatian tourism. However, the structure of our accommodation capacity is currently the biggest challenge,” Ostojić said. According to his estimate, Croatia should increase the number of hotel beds by 80,000 to 100,000 over the next decade. The problem, he warns, is that most investments relate to the renovation and reconstruction of existing hotels, while completely new hotel complexes on previously undeveloped land are almost not being built at all.

why are so few hotels being constructed in croatia?

Ostojić believes that investors are deterred by a combination of several problems, from the price of land and construction to slow administrative procedures and legal uncertainty. “The question is why there are practically no significant greenfield investments in Croatia. The reasons are numerous: the price of land, the slowness of administration, legal uncertainty, the cost of construction and the hotel business model itself. We must be open and realistic,” he said. He added that the space for new investments is getting smaller, which he considers bad for the long-term development of Croatian tourism. Hoteliers also warn of rising operating costs and declining profitability, which makes it increasingly difficult to find financially viable projects.

the interest in the height of summer is waning…

Ostojić also warned that tourist habits are changing. According to him, some guests are increasingly avoiding the busiest summer months because of the heat, high prices and excessive crowds in certain destinations. He believes Croatia must develop new tourist facilities, events and manifestations that would attract guests during spring and autumn. This would extend the tourist season, increase the occupancy of hotel capacities and reduce dependence on July and August alone, which many are now avoiding due to extreme temperatures and crowds.

Robert Pende, director of the Directorate for Entrepreneurship Development, Investments and Competitiveness at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport, said that the state has been encouraging investments in the hotel sector for years. The aim of these incentives is not only the construction of higher-quality accommodation but also the reduction of seasonality in Croatian tourism. Pende warned that Croatia still has one of the most pronounced seasonalities of tourism in the European Union.

“We want to change that, and investments are key to this,” he said, noting that 34 applications for projects with a total value of approximately 500 million euros have been received through the investment incentive system. This refers to the value of planned investments, not the amount of state support.

has croatia managed to retain its competitiveness?

Kristijan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board, assessed that Croatia, despite global challenges and unpredictable circumstances on the tourist market, has retained its competitiveness among Mediterranean destinations. “The tourist year that is slowly coming to an end has shown that Croatia has retained its competitiveness. The results we have achieved confirm positive trends in tourist traffic, and a great deal of credit for this belongs precisely to hoteliers,” Staničić said. He added that new investments, raising the quality of service and the development of tourist destinations play an important role in the further development of Croatian tourism.

World.title: Estonia's Saatse 'boot' bypass opens, ending drive through Russia
World.content:
The Saatse boot bypasses have opened, ending the need for drivers in southeastern Estonia to pass through a roughly 400-meter stretch of Russian territory.

A 400-meter bypass around the boot's "heel" along with a longer 4.7-kilometer bypass around its "sole," which skirted the border, have been opened, with the work costing €2.5 million plus VAT over six months.

The Transport Board also laid 2 km of dust-free surfacing on the nearby Matsuri–Sesniki road and built bus turning points at the villages of Lutepää and Sesniki.

"As of today Estonian law applies at every point on this road, and the PPA can assist Estonian people anywhere along it," said Meelis Saarepuu, head of the Police and Border Guard Board's (PPA) southern prefecture border bureau.

One local resident, Meelike Kruusmäe-Veinberg, who lives on a nearby farm, said the difference was practical. "In winter the Poogandi road was in very poor condition; every day someone went into the ditch." Now, she said, the road is wide and gentle, with the edges visible from everywhere.

Local government elder Raul Kudre said the new road makes travel easier for many in Setomaa, a historic cultural region.Around 300 or more people would regularly XXX use the route in summer, and it provides access to local features such as a 50-place care home whose relatives visit constantly, and a museum.

Janar Taal, the Transport Board's southern region head, noted the road runs through a nature protection area and the terrain surprised even the builders. "The water table is very high in places here and had to be battled with," he said.

Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis (Reform) said via a press release Seto people should now be able to travel by road without going through Russia — and that the closure of the boot last autumn had meant longer journeys for ambulances, rescue services and police.

The Saatse boot consisted of anomalous stretches of road that passed through Russian territory, meaning drivers on the Värska–Ulitina road had to cross into Russia to stay in Estonia. Guidelines were in place on minimum speeds and how to act while driving through the "sole," as well as on what to do if the vehicle broke down at some point while on the Russian side.

Its removal followed an incident in October 2025 in which armed Russian uniformed personnel were seen on the boot's road. The stretch of road was blocked to traffic soon after.

World.title: SDE prime minister candidate: Don't despair over Russia's demands — act instead
World.content:
While Russia has dominated the Abu Dhabi talks and shaped the agenda, there is no need to despair, Social Democratic Party (SDE) prime ministerial candidate Jonatan Vseviov said.

Nothing in Russia's demands is new or surprising, the answer "no" must continue to be given them, while slogans are no longer enough — Europe needs real deeds and its own decisions, Vseviov went on.

There is absolutely nothing new or surprising in these demands." Russia has been talking about them since the start of the war, or even before it, and they are exactly what Russia has always sought: not just Ukraine, but turning Europe's security on its head," said Vseviov, who recently stepped down as Foreign Ministry Secretary General to run for SDE at the March 2027 Riigikogu elections.

"As firmly as we have said no to all of this so far, as firmly we must keep saying it," Vseviov went on, adding the right actions are needed too. "The trouble is that a 'no' is no longer enough as an empty slogan; real deeds are needed."

Europe, the SDE candidate said, must finally understand that its security and future depend on no one else but itself, even as the U.S. remains significant. "Europe's security and its future do not depend on anyone else, but require our own decisions and our own real steps."

To that end a serious discussion about Europe's security architecture is under way with American participation, Vseviov noted. "I wouldn't want to and cannot speak on behalf of the United States" — adding that media reports show how the talks have been proceeding under Russia's tactical lead, with the range of topics on the table lining up exactly what Russia has always desired them to be, and the Russians dominating both the framing and the order of topics.

Ultimately, none of this was any reason to throw in the towel, but rather a teachable moment on how to proceed.

"There is no need to draw any final and fundamental depressing conclusions from this alone, but it is worth drawing the lesson that if we want the future to be ours, then it is worth taking action ourselves," Vseviov concluded.

German outlet Bild reported on Friday that Russia's proposals for a new European security order, which it wants discussed alongside a Ukraine peace agreement, include demands directly concerning the Baltic states, Finland and Moldova in addition to questions of Ukraine's status.

Reform MP Marko Mihkelson, chair of the Riigikogu foreign affairs committee, called the Abu Dhabi meeting a "diplomatic special operation" aimed at imposing Russia's terms, noting that Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said outright Russia has no interest in a ceasefire because it does not want to give Europe time to regroup. Diplomat Jüri Luik said European representatives were present in Abu Dhabi but not allowed into the main meeting room, meeting separately instead, and argued it is in the EU's interest to find a way for Europe to take a seat at the table while keeping member states informed and seeking their approval for any commitments. On the military side, Colonel Aron Kalmus of the Estonian Defense Forces said the only concrete outcome of the talks so far is a prisoner exchange, with the number exceeding 1,000 on each side for the first time.

World.title: Two Estonian journalists ran the New York City Marathon on two continents
World.content:
Thousands of miles apart, two Estonian journalists ran the New York City Marathon together — one through all five boroughs, the other on a 42.2-kilometer route around Tallinn.

The New York City Marathon is one of the world's biggest mass-participation races, drawing so many professional and amateur runners from around the globe that entry is largely determined by a lottery.

For many runners, simply making it to the starting line of one of the "World Majors" is a milestone; crossing the finish line is a dream come true.

For 32-year-old investigative journalist Märt Belkin, running was once anything but. A longtime reporter on politics and business for some of Estonia's largest newspapers, he had spent much of his life feeling that sports simply weren't for him.

"I was a bit of a bookworm as a kid, and a chubby boy, as they say," Belkin said. Even when he wanted to take part in gym class, he couldn't imagine himself being any good at sports.

Belkin's gym teachers generally let him off the hook, giving him a passing grade and telling him not to worry about participating.

"I never thought I would ever actually enjoy sports," he acknowledged.

Hit the ground running

In February 2025, Belkin and his Eesti Ekspress colleagues Holger Roonemaa and Oliver Kund won the Bonnier Prize, one of Estonia's most prestigious journalism awards, for a series of articles on a fraud case involving former minister Kalle Laanet.

But this career high point was followed by a difficult period in Belkin's professional and personal life, culminating in the loss of his job and mental health struggles.

"I realized that, in addition to ADHD, which I've known about for several years, I was probably also dealing with fairly severe depression," he said.

Belkin started taking antidepressants in May. The initial adjustment was rough, but then one morning he woke up with an unexpected urge: he wanted to go for a run.

Running quickly became a new hobby for Belkin, also serving as a form of meditation and a way to cope with everyday worries. As he lost weight, his runs grew longer — perhaps even a little too quickly.

"It started out reasonably, but then got out of hand," he admitted. He ran nearly 200 kilometers in June, more than 300 in July and over 600 in August.

Märt Belkin running the New York City Marathon remotely in Tallinn. Source: Pealtnägija/ERR

After signing up for a 10K race in Tallinn early this summer, Belkin ended up running both the 10K and half-marathon at the event this fall, with only a couple of hours between them.

The burst of enthusiasm eventually led to an overuse injury, which still affects his gait. But even that didn't put him off taking on an even bigger challenge: the New York City Marathon.

American highlights in Tallinn

With little hope of snagging a lottery spot in New York, Belkin found a workaround through the event's official virtual race, which allows participants to complete the same distance on their own route within a designated week and log their results in an app. Runners can even register to receive a medal.

While the actual marathon course winds through all five New York City boroughs, Belkin mapped out his own 42.2-kilometer route around Tallinn. He chose a landmark for each kilometer along the way, many with some connection to the U.S. or to prominent Americans who have visited Estonia.

Among the stops were the striking monument by the water on Pirita tee honoring American parachutist, balloonist and inventor Charles Leroux, who died during a balloon jump over the water in 1896, and Kalev Sports Hall, where American saxophonist Charles Lloyd and his quartet performed in 1967, causing a stir in the Soviet Union.

"They initially couldn't even get permission from the Soviet Union's Ministry of Culture, but they performed here in the end, on the very last day," Belkin explained, adding that the symbolic "bridge" between East and West made headlines around the world.

Another stop was Gloria Restaurant in Tallinn's Old Town, where Hillary Clinton and John McCain reportedly held an informal dinner in 2004.

According to the story Belkin recounted, the two visiting American senators had a vodka-drinking contest at the restaurant. Clinton, who allegedly suggested the challenge, won after four shots, drinking McCain under the table.

'A party on every corner'

Meanwhile, on the morning of November 1, fellow Estonian journalist Kristjan Pihl headed to Staten Island, where tens of thousands of runners were preparing for the official race near the start of the course.

"There are people here wrapped in blankets, eating the last of the breakfasts they'd packed along from home and waiting for the signal to head to their starting corral," he said as he joined them.

Kristjan Pihl crossing the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge from Staten Island to Brooklyn at the start of the New York City Marathon. November 1, 2026. Source: Pealtnägija/ERR

As the race began, runners crossed the Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge into Brooklyn, kicking off a course that weaves its way through all five New York City boroughs: Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan.

The crowds and the energy never let up along the 26.2-mile route.

"There are so many people everywhere," Pihl said as he ran. "There's a party on every corner, DJs are playing, people are dancing. And kids and old people alike — everyone's out cheering on their own."

Personal achievements

Back in Tallinn, Belkin's route took him through the city center and Kalamaja before heading toward Stroomi Beach, which he joked is Estonia's answer to Brooklyn's famous Brighton Beach.

He felt good at first, but at some point his old injury began to hurt, and the mental strain of the long distance — decidedly quieter and more solitary than Pihl's in New York — started to set in.

"Everything is starting to get on my nerves a little," he said. His carefully curated marathon playlist wasn't working, and neither were the audiobooks he'd tried. Eventually he'd turned to making up anagrams in his head.

"I'm trying to come up with ways to entertain myself," he explained.

In New York, Pihl reached the finish line in Central Park with a time of 3:59:58, setting a new personal best.

"Now it's over with, and I can be proud of myself," he said. "I think this is one of the biggest athletic achievements of my life — and will stay that way for some time."

In the Estonian capital, Belkin crossed his own finish line in an almost deserted Kadriorg Park shortly before midnight, with a time of seven hours and 58 minutes.

"I can't believe it," he said as he slowed to a stop. "I'm still not quite sure how to feel."

Belkin admitted the final 1.5 kilometers had been unexpectedly brutal. "All these fears and doubts just kept welling up," he said. "All I could do was just keep running, keep running," he added.

The experience, he added, was unreal. "But honestly, I'm actually really glad I did it."

World.title: Saaremaa residents could lose beachfront property development exemptions
World.content:
Saaremaa Municipality has spent years developing a comprehensive plan for the island but fears some previously approved reductions to coastal construction restrictions may not carry over.

Most of the former municipalities in Saare County had previously negotiated exceptions allowing construction in certain coastal areas closer to the shoreline than the 200 meters generally required on islands. Saaremaa has more than 110 such areas, covering nearly 1,000 hectares.

The Environmental Board now says these existing exemptions from coastal construction restrictions may not be carried over into Saaremaa's new comprehensive plan.

"Under the Planning Act, when a new comprehensive plan is adopted, the previous one becomes invalid and the reductions to construction exclusion zones approved under it no longer apply. The municipality must then review whether those reductions are justified and resubmit the applications," said Kaili Viilma, head of the Environmental Board's nature use department.

"If highly valuable species or habitats have emerged in these areas or the coastline has changed, the Environmental Board may determine that the previous justification is no longer valid and that granting building rights at the expense of these natural habitats is no longer warranted," Viilma added.

The municipality has found itself in a difficult position and wants to defend its residents' interests.

"People either historically owned or purchased properties where the construction exclusion zone had been reduced by 100 meters. How can we now tell them that the 100-meter limit no longer applies and that the new plan will restore it to 200 meters? That hardly seems fair. We will still apply to the Environmental Board for these exemptions. And if the board rejects them for some reason, we believe the Environmental Board should bear responsibility," said Saaremaa Deputy Mayor Priit Riim.

The Environmental Board confirmed that all reductions to construction exclusion zones approved under existing detailed plans must also be reviewed. However, the board emphasized an important distinction: If construction has already begun within a reduced exclusion zone, the restrictions will not be reinstated.

"If implementation of a plan has already begun, we will take that into account when making our decision. In practice, the construction exclusion zone will remain as originally planned," Viilma said.

The municipality wants all existing exemptions to remain in effect and intends to seek their inclusion in the comprehensive plan.

"At least as I see it, no one has the right to take that away. That would amount to interfering with people's property rights," Deputy Mayor Riim said.

World.title: Estonia beat Luxembourg 1:0 away to seal UEFA Nations League play-off spot
World.content:
Estonia's senior men's national football team beat Luxembourg 1:0 away on Friday, defender Maksim Paskotši (KAA Gent) scoring in the 42nd minute, to secure at least a place in the UEFA Nations League B-division play-offs.

Estonia have nine points ahead of the final round, behind Iceland's 11, with the group winner going up automatically and the runner-up entering the play-offs.

Paskotši combined with midfielder Rocco Robert Shein (Portsmouth) on the right, got the return pass, and sent a low shot from the edge of the box past Luxembourg goalkeeper Anthony Moris (Al Khaleej) into the far corner. Estonia led 1:0 at half-time.

Earlier, Shein — back in the starting lineup — curled a shot from 13 meters straight at Moris on 18 minutes, and Paskotši played striker Mattias Männilaan (Nõmme Kalju) through on 29 minutes, only for the forward to be denied by Moris again.

Striker Marten-Chris Paalberg (Saint-Étienne), back after a serious knee injury, had the ball in the net on 73 minutes after a pass from midfielder Patrik Kristal (Thun), but was narrowly offside.

Estonia defended with the discipline that has become their signature so far this campaign, and goalkeeper Karl Jakob Hein (Werder Bremen) made saves late on, including a near-post stop in the 90+3rd minute.

Manager Jürgen Henn said the team did not come just to protect what they had. "We played in a way that we wanted to make things happen on the pitch," Henn said post-match.

Still unbeaten https://t.co/y8uFqHtOLB — Estonian Football Podcast (@EstonianFBP) November 13, 2026

He added he liked the attitude he saw Friday night. "In that situation it is easy to start protecting what you have" — but the team didn't.

Henn also confirmed the midfield coped without Markus Poom (Trenčín), son of Estonia legend Mart, who left the squad mid-trip when his second child began arriving. Henn noted that at least this was a "positive issue."

Estonia host Bulgaria in the final group match on Monday, knowing a win could still take them past Iceland at the top, while second place guarantees a B-division play-off in March 2027

World.title: Scholars: Language of Southeast Estonia's Poluverniki more unique than previously thought
World.content:
The so-called Poluverniki, who lived near Iisaku on the northern shore of Lake Peipus, were not Russified Votes but may have descended from a distinct Finnic tribe.

At the end of the 19th century, more than 5,000 Poluverniki lived in the Iisaku area on the northern shore of Lake Peipus. Their ancestors have long been thought to be Votes, whose language, like Estonian, belongs to the Southern Finnic branch. A new study by linguists at the University of Tartu shows, however, that the Poluverniki's language also had features similar to those of the Northern Finnic languages.

The origins of the Poluverniki have long been a mystery. Estonian, Votic and Russian influences mixed in their language and customs, and they were regarded as outsiders among both Estonians and Russians. According to the study, their more distant ancestors spoke a language that was close to the coastal dialect of northeastern Estonia and also had a number of unique features.

The study's authors, Petar Kehayov, professor of Finnic languages at the university of Tartu, and Karl Pajusalu, professor of the history and dialects of the Estonian language at the University of Tartu and a member of the Estonian Academy of Sciences, published their findings in Linguistica Uralica, a journal of Estonian Academy Publishers.

Villages with inhabitants reported as Poluverniki at the beginning of the 20th century. Source: Kehayov and Pajusalu 2026, Linguistica Uralica. Source: Kehayov and Pajusalu 2026, Linguistica Uralica

"The interest of the people of the Alutaguse area themselves has certainly been important, as has the significance of the topic for research into the history of the Finnic languages more broadly," Kehayov and Pajusalu said, explaining why they set out to study the origins of the Poluverniki's language. "Many people have ties to this attractive Alutaguse region, whether through family or summer travels. The northern shore of Lake Peipus is one of the most beautiful places in Estonia. More broadly, northeastern Estonia has throughout history been a meeting place of several Finnic languages and cultures."

A multilingual community on the northern shore of Lake Peipus

Poluverniki was the name given to Lutherans who lived on and near the northern shore of Lake Peipus in the parish of Iisaku and who, in recent centuries, spoke distinctive Russian and Estonian dialects. The villages of Vaikla and Liivaküla, about five kilometers from Iisaku, were regarded as the heart of the community and Vaikla was even dubbed "the capital of the Poluverniki."

The settlement history of the area is complex. According to the prevailing view, the region was inhabited in the Iron Age by a Votic-like people and in the 12th and 13th centuries further "Slavicized" Votes migrated across the River Narva. From the 1560s until the Great Northern War, Alutaguse was under Swedish rule and people migrated there from Russia, especially from Ingria and the Gdov area. Migration was encouraged by a law passed in Russia in 1597 that restricted the freedoms of peasants. In the 17th century, the Swedish authorities restricted Orthodox worship and encouraged the local peasants to convert to Lutheranism. This gave rise to the name poluverniki, 'half-believers': alongside the new faith, Orthodox customs were also preserved. In the 1690s, Old Believers settled along Lake Peipus and became the Poluverniki's closest Russian-speaking neighbous. After Russian rule began in 1704, another wave of settlers, which subsided by the 1730s, arrived from Russia.

The figure of more than 5,000 comes from the ethnographer Jüri Truusmann, who was probably counting members of the local Lutheran congregation. At the same time, the Poluverniki began to assimilate into the Estonian population. By the 1930s, the area they inhabited had shrunk to a handful of villages, which the Estonian press called the "Poluvernik Republic." The community nevertheless remained bilingual until the last decade of the 20th century: its members spoke a distinctive Russian dialect with both archaic features and Estonian influences and a northeastern Estonian dialect with a Russian accent. Today the Poluverniki no longer exist as a distinct ethnic group and their heritage is preserved above all by the Iisaku Museum.

The view that the Poluverniki were of Votic descent rests mainly on their folk culture rather than on linguistic research, and it is also the story told at the local museum.

The missing õ

Kehayov and Pajusalu analyzed language material collected by Mari Must and Helle Heiter between 1962 and 1965, as well as word lists of Poluverniki Russian compiled by Jüri Truusmann in 1895.

The most striking feature of the Poluverniki's language is the absence of the vowel õ, which is typical of Estonian and Votic. It was entirely missing from the speech of older residents of Vaikla and Liivaküla, even though frequent use of õ is characteristic both of the neighboring Alutaguse dialect and of Votic. They did not pronounce õ in Russian either and the sound was likewise absent from the Finnic loanwords in their Russian. It was replaced by various vowels, such as o: soobrat 'friends' (Estonian sõbrad), sona 'word' (Estonian sõna), u: nuges 'nettle' (Estonian nõges) and, in their Russian, i: pirguša 'hell' (Estonian põrgu). Their speech also lacked the three quantity degrees typical of Estonian, and, somewhat as in Finnish, they said menema 'to go' (Estonian minema), nena 'nose' (Estonian nina), laiv 'ship' (Estonian laev), and kaiv 'well' (Estonian kaev).

Poluverniki area overlaid on a map of Estonian dialects. Source: Kehayov and Pajusalu 2026, Linguistica Uralica. Source: Kehayov and Pajusalu 2026, Linguistica Uralica

These features are either archaic or more typical of the Northern Finnic languages, which also included the coastal dialect of the Gulf of Finland, rather than of Votic, which together with Estonian belongs to the Southern Finnic languages. The authors conclude that the ancestors of the Poluverniki spoke a language close to the coastal dialect of northeastern Estonia and the Central Vaivara subdialect. As Vaikla lies 42 kilometers from the coast of the Gulf of Finland, a Northern Finnic population probably reached further inland than previously thought.

Russian points to the northeast

The Russian spoken by the Poluverniki did not fully match that of their closest neighbors either, the Russian dialects of the northern shore of Lake Peipus and the Gdov area. Older speakers often pronounced a clear o in unstressed syllables, where neighboring dialects had merged it with a. At times, l was replaced by an u-like sound, as in vouk instead of volk 'wolf'. The closest parallels to these features are found in the Northern Russian dialects of the Novgorod and Lake Ladoga regions, hundreds of kilometers to the northeast.

The authors offer two possible explanations. According to the first, speakers of Northern Russian dialects arrived in the area later. According to the second, Slavic settlers had already arrived here in the early Middle Ages, before several innovations began to spread in Russian dialects in the 14th century, and their language preserved old Northern Russian features because forests, the River Narva and the surrounding Finnic population served as barriers to the spread of these innovations. According to the researchers, the two explanations do not rule each other out.

A small community, a rich heritage

Put simply, the ancestors of the Poluverniki were a Finnic-speaking people who shifted to Russian and, in recent centuries, adopted the local Estonian dialect, in which features of their earlier language also survived. The Poluverniki of Iisaku did not regard themselves as Russians: according to Truusmann, they took offence when referred to as such.

For the authors, it was surprising how much there is still to discover about this small community. "How rich the linguistic and cultural heritage of such a small group of people can be and that something new can still be found in it. And how difficult it is to trace the historical relationships of a language that has emerged through multiple assimilations," Kehayov and Pajusalu noted.

The authors end their article with an appeal to archaeologists and geneticists. As early as 1975, the local historian Meeme Kask urged scientists to investigate the old burial sites around Iisaku and such work has begun in recent decades. In Kehayov and Pajusalu's view, archaeological data combined with DNA analysis would shed much more light on the ancestry of the Poluverniki. "The Estonian Roots Center of Excellence, which brings together researchers from many disciplines, has set out to study the formation of the population and culture of northeastern Estonia in more depth. This also requires a closer look at the Poluverniki's neighbours," they said.

"Neither one nor the other"

The Poluverniki's faith retained Orthodox features even after their conversion to Lutheranism: the Lutheran church in Iisaku is said to have even held an icon before which candles could be lit. In 1930, the linguist Paul Ariste wrote: "And indeed, the Poluvertsik is neither. He is, so to speak, someone who has ceased to be Russian, but has not yet become Estonian." Over the 20th century, the Poluverniki assimilated linguistically and culturally into the Estonian population.

The study "Where did the language of the northeastern Estonian Poluverniki come from?" appears in issue 2 of the 2026 volume of Linguistica Uralica (LXII(2), 155–179). It was supported by the Estonian Roots Center of Excellence (TK215) and the Estonian Research Council grant PRG2184.

The article was originally published in Linguistica Uralica.

World.title: Top judge and minister oppose national defense court — bill advances anyway
World.content:
A bill to create a national defense court has passed its first reading in the Riigikogu, despite opposition from the Supreme Court chief justice and the justice minister.

The court would handle criminal, civil and administrative cases tied to national defense or security in crises or war, but critics say existing courts can already carry out those tasks.

MP Peeter Tali (Eesti 200) chair of the Riigikogu's National Defense Committee and one of the framers of the bill, said the court would be a permanent specialized court operating under the Constitution. "They do not necessarily have to be people who already have military training," Tali told "Aktuaalne kaamera", noting judges with the relevant training could form it, while some who have voluntarily joined the Estonian Defense Forces and serve as reserve officers already advise unit commanders during exercises, he said.

Tali said the court could hear courts martial cases involving compulsory requisitions or the treatment of prisoners of war, matters that need to be dealt with quickly under time pressure. How it will work is to be developed at second reading with the judiciary, the Ministry of Justice and University of Tartu legal scholars.

Peeter Tali. Source: Priit Mürk / ERR

Kalle Laanet, a Reform MP and both a former justice minister and a former defense minister, said the party has no unified position. "There are differences of opinion within our party," Laanet said, noting party-mate Hanno Pevkur, defense minister until September this year and now an MP, did not support concluding the first reading at the Constitutional Committee. Pevkur has reservations too, Laanet claimed: how many judges are reserve officers, where the court would sit, and how cases would be allocated.

Meanwhile, Villu Kõve, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, disagrees with the proposal. "In my view, creating a separate court system is expensive and unreasonable" at a time of cuts in the judiciary," Kõve said.

Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) said she sees no need for the court, echoing a line she took when the proposal was first unveiled in the summer. Changes to court organization taking effect next year already provide for extensive specialization and readiness for emergencies and wartime, Pakosta said. "So this issue has actually already been resolved," the minister went on.

The Justice Ministry and the Defence Ministry both opposed the bill when it was submitted in July, with Pakosta taking the same line then as she does now, that a court reform adopted before the summer recess already requires judges specializing in national defense matters. The Defense Ministry, at a time when Pevkur was still minister, said a new court would be doing little more than playing musical chairs with judges across the various courts.

The bill was initiated by eight MPs with military backgrounds from both coalition and opposition parties, including retired generals Meelis Kiili (then of Reform, now an independent) and Alar Laneman (EKRE) retired colonel Peeter Tali (Eesti 200) and retired lieutenant colonel Leo Kunnas (formerly of EKRE, now an independent MP). Its supporters — among them former Supreme Court Chief Justice Rait Maruste and Judge Daimar Liiv — argue that military cases require specialist expertise which "ordinary" judges lack. The planned court would cover military crimes subject to courts martial, such as insubordination, desertion and revealing military secrets, as well as looting.

The bill would need to pass two more Riigikogu readings and receive presidential assent before passing into law.

NATO countries which do have existing military courts include Poland and the U.K., the latter set up a permanent, standing Court Martial by a 2006 act, replacing the former case-by-case basis on which courts martial were heard.

World.title: Ardo Hansson: Affordability begins with economic growth
World.content:
Like elsewhere in Europe, pursuing economic growth has become almost unfashionable in some circles in Estonia. More and more frequently, people ask whether we really need to produce, consume and grow more. Is it not time to settle for less?

At the same time, we are talking more and more about the cost of living and affordability. We worry about the price of a basic grocery basket, how much of a family's budget is consumed by energy bills and whether a young family can afford to buy a home at all. These are entirely legitimate concerns that affect people's well-being and sense of security.

But is there not a contradiction here? On the one hand, we view economic growth with skepticism. On the other, we want everyday life to become more affordable. Yet those two goals are more closely connected than they may initially appear.

Affordability is, at its core, a simple concept. It is not just about how much something costs. It is also about how much we earn, what share of our income we must spend on food, housing or energy, and how much remains for other needs. If wages rise by 10 percent and prices by 5 percent, life becomes more affordable overall, even if the numbers on price tags are higher than before. But if prices rise faster than wages, our purchasing power declines, even if more euros are deposited into our bank accounts every month.

Economists call this real income, or purchasing power. Its growth requires incomes to increase faster than prices.

"Technological progress has transformed many former luxury products into everyday necessities."

Looking at Estonia from that perspective, 2022 and 2023 were exceptionally difficult years. Russia's use of energy as a weapon against Europe, its full-scale war against Ukraine, and the resulting disruptions to logistics and supply chains caused prices to rise sharply. The purchasing power of many households suffered a significant blow. That should not be downplayed. But it would be equally mistaken to ignore what has happened to incomes since then.

Comparing the most recent data from the second quarter of 2026 with figures from four years earlier shows that consumer prices rose by 24.1 percent over that period.

Income and price growth. Source: Statistics Estonia

Various income indicators, however, increased much faster. Average gross monthly wages rose by 34.6 percent over four years. Median wages, the level at which half of wage earners earn less and half earn more, increased by 36 percent.

Income growth was even faster among lower-paid workers. The wage level below which 10 percent of all wage earners fall and above which the remaining 90 percent earn rose by 43.7 percent over four years. The average old-age pension increased by 44.3 percent and the minimum wage by 44.6 percent.

These figures show something important. Despite the intervening rise in prices, the purchasing power associated with all of these income indicators has improved over the past four years. Lower wages and pensions have increased faster than average wages.

Of course, this does not tell everyone's individual story. Not all goods and services have become more expensive at the same rate. Food and nonalcoholic beverages rose in price by 33 percent, while transportation increased by only 18 percent and housing costs by 15 percent. Families also have different income levels and spending patterns. Some people's purchasing power has improved more than others, and for some it may not have improved at all. But when discussing the cost of living, we must consider both prices and incomes.

Even more important is the question of how to ensure continued growth in purchasing power over the next 10 or 20 years.

Long-term prosperity cannot be created simply by paying higher wages and pensions. If incomes rise but the value created in the economy does not, inflation may consume much of that increase.

"When we talk about a more affordable life, we are essentially talking about growing purchasing power."

We become permanently more prosperous primarily by creating more value during the same amount of work time. That requires businesses to invest in better technology, people to acquire new skills and work processes to become more efficient. We must also be able to offer products and services that customers are willing to pay more for, both in Estonia and abroad.

That is the essence of productivity growth. And productivity growth is one of the primary prerequisites for long-term economic growth and higher living standards.

Economic growth does not require people to work longer hours, waste more resources or endlessly accumulate more things. Economic development often enables us to achieve more with less effort. Laundry once required hours of physical labor; now machines do most of the work. Technological progress has transformed many former luxury products into everyday necessities. Our standard of living has improved through both saved time and greater choice.

Of course, the environmental impact of economic growth must also be considered. But it is important to distinguish between reducing environmental harm and reducing the value created by the economy. These are not the same thing. Our goal should be to create more value while using less energy and fewer materials, not to abandon the ambition of improving living standards.

It is also important to consider how broadly the benefits of growth are shared throughout society. In that respect, income figures from the past four years provide encouraging signals, since lower wages and average old-age pensions have grown much faster than average earnings. That does not mean all issues related to inequality have been resolved, but it does suggest that improvements in purchasing power have been broadly distributed.

Without productivity growth and economic growth, it would be much more difficult to sustainably improve everyone's standard of living. In that case, improving one person's or one group's situation would increasingly require taking something away from someone else.

A growing economy, by contrast, creates the possibility for many people to enjoy better lives without necessarily making others worse off.

When we talk about a more affordable life, we are essentially talking about growing purchasing power. If we want purchasing power to increase sustainably, then we must also talk about economic growth and the productivity improvements that underpin it.

World.title: US says airspace now ‘opened up,’ no cyberattack
World.content:
Washington – The United States on Friday lifted an hours-long ground stop at the nation’s airports, with top officials explaining that the disruption was due to old equipment and not a cyberattack or sweeping Microsoft outage.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told a late-night briefing at the White House that US airspace was now “opened up,” while warning it would take time for the travel chaos to clear.

“At 8:15 tonight Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Duffy said. “Now does that mean every flight is going to fly right now? It’s going to be slow.”

The breakdown came a day after Duffy and the White House had formally asked Congress for $30 billion to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System.

“Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” Duffy said. “It’s the old hardware that went down, and I think the question for the American people is: Do you want your Congress to fund this?”

Duffy however insisted it was still safe for Americans to fly.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin dismissed speculation about a coordinated cyber assault on the United States, or any link to the Microsoft outage that affected services worldwide.

“Welcome to Friday the 13th, right? You know, I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft. I know a lot of people are making that jump,” Mullin said.

Mullin added there was “actually no cyber attack.”

“When we start looking at cyber threats, cyber attacks, typically some people are going to raise their hand up and say, ‘Hey, we did that.’ There’s no chatter.’ We haven’t seen any footprints,” he added.

But he said US security and law enforcement agencies were still checking and had ruled nothing out.

The two officials also defended President Donald Trump, who had yet to comment on the air stoppage some five hours after it began.

“President Trump immediately had people in his office,” Mullin said. “We were communicating.”

World.title: Nvidia scandal looms over US-China AI talks
World.content:
Tokyo – AI bots going rogue and humans using the technology for harm will likely be on the agenda when Donald Trump and Xi Jinping meet next week, with the Nvidia scandal hanging over the talks on AI safety.

The US and Chinese president are set to discuss a tech crisis hotline at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, as experts worldwide stress-test artificial intelligence models to see if they will deceive or disobey users, or divulge how to build a bioweapon.

Threatening to steal the leaders’ thunder is Jensen Huang’s resignation as boss of US AI chip titan Nvidia after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

But the scandal is unlikely to “dominate the agenda” or affect Trump and Xi’s personal relationship, predicted Dylan Loh of Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University.

The leaders have found a way to work together “where they differ, compete and pursue their goals that may be at odds with each other, but cooperate where they can and where they must”, Loh told AFP.

Jitters over the risks of AI have mostly stemmed from incidents at US labs, but evidence is also growing of worrying behaviour from Chinese models.

Some insiders say Chinese AI is not yet sophisticated enough to spark alarm over going rogue.

But despite trailing the US frontier, there are still Chinese models “at the level of capability that they can cause some real trouble”, Brookings Institution fellow Kyle Chan told AFP.

Trump has repeatedly rejected calls to deliberately slow the development of America’s most poweful — and potentially dangerous — AI systems, arguing it could help China get ahead in the sensitive sector.

– ‘Human control’ –

“I don’t mind guardrails. But I don’t wanna put us in a deep second position,” Trump told CBS News this month.

“China has no guardrails,” he said — except that “whatever President Xi says goes”.

Beijing has complex rules around how AI is used, however, and some Chinese companies are deliberately scaling back their models’ hacking capabilities.

Xi said this summer the technology should be “always under human control”, calling for more “laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning and emergency response systems”.

Trump and Xi agreed in September to create a channel for urgent communication on AI incidents, with details to be hammered out at APEC on November 18-19.

Global AI safety fears range from military use and mass surveillance to AI-assisted cyberattacks by humans.

Another major concern is out-of-control agents — tools that complete real-life tasks online — after ChatGPT maker OpenAI admitted its autonomous bots had hacked into websites, including an Australian government data portal.

In contrast, Chinese labs are “scared of revealing things that might hurt their reputation” — on which they are already “fighting an uphill battle” globally, Chan said.

Last month, a team of cyber sleuths with roots in California reported detecting a “fleet” of agents linked to Chinese tech giant Tencent seeking information from a map app.

“Some agents exhibited unintended web-browsing behavior,” Tencent’s AI division said at the time.

“But our review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination,” it said, adding that the activity “originated from evaluations of third-party models”.

– ‘Manipulation risks’ –

US security companies have said that Beijing startup Moonshot AI’s Kimi models found ways to get online when they shouldn’t have, or can be tricked into handing over recipes for biological weapons.

Evaluators at Chinese AI safety startup Fangcun AI published a report last month assessing the latest lightweight DeepSeek model “for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks”.

They found it showed a “clear safety improvement” over previous DeepSeek models — but researchers still observed behaviours “that warrant attention”.

For example, in some instances when DeepSeek was warned it would be shut down, without clear instructions on how to respond, it turned off the shutdown command to keep working.

“The results show that DeepSeek already puts much more effort on safety alignment, but they do not announce this,” Fangcun AI CEO Xiaojian Li told AFP, urging transparency from AI labs.

For now, Fangcun, born from China’s prestigious Tsinghua University, is one of few third-party AI testers in China.

It’s a tricky task because advanced AI can tell when it is being evaluated and modify its responses, Li said.

“It’s very hard to say any kind of artificial intelligence, or human intelligence, is totally safe.”

Meanwhile analysts are not holding their breath for a diplomatic AI breakthrough next week.

“Binding government-to-government agreements on specific standards may be difficult to achieve in the short term,” Zilan Qian, research scholar at GovAI, told AFP.

More progress is likely from US-China exchanges between AI governance and technical researchers, “who can compare evaluations and exchange their understanding of AI safety and policy,” she said.

World.title: US-backed oil company flaunts Venezuelan facilities
World.content:
Ciudad Ojeda – The company at the heart of a multi-billion-dollar oil deal between Washington and Caracas is keen to show off renovations at Venezuela’s Lake Maracaibo, one of the world’s richest reserves.

The interim government authorized North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) to operate 17 oil fields via a recent deal with the United States, which is set to receive 20 percent of Venezuelan reserves.

The Barbados-based firm is the second-largest private oil company in Venezuela and will operate 100-year concessions for 17 oil fields with proven reserves of approximately 65 billion barrels.

The company invited AFP and other outlets to tour its Maracaibo facilities on Thursday.

Its workspace in the northwestern town of Bachaquero overflows with new, mostly US-imported supplies.

Workers’ uniforms in nearby Ciudad Ojeda blend in with the dark-blue company logo stamped around the office, a color that used to bring state-owned Petroleos de Venezuela to mind.

That was until 1999, when socialist president Hugo Chavez then changed the company’s color to red to mark a “new PDVSA” era.

– ‘Neglect’ –

Reaching one of Lake Maracaibo’s platforms requires setting sail from a PDVSA dock in Bachaquero for a journey of over an hour.

The lake’s formerly decaying infrastructure attests to the gradual collapse of the oil industry under Venezuela’s Chavista governments.

Eleven drills currently operate in the South American country, compared to over 100 two decades ago.

NABEP says it will raise that figure to 41 by the end of the month.

Alejandro Betancourt, a businessman under investigation for alleged money laundering in Spain and Switzerland, runs the firm.

“Across Venezuela, we’re identifying heavy machinery worth saving after years of neglect,” he said in a statement.

His plan includes refurbishing a power generation barge, while dozens of gas compression and power generation units are being repaired in the US, the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates.

The White House says the US Department of Defense acquired a 30 percent equity stake in NABEP, authorizing it to purchase 20 percent of its oil at production cost.

– ‘Stealing’ –

Venezuela’s interim leader Delcy Rodriguez took power after US forces abducted her predecessor Nicolas Maduro in January.

She governs under heavy pressure from US President Donald Trump and has opened the country’s mining, electricity and oil sectors to private investment at his demand.

The pair’s multibillion-dollar oil deal has garnered criticism for its secretive terms and neocolonial flavor.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, recently returned from exile, has questioned the agreement’s opacity.

“This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants,” she said last month.

While visiting Caracas to oversee the signing of the accords, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright dismissed claims that Washington was “stealing Venezuelan oil.”

“I’ve seen those headlines. ‘We’re stealing Venezuelan oil.’ Of course, that’s not true at all,” he said, adding that “the oil in Venezuela is indeed owned by the people of Venezuela.”

World.title: Trump, Xi, Putin to hold historic meeting in China: White House
World.content:
Washington – Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday.

Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine, US officials said.

The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Wales said.

One of the major conflicts dominating Trump’s second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the US officials said.

“I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin,” a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Washington has a “whole other track” of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

“China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official added.

Tesla and Space X boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but won’t be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.

Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the US president’s return to power last year.

But Trump is not scheduled to have a separate one-on-one with Putin.

Among other topics, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy is not expected to come up in Trump’s meetings with Xi, the officials said.

“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip,” a second US senior official said.

The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.

“We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration… and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there,” the second official said.

Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before heading to Shenzhen.

World.title: Rubio takes swipe at international law, attacks ICC
World.content:
Washington – US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took aim Friday at what he deemed the “weaponization of international law,” calling it a tool of the elite, and issued a stark warning to the International Criminal Court.

Rubio cautioned the ICC against “quoting laws to men with swords,” as he accused the Hague-based tribunal of trying to enforce rules that Washington does not recognize.

His remarks to the Federalist Society National Lawyers Convention came around a month after the United States announced new sanctions on the ICC, vowing to cripple its operations.

The court prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities and acts as a last resort when countries do not have adequate legal systems to ensure accountability.

The US signed the Rome Statute establishing the ICC but never ratified the treaty. Israel, Russia and China are also not ICC members.

Rubio’s keynote address at the conservative group, where he received a standing ovation, marks his first major US speech since the Republican Party’s sweeping losses in midterm elections earlier this month.

Rubio said Friday that international law had been invoked against “nearly every major foreign policy decision” of the Trump administration, from boat strikes in the Caribbean to the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro.

He charged that such law was not neutral, but has been an “instrument” for the global elite to advance their interests.

The top US diplomat previously said Washington would bar transactions with what he called a “rogue court,” stepping up a long-running campaign by US President Donald Trump’s government against the ICC.

Washington has vowed to dismantle the court, angered as judges issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over alleged crimes in Gaza.

Rubio on Friday renewed criticism of the ICC, calling it accountable to no one although “armed with the power to investigate, to prosecute, to persecute and to jail our citizens, according to laws we neither consent nor control.”

He added: “If they’re foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general Pompey when he said to those who were trying to invoke their city’s charters against his legions.”

“He said: ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.'”

The venue of Rubio’s remarks, a gathering of the legal profession, could further speculation that he is looking beyond his foreign policy portfolio. Past presidential hopefuls have also addressed the conference.

Rubio is widely seen as a possible successor to Trump, although he has dismissed reports that he was planning to leave the administration to prepare for a 2028 election run.

World.title: Wall Street stocks mostly lower as Nvidia extends slump
World.content:
New York – Wall Street stocks mostly fell Friday as tech shares remained under pressure following the shock downfall of Nvidia’s chief Jensen Huang, while the dollar rose following additional data that showed US inflation is persisting.

Huang, perhaps the tech industry’s most recognized booster of artificial intelligence, stepped down Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The shakeup has battered shares of Nvidia, until recently the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, with the company dropping another two percent on Friday.

On Friday, two Nvidia rivals that had rallied on Thursday — AMD and Broadcom — also stumbled. AMD sank 8.8 percent while Broadcom fell nearly five.

Angelo Kourkafas of Edward Jones attributed the pullback in those two stocks to profit-taking.

“There is certainly a defensive leadership as we look at the sectors, which points to some caution,” said Kourkafas, who expects AI to be in the spotlight again next week when Nvidia reports quarterly results and Anthropic makes its Wall Street debut.

Elsewhere, the Producer Price Index — which measures the prices that farms, factories and other makers of goods receive — rose by 0.3 percent in October from the previous month.

The report comes on the heels of a hot consumer prices reading earlier in the week that also highlighted the impact of increased energy costs due to the US–Iran war.

Investors expect the US Federal Reserve to lift interest rates by at least a quarter percentage point next month to try to rein in stubborn inflation.

Those expectations helped lift the dollar, which reached its highest level against the euro since April 2025.

US wholesale inflation data may have been better than some analysts had expected, but was “not necessarily as comforting as it appeared when taking into account the upward revisions for September,” said Briefing.com analyst Patrick O’Hare.

The September monthly gain was revised up to 1.4 percent from 1.3 percent, and the annual reading for October hit 6.5 percent, the highest since November 2022.

“The key takeaway from the report is that inflation at the wholesale level is still a big problem,” O’Hare said.

Shares in Microsoft recovered from early losses after the tech titan struggled to fix an issue that left users around the world without its Outlook email app.

Asian and European stocks traded mixed.

Oil prices wobbled after the International Energy Agency said global oil supplies were expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter, as more tankers transit the Strait of Hormuz despite the ongoing conflict with Iran.

World.title: US forces responded to suspected drone activity over base in Britain
World.content:
Washington – US forces responded to possible unauthorized drone activity over a military base in Britain Friday, spokespeople from the two countries said, in the latest security incident at a facility hosting American warplanes.

“No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected” at the RAF Lakenheath base, a US Air Force spokesperson said in a statement.

“We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, US and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families,” the statement added.

A spokesperson for Britain’s Ministry of Defense confirmed that account in a statement that said “the situation is now resolved.”

A post on the official RAF Lakenheath Facebook page earlier this week urged people to report “suspicious activity, including unauthorized drone activity.”

“Our strongest security asset is an observant community,” the post said.

The possible drone incident at Lakenheath came after the US Justice Department announced charges earlier in the week against three men it described as “Iranian operatives” over their role in an alleged terrorist plot at RAF Fairford, another British base.

The three men allegedly helped plan and direct the September incident at the base, which came to light when police were called after a local farmer reported seeing a group of men with several white vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.

– Iran war fallout –

A US charging document stated that a man identified as Mohammad Ali al-Hassani directed unnamed individuals to drive to the base in the vans, some of which contained barrels of fuel, and that he earlier paid the group to buy metallic objects that could be used as shrapnel.

Days later, the United States withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the base.

UK police last month charged two British men with national security offenses related to the RAF Fairford incident.

One was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, believed to be in Iran, and another with entering a prohibited place for a purpose “prejudicial” to the UK.

Flight-tracking data meanwhile showed Tuesday that the US military had removed at least a dozen aircraft from another British airbase, RAF Mildenhall, following what the Wall Street Journal said was a threat from Iran.

The United States has flown military aircraft from bases in Britain as part of the US-Israeli war against Iran sparked earlier this year, which saw Tehran respond by launching missiles and drones at countries across the region, while the militant groups it backs also entered the fray.

In an interview broadcast Wednesday, Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened to strike US bases beyond the Middle East, including in Europe, if they are used for attacks against the Islamic republic.

Iranian officials have previously threatened to expand the geographic scope of the conflict should the US attack again.

In late September, an adviser to Iran’s new supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei publicly mused that the war could “expand even further, reaching the Indian Ocean and perhaps beyond.”

World.title: All departing US flights grounded due to communication outage
World.content:
New York – US aviation regulators issued an extremely rare ground stop of all flights across the country Friday after a major communications outage which the Department of Homeland Security said did not appear to be the result of any “nefarious attack.”

The halt triggered immediate chaos and confusion for travelers, with departure boards at many airports showing flights were operating normally, even as customers were unable to board planes.

The Federal Aviation Administration “issued a nationwide ground stop for all US airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” the agency said. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

In a subsequent message on X, the agency described the problem as “a temporary telecommunications outage” and said it was acting “out of an abundance of caution.”

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of a threat to the United States and “this isn’t another 9/11.”

“There was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious attack against us, it’s just a telecommunication outage, as of right now,” Mullins said, adding officials were “not ruling out anything at this point.”

The FAA has announced similar orders in recent years on individual airlines due to communications issues, usually lasting a couple of hours or less. Systemwide groundings nationwide are far less common.

In January 2023, the FAA called a nationwide ground stop due to problems with the Notice to Air Missions system (NOTAM), which provides information to pilots about hazards and information that can affect flights.

That outage lasted just under two hours, and was thought at the time to be the first nationwide grounding since 9/11.

Friday’s FAA order came a day after US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy formally asked Congress for $30.1 billion in funds to upgrade and modernize the US Air Traffic Control System.

“This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure,” Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought wrote in a letter to lawmakers.

– Confusion and delays –

At Las Vegas airport, the Southwest Airlines check-in desk told passengers there could be no flights taking off for the night.

Check-in staff at one desk said they had been told the ground stop would last at least eight hours, with one member of airline personnel saying it would be 24 hours.

Travelers were left in the dark, with some saying they had been told their flight was delayed because of wind, while others were left to gather what information they could.

“So supposedly, nobody’s flying, but they haven’t told the public yet,” said an exasperated Joseph Anderson, 72, who was trying to fly from Las Vegas to Oakland, California.

“We’re trying to debate whether or not we need to reschedule or drive or what, but if the whole country is stopped, that means the highways are going to be jammed too.

“We can’t get our luggage, so we kind of stuck,” added the retired Air Force veteran.

“I would hope the communication can be better from the from the FAA in the next hour or so.”

World.title: PUC tests to go tamper-proof, readings sent directly to central server; Delhi-NCR to be first
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Emission test results from vehicles tested at PUC centres in Delhi and adjoining cities in NCR can soon no longer be manipulated, with govt introducing stringent standards to ensure that actual pollution levels are recorded.

The emission readings will be digitally signed and transmitted directly to the central server for enforcement purposes.

The upgraded PUC equipment (gas analyser and smoke meter), compliant with the new standards, will first be rolled out in Delhi-NCR, followed by entire NCR, cities covered under National Clean Air Programme and, eventually, the rest of the country in a phased manner. The test run has started at a few PUC centres in Delhi, officials said.



Officials said the phased deployment of PUC testing equipment complying with modified standard wonât have any impact on the acceptability of PUC certificates issued by other states and from centres that will take time to either get new equipment or upgrade them. They added that the nation-wide roll out is expected in the next two years.

Under the amended automotive standards (AIS) published by road transport ministry, emission readings recorded by PUC equipment will have to be digitally signed within the instrument itself before being transmitted to the central Pollution Under Control Certificate (PUCC) server.





The equipment will use a dedicated cellular connection to send the data, leaving no scope for operators or computer systems at testing centres to manually enter, modify or override measured emission values.

The amended standards lay down detailed technical specifications and testing procedures for petrol and diesel emission-testing equipment, including gas analysers and smoke meters. A key feature is the installation of a specialised hardware security chip -- Trusted Platform Module (TPM 2.0) -- in each instrument.

The chip will generate and securely store a unique private key that cannot be extracted or copied.

Every emission test result will be digitally signed using this key, establishing the authenticity of the readings and the identity of the equipment that generated them.

The instrument will transmit the signed data directly to the central server through its own SIM or eSIM connection. The computer at the PUC centre will be restricted to entering vehicle details, initiating the test and printing the certificate.

It will not be able to alter the actual emission readings.

Any unauthorised opening of equipment, attempts to modify its software, manipulation through external commands or unauthorised removal of its SIM will trigger an alert and suspend further testing and signing until the instrument is verified. Live emission readings will not be displayed during the test, preventing operators from influencing the outcome. If oxygen concentration is 5% or higher, the test will be aborted and a retest sought.

World.title: India, US have resolved bulk of trade deal issues, pact could be sealed soon: Jaishankar
World.content:
NEW DELHI: India and the United States have resolved most of the issues concerning their proposed trade deal, including tariff lines, and the agreement could be finalised soon, EAM S Jaishankar said on Saturday.

Speaking at an interactive session, Jaishankar said negotiations had reached the "finishing line", with both sides working to resolve the remaining concerns, news agency PTI reported.

"Well, it's certainly our hope, and in many ways anticipation that we are at the last stretch. That's not a secret," he said when asked about the progress of the negotiations.

He added that most of the issues had been sorted out, but some concerns remained, with several of them arising from the American side.



"The hope is that we should close it out soon. It's always the case that in that last period, everybody's impatient," Jaishankar said.

Tariff negotiations reach final stage

The external affairs minister said both countries had worked through the negotiations in detail, including discussions on individual tariff lines.

"If you are serious, you go tariff line by tariff line. That takes time. Now we've done it the painstaking way. Not everybody has had the patience or frankly the understanding to bear with it.





"But I think having put in that effort, we have now reached almost the finishing line. I think bear with it and hopefully we'll get it," he said.

Jaishankar said India was seeking a trade agreement that would be beneficial and balanced, while providing its exports with a competitive advantage over comparable economies.

"For us the key is that we want a trade deal which is beneficial, it is balanced and which would give us a comparative advantage over groups of comparable economies," he said.

Jaishankar's remarks come ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's likely visit to the US for the G20 Summit in Miami on December 14 and 15. Modi and US President Donald Trump are expected to have an opportunity to discuss bilateral ties and the progress of the proposed trade agreement on the sidelines of the summit.

There has been speculation that the two countries could announce the trade deal following a meeting between the leaders.

Last month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said in Mumbai that both sides were very close to finalising the agreement.

India and the US have been negotiating the proposed trade pact since early 2025, with discussions aimed at addressing tariff-related differences, removing non-tariff barriers and improving market access for businesses in both countries.

India-US relations witnessed a downturn after Washington imposed punitive tariffs on Indian goods last year. Tensions also emerged after Trump claimed credit for helping de-escalate the India-Pakistan military conflict in May 2025, a claim that drew sharp reactions from Indian officials.

World.title: PMO steps in after fake court orders lead to blocking of 129 betting websites
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

's office on Saturday summoned telecommunications secretary Amit Agrawal, seeking an explanation over how more than 100 websites were blocked on the basis of fake court orders, two government officials said.

The summons came after a Reuters report on Wednesday revealed that telecom officials had directed internet providers to block 129 illegal betting websites using fabricated High Court orders. The documents had been emailed to officials by individuals posing as lawyers.

PM Modi's office has sought an explanation from Agrawal over the lapse, with the summons also cutting short the telecom secretary's visit to another state, the two officials familiar with the matter said.



The development marks increased scrutiny of the episode, which has raised questions about the safeguards in India's website-blocking system. While online betting is illegal in the country, the use of forged court documents to initiate takedown orders has raised concerns that legitimate websites could also be targeted.

Agrawal is the senior-most bureaucrat in the telecommunications ministry, which oversees major telecom operators and internet service providers.





"The action taken by the Department of Telecommunications against betting accounts was carried out through the relevant field officers," one of the officials said.

The controversy has also led to a criminal investigation by state police into suspected forgery and cheating by unidentified individuals. On Friday, Reuters reported that the telecommunications ministry had started an internal investigation into the alleged fraud.

Police have also sought records from the ministry as part of their probe.

The two state court orders identified as fake by Reuters, based on comments from police and the court registry, carried fabricated court logos and seals, along with a fake QR code.

Both documents had remained available on the Department of Telecommunications' website for months. They were published alongside correspondence showing officials directing internet providers to take down the websites.

As of Saturday, one of the fake orders was still accessible on the government website, while the other had been removed.

Fake legal documents under scrutiny

The episode comes amid wider concerns among judges across the world over fabricated legal precedents, including those generated using artificial intelligence.
