World.content: Anil Giri is a Chief Sub Editor covering diplomacy, international relations and national politics for The Kathmandu Post. Giri has been working as a journalist for more than two decades, contributing to numerous national and international media outlets.

World.title: Sundarpur bids farewell to crash victims in mass funeral
World.content:
Sundarpur bids farewell to crash victims in mass funeral

Thirteen residents of the Sarlahi village were among 14 people killed in Thursday’s Makawanpur crash. Twelve bodies were cremated together on the banks of the Lakhandeha river late Friday.

World.title: US to resume flights after air traffic network failure sparks chaos
World.content:
US to resume flights after air traffic network failure sparks chaos

A communications failure at air traffic control centres grounded flights nationwide for four hours, disrupting thousands of journeys and exposing vulnerabilities in the ageing US aviation system.

An aeroplane flies at Miami International Airport after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop “due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety” following the agency’s earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues, in Miami, Florida, US, November 13, 2026. Reuters

World.title: U.S. Air Force captain arrested in Okinawa for alleged drunk driving
World.content:
Japanese police arrested a U.S. Air Force captain Saturday on suspicion of drunk driving in Okinawa, a police spokesman said, in the latest twist to strains between the Pacific allies.

The arrest comes just a week after Tokyo and Washington agreed to measures aimed at preventing crimes by U.S. service members on the island of Okinawa after a murder allegedly involving an American marine triggered outrage.

The U.S. military has around 54,000 personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa. Crimes committed by its members have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.

U.S. officials also said last week they would extend a curfew to lower-ranking service members through Dec. 7, while banning all service members from drinking alcohol outside their homes between midnight and 5 am.

Police arrested the 27-year-old as he “was driving on a road in Okinawa City at around 3:09 am Saturday,” a spokesman for Okinawa prefectural police said.

“It is not clear if he violated the curfew” imposed by U.S. officials, he said.

The arrested captain was assigned to Kadena Air Base on Okinawa, Kyodo News reported.

Officials at the base were not immediately available for comment.

World.title: 6-year-old Gaza burn victim caught in Israeli dispute over aid
World.content:
The excruciating burns run around the side of Masa Yassin’s tiny face, behind her ear, over her scalp and down her neck.

Since her family’s tent burst into flames when a nearby cooking gas tank exploded in July, part of the 6-year-old girl’s treatment has been a clear plastic 3D-printed mask, which helps manage swelling and control the scars on her face.

But soon she will outgrow it, and the international medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres, which operates the only clinic in Gaza that can make her a new one, says it has been barred by Israel from importing the plastic.

World.title: Former Nvidia CEO Huang had a relationship with a second employee, sources say
World.content:
Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The revelation follows two other extramarital affairs that led to his resignation Thursday. The two women are Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy, and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care.

Reuters is not naming the second employee. Attempts to reach the woman were not successful.

Nvidia declined to comment. Powell, Jensen Huang, and a representative for Nvidia’s board did not reply to requests for comment. Alice Huang could not be reached for comment.

Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a Nov. 8 statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name.

The former Nvidia CEO’s decision to resign from the company could disrupt the AI industry that he helped shape. Nvidia has used its financial strength to help create an industry around AI through complex financial arrangements that ease the purchase of the company’s chips. It has backed cloud computing companies and AI labs in order to do so.

Pressure on Jensen Huang, who is 63 and married, to resign mounted after reports of his affair with Alice Huang.

Nvidia’s board appointed finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search to replace Jensen Huang. The board is considering internal and external candidates for the job.

Earlier this month, Nvidia’s board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.

World.title: Eddie Jones vows Japan will ‘play the house down’ in matchup with England
World.content:
Eddie Jones returns to Twickenham on Saturday promising his youthful Japan side will “play the house down” as it goes in search of a huge upset against England, the team he led to a World Cup final.

Japan, which suffered a narrow 28-21 defeat against Wales in its November Nations Championship opener in Cardiff last week, has lost all six of its previous tests against England.

But veteran Australian coach Jones oversaw one of rugby union’s greatest upsets in his first spell with Japan when the Brave Blossoms beat South Africa at the 2015 World Cup in England, and he is now plotting another shock success.

World.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after outage roiled world
World.content:
Microsoft Corp. said access has been fully restored to its flagship software, ending an outage that paralyzed government offices, traders and businesses around the world.

“All products are operational,” according to a service health status update on its website. A “backlog of email messages has been processed, thus this issue is remediated,” it said of its Microsoft 365 services.

That included Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence tool, whose users experienced missed meeting invitations and unresponsive web pages on Friday. Previous disruptions have rarely lasted more than several hours.

World.title: Japan and Philippines to ink deal on oil reserve cooperation
World.content:
Japan and the Philippines are expected to sign a memorandum of understanding on strengthening cooperation on oil stockpiling in the Southeast Asian country.

Under the partnership, Japan’s public and private sectors will help the Philippines develop a national oil reserve system as part of measures to enhance its energy security.

The MOU is set to be signed early next week by industry minister Ryosei Akazawa and a Philippine official ahead of a summit of the Asia Zero Emission Community framework in Manila on Tuesday.

The Philippines declared a state of national energy emergency in March amid growing turmoil in the Middle East and has since been working to bolster the resilience of its oil supply.

The memorandum will cover a joint study on cooperating with oil-producing countries such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates as well as the development of systems needed to establish a national oil reserve plan.

Meanwhile, Japanese engineering firm Chiyoda Corp. is expected to sign an MOU with Philippine National Oil soon on technological assistance for oil reserve facilities.

Japan’s Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia, or POWERR Asia, a framework announced in April to provide about $10 billion in financial aid to Asian countries for enhancing their energy supply networks, is seen as a possible source of funding for the measures.

Like Japan, the Philippines depends on the Middle East for more than 90% of its crude oil imports. As of May 3, the country held reserves of oil equivalent to only 53 days of domestic consumption, far below Japan’s public- and private-sector reserves capable of covering 207 days.

Having experienced fuel shortages and supply confusion following the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil transport waterway in the Middle East, the Philippines is working to establish a national oil reserve system while raising stockpiles at its private sector.

The country plans to construct storage tanks for national reserves for completion in 2027 and later, aiming to eventually increase its oil reserves by 15 million barrels, equivalent to 30 days of consumption.

World.title: Japan considers setting five-year defense spending plan at ¥60 trillion
World.content:
Japan is considering setting its total defense spending for the next five years at around ¥60 trillion, as it revises its three key national security-related documents by the end of this year.

The Defense Ministry estimates that necessary defense expenditures for the five-year period will total ¥70 trillion to ¥80 trillion, while the Finance Ministry is arguing for spending below ¥60 trillion, sources said Friday.

With Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reportedly reluctant to raise taxes to fund defense spending, a battle between the Finance and Defense ministries over spending levels and how to secure the necessary funding is intensifying.

World.title: Rubio labels international law a tool of elites and attacks ICC
World.content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered an aggressive and unrepentant challenge to international law in a speech on Friday, warning that the U.S. would never submit to the “sterile vision of radical judges or soulless global bureaucrats.”

His address singled out the International Criminal Court, as President Donald Trump and his administration have done many times over the course of his first and second terms. Rubio dismissed international law as an instrument that elites — whom he didn’t name — use to advance their own interests.

“If they’re foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general Pompey when he said to those who were trying to invoke their city’s charters against his legions, he said, ’Stop quoting laws to men with swords,’” Rubio said.

World.title: 17,000 Hong Kong Disneyland ticket QR codes stolen, online sales suspended
World.content:
Hong Kong Disneyland Resort has reported to police the theft of 17,000 ticket QR codes from its online ticketing system and suspended sales through its website, the South China Morning Post has learned.

A source said on Saturday that an IT worker at the amusement park on Lantau Island had detected anomalies in the resort’s computer system, only to discover the QR code theft.

Police have classified the case as access to a computer with a criminal or dishonest intent, and the Lantau district crime squad is investigating.

World.title: Catholic diocese asks parishes to hold special masses to mark Tai Po fire anniversary
World.content:
The head of Hong Kong’s Catholic diocese has asked all of the city’s parishes to hold special masses and prayers to mark the first anniversary of the deadly Tai Po fire later this month.

Cardinal Stephen Chow Sau-yan invited parishes to offer mass for the deceased on November 26, one year after the blaze broke out , according to a notice issued by the Hong Kong Catholic Diocesan Liturgy Commission on Friday.

The inferno at the Wang Fuk Court housing estate raged for more than 43 hours, killing 168 people and displacing nearly 5,000 residents.

World.title: A bad year for Hong Kong construction: 6 scandals that shocked city
World.content:
Hong Kong’s construction industry is facing mounting public scrutiny following a string of scandals involving substandard work, defective installations and questionable maintenance practices.

From malfunctioning hospital lifts and missing fire-safety components in lift door frames to defective columns at a railway station and structural flaws in residential projects, the incidents have raised concerns over construction quality, regulatory oversight and accountability.

Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho announced this week that the Construction Industry Council would form a task force to review site operations and address quality concerns after a series of substandard works were uncovered at building and infrastructure projects across the city.

World.title: Hong Kong nursery ordered to submit report after boy’s mystery head injury
World.content:
Hong Kong education authorities have ordered a nursery in Kowloon Tong to submit a report after it allegedly failed to explain why a two-year-old pupil had a large bump on the back of his head after classes.

The Education Bureau said it was highly concerned about the incident at Cannan Kindergarten (Waterloo Road) and had told the school to submit a report.

“Upon receiving the complaint from the parents, the bureau immediately contacted the parents and the school to understand the situation and requested that the school handle the matter seriously and submit a report on the incident,” it said.

World.title: Anthony Kwong destroyed Abby Choi’s things, discarded them with ‘pork bones’, court hears
World.content:
The brother-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has admitted in court to destroying her personal belongings after her death and discarding them at his father’s behest together with what he believed to be “pork bones” cooked with carrots and radishes.

Anthony Kwong Kong-kit also told the High Court on Friday that he had helped his father clean up knives and tools in a rural village flat where parts of Choi’s dismembered remains were found, while lying to her family and police about her whereabouts.

He said he had only followed his father’s instructions to help him dispose of “rubbish” without ever suspecting it could contain dismembered body parts.

World.title: Teachers working without new certificates face up to 2 years’ jail, HK$50,000 fine
World.content:
Schoolteachers found to be working without new practising certificates will face a maximum penalty a fine of up to HK$50,000 and two years’ imprisonment from the 2028-29 academic year, as Hong Kong authorities tighten requirements for educators.

However, short-term supply teachers will be exempted from needing the newly required certificates.

Teachers in international and private schools, as well as kindergartens, applying for or renewing the certificate will have to complete 60 hours of continuing professional development in the 36 months before their application. Teachers in publicly funded schools will have to complete 150 hours per three-year cycle.

World.title: Hong Kong to exempt medical device imports for personal use from new regulation
World.content:
Medical devices bought from online platforms based outside Hong Kong for self-use or as personal gifts will not be targeted by a proposed law requiring medical device traders to register with the government, the city’s health minister has said.

Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau on Friday set out to lawmakers the circumstances in which some medical devices would face more stringent regulation under a proposed bill to strengthen public health protection. The bill is scheduled to be submitted next year.

Under the proposed regulation, medical devices with higher risks, such as corrective contact lenses and hypodermic needles, would need to be registered with the Department of Health before they are sold in Hong Kong.

World.title: Hong Kong raises 2026 growth forecast to 4.8% as AI-driven exports power economy
World.content:
Hong Kong has upgraded its 2026 economic growth forecast to 4.8 per cent, buoyed by recent strength in artificial intelligence-related exports, with the full-year performance expected to be the strongest in five years.

The government’s latest projection, released on Friday, was raised from the 3.5 to 4.5 per cent range predicted in August and the 2.5 to 3.5 per cent growth it forecast in February.

The city’s economy expanded by 6.5 per cent in 2021.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019262/China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
World.title: China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019262/China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
World.content:
An AI-generated short drama made by amateurs, including a former rideshare driver and a stay-at-home mother, has gone viral in China for its high production quality and historical accuracy, challenging the genre’s reputation for simple, brainless plots.

First released in August, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” already has 10 seasons and comprises roughly 1,000 3-minute episodes. As of Thursday, the show has amassed over 12 billion views across platforms including Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, and streaming site Bilibili, local media reported.

In the first nine months of this year, 490,000 micro-dramas were released in China, 13 times more than in all of 2025. AI is also reshaping the micro-drama industry, with AI-generated productions now accounting for more than 90% of all such content, according to a report the National Radio and Television Administration released in October. The report also found that China’s short-drama audience had surpassed 600 million active monthly viewers.

Adapted from a web novel published in installments beginning this April by a writer under the pen name Chagen’er, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” follows five modern-day soldiers who unwittingly travel back to the late Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), bringing their weapons and military expertise with them.

The late Northern Song period is a popular setting for Chinese time-travel fiction, as it offers viewers an alternative reality to the dynasty’s end, when invading Jurchen tribes captured two of its emperors — widely remembered as a national disgrace.

Fans have praised the drama’s carefully crafted script, elaborate fight scenes, and rounded characters who grapple with everything from the imperial examination system to weapons, food, and military equipment shortages during invasions by northern nomadic groups.

The historical details have prompted some viewers to look up Song-era official ranks, military organizations, and historical records and compare them against the drama’s depictions.

The production team behind “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” reportedly comprises six members — including a former pharmaceutical sales representative, interior designer, rideshare driver, stay-at-home mother, and wholesale business owner — who met during an online course on how to use AI to make short dramas.

Zhang Hansheng, 54, the production team’s head, told domestic media that the series has so far cost roughly 1 million yuan ($150,000) to produce, but declined to disclose the team’s earnings. However, rumors of hefty returns have drawn fresh attention to AI drama production, which many see as a potential source of new opportunities for grassroots content creators.

In the comments on a video interview with Zhang by the domestic outlet Yicai, some viewers said the project had inspired them to learn AI tools and try making dramas themselves. Others urged caution, noting the rise of scams disguised as AI-related courses.

The show’s success comes as the genre shifts toward higher production values. Until recently, short dramas were widely considered mindless entertainment defined by exaggerated interpersonal conflicts, formulaic characters, and implausible plots.

Recently, multiple AI short dramas exploring Chinese history have changed this perception. They include “Assuming a Noble Identity,” which premiered last year, and “Inkstone Edge Green Plum,” released this fall.

Critics, however, have called for tighter scrutiny of how AI-generated content depicts China’s past. Last year, China’s National Radio and Television Administration launched a campaign against AI-generated videos that alter or distort classic literary, film, and television works, particularly those based on historical, revolutionary, and heroic themes.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “Armed Into the Song Dynasty.” From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019263/How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
World.title: How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019263/How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
World.content:
Editor’s note: Zhang Li is a professor of anthropology at the University of California, Davis, and the author of “Anxious China: Inner Revolution and Politics of Psychotherapy,” which explores how a new psychotherapeutic culture is taking root in China amid profound socioeconomic change. A Chinese version of the book was released this summer. Here, Zhang, who grew up in Kunming, capital of the southwestern Yunnan province, talks with The Paper about her personal journey, trends in mental health care, and the potential impact of artificial intelligence.

The Paper: In your book, you say that returning home to Kunming to conduct research into the city’s mental and psychological landscape was a “deeply emotional experience” that sometimes left you feeling vulnerable. How did your personal connection with Kunming shape this project?

Zhang: The idea for the book first came to me when I learned that my best friend from middle school had become a therapist. I was quite surprised. This was around 2000, when interest in psychology was just beginning to take off in China and few people knew anything about mental health counseling. When I talked to my friend about her work, I realized that it touched on all kinds of everyday issues but was relatively unexplored. Most of the anthropological field research I’d come across had been conducted outside China.

As I worked on the project, I discovered how deeply it was connected to my family. My mother died 13 years ago. Looking back, I realized she’d lived with post-traumatic stress disorder for much of her life. She lost her mother when she was 8 years old. Her father remarried, and her stepmother treated her and her siblings very badly.

Growing up, we became accustomed to her extreme emotional reactions, but we had no idea they were symptomatic of a psychological disorder. Back then, people simply described this behavior as having “a bad temper.” It was only after reading up on the subject that I came to understand that my mother had suffered from chronic anxiety and depression, but she lacked the language to express it.

Seeing a psychiatrist is more normalized now; back then, mental health was a taboo topic. When I began my fieldwork, my mother was 80. I repeatedly urged her to see a psychiatrist, and eventually she agreed. After a complicated and rather haphazard diagnostic process, she was prescribed a short course of Prozac, which helped improve her condition. In the final three years of her life, she was relatively at peace, and we could have calmer, more constructive conversations.

I chose Kunming for my fieldwork because it allowed me to leverage personal connections and familiarity with the local environment. In addition, scholars were already conducting similar research in major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai, so I wanted to look at a medium-sized city. Kunming was experiencing many of the same problems as larger cities amid China’s economic reforms and social transformation. Rapid, large-scale change inevitably causes disruption, and the psychological disruption individuals experience manifests in all kinds of ways.

Another factor, as I discuss in the book, is Kunming’s place in the history of psychotherapy in China. In 1988, the city hosted the country’s first Advanced Sino-German Psychotherapy Symposium. This earned Kunming a reputation as the “cradle of Chinese psychotherapy.”

The Paper: Why do you consider anxiety a key indicator for the pulse of contemporary Chinese society, and what distinguishes the anxiety here from that elsewhere in the world?

Zhang: Over the years, through interactions with people from diverse backgrounds, I’ve come to feel that Chinese people are an exceptionally anxious population, or as we say, neijuan, “involuted.” Some people are depressed or “low energy,” while others are energetic and highly strung, but anxiety is pervasive across social classes and age groups.

At the same time, anxiety is a global phenomenon. With our digital devices always at hand, constant exposure to news about climate change, geopolitical crises, and the threat of artificial intelligence further exacerbates our anxiety. Anthropologists in other countries, including India, Russia, Japan, and the United States, have found that people in all of these places experience anxiety. But while a general sense of anxiety may be shared across populations, specific trigger issues closely reflect local political, economic, and cultural pressures.

The Paper: The localization of psychotherapy is a central theme of the book. Based on your observations and personal experiences, what similarities and differences do you see between China and the United States?

Zhang: Psychotherapy began to take off in China in the late 1990s and early 2000s. In the West, psychotherapy has a much longer history and has undergone a lengthy process of professionalization. To become a licensed therapist in the U.S., you must complete an undergraduate degree and a master’s in counseling or psychology, and then accumulate a certain amount of clinical experience.

In China, the profession is relatively immature and poorly regulated. With low barriers to entry, practitioners vary widely in competence, and this makes it difficult to find a reliable, qualified therapist. A one-hour therapy session can cost 500 to 1,000 yuan ($75 to $150), making trial and error an expensive process.

In terms of specific techniques and theoretical schools, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the predominant approach in Europe and the U.S. In China, a wide range of therapeutic approaches are popular. In my book, I focus primarily on Satir-based systematic family therapy, CBT, and Jungian psychology-inspired sandplay therapy.

I have a great deal of respect for Jungian sandplay therapy because it resonates in many ways with traditional Chinese culture. However, many young urban Chinese tend to favor therapeutic methods they consider to be “scientific,” and have little interest in methods associated with traditional culture. The Satir model was influential in the U.S. in the ’70s and ’80s, but is no longer popular. However, its emphasis on family relationships resonates with Chinese cultural values and has helped make the Satir model hugely popular here.

Another difference is that Western practitioners emphasize language and narrative, with sessions generally taking the form of a conversation between therapist and patient. Chinese people are less comfortable with talk therapy approaches, and the popular models tend to use both nonverbal and verbal methods.

The Paper: In the book, you argue that Chinese therapists have not just absorbed and imitated Western therapeutic methods but rather selected and adapted approaches suited to the needs of the Chinese population. Where have these localization efforts worked, and what role has the market played?

Zhang: Whenever psychotherapy enters a new country, it always undergoes a process of localization. The efforts and experiments therapists undertook to adapt Western therapies to Chinese contexts were necessary, but also challenging. It’s difficult to say definitively how successful they’ve been.

Some have made a significant impact. However, some localization efforts failed to preserve the essence of the original approaches, instead veering into something resembling ideological indoctrination — not a desirable outcome. But China’s psychotherapy field is still young, and there’s ample room for development.

The market has played a crucial role, because therapy is extremely expensive. In China and the West, therapy is mainly accessible to the middle and upper classes; it’s a luxury for the working class. With the exception of some mental health counseling services provided through psychiatric departments that can be covered by medical insurance, most therapy in China is paid for out of pocket. As a result, individuals’ ability to pay is an important factor shaping the development of the profession.

The Paper: You observe that by 2008, more than 100,000 people in China had obtained certification to work as counselors, yet less than 15% went on to work in the field, with many pursuing psychotherapy training as a form of self-care. Can psychotherapy training that excludes the patient-therapist relationship have a therapeutic effect?

Zhang: I found this phenomenon very interesting. When I spoke with individuals who had completed training programs, I discovered that many were facing difficulties in their lives, or problems in their marriages or relationships with their children. They wanted help, but when they sought a therapist, they found the cost prohibitively expensive. They figured they might as well spend that money on a counseling certification that could give them tools to help themselves and support their loved ones, as well as skills they could apply professionally. About 90% of interviewees had full-time jobs, including as teachers, police officers, and government employees. None of them intended to pursue careers in mental health care.

The therapeutic relationship is central to mental health care, and the effectiveness of therapy often depends on the rapport between client and counselor. However, these certification programs also involve close interactions among instructors and participants. Role-playing exercises add to this dynamic. The training environment functions as a safe therapeutic space, and the courses can have some therapeutic value for people dealing with relatively mild emotional difficulties.

When participants return home to their children or partners, they may not necessarily assume the role of a therapist, but the knowledge they’ve acquired may give them a new perspective on how to understand and interact with them.

The Paper: Why is it predominantly urban middle-class women participating in such programs?

Zhang: The people I interviewed were almost all middle class. A counseling certification program can cost thousands of yuan in tuition, and there may be additional expenses down the line. Lower-income urban residents already have their hands full making ends meet — they don’t have the time, energy, or financial resources to invest in these kinds of things. There are exceptions, of course. I encountered two migrant workers who pursued certifications after their children experienced serious mental health problems.

In the training courses I attended, the ratio was roughly nine women to every man. This discrepancy is partly related to gender stereotypes. In one course, I spoke with the sole male participant, a police officer, who told me his family was baffled by his decision to study counseling. They thought that when he encountered problems, he should just grin and bear it. But he found the training extremely helpful.

Generally, looking after the emotional well-being of family members is considered women’s responsibility, particularly when it comes to children’s emotional problems. This may be changing among younger generations, of course.

The Paper: Your book mentions the late-night talk show Xinli Fangtan, or “Psychological Time,” in the 2000s. Through counseling sessions, its guest experts sought to destigmatize family and work problems, framing them as social rather than medical problems. But today, mental health issues are increasingly medicalized, with hospital psychiatrists booked solid, and social media awash with clinical terms like “trauma” and ADHD. What’s behind this reversal?

Zhang: The medicalization of mental health problems and the individualization of structural problems are not phenomena unique to China; they are happening around the world. In the West, where psychology is much more developed, there has been considerable criticism of this trend. One of the main arguments is that psychology turns many social problems into individual problems, thereby eliminating the impetus to address the underlying structural issues.

But this is one side of a two-sided problem. On the other side, you have what my mother’s generation experienced: people talked only about social problems, never psychological ones. Many people were suffering, yet no medical resources or treatments were available to them. Now we’ve swung to the opposite extreme, where it seems every problem can be solved through therapy or medication. I don’t think this kind of binary thinking is helpful. Rather than treating every problem as either an individual medical issue or a social one, we need to understand how these factors interact and adopt corresponding approaches.

The Paper: You observe that corporate psychotherapy and mental health initiatives, framed as “psychological care,” are becoming new tools of management and control. What does this mean for employees?

Zhang: This is not limited to Chinese companies. In Western capitalist societies, it is very common for businesses to use mental health care as a tool of management and control.

For individuals in China, this approach has some appeal. In my interviews, many employees told me they liked it. Companies have outside experts or human resources staff lead sessions with employees. Rather than simply issuing instructions from above, they take a more egalitarian approach, offering advice on managing family and workplace relationships, or leading group activities such as meditation.

On the other hand, this form of management has attracted considerable criticism in the West. The mechanisms underlying it are often invisible: control over employees may operate at an unconscious level, potentially making it even more effective than overt coercion. However, based on my observations, this approach has some merits and should not be dismissed outright.

The Paper: Your fieldwork for the book ended in 2018. Have you continued to follow developments in this “inner revolution”?

Zhang: I’ve observed three major trends. First, public interest in psychology and mental health has increased. Second, many therapists report that their client numbers have declined in recent years and that fees have decreased. Many people are turning instead to online counseling services, which are cheaper and anonymous.

Third, the emergence of artificial intelligence has had a considerable impact. When people encounter problems, many turn first to free AI tools. Some even feel AI is more trustworthy than a therapist. Therapists have found that many clients who have consulted AI come into sessions with a clearer understanding of their problems. However, in more serious cases, timely medical intervention and medication may be necessary, which is where AI cannot replace a professional.

Reported by Zhu Fan.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from the book cover of “Anxious China: Inner Revolution and Politics of Psychotherapy” and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019255/China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
World.title: China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019255/China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
World.content:
SHANGHAI — When prospective clients contacted Li Shuping’s medical companion agency in Shanghai, their first question often had little to do with the hospital visit they were arranging.

“Patients used to ask first whether we were individuals or a legitimate agency,” Li tells Sixth Tone. Patients hire her company, Qingbeihu, to send a trained companion with them to hospital, helping with appointments, consultations, and paperwork.

The agency opened in September 2025, when almost anyone could advertise the same service on social media. And with people aged 60 or older accounting for 23% of China’s population by the end of 2025 and 59 million forecast to need care by 2030, more families were turning to companions to guide elderly relatives through hospital visits.

But written contracts were often absent, leaving services and fees unclear. Some patients faced unexpected charges once a visit was underway, with little recourse if they disputed them, prompting calls for tighter oversight.

But since Shanghai announced new rules for medical companion services effective July 1, Qingbeihu has received more inquiries, Li says. “Orders are growing steadily, and prospective clients seem more willing to trust the service.”

The rules cover medical companion services for Shanghai residents aged 60 and older and set requirements for worker qualifications, pricing transparency, and written contracts. They also require companions to wear identity badges, provide public lists of qualified agencies, and define responsibilities that include helping patients communicate with doctors and offering psychological support.

More recently, a national standard that took effect Nov. 1 covers medical companion services for patients of all ages across China. It also sets limits on what companions can do, prohibiting them from giving medical advice or making treatment decisions on patients’ behalf.

Following Shanghai’s new rules, Li says Qingbeihu now uses written risk and privacy agreements with patients and companions, as well as accident insurance for companions. For elderly clients unfamiliar with digital services, the agency also provides paper consent forms before a visit.

“Elderly people are very willing to have young people accompany them to seek care — it is also a kind of emotional support,” Li says.

For Qingbeihu’s six full-time companions, all under 30, the working day often begins as early as 5 a.m.

Patient work

By the time Li Suyu, not related to Li Shuping, meets a patient at the hospital around 7:30 a.m., she has already asked about their medical history, drug allergies, and mobility. She then checks registration details and organizes medical records and examination reports before the hospital opens at 8.

Once consultations begin, the 22-year-old accompanies patients to see their doctors, records treatment plans and prescribed medications, and arranges any examinations ordered. She also keeps family members informed and, after the visit, helps patients keep track of follow-up appointments and medication reminders.

In the afternoon, she takes patients for blood tests or ultrasounds, then collects their reports and mails them out. She often handles about 28 bookings a month, with as many as four on a busy day, each lasting two to four hours. At Qingbeihu, a two-hour booking costs 188 yuan ($26), while four hours of surgery accompaniment costs 360 yuan.

Li previously worked in sales and became interested in medical companionship after accompanying a family member to hospital and struggling with some of the procedures herself.

“I had no medical background, so even understanding the doctors’ terminology was difficult at first,” she recalls. When she encountered unfamiliar terms, she consulted more experienced colleagues.

At Qingbeihu, training covers first aid, hospital procedures, and organizing patient records. Companions also attend training at a Red Cross first-aid center and must pass an assessment organized by the Shanghai Association of Elderly Care Services and Aging Industry to obtain a medical companion certificate.

Much of the initial training is theoretical. Even after certification, newcomers must shadow experienced colleagues before taking bookings on their own.

“Many elderly patients become anxious in crowded hospitals, especially when they don’t know their way around,” Li says. She learned to calm them through conversation or small gestures, such as offering a bottle of water or some snacks.

One elderly patient with mid- to late-stage cancer initially refused to engage with her. He believed his illness was incurable and saw little point in spending money on treatment.

Li began talking to him about his family, listening as he spoke about his grandchildren. As he grew more comfortable with her, she encouraged him to continue treatment, reminding him that his relatives wanted him to recover. Li says he eventually agreed to cooperate with treatment.

Ma Xunru, a 60-year-old Shanghai retiree, had reservations when she hired a medical companion while her daughter was away on a business trip. She needed to visit a hospital for dizziness and cervical spine problems but worried that the companion might not be professional.

The crowds at the top-tier hospital made her dizziness worse. But her companion arranged appointments with two departments so she could see the doctors and complete the necessary examinations. Ma says that if she had gone alone or with her daughter, they would have registered with only one department.

“It was such a relief to have the companion with me. Otherwise I wouldn’t have known where to go,” Ma says. She now plans to use the service again.

“I think in the future I’ll ask my daughter to book a companion as well, so that I don’t need to bother her, since she’s busy with her work and life.”

Doctor’s orders

When Wang, a rehabilitation doctor in Shanghai, needed someone to accompany her for a gastroscopy, she hired a medical companion. Most of her friends were doctors, too, and asking one of them to come along would have meant rearranging a hospital shift.

She expected help preparing for the procedure and someone to talk to while she waited. “When taking the order, they only asked what time and where. And they were on their phone the whole time,” she recalls.

The experience helped prompt Wang, 25, to establish Zhuoyu Health with Zhou, 30, a gynecology and reproductive medicine doctor. Both asked to be identified only by their surnames.

Both had seen elderly patients struggle with hospital equipment such as self-service machines. Zhuoyu now has more than a dozen part-time companions drawn from rehabilitation, gynecology, anesthesiology, and the medical device industry.

Wang and Zhou found that questions they considered straightforward could leave patients at a loss, from what to do if they lost their ID card at a hospital to how to prepare for a CT scan. During consultations, they also help patients ask questions they might otherwise overlook and, afterward, understand their doctors’ instructions.

Wang’s first booking, in early June, involved an elderly woman whose health had suffered, she says, from using folk remedies during a long illness.

Before the visit, Wang and the woman’s son-in-law reviewed her medical records and the remedies she had been taking. With heavy rain that day, Wang rented a wheelchair for her. During an echocardiogram, she helped the woman adjust her clothing and explained each step.

Wang admitted to the family that she was handling her first booking. “I was very nervous taking my first order, and the patient’s family comforted me instead,” she recalls.

Zhou encountered a different problem while accompanying an elderly woman with poor hearing and limited Mandarin for a contrast-enhanced CT scan. The patient struggled to follow instructions requiring specific movements, and her anxious daughter began scolding her.

Zhou took the woman out of the examination room and explained what she needed to do. The second attempt went smoothly. “She wasn’t being uncooperative. She genuinely didn’t understand what she was supposed to do,” Zhou recalls telling the daughter.

Yang Hanxue, 25, decided to become a medical companion after seeing elderly people living alone and out-of-town patients struggle through hospital visits while she was working as a nurse.

Now at Qingbeihu, she adjusts her approach to different patients, explaining delays to those who are anxious, listening to those who want to talk, and keeping small talk to a minimum with people wary of the service.

Yang recalls a family wanting an elderly relative to undergo a full set of examinations, although the patient might not have been able to tolerate them. In such situations, she says, companions should remain neutral, relay the doctor’s advice, help families raise questions during consultations, and work toward an arrangement that accounts for the patient’s condition and the family’s wishes.

“Many people don’t understand this profession and mistakenly think we are experts, consulting us on how to treat illnesses,” Yang says. She tells patients and families to follow their doctor’s advice rather than offering treatment recommendations herself.

Wang recalls a patient who fell into a deep coma. The family eventually decided to discontinue treatment. Wang and Zhou say companions should not influence such decisions, but can offer support to relatives struggling with the choices they face.

Despite being a practicing doctor, Wang believes the boundaries of medical companionship need to be more clearly defined, particularly when patients ask companions to weigh in on treatment decisions.

“Patients often ask me, ‘The doctor recommended this — should I do it? Should I keep taking this medicine?’” she says.

Contributions: Marianne Gunnarsson; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A trained medical companion explains prescribed medication to an elderly couple at a traditional Chinese medicine hospital in Beijing, May 22, 2025. Jade GAO/AFP/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.title: Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.content:
A pair of Chinese noodle shops serving free meals sparked debate this week after their popularity reportedly disrupted neighboring shops’ business.

“Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop,” which opened two outlets last month in the densely populated Jiangning and Yuhuatai districts of Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, offers only one dish: noodles with braised vegetarian chicken and shiitake mushrooms. Each restaurant has around 50 seats, and since opening have been frequented mainly by middle-aged and elderly customers, according to domestic media.

Jiangning is home to a large migrant worker population, while Yuhuatai has the city’s largest public housing project. Signs outside the restaurants read, “A bowl of pure intention, with no fixed price; three meals a day, offered with warmth to those in need.”

The owner, surnamed Zhang, told domestic media he opened the shops for two reasons: promoting vegetarianism and charity. He said he had previously donated to charities and operated low-cost vegetarian restaurants but found that offering free noodles was the most effective way to achieve his philanthropic goals.

The two shops have served more than 1,000 bowls of noodles each day, Zhang said. He added that he had initially planned to open 10 stores, each serving 500 bowls a day, but demand had exceeded his expectations.

“Our idea was simple: get more people to come eat,” he said.

The topic has garnered more than 10 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many questioning whether the measures can genuinely help those in need.

Asked what they thought about the initiative, a local resident told domestic media, “It’s both good and bad. The good thing is that people who are genuinely struggling can come here to get a meal and meet their basic needs. The bad thing is, how can you tell who has money and who doesn’t?”

Other users suggested requiring customers to show their ID cards to exclude locals and help migrant workers.

In an interview with domestic media, Zhang rejected the idea of screening customers. “We want to give people facing difficulties a sense of dignity and respect,” he said.

Domestic media reported that one nearby restaurant’s daily revenue had fallen from 3,000 yuan ($450) to just a few hundred yuan. Another shop owner said he was considering not renewing his lease over concerns about declining customer traffic.

However, some shop owners said customer traffic along the street had already fallen after the relocation of several nearby factories. Others said the free noodle shops had not significantly affected their business.

Zhang told domestic media that affected business owners could work at his stores if they were willing.

He added that the two shops could lose up to 10 million yuan a year. The stores do not have payment QR codes, and he has also turned down donation offers from friends.

The shops have reportedly recently installed barriers to keep lines orderly and stopped providing noodle refills and napkins to discourage those who don’t truly need help from taking advantage of the offer.

Authorities told domestic media they had found no evidence that the restaurants were providing free meals as a publicity stunt. Local authorities also said they had visited the shops to check food safety compliance and help maintain order among customers queuing outside.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Crowds gather at a “zero-yuan noodle shop” in Nanjing, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019244/What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
World.title: What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019244/What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
World.content:
Fufeng County, some 110 kilometers west of the northwestern Chinese city of Xi’an, is best known for its stunning Tang dynasty (618–907) relics, unearthed from an underground crypt beneath Famen Temple in the late 1980s.

But ask a Chinese archaeologist about Fufeng, and they’ll likely point you in another direction: toward a quiet cluster of more than 20 villages located along the border with neighboring Qishan County. There, hidden beneath unassuming farms and village houses, lies what a growing number of experts believe was the first capital of the Western Zhou (1046–771 BC) — one of China’s earliest and most important dynasties.

Known as Zhouyuan — literally “The Plains of Zhou” — its excavation sites have produced some of China’s most famous bronze ritual vessels. In the 1940s, those discoveries led archaeologist Shi Zhangru to survey the area and eventually propose that this was Qiyi, the center of Zhou culture before the Zhou toppled the Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC).

In the decades that followed, archaeologists worked on the site sporadically, uncovering large rammed-earth building foundations, cemeteries, craft workshops, bronze hoards, and oracle bones, all dating to the Zhou period.

Yet planned, continuous excavation at Zhouyuan began only at the turn of the 21st century, when the Institute of Archaeology at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, and Peking University’s School of Archaeology and Museology formed a joint team to systematically explore the site.

Why the delay? Part of the problem was historiographical. Chinese scholars have long relied on written texts to locate historic sites, and for more than 2,000 years historians placed the Western Zhou capital dozens of kilometers away, in a place called Fenghao, near Xi’an.

This drew attention and resources from other sites in the region, including Zhouyuan. But over the past decade or so, the joint archaeological team at Zhouyuan has made a string of breakthroughs that suggest Shi Zhangru’s near-century-old hunch might be right — and possibly even show that Zhouyuan, not Fenghao, was the Western Zhou’s first capital.

“Modern excavations are revealing more and more contradictions between the archaeological record and traditional accounts,” Cao Dazhi, a Peking University-based archaeologist and co-leader of the Zhouyuan team, wrote in a 2023 paper. Cao’s analysis attracted widespread attention in China for arguing that Zhouyuan was the Zhou capital, while the Fenghao region was merely an important hub and site of the royal hunting grounds.

But the dispute over ancient capitals may not be the biggest revelation to emerge from the Zhouyuan excavations.

While the exact significance of the discoveries remains a matter of debate even within the team, mounting evidence suggests the Zhou capital’s population was far more diverse than previously thought. In addition to the core Zhou population, it was home to large numbers of conquered Shang, as well as migrants from the northwest and south.

That matters because, over time, the Zhou would establish a very different political and moral order from the Shang, one combining military power with ritual, moral claims to legitimacy, and the incorporation of conquered peoples. This order would help shape Chinese political culture for the next 3,000 years, but where did it come from? And could the answer lie in the palaces, streets, and workshops of Zhou’s most prominent early settlement?

“Sweet as sugar”

Zhouyuan was founded by a people on the move.

According to legend, an ancestor of the Zhou people had served as an agriculture official under the Xia — a legendary state traditionally regarded as China’s first dynasty — and the clan made its living farming the land north of what is now Xi’an.

After the Xia declined, the clan lost its fief. For most of the Shang, the Zhou wandered from place to place.

Finally, around the 12th century BC, their leader Gugong Danfu set out with his people in search of a land where they could finally settle and prosper.

“Mian,” a poem from the “Book of Songs,” China’s oldest surviving poetry anthology, tells this story in just 400 characters: After a long journey, the Zhou arrive at a place called Mount Qi, where they find wild herbs “sweet as malt sugar.” They carve a turtle shell for divination, and the resulting oracle tells them to settle there.

Laborers toil under the direction of officials, stretching cords to mark straight lines and raising frames to tamp the earth. Soon, “a hundred walls rise together.” Ancestral temples, palaces, and homes are built, roads are laid down, and the local barbarian tribes, awed by the magnificent new city, can only flee in disarray.

The claim that Zhouyuan’s wild grass tasted as sweet as sugar may be poetic license, but modern archaeological discoveries support the outlines of the story. Archaeological and environmental evidence suggests that the region offered favorable conditions for early agriculture, with fertile loess soils and plentiful rainfall.

That supported the Zhou as they developed a mixed agricultural system dominated by millet and, later, wheat. The region’s abundance is reflected in the contents of a predynastic Zhou storage pit — a kind of primitive refrigerator with walls plastered in straw-tempered mud — containing some 500 apricot pits, more than 150 melon seeds, and a handful of plum pits, some still glossy after 3,000 years.

But the crucial evidence for Zhouyuan as the site of the Zhou’s foremost settlement only came in 2020, with the discovery of a building archaeologists call Wangjiazui No. 1. Covering more than 2,500 square meters, the compound is divided into front and rear sections, with a front courtyard framed by gatehouses, side chambers, and a front hall. In the rear lies another courtyard, surrounded by a hall, side chambers, and a back chamber.

It’s a structure of truly royal proportions, and Wangjiazui No. 1 quickly caught the attention of the archaeological team. “Ever since Shi Zhangru proposed in the 1940s that Zhouyuan was where Gugong Danfu migrated, the bronze hoards and large building foundations unearthed here have steadily reinforced that judgment — but hard proof of a high-ranking predynastic building was always missing,” Chong Jianrong, director of the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, tells Sixth Tone. “Large rammed-earth foundations are the most direct indicator of a settlement’s rank: Only a settlement with capital-level political functions could build such a structure. Wangjiazui No. 1 provides that key evidence.”

Based on stratigraphy and radiocarbon dating, the team confirmed that the building dated to the predynastic Zhou period, before the conquest of Shang, thereby verifying the existence of a “central settlement” within the Zhouyuan cluster. Wangjiazui No. 1’s size and clearly defined layout are unmatched among predynastic finds, and archaeologists were also able to trace a belt of predynastic structures stretching over 150 meters from north to south — evidence of a deliberately planned settlement that was developed continuously, rather than a temporary encampment.

Yet even the grandest predynastic building at Zhouyuan pales next to contemporary Shang architecture: the No. 1 palace at the Shang city of Huanbei, built at least a century earlier, covers some 16,000 square meters — six times the size of Wangjiazui No. 1.

The gulf in scale reflected a gulf in power. In the 12th century BC, the Shang were a powerful empire built on violence and tight state control, with formidable armies, complex cities, and impressive industry.

The Zhou, meanwhile, were still a small tribe on the distant fringes of the Shang cultural sphere. But after centuries of wandering, they had finally found land to farm and walls to call home. And within a few generations, their roles would flip as the Zhou destroyed the Shang and conquered the Chinese heartland.

A melting pot

In early 1046 BC, on a plain in what is now the central province of Henan, the Battle of Muye — a clash that would transform the course of Chinese history — was about to begin.

According to traditional accounts, Ji Fa, Gugong Danfu’s great-grandson, led a coalition of allied tribes numbering fewer than 50,000 men. Opposing them was a Shang army said to number hundreds of thousands. Yet despite its supposed numerical superiority, the Shang force offered little resistance, and its defenses collapsed almost immediately. The decisive battle was over in a single day — and with it, nearly six centuries of Shang rule.

Zhou’s conquest of Shang greatly expanded their territory. To administer their new lands, the Zhou established two capitals. One was Luoyi, near present-day Luoyang in Henan. Close to the conquered Shang heartland, it was intended to keep watch over Shang remnants and the eastern lords.

For centuries, the other was believed to be Fenghao, in what is now Xi’an’s Chang’an District, roughly 90 kilometers from Zhouyuan as the crow flies.

But recent finds at Zhouyuan have uncovered hard evidence against that view: in particular, the presence of a walled city of about 1.75 million square meters, with a palace complex at its core.

The palace lies at the exact center of the city’s northern half, says Cao, the Peking University archaeologist whose article kickstarted the Fenghao-Zhouyuan debate. Covering roughly 500,000 square meters, it is the largest and best-preserved pre-Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) palace complex ever discovered.

A comprehensive coring survey in 2023 revealed buildings across almost the entire site. Roads crisscross the area: the avenue leading into the city was paved with a foundation of large stones topped with soil and gravel, not unlike a modern gravel road. And in the moats outside the palace city’s walls, archaeologists found oracle bones used in royal divination.

“By comparison, no city walls have yet been found at Fenghao,” Cao says. “In fact, Zhouyuan’s remains of every kind are richer than Fenghao’s: more people, more nobles and officials, more wealth.” He adds that a building he is currently excavating is the largest structure ever found from the Western Zhou.

Inside the palace district, members of the royal house would have enjoyed the highest luxuries the age could offer. Beyond the palace walls, the settlement hummed with industry. Archaeologists have identified 61 craft production sites within the settlement, which produced bronzes, bone objects, pottery, jade ware, and lacquered wood.

Notably, many of the laborers staffing these workshops were not from the Zhou. Strontium isotope analysis of human bones and teeth from sites across the Yellow River basin found that populations at predynastic Zhou and Western Zhou sites were among the most heterogeneous on record in China, pointing to large-scale migration to Zhouyuan.

The influx began even before the conquest of Shang, says Chong of the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology. He identifies two early waves of migration: people associated with the Nianzipo culture to the north, whose graves featured distinctive vertical shafts, followed by people associated with the Liujia culture to the west, who used catacomb-style tombs.

Once the Western Zhou was established and Zhouyuan became a dynastic capital, people and cultural influences converged there from every direction — including the Chu from the south and the Qin from the west. Two shell carvings of human heads unearthed in 1980 feature high-bridged noses and deep-set eyes reminiscent of depictions of the Saka, a Scythian-related people of the Eurasian steppe — a hint that even more distant groups may have lived at Zhouyuan.

But the largest group of migrants came from the east: the conquered people of the Shang. In fact, the Shang may have been the city’s second-largest demographic after the Zhou themselves.

“The population structure of Zhouyuan was highly complex, and the available material doesn’t yet support precise ratios,” Chong tells Sixth Tone. “But what is certain is that, while the Zhou formed the ruling core, other groups from the northwest and south were integrated in different ways; and Shang remnants were a major group of considerable size.”

Learning from the conquered

So why were so many Shang people living in the Zhou capital?

Immediately after their victory at Muye, the Zhou were faced with a challenge: how to integrate this distant power center into their new state. They moved quickly to extend their rule east, building Luoyi to strengthen their position in the Shang heartland, while planting their agents and allies at strategic points throughout the new territory.

They also pursued a deliberate strategy of breaking up the close-knit Shang clans and resettling them across their empire.

It must have been a colossal undertaking. At its peak, the Shang capital alone is estimated to have had a permanent population in the hundreds of thousands. But in the eyes of the Zhou rulers, the effort of relocating large numbers of people hundreds of kilometers was worth the trouble. Not only did it allow them to keep a close eye on their new subjects, but it also made a powerful political statement: the remnants of the fallen dynasty had fully submitted to the Zhou order.

Then there were the practical reasons for the relocation: Archaeological finds suggest that Zhouyuan’s new Shang residents clustered around the city’s workshops, where they would have put their technological know-how and skills to work for their new rulers.

“In the predynastic period, bronze casting across the Guanzhong region (surrounding Zhouyuan) was scarce, and only very simple vessels could be made,” Cao tells Sixth Tone. “Then, at a certain point, large numbers of exquisite bronzes suddenly appear, essentially identical to late Shang products.”

Scholars such as Cao speculate that this sudden shift was connected to the Zhou bringing Shang artisans — along with bronzes seized in war — back to Zhouyuan.

Bronze was just one of many crafts and cultural practices the Zhou learned from the Shang. Li Xueqin, the late chief scientist of the state-sponsored Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project, compared the oracle-bone inscriptions of Yinxu and Zhouyuan and found them “more alike than different” — evidence of continuity in the writing system and divination practices across the two dynasties.

Song Jiangning, who heads the CASS Institute of Archaeology’s Zhouyuan project, argues that several early Western Zhou buildings imitate Shang architectural forms, and believes that their designers were most likely Shang people.

The evidence suggests the Zhou allowed these people to maintain many of their cultural practices. Excavations at multiple Zhouyuan workshops show that Shang people carried on key traditions, including burying their dead close to home and organizing production around clan lines.

Production and daily life were concentrated within the workshop quarters; the dead were buried there in their clan’s customary way; and children inherited the family trade. In other words, the Zhou rulers treated them with relative leniency — especially in contrast to the Shang’s own brutal treatment of outsiders, as attested by the large numbers of human sacrifice victims unearthed at the former Shang capital.

“The archaeological material tells us that the early Western Zhou inherited many Shang practices across the board — crafts, writing, architectural layouts, and even the ‘hereditary artisan clan’ mode of organizing production,” Chong tells Sixth Tone.

Running dry

As Zhouyuan attracted more and more people, its workshops continued to grow, eventually outpacing the city’s initially planned borders.

Toward the end of the Western Zhou period, the dynasty established a new, far larger settlement southeast of the original city, roughly tripling Zhouyuan in size and turning it into the largest known Chinese city of the Western Zhou. Excavations have uncovered walls and gates on a scale unprecedented for the pre-Qin period. It was a clear display of power and order.

Yet the city’s residents had little time to enjoy their magnificent new metropolis. In 771 BC, after 275 years of rule, the Western Zhou fell. Nomadic tribes from the west invaded the Guanzhong Basin, and King Ping fled east with his lords to the dynasty’s second capital of Luoyi. The Zhou would survive as the Eastern Zhou, but royal power quickly declined, and China descended into centuries of conflict and war.

Curiously, archaeologists have found almost no Eastern Zhou artifacts at Zhouyuan.

That might seem natural enough: after all, Zhouyuan was no longer the capital. But experts say it is highly unusual. “Think about it,” Song Jiangning of CASS tells Sixth Tone. “Chinese history is full of cities — Xi’an, Nanjing, Hangzhou — that were once capitals and later weren’t. When a city loses capital status, the royals and officials leave, sure. But do ordinary people leave? No. They go on with their lives. Zhouyuan is different. After the Western Zhou, the people of that city disappeared almost completely.”

The bronze hoards found densely packed across the site suggest the city’s abandonment was sudden.

“Picture the scene: the city suffers a sudden disaster, and the noble families must flee with the royal house,” Cao explains. “Their bronzes are incredibly precious — and far too heavy to carry — so they hastily dig pits and stash them away. The density of bronze hoards at Zhouyuan makes it easy to picture the rows of aristocratic mansions that once stood here, and the panic of their owners’ flight.”

But what exactly was the catastrophe? Many historians attribute the city’s fall to invasions by groups from the west. Song, however, wonders whether the city succumbed to something deadlier than war.

“Down through the ages, cities have generally met one of two fates,” he says. “The first is ‘rise and decline’: once a capital, then no longer; once prosperous, then decayed. That kind of story is common, and behind it are human factors.”

“The second fate, less common, is ‘life and death,’” he says. “Liangzhu died, Shimao died, Taosi died, the capitals of the 36 states of the Western Regions almost all died. Perhaps that is what happened to Zhouyuan. The death of a city means its people simply could no longer live there — and behind that usually lie forces of nature.”

For years, Song has studied the relationship between Zhouyuan’s water resources and its urban planning, hoping to crack the mystery of the city’s disappearance. Zhouyuan sits on a loess tableland, and its inhabitants drew water from two rivers descending from the mountains. To secure a sufficient, stable supply, they built a hydraulic system covering more than 30 square kilometers — enormous in scale and remarkably complex and refined in design.

For a time, the artificial canals worked well. But rivers rushing down from the mountains continually cut deeper into their channels; as the water levels fell, the canals had to be dug ever deeper, and at ever greater cost. Meanwhile, Zhouyuan kept expanding, and the demand for water kept growing.

To make matters worse, sediment analysis suggests that the city’s water-management authorities maintained the system diligently in the early Western Zhou, but grew lax in the middle period, and had ceased to function entirely by the dynasty’s collapse.

Although the evidence is inconclusive, water scarcity may be one reason Zhouyuan was abandoned. The same may have happened to several large Western Zhou dozens of kilometers to the west.

To Song, the quest to understand how Zhouyuan collapsed is almost as important as the answer itself. “To attend to one thing is inevitably to neglect another — and on that, we are no different from the ancients,” he says. “What the ancients did is done and cannot be redone. But we can study them, assess them, and learn from them. Zhouyuan is a modern-day revelation — how it rose, prospered, and died.”

A new order

The death of Zhouyuan was a catastrophe for the nobles and commoners who called it home. For archaeologists today, it has proven an unexpected gift.

One need only compare it with Luoyi — modern-day Luoyang — the Zhou’s eastern capital. Celebrated in China as the “ancient capital of thirteen dynasties,” Luoyang has served as a seat of power longer, and for more dynasties, than almost any other city in China. But that very longevity is the archaeologist’s headache: wave upon wave of construction has left cultural layers piled one atop another, making dating unearthed remains a thorny task.

Zhouyuan is different. No major city has stood there since the Western Zhou. The land has been farmed for nearly 3,000 years, and remains so today.

For China’s archaeologists and historians, that is rare good fortune, especially given that Zhouyuan may contain the answer to one of the longest-standing riddles in Chinese history: How China transitioned from the Shang to the Zhou, whose focus on ritual, order, and moral justifications for rule would shape future Chinese states for millennia.

Over a hundred years ago, the renowned scholar Wang Guowei called the Shang-Zhou transition “the most drastic transformation in Chinese politics and culture.” In essence, it shifted the basis of political order — from sacrificial ritual to political ethics. The Shang revered gods and ghosts, seeking to appease them with elaborate sacrifices, including human sacrifice; the Zhou, while not immediately breaking from Shang practices entirely, set out to build an alternative justification for their rule.

Historians have read this shift in many ways. According to one widely shared view, the Shang placed their faith in divination and sacrifice, trusting that so long as the rituals never lapsed, their ancestors and the spirits would protect them.

The Zhou advanced a different argument: Heaven favored virtue, and political legitimacy depended on the moral conduct of the ruler. Through the patriarchal clan system and the strategic allocation of titles and fiefs, they wove political and ethical order into a single fabric.

Dynasties rose and fell over the nearly 3,000 years that followed, and the machinery of government was rebuilt many times — but the Zhou ideal of “governing through virtue” endured. “By the Western Zhou, Chinese civilization had its ‘final draft,’” says Song.

Now, archaeologists can look for the physical evidence of that transition. The numerous tombs of Shang survivors found around Zhouyuan’s craft workshops, for instance, reveal a dynasty that inherited Shang culture and technology on a massive scale even as it labored to build a new ethical and moral order — one that could legitimize Zhou rule while incorporating conquered peoples and other groups.

“What did not change between Shang and Zhou dwarfs what did,” says Chong. “But that is precisely why we focus on the change — on how the Zhou built the ritual order that would define Chinese political culture for the next 3,000 years.”

(Header image: Visuals from Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, reedited by Fu Xiaofan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: ‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.content:
“Sisters, stand up!” reads a slogan written in pink on the mirror above three pink-and-white urinals. Alongside each sits a stack of disposable paper funnels, waiting for those willing to heed the call.

The scene, reportedly captured in the women’s restroom of a bar in China’s eastern city of Wuxi, began circulating online last week, sparking debate and prompting a related hashtag to garner over 54 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

“I stood there in disbelief for two minutes, thinking I’d walked into the wrong restroom,” one user wrote on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, attaching photos of the urinals. “I kept checking until a cleaner confirmed it was indeed the women’s restroom.”

The user, a Wuxi resident in her 30s surnamed Shi, told domestic media she was unsure how to use the urinals as there were no instructions nearby. She said she eventually opted for a traditional squat toilet in the same restroom instead because she worried about making a mess or soiling her clothes.

“I’d actually love to try this,” one commenter wrote. “In winter, it’s a hassle to squat with all those thick, long layers on, especially when you’re also carrying a bag.”

“Better yet, let the brothers sit down,” read another comment, which received nearly 1,400 likes.

On Tuesday, a woman surnamed Tang, who runs Gungun Folk Theater, the bar where the urinals were reportedly installed, told domestic media that they were intended for women who find it difficult to squat, including those wearing long dresses or with limited mobility. “We just wanted to make things easier and give women another option,” she said.

Studies suggest that standing to urinate may be easier for pregnant women and those with knee osteoarthritis, while standing, crouching, and sitting have been found to make no significant difference to bladder emptying in healthy women.

Standing urinals are increasingly common worldwide at music festivals to save space and reduce restroom queues, and at outdoor activities where toilets are scarce.

In China, efforts to introduce standing urinals for women reportedly date back to 2004. At that time, Ye Ganlin, a retired senior engineer, spent 10,000 yuan ($1,400) developing a portable standing urinal for all genders, and offered free disposable funnels to female users. She said the idea grew out of her own experience with a spinal condition that made squatting increasingly difficult as she aged.

Her toilet was tested in busy public areas of neighboring cities Xi’an and Xianyang, in the northwestern Shaanxi province, and reportedly drew around 200 users a day. However, women were in the minority, Ye said.

In 2010, Shaanxi Normal University, also in Xi’an, installed six standing urinals for women, an initiative championed by professor Qu Yajun to conserve water. Female students welcomed the idea but said it would take practice to get used to the fixtures.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Urinals installed in a women’s restroom at a bar in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)
