The declaration, signed on 5 May by then UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, also identifies three main areas of cooperation. The first two are similar to those outlined in the declaration with Azerbaijan: defence and security, and economic growth and development.

However, the third area differs. In the declaration with Armenia, it is titled “Governance and Democratic Resilience”, while the document with Azerbaijan focuses on “Education and Innovation”.

In the declaration with Armenia, the two countries commit to protecting democracy, human rights and the rule of law. The document also provides for creating an enabling environment for independent media and civil society.

By contrast, the declaration with Azerbaijan makes no mention of democracy, human rights or the media. The term “civil society” appears only once, in the context of strengthening people-to-people ties between the two countries.

Furthermore, the declaration with Armenia provides for the development of a joint “Results Framework” to monitor the implementation of the agreements. No equivalent mechanism is included in the declaration with Azerbaijan, with the two countries agreeing only to hold annual meetings.

The declaration with Armenia also explicitly states that it does not constitute an international treaty and that either party may terminate cooperation by giving six months’ written notice.

What is the wider context behind these differences?

The declaration was signed amid continuing international criticism over the arrests of journalists in Azerbaijan. According to Amnesty International, 12 people detained in connection with the Meydan TV case are being persecuted for their journalistic work. The human rights organisation has also reported serious health problems among some of those detained.

In February this year, the detained journalists appealed to diplomatic missions in Baku, including the British embassy, asking them to monitor the court proceedings.

In response to calls for the journalists’ release, Azerbaijani officials have said that the legal proceedings are ongoing and that a fair decision will be reached.

The British government’s statement announcing the signing of the declaration makes no mention of the issue.

What do the two countries expect from each other?

The UK has long been one of the largest foreign investors in Azerbaijan, largely through BP, which operates the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli and Shah Deniz oil and gas fields. According to Azerbaijani officials, British investment in the country’s economy has exceeded $39bn.

However, the two countries’ figures for bilateral trade differ. According to Azerbaijan’s State Customs Committee, trade turnover between the two countries reached $3.72bn in the first nine months of this year.

According to official UK government statistics, trade in goods and services totalled £1.2bn in the 12 months to June, making Azerbaijan the UK’s 89th-largest trading partner.

British exports to Azerbaijan amounted to £724m, down 2.9% from the previous year. Imports from Azerbaijan, meanwhile, increased more than 2.6-fold to £453m.

Preparations for the declaration began well before its signing. In August 2025, UK Minister for Europe Stephen Doughty announced during a visit to Baku that the two countries had agreed to upgrade bilateral relations to a strategic partnership.

In December, UK Minister of State for Defence Lord Coaker visited Baku. In October this year, UK Trade Minister Lord Anas Sarwar announced at a meeting of the Intergovernmental Commission in Baku that the text of the declaration had been agreed.

The two countries also signed a roadmap for developing transport and digital infrastructure. Sarwar outlined the areas the partnership would cover:

“Of course, it will include energy and port infrastructure, investment, education and other areas.”

The UK government’s statement on Doughty’s 2025 visit also mentioned the peace process, the Russia-Ukraine war, the Middle Corridor, energy, defence, cybersecurity and education.

Human rights and media freedom were not mentioned on that occasion either.

What meetings took place in Dublin?

The signing of the declaration was one of several events on Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev’s busy schedule in Dublin. On the same day, he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and the prime ministers of Bulgaria, Greece and the Czech Republic. His meeting with the Bulgarian prime minister focused on a proposed electricity corridor between the two countries.

According to the Azerbaijani side, Aliyev and Pashinyan discussed the peace agenda under the joint declaration signed in Washington in August 2025, border delimitation, transport links and the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).

The two leaders also welcomed the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and in the opposite direction.

The UK signed strategic partnership declarations with Armenia and Azerbaijan six months apart. Both documents provide for support for the peace process in the South Caucasus. However, the third area of cooperation differs: the declaration with Armenia focuses on democracy, while the one with Azerbaijan emphasises education.

Azerbaijani human rights activists and opposition figures have yet to comment on the signing of the declaration.

World.title: Azerbaijani Chamber of Accounts reveals additional fiscal risks for state budget
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Rising costs for servicing state debt, the need to refinance domestic debt, and a growth in tax overpayments can pose additional risks to public finances in Azerbaijan in the medium term, according to the opinion of the Chamber of Accounts on the draft law “On the state budget for 2027”.

In addition to the above risks, the Chamber of Accounts has emphasized the importance of providing more comprehensive information in budget documents regarding the financial position of state-owned enterprises and debts incurred under state guarantees.

The chamber remarked that in the explanatory note to the 2027 draft state budget, awareness and the quality of analysis of risks affecting fiscal sustainability have been improved compared with previous years. Specifically, the document provides a more concrete definition of "fiscal risk" for the first time; it conducts an analysis of these risks at the level of public finance, assesses their probability of occurrence and potential impact, and outlines measures for risk mitigation.

According to the Chamber of Accounts, the inclusion of information on fiscal risks within budget documents is significant for managing such risks over the medium term. The chamber recalled that, in its opinion on the 2026 draft state budget, it had already highlighted the measurement of the potential impact and probability of occurrence of risks as a key requirement of international fiscal diagnostic tools.

Unlike in previous years, the explanatory note for the 2027 draft budget places primary focus on macroeconomic risks. The document identifies the volatility of oil and natural gas prices, the growth rate of the non-oil-and-gas GDP, and the dynamics of inflation as the primary fiscal risks for the medium term.

However, according to the chamber, the scope of these risks should be broadened. In particular, there is a need for more comprehensive disclosure within the budget documents regarding the potential impact of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and debt incurred under state guarantees on public finances.

The opinion states that disclosing information on fiscal transfers to SOEs, including funds allocated to their authorized capital, their capital value, net profit, debt incurred under state guarantees, quasi-fiscal activities, and dividends paid, would enhance the quality of the budget documents. Furthermore, conducting relevant ratio analyses based on these indicators would allow for a more accurate assessment of the financial condition of state-owned enterprises and the risks they may pose to the budget. Going beyond the risks outlined in the budget documents, the Chamber of Accounts has highlighted three additional risks that could impact public finances in the medium term.

The first risk is an increase in benchmark interest rates. According to the Chamber’s assessment, if benchmark interest rates turn out higher than expected, this could drive up debt-servicing costs for external public debt with variable interest rates. As of October 1 of the current year, 48.8% of the external public debt consisted of obligations with variable interest rates. Consequently, should interest rates rise in international financial markets, the likelihood of an increased debt-servicing burden for the state grows.

The second risk relates to the refinancing of public debt. The chamber noted that refinancing maturing debt obligations at higher interest rates could lead to an increase in the costs associated with servicing public debt. As of October 1, 2026, 56% of domestic government securities had been issued with maturities of up to five years. This indicator suggests that a need may arise to repay or refinance a significant portion of the domestic public debt in the medium term.

A third risk is the increase in tax overpayments. The report notes that during the first nine months of the current year, the amount of tax overpayments, tracked via the State Tax Service (STS), increased by 339.9 million manat ($200 million) compared to the beginning of the year, reaching 2.74 billion manat ($1.61 billion).

According to the chamber’s assessment, the offsetting of these overpayments against future tax liabilities could lead to a discrepancy between the calculated tax amounts and the actual receipts into the state budget. This is a factor that must be taken into account when forecasting and executing budget revenues.

According to the Chamber of Accounts, while the efforts made to identify and mitigate fiscal risks are positive, further measures in this area are required. The chamber pointed out the importance of broadening the scope of risks, specifying the actions to be taken should these risks materialize, and justifying the effectiveness of such measures.

The opinion emphasized that improving the quality and comprehensiveness of data on fiscal risks can contribute to strengthening the sustainability of public finances in the medium term, as well as ensuring that budgetary decisions are made on the basis of more complete information.

World.title: Fitch affirms AIIB's 'AAA' rating with Stable Outlook
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Fitch Ratings has affirmed the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank's (AIIB) Long-Term Issuer Default Rating (IDR) at 'AAA' with a Stable Outlook, citing its excellent capitalization, low risk profile and strong liquidity position.

According to Fitch, the bank's 'AAA' rating is anchored in its Standalone Credit Profile (SCP), supported by 'excellent' capitalization and a 'low' risk profile, with a one-notch uplift reflecting its 'medium risk' business environment.

The Stable Outlook reflects Fitch's expectation that AIIB's SCP will remain commensurate with the 'AAA' rating over the medium term, supported by strong capital and liquidity buffers.

Fitch described AIIB's capitalization as a key rating strength, noting that its capital ratios remain stronger than those of most 'AAA'-rated peers. The agency expects the usable capital to risk-weighted assets (FRA) and equity-to-assets (E/A) ratios to remain above their respective 'excellent' thresholds of 35% and 25% through 2028.

The agency assessed AIIB's credit risk as 'low'. The bank's asset quality remains strong, with non-performing loans, including investment operations bonds, declining to zero at the end of the first half of 2026 from 0.2% a year earlier.

"AIIB also benefits from 'strong' preferred creditor status (PCS), which supports the performance of its sovereign loans, with no sovereign arrears since inception," Fitch said.

AIIB's liquidity profile was assessed as 'excellent'. Treasury assets represented 48% of total assets at the end of the first half of 2026, while liquid assets covered short-term debt by 3.1 times. The bank also benefits from excellent access to capital markets and a diversified investor base.

AIIB's business profile is supported by its public mandate, high governance standards and banking portfolio, which stood at $35.5 billion at the end of the first half of 2026. The share of non-sovereign sector financing is expected to reach 50% by 2030.

Fitch assesses extraordinary shareholder support at 'a', reflecting shareholders' capacity to support the bank and their 'strong' propensity to do so.

World.title: Azerbaijan's Chamber of Accounts warns $176M risk to budget revenues from customs
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. 300 million manat ($176 million) risk has emerged for Azerbaijan's budget revenues from customs.

The Chamber of Accounts' opinion on the draft law "On the state budget of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027" noted that in 2027, state budget revenues of nearly 6.87 billion manat ($4.04 billion) are projected through the State Customs Committee (SCC). However, previous year's execution figures, actual results for the current year, and the possibility that imports will fall short of the projected level pose a risk that this forecast may not be fully met.

According to the document, 2027 revenues through the SCC are projected to exceed the actual 2025 figure by 498.1 million manat ($293 million), or 7.8%, and the 2026 forecast by 6 million manat ($3.5 million), or 0.1%.

One of the key assumptions underlying next year's revenue projections is that imports will reach 32.2 billion manat ($18.9 billion). At the same time, exemptions and concessions applied to imported goods are expected to reduce budget revenues.

According to the assessment of the Chamber of Accounts, the ratio of revenues to be collected via the State Customs Committee in 2027 to the volume of imports will be 0.6 percentage points higher than the actual figure for 2025, and 0.3 percentage points lower than the forecast for 2026.

Risks to customs revenue execution

The opinion emphasizes that in 2025, amid imports totaling $18.1 billion against the projected $18.4 billion, the state budget revenue target of 6.6 billion manat ($3.88 billion) through the SCC wasn’t fully met. Actual revenues amounted to nearly 6.37 billion manat ($3.75 billion), falling short of the forecast by 230.1 million manat ($135.4 million), or 3.5%.

In 2026, imports are projected at $18.7 billion. Actual imports in the first nine months of this year amounted to $13.2 billion. During the same period, 4.97 billion manat ($2.93 billion) was transferred to the state budget through the SCC, against the projected 4.98 billion manat ($2.93 billion). Thus, revenues fell short of the forecast by 10.7 million manat ($6.3 million), or 0.2%.

According to the chamber's estimates, given that imports are expected to fall below the projected level this year, revenues through the SCC are expected to reach 6.6 billion manat ($3.88 billion). This is 300 million manat ($176.5 million), or 4.3%, below the approved forecast.

The document noted that, despite this, the practice of determining the forecast for the SCC revenues for the coming year, based on a cumulative, year-over-year increasing total, has been continued.

The Chamber of Accounts pointed out that the persistence of uncertainties in the international economic environment, particularly shifts in economic behavior among key trading partners, could impact import volumes. Under these conditions, threats to the uninterrupted movement of goods within trade and supply chains could reduce foreign trade turnover and, consequently, hinder the full realization of projected customs revenues.

VAT on imported goods projected at 4.7 billion manat ($2.76 billion)

In 2027, revenues from value-added tax (VAT) on imported goods are projected at 4.7 billion manat ($2.76 billion). This is 50 million manat ($29.4 million), or 1.1%, below the 2026 forecast, but 377.7 million manat ($222.2 million), or 8.7%, above the actual 2025 figure.

According to the opinion, the increase compared with the actual 2025 figure is mainly due to the higher import volume projected for next year. Specifically, imports are expected to reach $19 billion in 2027, up $900 million, or 5%, from the actual 2025 figure.

Meanwhile, the projected decline in VAT on imports compared with the 2026 forecast was attributed to the impact of the lower share of VAT-taxable turnover in total imports in 2025 on the forecast for the following year.

At the same time, the 2027 draft state budget envisages a decline in VAT revenues on imported goods in some categories and an increase in others.

In particular, VAT revenues from entities operating in the non-oil and gas sector, in which 51% or more of shares or ownership interests are directly or indirectly state-owned, are projected to decrease by 80 million manat ($47.1 million), or 40%. Revenues from other resident and non-resident legal entities are expected to decline by 45 million manat ($26.5 million), or 1.2%.

Conversely, VAT revenues from goods imported by individuals are expected to increase by 10 million manat ($5.9 million), or 1.7%. Revenues from budgetary organizations, public legal entities established on behalf of the state, and other entities financed by state-owned funds are projected to rise by 5 million manat ($2.9 million), or 5.9%.

Excise revenues on imports to reach 240 million manat ($141.2 million)

In 2027, state budget revenues from excise taxes on imported goods are projected at 240 million manat ($141.2 million). This is 6 million manat ($3.5 million), or 2.6%, above the 2026 forecast and 7.3 million manat ($4.3 million), or 3.1%, higher than actual revenues in 2025.

According to the Chamber of Accounts' opinion, amendments to legal acts providing for the inclusion of sweetened mineral and carbonated drinks, as well as chips, on the list of excisable goods have contributed to the increase in revenues from this source.

Nevertheless, the forecasts for excise revenues across individual product groups envisage both increases and decreases.

Excise revenues from petroleum products are expected to increase by 6 million manat ($3.5 million), or 31.6%; those from other alcoholic beverages by 4 million manat ($2.4 million), or 8%; and those from other products by 6.8 million manat ($4 million), or 17.5%.

On the other hand, excise revenues from potable alcohol are projected to decrease by 3.7 million manat ($2.2 million), or 31.6%; those from beer and other beer-based beverages by 2.1 million manat ($1.2 million), or 20%; and those from tobacco products and their substitutes by 2 million manat ($1.2 million), or 10%.

A decline of 2 million manat ($1.2 million), or 2.6%, is also expected in excise revenues from passenger cars, motorcycles subject to state registration, and buses, while revenues from energy drinks are projected to fall by 1 million manat ($588,000), or 16.7%.

Customs duty revenues to increase

In 2027, customs duty revenues are projected at nearly 1.87 billion manat ($1.1 billion). This is 49 million manat ($28.8 million), or 2.7%, above the 2026 forecast and 96.2 million manat ($56.6 million), or 5.4%, higher than actual revenues in 2025.

According to the chamber, the increase in customs duty revenues will be driven mainly by higher import duties paid by legal entities.

Thus, import duties paid by individuals are projected to decrease by 34 million manat ($20 million), or 13.1%, while those paid by legal entities are expected to increase by 93 million manat ($54.7 million), or 7.2%.

The increase in revenues from this source is also justified by the projected import volume of $19 billion next year.

Road tax revenues to reach 61 million manat ($35.9 million)

In 2027, state budget revenues from road tax are projected at 61 million manat ($35.9 million). This is 1 million manat ($588,000), or 1.7%, above the 2026 forecast and 17 million manat ($10 million), or 38.6%, higher than actual revenues in 2025.

The opinion noted that the main reason for the increase compared with the actual 2025 figure is the higher tax rate applied per liter.

At the same time, road tax revenues from imported fuel are projected to decrease by 3.5 million manat ($2.1 million), or 12.5%. This decline will mainly result from a decrease of 2.6 million manat ($1.5 million), or 83.7%, in revenues from diesel fuel; 900,000 manat ($529,000), or 3.4%, from motor gasoline; and 100,000 manat ($58,800), or 100%, from liquefied gas.

Conversely, road tax revenues paid by owners or drivers of motor vehicles registered in foreign countries entering Azerbaijan or transiting through its territory are projected to increase by 4.5 million manat ($2.65 million), or 14.1%.

The opinion of the Chamber of Accounts highlighted that actual execution figures from previous years, results from the first nine months of the current year, and the possibility that import volumes may fail to reach projected levels create a risk that budget revenues collected via the SCC will not be fully realized in 2027. In this regard, when forecasting customs revenues, it's essential to consider not only import volumes but also the impact of changes in the international trade environment and the effects of various concession mechanisms.

World.title: Azerbaijan plans concessions for tax debts, new limit on SOFAZ transfers since 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Concessions for tax debts and a new limit on transfers from the State Oil Fund of Azerbaijan (SOFAZ) to the state budget can be imposed since 2027.

According to the opinion presented by the Chamber of Accounts regarding the draft state budget for 2027 and fiscal policies for the medium term, starting from 2027, it’s envisaged that transfers from SOFAZ to the state budget will be gradually reduced, with these transfers being aligned with the income generated from the management of the fund’s assets. At the same time, consideration is being given to simplifying the deferral mechanism for economically active taxpayers who face difficulties in settling their tax liabilities, as well as to the possibility of introducing concessions regarding financial sanctions.

The opinion remarked that in the fiscal policy covering the years 2027–2030, the gradual reduction of transfers from SOFAZ to the state budget has been identified as a key priority. The objective is to bring the volume of these transfers in line with the income generated from the management of the Fund’s assets.

The Chamber of Accounts noted that this approach is significant for reducing the state budget's dependence on oil revenues and strengthening fiscal sustainability. In its previous opinions, the chamber had also recommended establishing a direct limit on the volume of transfers from SOFAZ to the budget.

The document also addressed the improvement of the mechanism for managing tax liabilities. Specifically, it proposes simplifying the procedure for granting deferrals for the installment payment of tax debts, as well as considering the possibility of offering concessions on financial penalties and interest for taxpayers who face payment difficulties but continue their economic activities.

According to the chamber’s assessment, the accumulation of tax arrears represents a fiscal risk. Financial penalties and interest account for approximately one-third of these debts. Therefore, the implementation of mechanisms to facilitate debt repayment could help increase state budget revenues while preserving the solvency of taxpayers.

The opinion also highlighted, for the first time, the disclosure of specific targets for revenue policy over the medium term. Under these targets, the level of tax and customs concessions, relative to the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of the non-oil and gas sector, is intended to be maintained within a range of 7.4% to 8%.

Furthermore, the objective is to keep the variance between the projected non-oil and gas revenues and the actual budget execution within a margin of ±5%. According to the Chamber of Accounts, these indicators are significant for evaluating the outcomes of revenue policy and enhancing the quality of budget forecasting.

At the same time, the chamber considered it appropriate to establish similar quantitative targets for expenditure policy. The opinion noted that, although the main directions of budget expenditure policy have been defined, the absence of specific quantitative metrics and measurable outcome indicators for these areas makes it difficult to evaluate their implementation.

According to the chamber, establishing measurable targets for expenditures, much like those for revenue policy, could strengthen oversight regarding the efficiency of budget fund utilization and enable a more objective assessment of the outcomes of fiscal policy.

World.title: Uzeltexsanoat, China's SIASUN explore industrial robotics cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Uzbekistan's electrical engineering industry is exploring opportunities to introduce industrial robots and advanced automation technologies through cooperation with Chinese robotics manufacturer SIASUN Robot & Automation Co., Ltd., at a meeting on November 13.

According to Uzeltexsanoat, the issue was discussed during a meeting between Mirziyod Yunusov, Chairman of the Uzeltexsanoat Association, and a delegation from SIASUN led by the company's Vice President Liu Zijun.

The discussions focused on modernizing production processes, improving the technological efficiency of Uzbek electrical engineering enterprises and introducing industrial robots and other automation solutions.

The parties also examined opportunities for technology transfer, localizing production, implementing joint investment projects and training qualified specialists in robotics.

Both sides expressed interest in developing cooperation through specific initiatives and practical projects. No investment amount or project implementation timeline was disclosed.

Founded in 2000, SIASUN specializes in the development and implementation of robotics and industrial automation solutions. According to company data, its products have been exported to more than 40 countries, while it has served over 4,000 enterprises and completed more than 18,000 projects.

Uzeltexsanoat is Uzbekistan's association of electrical engineering enterprises, bringing together manufacturers operating across the country's electrical and electronics industries. The association works to support industrial development, expand production capacity, promote exports, attract investment and introduce advanced technologies. Its activities also include strengthening cooperation between domestic manufacturers and international partners to increase the competitiveness of Uzbekistan's electrical engineering sector.

World.title: Tajikistan’s natural gas imports fall 24.3% to 200 million cubic metres - Eni
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Tajikistan imported 200 million cubic metres of natural gas in 2025, down 24.3% year-on-year (based on unrounded figures) from 270 million cubic metres in 2024, according to Italian energy company Eni’s World Energy Review 2026.

Eni’s data show that the country’s natural gas imports amounted to 230 million cubic metres in both 2019 and 2020, before increasing to 240 million cubic metres in 2021. Imports then declined to 190 million cubic metres in 2022, rose to 220 million cubic metres in 2023 and reached 270 million cubic metres in 2024, before falling back to 200 million cubic metres in 2025. The company did not provide a figure for 2015.

For comparison, natural gas imports in Russia and Central Asia as a whole stood at 38 billion cubic metres in both 2024 and 2025, up 0.5% year-on-year. Regional imports amounted to 19 billion cubic metres in 2015 and 31 billion cubic metres in 2019, before falling to 27 billion cubic metres in 2020, 18 billion in 2021 and 17 billion in 2022. They then rose to 20 billion cubic metres in 2023 and almost doubled to 38 billion in 2024. The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) for 2015–2025 was 7.3%.

Eni also reported that Tajikistan’s population reached 10.8 million in 2025, compared with 10.6 million in 2024. The country’s population increased by 1.8% year-on-year, while its CAGR for 2015–2025 stood at 2.2%.

According to the report, Tajikistan’s population amounted to 8.6 million in 2015 and 9.5 million in 2019. It then rose to 9.7 million in 2020, 10 million in 2021, 10.2 million in 2022 and 10.4 million in 2023, before reaching 10.6 million in 2024 and 10.8 million in 2025.

World.title: 'We're still standing': King Charles jokes with Elton John in birthday clip
World.content:
Britain's King Charles has joked that he and Sir Elton John were "still standing" in a clip recorded for the singer's radio show which was aired on the monarch's 78th birthday.

King Charles had joined Sir John for a special edition of the singer's Elton John's Rocket Hour on Apple Music to celebrate 50 years of The King's Trust and musicians who have supported his youth charity.

During the episode, which was first broadcast on Saturday to coincide with the king's birthday, the pair discussed benefit concerts held in support of the Trust.

This included a Rock Gala held at Wembley Arena in 1986 where Sir Elton performed his 1980s hit, I'm Still Standing.

King Charles and Sir Elton John at the Royal Variety Performance in 2024. (Reuters: Toby Melville/Pool/File Photo)

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience," King Charles said.

" And certainly 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing. "

Sir John, who turns 80 in March, replied, "I'm still sitting now, though", prompting laughs from the king.

"With occasional bits dropping off here and there," King Charles said.

"I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

Both men have suffered well-documented health problems in recent years, with the king still undergoing treatment for cancer and Sir Elton suffering problems with his eyesight.

When he was the heir, King Charles founded the Prince's Trust in 1976 using his Royal Navy severance pay to help disadvantaged young people prepare for work, find jobs or start businesses.

It was renamed the King's Trust after Charles became king in 2022.

The charity says it has supported more than one million young people since its launch.

Rocket Hour is a weekly show that has aired globally on Apple Music 1 since 2015.

Reuters

World.title: Heat hammer Hurricanes to hand WBBL champions sixth straight loss
World.content:
Brisbane have continued their stunning WBBL rejuvenation in spectacular style, annihilating hapless Hobart by 10 wickets with a staggering 86 balls to spare.

After skittling the Hurricanes for just 86 in 17.5 overs at Bellerive Oval on Saturday, the Heat wasted no time securing themselves a fourth win in six matches, taking just 5.4 overs to race to 0-88 in reply.

Grace Harris (52 not out off 22 balls) and Charli Knott (34no off 12) looked like they were batting on a different deck to Hobart's confounded batters, who struggled to hit the ball off the square.

The 'Canes hit just six boundaries. Harris and Knott, in contrast, combined for 12 fours and four sixes.

Brisbane's 62-run powerplay set a new competition record.

Their intent was obvious as they crushed 17, 18, 20, seven and 13 off the five completed overs, Harris teeing off from the outset, before Knott applied the finishing touches, raising victory with back-to-back fours.

After going winless for 706 days, the Heat have now notched four victories in the past 10 days to consolidate third position on the ladder.

Meanwhile, reigning champions Hobart have crashed to a 0-6 record.

When captain Nicola Carey was castled by Lily Bassingthwaighte, the Hurricanes were staring down the barrel at 3-11 inside their own powerplay.

That soon became a perilous 6-42.

No 9 Lauren Smith top-scored with 20 before being bowled by Knott, ending Hobart's disappointing innings.

Bassingthwaighte (3-25) was the early destroyer, while Sianna Ginger (2-8), Lucy Hamilton (2-15) and Sarah Glenn (2-16) shared the spoils.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Vescio stars in milestone game as Blues and Swans reach preliminary finals
World.content:
Carlton has claimed a thrilling five-point semifinal win over Hawthorn, with 100-gamer Darcy Vescio starring as the Blues set up an AFLW preliminary final against Melbourne.

Hawthorn started fast at Princes Park, but the Blues fought back, with Vescio slotting the match winner to deliver a 6.7 (43) to 6.2 (38) win in front of 4,701 fans.

Hawthorn star Aine McDonagh could have kicked the winner with two minutes left but missed everything from close range.

Earlier, Sydney pulled off an upset, defeating Geelong by three points in the other semifinal to progress to a final-four clash with North Melbourne.

Hawthorn was without Eliza West for the pivotal final moments after the star on-baller suffered a left knee injury.

West was clearly best on ground and had 25 disposals, 10 tackles, 14 contested possessions and three clearances in the first half alone, before finishing with 31 touches.

Defender Jenna Richardson was important while Jac Dupuy kicked two goals and had an entertaining duel with Carlton's Harriet Cordner (six marks, 11 intercepts).

Carlton skipper Abbie McKay lifted and had 29 disposals and nine clearances.

The Hawks dominated the early exchanges, at one point leading clearances 10-1, kicking three goals to race to a game-high 19-point lead in the first term.

Carlton stopped the rot when Tara Bohanna cut the quarter-time margin to 11.

Lila Keck sparked Carlton before Lily Goss made the most of a contentious 50-metre penalty against Casey Sherriff to cut the half-time deficit to four.

Then, in the third quarter, Vescio won a free kick and kicked truly to put Carlton in front for the first time.

Mackenzie Eardley restored Hawthorn's lead before Vescio forced the ball forward and Sophie McKay spun on a dime in the square, beating three Hawks to put the Blues back in front.

Eardley struck again to make for a thrilling finish, but Vescio took a strong contested mark then snatched victory with her second goal of the game.

Concern for Cats ruck as Swans reach maiden preliminary final

Piper Dunlop collapsed after what looked like a glancing blow in a head knock with Tanya Kennedy. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

Earlier, there were concerning scenes as Geelong ruck Piper Dunlop was stretchered from the field on a motorised cart in the Cats' shock loss to Sydney.

Dunlop went down after a head clash with Sydney's Tanya Kennedy during the third quarter at Kardinia Park.

She initially returned to her feet before becoming unsteady and falling on the edge of the centre circle, caught by Sydney's Lexi Hamilton before trainers sprinted onto the ground to attend to her.

The game was stopped for nine minutes as medical staff gathered on the field, Dunlop eventually leaving the field on the motorised cart.

Geelong has since said Dunlop was taken to hospital for "further precautionary assessment".

Forward Chloe Molloy was the star for the Swans, kicking three goals and taking a key late mark to see her side through to its first-ever AFLW preliminary final.

The 8.2 (50) to 7.5 (47) victory means Sydney will face two-time defending premiers North Melbourne next weekend.

Geelong, meanwhile, bows out of the finals series in straight sets after just one loss in the regular season.

The Swans led by 16 points early in the final quarter, but goals to Chloe Scheer and Jacqueline Perry cut the deficit to four points minutes later.

Scheer proceeded to hit the post, with her behind proving the final score of the game.

Geelong experienced a torrid afternoon on the injury front.

In addition to Dunlop's concerning head knock, the Cats lost Amy McDonald to a hamstring injury in the shadows of half-time, Rachel Kearns was absent for most of the second half, and star midfielder Georgie Prespakis spent time off the field after a heavy collision.

All three of Molloy's goals came in the first half, including one spectacular effort in which she gathered and snapped from an acute angle on the right.

Young key forward Maddie Quinn (22 disposals, one goal) was also impressive for the Swans, while Scheer finished with three majors for Geelong.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Father Christmas greeted by estimated 335,000 at Adelaide pageant
World.content:
More than 300,000 people are estimated to have lined the streets for this year's Adelaide Christmas Pageant, the 94th edition of the annual yuletide parade.

Pageant-goers arrived in the city early, along with hundreds of performers who gathered near South Terrace and King William Road, ahead of the much-loved parade.

Young faces lined the CBD streets to watch the floats pass by, ahead of the arrival of Father Christmas. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Five new floats were added to this year's line-up, including The Magic Hat and A Bumper Christmas.

"Seeing all the floats go past, they love it," one parent said while sitting with his family.

" It makes it all kind of worth it, getting up super early. "

Hundreds of performers took part in the event. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Organisers believe about 335,000 people turned out for the event, which culminated with the much-anticipated arrival of Father Christmas.

Beneath grey skies, a slight shadow was cast on proceedings by the collapse of David Jones, whose Adelaide store has hosted the children's Christmas attraction, the Magic Cave, for almost three decades, although it will continue operating for the time being.

But, overwhelmingly, there were beaming smiles along the event's route.

Five new floats were added to this year's line-up. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Renowned children's entertainer Emma Watkins, better known by her stage name Emma Memma, said she was thrilled to be back after making her debut last year.

"The buzz is real, the festive spirit is out," she said.

This year Watkins was part of the float The Sounds and Signs of Christmas, a reference to her push to help make entertainment more accessible for deaf and and hearing children alike.

Emma Memma says she is thrilled to be back for the Christmas Pageant. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

"Today is the first time that my co-performer Elvin Lam is actually joining me in the pageant," she said.

"It's his first Christmas pageant ever, and Elvin is profoundly deaf, and he will be signing throughout the whole parade."

A delight for all generations

Kunal Dhingra and his family were among those who rose early to secure good spots.

"I can see a lot of people are here from different backgrounds. All the kids are really happy," he said while holding his slightly tired infant daughter.

"We're here from 6am, she woke up pretty early."

Kunal Dhingra and his family were among the early risers. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

A cross-section of the community was present at the time-honoured parade, with young pageant-goer Miabelle saying she relished "spending time with my cousins" and seeing the floats.

"There's one big teddy bear I'm looking forward to," she said.

Another attendee, a local grandmother, said her connection to the event went back decades.

"My dad used to drive trucks, and I remember when we were kids we used to get on the back of his truck and watching the pageant on King William Street," she said.

"Now I get to enjoy it with my grandchildren.

"I just love it. I think I'd come without the kids, if I had to."

The event brings Christmas magic to the streets of Adelaide. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The Magic Cave, currently held in David Jones at the Adelaide Central Plaza, has been part of the city's Christmas landscape since the 1890s. David Jones took over in 1998 when its original host John Martin's closed down.

While the Magic Cave welcomed Father Christmas this year, questions have emerged about what lies ahead for the attraction.

Last week, David Jones went into voluntary administration, with 19 of its 38 stores slated for closure across Australia and New Zealand.

Organisers estimate more than 300,000 people attended. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

In SA, stores in Westfield Marion and Westfield West Lakes will shut down by the end of the year.

But the store in Rundle Mall will remain open, and locals are keen to keep the Magic Cave as part of Adelaide's Christmas festivities.

"It's an Adelaide icon, bringing my now baby like when I was a kid, and now letting her do it," local woman Erin said.

"We need David Jones … we need the Magic Cave, the kids love it, it's one thing they look forward to."

World.title: Australia's newest fast-bowling sensation tipped for big things from a young age
World.content:
While Mahli Beardman's record-setting demolition of England may have stunned the visitors, those who watched his development as a junior say it's no surprise.

On a day when fresh hostilities in the Sandpaper scandal dominated the headlines, the West Australian fast bowler's 6/24 skittled the visitors and gave Australian cricket a much-needed bit of good news.

But for West Pilbara Cricket Association secretary Christy Reed, Beardman's talent was always obvious.

Beardman (right) receives a representative cap while playing junior cricket in WA's Pilbara. (Supplied: Christy Reed)

While hailing from Cowaramup in WA's South West, the 21-year-old played his initial junior and representative cricket for Dampier in WA's Pilbara.

Initially spotted by scouts at a talent clinic in Karratha in 2017 as a 12-year-old, Beardman progressed quickly through the junior representative ranks, eventually landing at WA Premier Cricket Club Melville when he moved to Perth.

Ms Reed said he made an impression early.

"He was a tiny little kid, but his bowling was absolutely natural talent," she said.

Beardman (left) was identified early as a talented young bowler. (Supplied: Andrew Hayes)

"So fast for his size, and he absolutely loved his cricket.

" He would even go down to the senior team, Dampier Taverners, training and bully them in the nets. "

She hoped Beardman's success would show other talented junior cricketers across the Pilbara what could be achieved.

"For years it was really hard for kids to have a pathway through to that upper level, but I imagine this would get more kids interested in the sport," Ms Reed said.

"I couldn't be happier for him, his family and for Cricket Australia."

WA Cricket country area manager Andrew Hayes was working in the Pilbara around the same time Beardman and fellow Dampier quick Josh Vernon were making their way through the system.

"To take six wickets against our old foe on debut is an incredible achievement, and we couldn't be prouder," he said.

Mahli Beardman (back row, second from right) representing the West Pilbara at Junior Country Week. (Supplied: Christy Reed)

Hometown pride

The pride was echoed in Cowaramup, who are keen to embrace Beardman as a favourite son despite competing claims from nearby Dunsborough and Margaret River.

Loading...

Cowaramup Cricket Club stalwart and secretary Bob Biddulph coached a six-year-old Beardman before his family moved north.

"Unfortunately, he was only there for one year … but it was the start of his cricket journey, so we're very proud of him," he said.

"We're claiming it down at Cowaramup that's for sure; I think everyone associated with the cricket club is very proud of that."

Mahli Beardman walks off Perth Stadium after taking 6/24 on debut for Australia in ODI cricket. (ABC News: Sam Tomlin)

Mr Biddulph echoed the importance of seeing regional cricketers performing well at international level.

"It just goes to show that it doesn't matter where you are; if you start off and you enjoy the game and stick at it and keep practising, the sky is the limit," he said.

"We've got quite a few junior teams this year, so for them to actually see one of their own making it on the big stage is quite exciting."

Game two of the three-match ODI series is at Adelaide Oval on Sunday.

World.title: Newcastle climate protest goes ahead, no arrests made
World.content:
Protest organisers and NSW Police say no arrests were made as hundreds of kayakers took to Newcastle Harbour in New South Wales, to protest against coal exports and fossil fuels.

Climate activism group Rising Tide began promoting its "Paddle for the Planet" event in August, but Newcastle Council this week moved to ban the group from holding any of its events on council land.

NSW Police attempted to block the protest, citing safety concerns and potential resourcing pressures.

However, the court dismissed the application on Friday, deciding the event was in the public interest.

The Supreme Court of NSW dismissed an application by NSW Police to stop the on-water protest. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

Speaking after the paddle-out, Rising Tide spokesperson Joe Hallenstein labelled Anthony Albanese "hypocritical", as the prime minister and climate change minister engage in the COP31 summit.

"[Albanese] is over in Türkiye telling the world that Australia is a leader in climate action, when the opposite is true," Mr Hallenstein said.

"Both Albanese's federal Labor government, and Chris Minns's state Labor government continue to approve new coal and gas projects, which is the opposite of action on climate change."

Rising Tide spokesperson Joe Hallenstein spoke out at the event. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

The event was held off Horseshoe Beach, which is managed by Transport for NSW.

A NSW Police spokesperson confirmed, by the completion of the event, officers had not made any arrests.

On-water demonstration

Organisers say more than 900 people registered for the event, with more than 600 taking to the water.

Hundreds more lined the shore of Horseshoe Beach for the hour-long demonstration.

"I'm tired of governments, from the federal government down to the local government, not doing enough about reducing [climate impact]," attendee Scott Alcorn said.

"I can see there's plenty of enthusiastic people who feel just the same way as I do."

Protesters formed a line across Newcastle's harbour during the one-hour paddle-out. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

A limited police presence, mostly on foot, attended the protest.

In the Supreme Court hearing, Assistant Commissioner David Waddell and NSW Police's legal representative argued there were serious safety concerns for large amounts of people on the water.

A cap of 785 vessels was placed on the event.

The Port of Newcastle did not run any shipping movements between 10am and 2pm.

Election approaches

NSW Greens spokesperson for climate change and justice Sue Higginson said climate change and fossil fuel projects must be a key concern in the NSW election, scheduled for March 13, 2027.

She argued while the cost of living is the biggest issue for voters coming into the campaign period, it "does not mean people are not also concerned about the health of their local environment".

"Labor and the Coalition, all they want to do is talk about One Nation … what we are doing is providing the people with a real alternative and a real vision for their future."

NSW Greens MLC Sue Higginson declared her support to the Rising Tide movement. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

Ms Higginson also referred to a recent decision by the Minns government to make legislative changes allowing the Mount Pleasant coalmine in the Upper Hunter to increase its life and output.

The premier announced the move despite a High Court ruling relating to the mine that concluded global climate emissions must be considered in approvals.

"[The government] is literally carving laws that defy the High Court's ruling because a coal company is threatening to lay off workers before Christmas," she said.

Ms Higginson said the matter is set to be debated in NSW parliament next week.

A Rising Tide spokesperson confirmed the group plans to hold a larger on-water protest at the end of February on Newcastle Harbour, a fortnight before the election.

World.title: Camping, sightseeing booking portal disabled while data breach investigated
World.content:
The ACT government is stressing vigilance after a cybersecurity breach of a booking platform for campgrounds in territory parks and reserves.

The government said another of its departments, VisitCanberra, used for accommodation and attraction bookings in the ACT, had also been compromised.

The third-party platform, Bookeasy, processes bookings and permits for the National Parks booking system in the ACT and other Australian states, storing personal data from emails to addresses and phone numbers.

It comes as systems in Queensland, Victoria and South Australia were hacked this week.

In a statement, Bookeasy said it was continuing to investigate, and so far had identified potential compromising of customers' personal and booking information.

The platform says it has not identified any breaches of financial details. (Supplied)

"Following a security alert, we were able to take immediate containment action. This included engaging cyber experts to assist with our investigation and provide advice," Bookeasy said.

It said it had not detected any access to credit card details.

The ACT government said it has emailed around 6,000 users, warning them of attempts to scam or phish in the wake of the breach.

Platform suspended

The territory government said some Canberran campers had received "suspicious messages via email of WhatsApp applications".

"We urge extreme caution and to consider that there is a risk of being scammed," the department's executive group manager Bren Burkevics said.

Mr Burkevics said the government has temporarily disabled the platform while it assessed the fallout.

National Parks hacked The National Parks booking system for Queensland, Victoria and South Australia has suffered a data breach, with hackers stealing personal user information.

"Bookeasy has notified the ACT government that they have incurred a cyber incident and potentially the unauthorised release of information," he said.

"So in the abundance of caution, the ACT government has suspended the use of that website."

Mr Burkevics said people could make bookings directly via the parks government website.

"The usual message is that avoiding scams is critical in these times," he said.

"Further information is available from scamwatch.gov.au, but avoid clicking on links and providing sensitive information, particularly credit card information, to third-party applications."

World.title: Cape Town inquiry spoke to all Aussie bowlers, ABC understands
World.content:
All four bowlers from the 2018 Cape Town Test spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into ball tampering, the ABC understands, running counter to claims by former opening batter David Warner.

Warner wrote on social media that Cricket Australia's investigation — which saw him and Steve Smith banned for a year, and Cameron Bancroft rubbed out for nine months — was poorly handled and had a pre-determined outcome.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation. If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?" Warner wrote.

But sources connected to the bowling group said Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc were interviewed. The other front-line bowler from Cape Town, current Test captain Pat Cummins, said during a marathon press conference on Friday that he spoke to investigators.

Sources close to the bowlers said they all spoke to investigators. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour/Cricket Australia)

"They were all interviewed. [Warner's] comments are just not true," one source told the ABC.

The ABC also understands Tim Paine was interviewed as part of the investigation.

Cummins is sadly mistaken In his detailed 70-minute press conference, Pat Cummins said he hoped he could draw a line under the brewing Sandpapergate civil war. David Warner quickly proved that won't be happening.

After Cummins's press conference, Warner said Cummins had "thrown [Usman Khawaja] under the bus" by rejecting Khawaja's claims that more people were responsible for sandpaper entering the field of play than Warner, Bancroft and Smith.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence," Warner said on Fox Sports before Friday's ODI between Australia and England.

"I feel like it was a botched investigation. It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us [Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft] and we had to move on and just accept responsibility."

Usman Khawaja (right) said it wasn't fair for three players to bear all the responsibility for ball tampering. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

And Warner has doubled down on social media.

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that bowlers had no idea," he wrote.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Cricket Australia said in response: "As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since.

"Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players right to provide their own version of events."

In his new book, Khawaja said he was never spoken to despite sitting next to Cameron Bancroft during discussions about using sandpaper on the ball.

What did Khawaja say about Sandpapergate in his book? Much has been written and said about Usman Khawaja's new book — but what's actually in the pages of Sabr?

Cummins on Friday said he spoke to investigators and there were calls at the time for anyone with more information to come forward.

On Tuesday, Starc was one of the first players to be asked about Khawaja's claims and said there were "differing opinions of eight years ago".

"We were heavily grilled through the process at the time and since," he said.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021."

In 2021, Bancroft implied in an interview that the bowlers likely knew what was going on.

"Obviously what I did benefits bowlers and the awareness around that, probably, is self-explanatory," he said.

Starc, Cummins, Lyon and Hazlewood released a joint statement in response, saying they were disappointed to have their integrity questioned.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands," they wrote five years ago.

World.title: A Cat collapsed in an AFLW final. Her trained paramedic rival leapt to her aid
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFLW A Cat collapsed in an AFLW final. Her trained paramedic rival leapt to her aid Hannah Kennelly and Roy Ward Updated November 14, 2026 — 10:11pm ,first published 5:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. In the heat of battle on Saturday, Lexi Hamilton’s instincts took over. The Swans star watched as her teammate Tanya Kennedy and Cat Piper Dunlop clashed in a ruck battle, with the latter crumbling to the turf after receiving an accidental knock to the temple. Piper Dunlop receives medical attention after an accidental head knock. Getty Images Hamilton saw Dunlop struggling and rushed over to her, using her paramedicine and nursing training to ease her to the ground and hold her head in place as medical staff rushed onto the field. It was a heart-warming act within an extraordinary fiery clash, in which Sydney ultimately secured their maiden AFLW semi-final win, overpowering an injury-stricken Geelong to win by three points in a stunning upset.



Swans coach Colin O’Riordan later said watching Dunlop fall was “really scary to witness” and praised Hamilton’s immediate response. “Lexi’s first reaction was, ‘How can I help someone?’” he explained. “It’s credit to her and how she goes about it. “Obviously, [a] qualified nurse, just incredible ... It’s just testament to the person Lexi is in the heat of battle. You can still turn someone on the recovery position and make sure that they’re OK.” A Chloe Molloy goalkicking masterclass propelled the Swans to victory, beating the Cats on their home GMHBA Stadium turf, 8.2 (50) to 7.5 (47).



The result dumped the Cats from the finals in straight sets after two losses by under a goal. It’s been a challenging few months for the Swans’ women’s program, which was hit by collateral damage from the Pullman Hotel scandal. Maddie Quinn celebrates a key goal for the Swans. AFL Photos On Friday, news broke that suspended Swans players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and James Jordon, and North Melbourne recruit Nick Blakey had been cleared by Victoria Police after an investigation into alleged sexual assaults. The announcement ended three months of scrutiny, however the women at the centre of the complaints have vowed to push on with civil action.



In his post-match press conference, O’Riordan reiterated CEO Matthew Pavlich’s statements that the decision by Victoria Police “was not a day for celebration”. Lexi Hamilton came straight to her rival Dunlop’s aid. AFL Photos “I think ‘Pav’ touched on it yesterday in how he spoke to the media, and it’s not a day for celebration,” said O’Riordan . “Like he said, it’s a time now that we have to reflect, look back, and plan what’s next for the footy club, and hopefully, we can do that in the coming weeks.” Swans president Andrew Pridham was in Geelong supporting the women’s team on Saturday as they looked to reach a preliminary final for the first time.



It was a dream opening for Geelong, with dependable Irishwoman Aishling Moloney slotting a goal within the first 30 seconds of the game – an apt celebration for her 50th game milestone. But Molloy immediately posed a problem for the Cats. The league’s leading goal-kicker was last to line up for the national anthem before the siren, spending as much time as possible slotting practice goals in. That would prove telling. Molloy added to her goal tally, firing two goals in the first quarter to give her Swans the lead, followed by another goal in the second that seemed to defy physics, bending through then air to sail through the goals. View post on X



It was injury carnage for the cats before half-time, with Amy McDonald out with a hamstring issue, and star midfielder Georgie Prespakis briefly leaving the field after getting crunched. Rachel Kearns also sustained a nasty-looking hip injury. Prespakis was back on field after half-time, however her influence was significantly dulled by defender Tanya Kennedy. After tagging Bulldogs co-captain Isabelle Pritchard last week, Kennedy had the job on Prespakis and curbed the usually explosive Cats star. Play was temporarily halted in the third quarter for around eight minutes after Dunlop’s horror moment. As Hamilton eased her to the ground, concerned Cats and Swans players looked on and medical staff swarmed around Dunlop, supporting her head and easing her on a stretcher in front of the 5656-strong crowd. The 23-year-old appeared to be conscious, received a standing ovation and cheers from the crowd as she was stretchered off on a medical cart.



Play resumed, and both sides continued to wrestle for the lead. Cynthia Hamilton piled on another goal in the fourth, and suddenly Sydney were up by 16 points. View post on X But Geelong’s Chloe Scheer was eager for redemption after last week’s loss to Melbourne. Scheer missed a set shot at the end of that nail-biting game, handing the victory to the Demons. But she bounced back and kicked three goals on Saturday, including a pivotal major in the final quarter to give the Cats a sniff. Jacqueline Parry kicked another, and suddenly the margin was only four points.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The devastating loophole the AFL must immediately close Kelli Underwood Columnist An arm-wrestle continued by the next 10 minutes, with both sides belting the ball back and forth, desperately trying to score a goal. As the clock ticked down, the Cats’ home crowd screamed and cheered as the ball soared towards their goal square. But, there was Molloy again – taking a telling mark and preventing what would have been a crucial Cats goal. Moments later, the siren went and pandemonium ensured. Cats players fell to their knees as Sydney rushed to embrace each other, ignoring the boos that rained down.



AFLW commentator, and columnist for The Age, Kelli Underwood said on Kayo that the game was one of the best in the league’s history, and long-time AFLW star Ellie Blackburn agreed with her. “That game was amazing, we stuck to our system and our contest pressure – it was just the best,” Swans ruck-forward Maddie Quinn told Kayo Sports. “We got the job done, and I’m just so excited for next week [the preliminary final]. “I had one main focus and that was to be physical in the ruck and then everything else came from that. “You can feel the belief around the club. All our coaches have belief in us, the rest of the club believes in us and that’s why we are winning games and are into a prelim.”



In Cats coach Mick Stinear’s post-match press conference, he confirmed Dunlop had been sent to hospital for scans. “Piper’s in hospital now, just getting some further imaging done,” he explained. “I think she’s doing OK but, yeah, we won’t know more until we get the imaging results. “She’s in good hands, and we’ll find out more shortly.” Stinear said his Cats were shattered by the nail-biting loss, but conceded they were not good enough to beat the Swans.



“We’re bitterly disappointed because I think [with] the season we’ve had, we really should have been competing in a prelim with the kind of footy we put together,” he said. View post on X “Ultimately, we weren’t good enough, so that’s that’s on us. So yeah, it does feel like a little bit of a failed season.” The Swans easily got the better of the free-kick count, 18-9. They trailed significantly in the inside-50 and disposal counts, but were more efficient moving forward and had fewer turnovers. Stinear, who left the Demons to join Geelong, said the Cats would continue to evolve so they could “be on the right side of this” next season.



Meanwhile, a beaming O’Riordan was thrilled with the Swans’ efforts, hailing the performances of Molloy, Quinn and Kennedy. The Swans will next face rampant two-time reigning premiers North Melbourne in a preliminary final next Saturday from 1.05pm at Ikon Park.

- Hannah Kennelly Vescio fires Blues to victory in game 100 as McKay sends a message to Dees Darcy Vescio wound back the clock in game 100 on Saturday night to lead their beloved Carlton to a preliminary final berth against the Demons next week. Vescio kicked two goals and created a third as the Blues stormed back from 19 points down to beat Hawthorn in a thrilling five-point win in front of 4701 fans at Ikon Park, 6.7 (43) to 6.2 (38).



Darcy Vescio of the Blues celebrates a goal against Hawthorn. AFL Photos Vescio’s second major with five minutes ago gave the Blues the lead for the last time as the team navigated a frantic finish. “I was having some flashbacks to junior footy and reminded myself I have done this plenty of times,” Vescio told Kayo Sports. “This week has been very overwhelming and people have sent me the nicest messages, but I haven’t been able to take it all in as I would be a puddle of tears. “I’m so happy to remain in the game so long, a few years ago I saw 100 on the horizon and I thought it would be special to make it there.”



Blues forward Sophie McKay was a child in the crowd in Vescio’s first game, but on this night she was celebrating the win alongside them. “It’s just full circle. I love Darce,” McKay told Kayo Sports. “They are Carlton encapsulated. It’s so surreal for someone like me – I watched them and realised I could do my dream job. “It was true Darcy style to kick the sealer, and I couldn’t be happier.” The feisty McKay also had a message for the waiting Demons, who the Blues will face in the second of a preliminary final double-header back at Ikon Park next Saturday from 4.05pm (AEDT).



Darcy Vescio of the Blues celebrates a goal with teammates. Getty Images “We are coming for ya,” McKay said. “We are not afraid of anyone, and we will fight to the end. Come at us.” The Hawks burst out of the blocks, kicking the first three goals and laying more than 30 tackles in the first term, but the Blues gradually found their feet with late goals to Lila Keck and Lily Goss bringing the home side close at half-time. Vescio kicked four goals, including the Blues’ first, in the league’s inaugural match at Ikon Park in 2017, and in December 2021 Vescio introduced many footy fans to a new term when they announced they are non-binary. Ever since, they have been a beacon for the benefits of inclusion and recognising people the way they want to be recognised.



On this night, Vescio, now a celebrated veteran, was in and out of the match until they won a free kick in front of goal after being awkwardly taken to ground during a red-hot third term. They booted the goal to give the Blues the advantage. Dayna Finn of the Blues and Hayley McLaughlin of the Hawks compete for the ball. AFL Photos Carlton players and fans celebrated accordingly, although their lead was temporarily lost when Hawthorn’s Mackenzie Eardley kicked truly early in the last term. Vescio bobbed up again moments later to mark at centre half-forward and send a long kick to the square, which Sophie McKay grabbed and then snapped truly – bowing down to Vescio during her celebration. Eardley marked a pass from Jacqui Dupuy and kicked her second goal soon after the restart, although Hawks onballer Eliza West injured her knee in the lead-up and limped to the bench.



As rain fell and the pressure lifted, Vescio rose to the occasion yet again, forcing their way to front position and pulling in a telling mark before kicking goal number two for the night – coming with just five minutes remaining. View post on X Goss executed a crucial smother in the last minute, while Vescio was among the Blues who got hands on the ball and cleared it from defence. There were hugs galore after the siren, and Vescio was covered in Gatorade before they sang the team song. “That was disgusting, but I’m all for trying new things – it keeps me young,” Vescio told Kayo with a laugh.



The Blues believe they can win from any position, and on this night they proved it.

- Roy Ward Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

A lightning bolt has struck a man swimming on the NSW Central Coast on Saturday afternoon, with bystanders forced to pull him from the water.

The man was among a crowd enjoying the warm and sunny afternoon at Umina, north of Sydney, on Saturday afternoon.

Bystanders pulled the man from the water. NSW Central Coast Incident Alerts

“It came out of the blue, we could see a bit of storm happening towards Palm Beach. Where we were was sunny, clear skies - it really came out of nowhere,” witness Ed Alvarez told Nine News.

The man was pulled from the water by bystanders just before 4pm, then taken off the sand in a beach buggy.

World.title: ‘You have to understand the impact’: Inside the battle to stop schoolyard bullies
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation ‘You have to understand the impact’: Inside the battle to stop schoolyard bullies Emily Kowal November 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Tears well in Winmalee High School principal Voula Facas’ eyes as she sits across from the mother of a badly bullied child. The mother says to Facas: “I am not the sort of person who comes in and yells the place down. I just didn’t want to see my child so depressed.” Winmalee High School principal Voula Facas with students. Wolter Peeters Facas listens intently, as she has every time the parent has visited the school to report the bullying their child faces. Together, the pair has worked through the problems, creating a safety plan centred on making sure the child who was causing harm understood the consequences of their actions. “That’s what restorative practice is about – it’s getting kids to understand their impact,” Facas said.



“You can discipline a child for doing the wrong thing, but if they don’t truly understand the impact, then nothing will change.” This belief in restorative justice is the approach all NSW schools must soon follow. By the end of the year, schools are required to overhaul their anti-bullying practices to meet a new statewide framework, or face deregistration. Under the new framework, bullied students must be given personalised safety plans that could include more supervision and their own “safe zone”, such as a library. Schools must prioritise student wellbeing, explicitly teaching kindness, respect and inclusion, and counsel bullies rather than simply punish them. Winmalee High School’s adherence to the framework is the reason the mother decided to keep her child in the school.



Related Article Exclusive

Education The classroom moment changing how new teachers see western Sydney “If we pulled them out, then we just thought we’d have the same thing happen again because it happens in all schools. They’re all going to get bullied, and then we’d be back to square one, and I’d have no support,” she said. A study of more than 20 countries found Australian students were among the most exposed to bullying, with nearly one in five saying others had made fun of them, and one in 10 saying they had been deliberately excluded. The framework is underpinned by research conducted by NSW behavioural expert Professor Donna Cross, who found “zero tolerance” policies involving suspension and expulsion were ineffective and potentially harmful. The mother, whose child is today much happier at the school, agreed. She said students must consider the cumulative effect of bullying, and be asked to imagine being targeted “15, 20 times” a day.



Schools will also be required to introduce a triage system that categorises bullying incidents into low, medium or high risk based on factors such as physical harm, emotional impact and recurrence. Each triggers a specific response, from counselling to external referrals. School captain Robbie Pigram said the school’s focus on creating a safe community empowered him to stand up when he saw children acting poorly. “There’s been a couple of times throughout my time in high school where I just happened to find myself near something that is clearly not right,” Pigram said. “I can’t leave it be. I need to step in and help. I tell them to pull their head in.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Meet the Sri Lankan immigration lawyer handing out for Pauline Hanson at the election
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As a One Nation-supporting, Sri Lanka-born migration adviser, Lalin De Silva is alive to the irony. He mentions it immediately. “It’s very ironic that I’m a registered migration agent who is supporting Pauline Hanson against mass immigration. Plus, my best friend happens to be a Muslim,” says the 65-year-old lawyer, enjoying a late afternoon coffee. In the fading light, the main street is virtually empty, while the Pakenham Marketplace shopping centre is still going strong. De Silva continues: “Third irony: I am a Buddhist.” Lalin De Silva is volunteering for One Nation. Joe Armao We’re in Pakenham, the lower house seat on Melbourne’s eastern fringe where One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering is hoping to make history as the right-wing populist party’s first Victorian lower house MP. Back in the late 1990s, the first wave of momentum for Hanson’s party was met with protests in Victoria and defeat for the party electorally in Australia’s most progressive state. Now, with less than two weeks until the election, One Nation’s primary vote is at 23 per cent, according to The Age’s Resolve Political Monitor – 1 point ahead of Labor. Pollsters expect Victorians will elect several One Nation MPs, particularly in the upper house, where Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell is the party’s sole representative. Pickering himself wants to be the premier – as he told the Melbourne Press Club this week, his party is “here to govern”.



“We are now part of the permanent political landscape here in Victoria, whether people like it or not,” he said. “Get used to it.” This is One Nation in 2026: a truckie who stops outside Coles to tell us Labor is stuffed; a cleaner raising three kids with his Samoan ex-partner; a retired tuckshop lady who lived in Traralgon for 44 years but would leave tomorrow if she could; a lifelong Labor-supporting staunch unionist who turned his back on the party because he says Labor turned its back on him. For many, life has simply got worse. It’s a bitter given that the government doesn’t act in the interests of the people out here. Their mood boards range from disillusioned to outright conspiracy theories. De Silva advises prospective migrants about working in Australia or settling here permanently. A member of Sri Lanka’s Sinhalese community, he will volunteer at polling booths for One Nation near his home in neighbouring Berwick. “I like people who are skilled,” he says, explaining how his immigration stance aligns with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s. “Let them be plumbers, carpenters, lawyers. I came as a lawyer to this country.” That was 19 years ago with his Catholic wife, Manjula, a qualified chef, and two children, now both in their 30s.



Denis Fahy and Jacqui Fahy have two One Nation corflutes on their Traralgon home. Joe Armao “We wanted to have a Western culture, which loved people from different ethnicities to come and live within that monoculture of Western civilisation,” he says. “Each one’s religion can be very private. I do a lot of Buddhist meditation, but I don’t try to force it on other people. I don’t go around standing in the middle of the road, laying down and praying or meditating. I’ll do it at my home. I’ll go to a monastery and do it.” That, he feels, has been lost, along with the primacy of the Australian flag he moved here under, now often displayed alongside the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags. De Silva is also against the Victorian government’s First Nations treaty, which he feels is undemocratic given the public voted down the federal Voice to parliament. His teammates at the Endeavour Hills Cricket Club’s veterans team, where he is one of only three non-white players, were surprised when he announced he was supporting One Nation. “People think when they see a dark skin, ‘Oh boy, they are against the whites,’” he says.



“They were quite surprised. Then they started coming and whispering, ‘Lalin, do you know that I’m also member of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation?’ “Most of the Sri Lankan Sinhalese community, whom I associate with, are dead set for Pauline Hanson’s One Nation.” Further east from Pakenham lies Morwell, the urban centre and administrative heart of the Latrobe Valley that gives its name to the electorate that includes Moe, Traralgon and the coal-fired power stations of Yallourn and Loy Yang. The electorate is held by the Nationals’ Martin Cameron, a 57-year-old plumber; pollsters regard it the most likely lower-house seat to fall to One Nation. On Commercial Road, inherent suspicion has replaced rural friendliness. “But I don’t know you,” says one local woman, astonished, when The Age bowls up to her in the street. Suppressing the urge to explain that strangers are merely friends you haven’t met yet, we instead ask her voting intentions in the November 28 poll.



She looks at us, torn between temptation and self-censorship, before gaining control and passing swiftly by. This week at least, Morwell is Nationals country. Even though at the last state election Labor scored more than 31 per cent of the primary vote, preferences put Cameron over the line. He is standing again. Ricky Muir, the ex-federal senator for the Australian Motoring Enthusiasts Party, tried his luck here in 2018 for the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party but only managed fifth. This year he is standing for the upper house for the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers. Related Article Victorian election The 13 seats to watch – and why they will determine the Victorian election Commercial Street is a collection of council offices, charity shops, a florist, a cafe, lawyers’ offices and the Latrobe Valley Law Courts – briefly world-famous when they hosted the Erin Patterson mushroom murder trial. Where once power plant operators, timber mills and coal miners, which sustained the valley last century, might have strolled the streets, they have been replaced by lanyard-wearing public servants employed by Latrobe Valley Council, the courts and regional departmental centres for housing, jobs and transport, and federal department Services Australia. At least when they are not working from home, which has had a big negative impact in the past six months.

World.title: Killed on the Somme at 35, ‘Australia’s Chopin’ is finally getting his due
World.content:
NationalWorld War I Killed on the Somme at 35, ‘Australia’s Chopin’ is finally getting his due Rob Harris November 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
