A century after his death on the battlefields of France, the lost masterpieces of one of Australia’s most gifted composers will be brought back to life at Melbourne’s Shrine of Remembrance in a major effort to reclaim a forgotten figure in the nation’s musical history. Frederick Septimus Kelly, hailed as Australia’s answer to Chopin, was killed at the Battle of the Somme in November 1916, aged just 35, leaving behind a remarkable body of compositions and ambitious unfinished works that have remained largely unknown for generations. Australian composer, concert pianist and Olympic gold medallist Septimus Kelly, who was killed on the Western Front in 1916, is being celebrated as part of a campaign to revive his lost musical legacy 110 years after his death. Australian War Memorial A new biography of the Sydney-born composer will be launched at the Shrine on Sunday, alongside performances of his long-neglected piano music and a screening of an award-winning documentary examining his extraordinary life. The Australian War Memorial’s first musical artist-in-residence, Chris Latham, has spent almost two decades recovering Kelly’s compositions and believes his death represented one of the greatest cultural losses suffered by Australia during World War I.



“Sep, in order of his talents, was an Olympic gold medal-winning rower, a great pianist and an even greater composer,” Latham said. “It’s time for our long-lost son to come home.” Born in Sydney in 1881, Kelly grew up in a musical household before travelling to England, where he attended Eton College and subsequently studied piano and composition in Frankfurt alongside fellow Australian musician Percy Grainger. His talent was evident from childhood. At 14, he performed for Antoine Marmontel, one of Chopin’s last surviving pupils, who enthusiastically endorsed his musical ambitions. Kelly went on to perform with major orchestras and collaborate with some of Europe’s most accomplished musicians, including cellist Pablo Casals and violinist Jelly d’Aranyi. He was also an exceptional athlete, winning a rowing gold medal at the 1908 London Olympics before pursuing a professional music career that took him across Europe and Australia.



The grave of F.S Kelly at Martinsart, Somme, France. Australian War Memorial When war broke out in 1914, Kelly enlisted in Britain’s Royal Naval Division, serving alongside the celebrated English poet Rupert Brooke. Brooke died from an infected mosquito bite while moored of the Greek island of Skyros in the Aegean Sea, while on their way to the landings at Gallipoli. His death in 1915 inspired Kelly’s best-known composition, Elegy for Strings, which was written during the campaign and has since become the subject of an internationally award-winning documentary, Elegy. Despite the demands of military service, Kelly continued composing, completing two substantial collections of piano works inspired by Chopin’s études and preludes.



In May 1916, while on leave before deploying to France, he delivered corrected proofs of his 12 Studies and 24 Monographs to his London publisher. Six months later, on November 13, he was killed on the Somme. His wartime diaries reveal an artist acutely conscious that his creative ambitions might be cut short. Before leaving for the front, Kelly invoked the poet John Keats and his fear of dying before completing his work. Related Article Exclusive

Remembrance Day The war widow, the love story – and the Australian flag stitched from Japanese rags He listed a symphony, piano sonata, string quartet and numerous other compositions still forming in his imagination. Much of that music was never committed to paper. Latham believes Kelly’s decision to serve in a British military unit rather than an Australian battalion contributed to his subsequent neglect, leaving his musical achievements stranded between two countries.



“One can only speculate what would have happened if Kelly had lived,” Latham said. “Had he returned to Australia, he would have likely risen to be the head of music at the ABC or perhaps at the Sydney Conservatorium. The loss of Kelly and similar talents from his generation too often are stories we don’t know.” The new biography by Melbourne author Therese Radic and Olympic gold medallist Martin Cross forms part of a broader campaign to restore Kelly’s reputation, with his recovered compositions being made freely available to musicians and cultural institutions. Sunday’s event will feature performances by pianists Edward and Stephanie Neeman, alongside readings from Kelly’s diaries by Melbourne arts figure Carrillo Gantner. The concert, beginning at 2pm, will conclude a commemorative tour through Sydney, Canberra and Melbourne marking the 110th anniversary of Kelly’s death. World.title: Nvidia scandal raises new concerns about scale of Chinese spying
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaChina relations Nvidia scandal raises new concerns about scale of Chinese spying Peter Martin and Philip J. Heijmans November 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Singapore: The Jensen Huang saga is the latest example of what governments around the world say is a broad push by China to steal commercial and technological secrets and gather intelligence on foreign leaders and military plans. The revelation that Nvidia’s now ex-CEO had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China has rocked the US artificial intelligence boom and thrust allegations that Beijing is seeking to infiltrate Western tech giants into public view. It fits into what foreign officials say is a globe-spanning project. In Germany, prosecutors allege a married couple posing as interpreters and car industry employees cultivated professors in AI, computer science and aerospace, drawing some to China for paid “civilian” lectures delivered to state arms companies. New Zealand intelligence says a Chinese observatory with close government ties tried to install space-tracking equipment through a local company – gear that could also collect military intelligence. Taiwan says Chinese operatives trawl social media for indebted soldiers, offer loans, then press them for secrets and introductions to colleagues. The revelation that Nvidia’s now ex-CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China has rocked the tech world. AP Security agencies around the world have raised the alarm. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) calls Chinese espionage “a grave threat to the economic well-being” of the US. Britain’s MI5 said it was running seven times as many China-related investigations in 2022 as four years earlier. Canadian intelligence calls China its “greatest counter-intelligence threat”, while Dutch intelligence says Chinese digital espionage against technology companies is happening on a “large scale”.



Beijing has dismissed the Huang espionage allegations as a smear, accusing Washington of fabricating “Chinese spy narratives” to justify restrictions on technology exports. Despite those denials, the suspected spy at the centre of the scandal that toppled Huang is now in China with the knowledge of the Chinese government. Related Article Analysis

Billionaires There has never been another scandal like this At stake is the balance of power between the world’s two largest economies. America has bet that its lead in AI and advanced semiconductors will underpin its continued economic strength and military superiority, while its ability to project force across the Pacific constrains Beijing’s ambitions over Taiwan. Espionage offers China a way to erode those advantages, accelerating its technological rise while gaining insight into Washington’s military plans and political decision-making. “There is a lack of appreciation for how professional the Chinese services have become,” said Holden Triplett, who ran the FBI’s office in Beijing and founded Trenchcoat Advisors, noting that parts of China’s intelligence service now rivalled the US Central Intelligence Agency and Russia’s Federal Security Service. “They’re hitting on human frailty and vulnerability and they’re spending all day thinking about how to do this,” he added. “Anyone can fall for it.”



China’s spying push is intensifying in its backyard as Beijing continues to expand its military footprint in the South China Sea. In the Philippines, suspected Chinese spies claimed to be using drones to carry fishing bait as they monitored warships around Subic Bay. Others posed as seafood buyers while flying drones near a naval base. In Manila, hired drivers cruised past the presidential palace, military camps and the US embassy in cars fitted with fake mobile phone towers capable of collecting data from nearby phones. Another vehicle, equipped with cameras and mapping technology, visited more than 120 locations, including bases used by American forces. Loading The alleged operations reached deep inside the Philippine government. Authorities say suspected Chinese agents also recruited people inside the country’s defence establishment, obtaining names of naval personnel and schedules for troop rotations and resupply missions to disputed South China Sea outposts. The cases offered a rare glimpse into the scale and sophistication of Beijing’s espionage operations – which an investigator said were carried out by a spy network that numbered in the hundreds. China has dismissed the allegations as baseless.



“It is extremely widespread because that is the modus operandi of the Chinese,” Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said in an interview. “It’s not only here – the United States. How many are being arrested? Within Australia, how many? In the UK, how many?” Related Article Technology & democracy Who is Alice Huang? The suspected Chinese spy at the centre of the Nvidia scandal China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) is at the centre of Beijing’s increasingly brazen espionage push. The country’s main civilian spy service combines the overseas remit of the CIA with a domestic remit like that of the FBI. Under Chinese President Xi Jinping, reforms have tightened Beijing’s control over provincial and municipal intelligence bureaus, allowing the MSS to co-ordinate operations across the country and pursue more ambitious missions overseas. “It’s become more aggressive,” said Randy Phillips, a former CIA Beijing station chief. “If you look at the kinds of targets they’ve gone after in the last 10 years, they’ve become a much more emboldened organisation.” The MSS is only one arm of what Britain’s parliamentary watchdog has called “the largest state intelligence apparatus in the world”: the People’s Liberation Army runs military, signals and cyber intelligence; the Ministry of Public Security operates at home and abroad; party bodies cultivate political, business and academic networks overseas.



Xi has also handed intelligence agencies broader powers and obliged citizens and institutions to help them. The 2017 National Intelligence Law says every organisation and citizen must “support, assist, and co-operate” with intelligence work. While the US and other countries spy on adversaries and allies, most argue that they don’t engage in industrial espionage the way that the MSS does and none has its scale. ‘They’re hitting on human frailty and vulnerability and they’re spending all day thinking about how to do this.’ Holden Triplett, who ran the FBI’s office in Beijing and founded Trenchcoat Advisors “The numbers in military and civilian intelligence and in the public security apparatus that feeds into intelligence are probably well into the millions,” Phillips said. As the AI revolution has taken off, the technology that underpins it has become a crucial target for Chinese spy agencies, including obtaining it through hacking and human sources, which has made people working at the cutting edge in government, industry and academia potential targets, according to Western officials familiar with the matter.



“The CCP considers itself as in pretty much an existential contest with the United States and other democracies. The hinge on which this contest will turn is scientific and technological power and central to that will be artificial intelligence,” said Peter Mattis, a former CIA counterintelligence analyst who is now president of the Jamestown Foundation. “Any C-suite in the AI industry is going to be an interesting target.” Related Article Analysis

China relations Downfall of world’s chipmaker-in-chief a potential headache for Beijing as well as US AI is also reshaping Chinese spycraft. The biggest gains come early in recruitment, helping services sift huge pools of potential targets and tailor approaches before a human officer steps in. In June, the FBI and Justice Department said suspected Chinese spies used fake consulting firms, lucrative job offers and AI-generated photographs to lure Americans with security clearances onto encrypted messaging apps. In October, US counterintelligence officials warned that Beijing was using AI tools, including DeepSeek, to profile American executives and government officials, identify their vulnerabilities and gain leverage over them. “With AI, you just set up the algorithm to go after targets. You save a tremendous amount of manpower and searching – it’s a force multiplier,” said Dennis Wilder, the CIA’s former deputy assistant director for East Asia and the Pacific. Then, once targets were identified, Chinese agents could meet them online instead of undertaking risky travel overseas, Wilder said. “Human espionage doesn’t any more have to be sneaking around back alleys.”



AI is also bolstering China’s already formidable cyber capabilities. Microsoft said last month that the China-linked group Storm-0940 used agentic AI to automate attacks against hundreds of organisations worldwide. In September, Britain’s MI5 warned that the China General Technology Research Institute was funding research in AI and cybersecurity primarily to strengthen the Ministry of State Security’s espionage capabilities. More than 100 UK-linked academics had contributed to projects ultimately funded by the MSS, MI5 said, sometimes without knowing who was paying. “This isn’t the only [alleged] operation against Nvidia. You should assume there are another 10 or more going on and, of course, it’s not the only operation going on against US tech,” said Triplett, the former FBI agent. “My guess is that they’ll be encouraged by how this worked out and they’ll do more and more of these operations.” Bloomberg Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: A Cat collapsed in an AFLW final. Her trained paramedic rival leapt to her aid
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFLW A Cat collapsed in an AFLW final. Her trained paramedic rival leapt to her aid Hannah Kennelly and Roy Ward Updated November 14, 2026 — 10:11pm ,first published 5:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. In the heat of battle on Saturday, Lexi Hamilton’s instincts took over. The Swans star watched as her teammate Tanya Kennedy and Cat Piper Dunlop clashed in a ruck battle, with the latter crumbling to the turf after receiving an accidental knock to the temple. Piper Dunlop receives medical attention after an accidental head knock. Getty Images Hamilton saw Dunlop struggling and rushed over to her, using her paramedicine and nursing training to ease her to the ground and hold her head in place as medical staff rushed onto the field. It was a heart-warming act within an extraordinary fiery clash, in which Sydney ultimately secured their maiden AFLW semi-final win, overpowering an injury-stricken Geelong to win by three points in a stunning upset.



Swans coach Colin O’Riordan later said watching Dunlop fall was “really scary to witness” and praised Hamilton’s immediate response. “Lexi’s first reaction was, ‘How can I help someone?’” he explained. “It’s credit to her and how she goes about it. “Obviously, [a] qualified nurse, just incredible ... It’s just testament to the person Lexi is in the heat of battle. You can still turn someone on the recovery position and make sure that they’re OK.” A Chloe Molloy goalkicking masterclass propelled the Swans to victory, beating the Cats on their home GMHBA Stadium turf, 8.2 (50) to 7.5 (47).



The result dumped the Cats from the finals in straight sets after two losses by under a goal. It’s been a challenging few months for the Swans’ women’s program, which was hit by collateral damage from the Pullman Hotel scandal. Maddie Quinn celebrates a key goal for the Swans. AFL Photos On Friday, news broke that suspended Swans players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and James Jordon, and North Melbourne recruit Nick Blakey had been cleared by Victoria Police after an investigation into alleged sexual assaults. The announcement ended three months of scrutiny, however the women at the centre of the complaints have vowed to push on with civil action.



In his post-match press conference, O’Riordan reiterated CEO Matthew Pavlich’s statements that the decision by Victoria Police “was not a day for celebration”. Lexi Hamilton came straight to her rival Dunlop’s aid. AFL Photos “I think ‘Pav’ touched on it yesterday in how he spoke to the media, and it’s not a day for celebration,” said O’Riordan . “Like he said, it’s a time now that we have to reflect, look back, and plan what’s next for the footy club, and hopefully, we can do that in the coming weeks.” Swans president Andrew Pridham was in Geelong supporting the women’s team on Saturday as they looked to reach a preliminary final for the first time.



It was a dream opening for Geelong, with dependable Irishwoman Aishling Moloney slotting a goal within the first 30 seconds of the game – an apt celebration for her 50th game milestone. But Molloy immediately posed a problem for the Cats. The league’s leading goal-kicker was last to line up for the national anthem before the siren, spending as much time as possible slotting practice goals in. That would prove telling. Molloy added to her goal tally, firing two goals in the first quarter to give her Swans the lead, followed by another goal in the second that seemed to defy physics, bending through then air to sail through the goals. View post on X



It was injury carnage for the cats before half-time, with Amy McDonald out with a hamstring issue, and star midfielder Georgie Prespakis briefly leaving the field after getting crunched. Rachel Kearns also sustained a nasty-looking hip injury. Prespakis was back on field after half-time, however her influence was significantly dulled by defender Tanya Kennedy. After tagging Bulldogs co-captain Isabelle Pritchard last week, Kennedy had the job on Prespakis and curbed the usually explosive Cats star. Play was temporarily halted in the third quarter for around eight minutes after Dunlop’s horror moment. As Hamilton eased her to the ground, concerned Cats and Swans players looked on and medical staff swarmed around Dunlop, supporting her head and easing her on a stretcher in front of the 5656-strong crowd. The 23-year-old appeared to be conscious, received a standing ovation and cheers from the crowd as she was stretchered off on a medical cart.



Play resumed, and both sides continued to wrestle for the lead. Cynthia Hamilton piled on another goal in the fourth, and suddenly Sydney were up by 16 points. View post on X But Geelong’s Chloe Scheer was eager for redemption after last week’s loss to Melbourne. Scheer missed a set shot at the end of that nail-biting game, handing the victory to the Demons. But she bounced back and kicked three goals on Saturday, including a pivotal major in the final quarter to give the Cats a sniff. Jacqueline Parry kicked another, and suddenly the margin was only four points.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The devastating loophole the AFL must immediately close Kelli Underwood Columnist An arm-wrestle continued by the next 10 minutes, with both sides belting the ball back and forth, desperately trying to score a goal. As the clock ticked down, the Cats’ home crowd screamed and cheered as the ball soared towards their goal square. But, there was Molloy again – taking a telling mark and preventing what would have been a crucial Cats goal. Moments later, the siren went and pandemonium ensured. Cats players fell to their knees as Sydney rushed to embrace each other, ignoring the boos that rained down.



AFLW commentator, and columnist for The Age, Kelli Underwood said on Kayo that the game was one of the best in the league’s history, and long-time AFLW star Ellie Blackburn agreed with her. “That game was amazing, we stuck to our system and our contest pressure – it was just the best,” Swans ruck-forward Maddie Quinn told Kayo Sports. “We got the job done, and I’m just so excited for next week [the preliminary final]. “I had one main focus and that was to be physical in the ruck and then everything else came from that. “You can feel the belief around the club. All our coaches have belief in us, the rest of the club believes in us and that’s why we are winning games and are into a prelim.”



In Cats coach Mick Stinear’s post-match press conference, he confirmed Dunlop had been sent to hospital for scans. “Piper’s in hospital now, just getting some further imaging done,” he explained. “I think she’s doing OK but, yeah, we won’t know more until we get the imaging results. “She’s in good hands, and we’ll find out more shortly.” Stinear said his Cats were shattered by the nail-biting loss, but conceded they were not good enough to beat the Swans.



“We’re bitterly disappointed because I think [with] the season we’ve had, we really should have been competing in a prelim with the kind of footy we put together,” he said. View post on X “Ultimately, we weren’t good enough, so that’s that’s on us. So yeah, it does feel like a little bit of a failed season.” The Swans easily got the better of the free-kick count, 18-9. They trailed significantly in the inside-50 and disposal counts, but were more efficient moving forward and had fewer turnovers. Stinear, who left the Demons to join Geelong, said the Cats would continue to evolve so they could “be on the right side of this” next season.



Meanwhile, a beaming O’Riordan was thrilled with the Swans’ efforts, hailing the performances of Molloy, Quinn and Kennedy. The Swans will next face rampant two-time reigning premiers North Melbourne in a preliminary final next Saturday from 1.05pm at Ikon Park.

- Hannah Kennelly Vescio fires Blues to victory in game 100 as McKay sends a message to Dees Darcy Vescio wound back the clock in game 100 on Saturday night to lead their beloved Carlton to a preliminary final berth against the Demons next week. Vescio kicked two goals and created a third as the Blues stormed back from 19 points down to beat Hawthorn in a thrilling five-point win in front of 4701 fans at Ikon Park, 6.7 (43) to 6.2 (38).



Darcy Vescio of the Blues celebrates a goal against Hawthorn. AFL Photos Vescio’s second major with five minutes ago gave the Blues the lead for the last time as the team navigated a frantic finish. “I was having some flashbacks to junior footy and reminded myself I have done this plenty of times,” Vescio told Kayo Sports. “This week has been very overwhelming and people have sent me the nicest messages, but I haven’t been able to take it all in as I would be a puddle of tears. “I’m so happy to remain in the game so long, a few years ago I saw 100 on the horizon and I thought it would be special to make it there.”



Blues forward Sophie McKay was a child in the crowd in Vescio’s first game, but on this night she was celebrating the win alongside them. “It’s just full circle. I love Darce,” McKay told Kayo Sports. “They are Carlton encapsulated. It’s so surreal for someone like me – I watched them and realised I could do my dream job. “It was true Darcy style to kick the sealer, and I couldn’t be happier.” The feisty McKay also had a message for the waiting Demons, who the Blues will face in the second of a preliminary final double-header back at Ikon Park next Saturday from 4.05pm (AEDT).



Darcy Vescio of the Blues celebrates a goal with teammates. Getty Images “We are coming for ya,” McKay said. “We are not afraid of anyone, and we will fight to the end. Come at us.” The Hawks burst out of the blocks, kicking the first three goals and laying more than 30 tackles in the first term, but the Blues gradually found their feet with late goals to Lila Keck and Lily Goss bringing the home side close at half-time. Vescio kicked four goals, including the Blues’ first, in the league’s inaugural match at Ikon Park in 2017, and in December 2021 Vescio introduced many footy fans to a new term when they announced they are non-binary. Ever since, they have been a beacon for the benefits of inclusion and recognising people the way they want to be recognised.



On this night, Vescio, now a celebrated veteran, was in and out of the match until they won a free kick in front of goal after being awkwardly taken to ground during a red-hot third term. They booted the goal to give the Blues the advantage. Dayna Finn of the Blues and Hayley McLaughlin of the Hawks compete for the ball. AFL Photos Carlton players and fans celebrated accordingly, although their lead was temporarily lost when Hawthorn’s Mackenzie Eardley kicked truly early in the last term. Vescio bobbed up again moments later to mark at centre half-forward and send a long kick to the square, which Sophie McKay grabbed and then snapped truly – bowing down to Vescio during her celebration. Eardley marked a pass from Jacqui Dupuy and kicked her second goal soon after the restart, although Hawks onballer Eliza West injured her knee in the lead-up and limped to the bench.



As rain fell and the pressure lifted, Vescio rose to the occasion yet again, forcing their way to front position and pulling in a telling mark before kicking goal number two for the night – coming with just five minutes remaining. View post on X Goss executed a crucial smother in the last minute, while Vescio was among the Blues who got hands on the ball and cleared it from defence. There were hugs galore after the siren, and Vescio was covered in Gatorade before they sang the team song. “That was disgusting, but I’m all for trying new things – it keeps me young,” Vescio told Kayo with a laugh.



The Blues believe they can win from any position, and on this night they proved it.

- Roy Ward Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

A lightning bolt has struck a man swimming on the NSW Central Coast on Saturday afternoon, with bystanders forced to pull him from the water.

The man was among a crowd enjoying the warm and sunny afternoon at Umina, north of Sydney, on Saturday afternoon.

Bystanders pulled the man from the water. NSW Central Coast Incident Alerts

“It came out of the blue, we could see a bit of storm happening towards Palm Beach. Where we were was sunny, clear skies - it really came out of nowhere,” witness Ed Alvarez told Nine News.

The man was pulled from the water by bystanders just before 4pm, then taken off the sand in a beach buggy.

World.title: For our children’s sake, we must protect the environment
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters For our children’s sake, we must protect the environment November 14, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Nature’s bounty

I completely agree with your correspondent that we must consider younger generations when planning high-rise developments (Letters, 13/11). Prioritising their physical and mental health means placing climate and environmental considerations at the centre of urban design.

As discussed in the article ″⁣Doctors keen to prescribe fresh air and nature″⁣ (9/11), regular access to nature and open space is essential. Because high-density projects inevitably clear existing trees and gardens, developers must actively replace this greenery within their designs.

Removing tree canopies, biodiverse gardens, and permeable ground surfaces will only worsen the urban heat island effect, drive up carbon emissions, and increase flood risks.

If we want to enhance the lives of younger generations, we must ensure their future living environments are resilient, and safe.

Jennie Epstein, Little River Impossible task

The Liberal Party Sussan Ley led for a short time was never going to create the world she now seems to yearn for (″⁣Empathy, democracy’s biggest threat″⁣, 14/11).

Judy Kevill, Ringwood Political discourse

Sussan Ley succinctly summarises the depressing state of political discourse both here and in the US. She captures the growing apathy and disillusionment of the average voter with our political class. The only thing that she fails to acknowledge is that she was part of the problem.

Ross Hudson, Mount Martha



Vote for future

The latest polls predict there will be a total wipeout of Labor in Victoria.

Any acknowledgement of the range of achievements by Labor over the past 12 years are ignored, including the massive number of infrastructure projects overtaken by scandals and the level of corruption in the unions associated with the Big Build program aimed at the growth of Melbourne over the next 30 years.

The rising costs on these projects is disturbing as reported that government ministers were reluctant or ignored corruption advice when told by their departmental heads.

It is a fact that any government can run out of steam while oppositions can offer all sorts of inducements to voters without evidence or experience.

We the voters need to assess Victoria’s current challenges and vote in the best interests of the state’s future not simply on outrage, ideology, anger and failure but on the basis of greater attention to integrity oversight and regulation and take the politicians out of infrastructure decision-making once programs have been approved. This applies also to unions and business and corporate elites. Regulators must be put in place to ensure any infrastructure project is completed according to sound economics.

Ray Cleary, Camberwell The Lasso approach?

What a mess the sandpapergate saga has become. Sadly, many seem to be taking sides. Perhaps, we might do better to adopt the Ted Lasso approach: be curious but not judgmental.

Terry Kelly, Coburg Show Treaty respect

I am increasingly frustrated at Jess Wilson’s response to questions on her decision to repeal the Treaty Act passed by the Victorian Parliament exactly a year ago. She equates the Act with the Voice Referendum and states that Victorians gave a very clear message. The actual result in Victoria was 54 per cent No and 46 per cent Yes. A significant cohort – around 15 per cent of No voters cited fears centred on the amendment of the Constitution as the main reason for their decision. The Treaty does not involve any constitutional change and it does not preclude any existing or future First Nations programs. It is simply a way of showing respect for our Indigenous heritage and a step towards change and greater opportunities for our First Nations people.

Judy Nicol, Sandhurst Acknowledge history

Your correspondent correctly asserts that Jess Wilson, if elected, has an ″⁣undeniable mandate″⁣ to repeal Victoria’s First Peoples Treaty (Letters, 13/11). What I take issue with, however, is their claim that because of the No vote in the 2023 Voice referendum, the Treaty ″⁣should never have been brought before parliament″⁣.

The Treaty-making process began in 2016, in other words, a decade-long commitment to advance justice and self-determination for First Peoples.

Whereas the referendum was a model not tried and tested, Victoria was implementing something that had existed successfully for the First Peoples’ Assembly for the preceding six years.

The Treaty is (or was) an opportunity for all Victorians to acknowledge our shared history and move forwards together.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne Kew here for doubt

The profile of the Opposition Leader Jess Wilson (″⁣How a daggy Millennial came to hold a party’s hope in her hands″⁣, 13/11) overlooks one crucial detail: Kew is a marginal seat.

Wilson holds it by around 4 per cent, and former Boroondara mayor Sophie Torney is standing again as an independent. If the Coalition wins government but Wilson loses Kew, who becomes premier? Would the policies change? Voters across Victoria might want to consider this before they cast their vote.

Amy Hiller, Kew



Give Treaty a go

The article on Jess Wilson covered many reasonable questions about her beliefs and approach to politics. Sadly, an important subject to many Victorians was never broached: Treaty. Why is Wilson dead set on removing Treaty? Why would it not be fairer to at least give Treaty a chance to prove its value over a reasonable timeframe, to follow Treaty for a year at least? Please, give Treaty a fair go.

Lynn Heath, Doncaster Counting the coast

The two medically qualified correspondents (Letters, 13/11) commented that the deinstitutionalisation of Victoria’s mental health services in the 1980s was, in itself, a good idea. However the equivalent resources were subsequently never allocated into community mental health services and we continue to see the social consequences today.

There is an opportunity cost in not properly funding mental health care and that is found in the news every day in reports of homelessness, crime and domestic violence. The only conclusion one can reach is that the bureaucrats and politicians who went down this path believed that society should bear the social cost of the cynical funding priorities that they foisted upon us.

David Fry, Windsor Debt benefits

So Labor has notched up unbearable levels of debt, at about 30 per cent of the state’s GDP. Debt under the Liberals reached 58 per cent when Henry Bolte was premier. And in both instances the expenditure was on much needed infrastructure – schools, hospitals, roads, public transport.

John Andrews, North Fitzroy AI’s failure

Recent developments have made it clear that where human relationships are concerned, artificial intelligence does not have all the answers.

Melanie Carter, Semaphore, SA Exterminate!

Your correspondent (Letters, 13/11) calls for AI to be asked how to attain world peace, end poverty and solve climate change. AI’s obvious answer would be to remove the human race. Then there would be nobody left to care about Essendon’s AFL flag prospects.

Phil Bodel, Ocean Grove

World.title: ‘You have to understand the impact’: Inside the battle to stop schoolyard bullies
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation ‘You have to understand the impact’: Inside the battle to stop schoolyard bullies Emily Kowal November 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tears well in Winmalee High School principal Voula Facas’ eyes as she sits across from the mother of a badly bullied child. The mother says to Facas: “I am not the sort of person who comes in and yells the place down. I just didn’t want to see my child so depressed.” Winmalee High School principal Voula Facas with students. Wolter Peeters Facas listens intently, as she has every time the parent has visited the school to report the bullying their child faces. Together, the pair has worked through the problems, creating a safety plan centred on making sure the child who was causing harm understood the consequences of their actions. “That’s what restorative practice is about – it’s getting kids to understand their impact,” Facas said.



“You can discipline a child for doing the wrong thing, but if they don’t truly understand the impact, then nothing will change.” This belief in restorative justice is the approach all NSW schools must soon follow. By the end of the year, schools are required to overhaul their anti-bullying practices to meet a new statewide framework, or face deregistration. Under the new framework, bullied students must be given personalised safety plans that could include more supervision and their own “safe zone”, such as a library. Schools must prioritise student wellbeing, explicitly teaching kindness, respect and inclusion, and counsel bullies rather than simply punish them. Winmalee High School’s adherence to the framework is the reason the mother decided to keep her child in the school.



Related Article Exclusive

Education The classroom moment changing how new teachers see western Sydney “If we pulled them out, then we just thought we’d have the same thing happen again because it happens in all schools. They’re all going to get bullied, and then we’d be back to square one, and I’d have no support,” she said. A study of more than 20 countries found Australian students were among the most exposed to bullying, with nearly one in five saying others had made fun of them, and one in 10 saying they had been deliberately excluded. The framework is underpinned by research conducted by NSW behavioural expert Professor Donna Cross, who found “zero tolerance” policies involving suspension and expulsion were ineffective and potentially harmful. The mother, whose child is today much happier at the school, agreed. She said students must consider the cumulative effect of bullying, and be asked to imagine being targeted “15, 20 times” a day.



Schools will also be required to introduce a triage system that categorises bullying incidents into low, medium or high risk based on factors such as physical harm, emotional impact and recurrence. Each triggers a specific response, from counselling to external referrals. School captain Robbie Pigram said the school’s focus on creating a safe community empowered him to stand up when he saw children acting poorly. “There’s been a couple of times throughout my time in high school where I just happened to find myself near something that is clearly not right,” Pigram said. “I can’t leave it be. I need to step in and help. I tell them to pull their head in.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Meet the Sri Lankan immigration lawyer handing out for Pauline Hanson at the election
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As a One Nation-supporting, Sri Lanka-born migration adviser, Lalin De Silva is alive to the irony. He mentions it immediately. “It’s very ironic that I’m a registered migration agent who is supporting Pauline Hanson against mass immigration. Plus, my best friend happens to be a Muslim,” says the 65-year-old lawyer, enjoying a late afternoon coffee. In the fading light, the main street is virtually empty, while the Pakenham Marketplace shopping centre is still going strong. De Silva continues: “Third irony: I am a Buddhist.” Lalin De Silva is volunteering for One Nation. Joe Armao We’re in Pakenham, the lower house seat on Melbourne’s eastern fringe where One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering is hoping to make history as the right-wing populist party’s first Victorian lower house MP. Back in the late 1990s, the first wave of momentum for Hanson’s party was met with protests in Victoria and defeat for the party electorally in Australia’s most progressive state. Now, with less than two weeks until the election, One Nation’s primary vote is at 23 per cent, according to The Age’s Resolve Political Monitor – 1 point ahead of Labor. Pollsters expect Victorians will elect several One Nation MPs, particularly in the upper house, where Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell is the party’s sole representative. Pickering himself wants to be the premier – as he told the Melbourne Press Club this week, his party is “here to govern”.



“We are now part of the permanent political landscape here in Victoria, whether people like it or not,” he said. “Get used to it.” This is One Nation in 2026: a truckie who stops outside Coles to tell us Labor is stuffed; a cleaner raising three kids with his Samoan ex-partner; a retired tuckshop lady who lived in Traralgon for 44 years but would leave tomorrow if she could; a lifelong Labor-supporting staunch unionist who turned his back on the party because he says Labor turned its back on him. For many, life has simply got worse. It’s a bitter given that the government doesn’t act in the interests of the people out here. Their mood boards range from disillusioned to outright conspiracy theories. De Silva advises prospective migrants about working in Australia or settling here permanently. A member of Sri Lanka’s Sinhalese community, he will volunteer at polling booths for One Nation near his home in neighbouring Berwick. “I like people who are skilled,” he says, explaining how his immigration stance aligns with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s. “Let them be plumbers, carpenters, lawyers. I came as a lawyer to this country.” That was 19 years ago with his Catholic wife, Manjula, a qualified chef, and two children, now both in their 30s.



Denis Fahy and Jacqui Fahy have two One Nation corflutes on their Traralgon home. Joe Armao “We wanted to have a Western culture, which loved people from different ethnicities to come and live within that monoculture of Western civilisation,” he says. “Each one’s religion can be very private. I do a lot of Buddhist meditation, but I don’t try to force it on other people. I don’t go around standing in the middle of the road, laying down and praying or meditating. I’ll do it at my home. I’ll go to a monastery and do it.” That, he feels, has been lost, along with the primacy of the Australian flag he moved here under, now often displayed alongside the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags. De Silva is also against the Victorian government’s First Nations treaty, which he feels is undemocratic given the public voted down the federal Voice to parliament. His teammates at the Endeavour Hills Cricket Club’s veterans team, where he is one of only three non-white players, were surprised when he announced he was supporting One Nation. “People think when they see a dark skin, ‘Oh boy, they are against the whites,’” he says.



“They were quite surprised. Then they started coming and whispering, ‘Lalin, do you know that I’m also member of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation?’ “Most of the Sri Lankan Sinhalese community, whom I associate with, are dead set for Pauline Hanson’s One Nation.” Further east from Pakenham lies Morwell, the urban centre and administrative heart of the Latrobe Valley that gives its name to the electorate that includes Moe, Traralgon and the coal-fired power stations of Yallourn and Loy Yang. The electorate is held by the Nationals’ Martin Cameron, a 57-year-old plumber; pollsters regard it the most likely lower-house seat to fall to One Nation. On Commercial Road, inherent suspicion has replaced rural friendliness. “But I don’t know you,” says one local woman, astonished, when The Age bowls up to her in the street. Suppressing the urge to explain that strangers are merely friends you haven’t met yet, we instead ask her voting intentions in the November 28 poll.



She looks at us, torn between temptation and self-censorship, before gaining control and passing swiftly by. This week at least, Morwell is Nationals country. Even though at the last state election Labor scored more than 31 per cent of the primary vote, preferences put Cameron over the line. He is standing again. Ricky Muir, the ex-federal senator for the Australian Motoring Enthusiasts Party, tried his luck here in 2018 for the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party but only managed fifth. This year he is standing for the upper house for the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers. Related Article Victorian election The 13 seats to watch – and why they will determine the Victorian election Commercial Street is a collection of council offices, charity shops, a florist, a cafe, lawyers’ offices and the Latrobe Valley Law Courts – briefly world-famous when they hosted the Erin Patterson mushroom murder trial. Where once power plant operators, timber mills and coal miners, which sustained the valley last century, might have strolled the streets, they have been replaced by lanyard-wearing public servants employed by Latrobe Valley Council, the courts and regional departmental centres for housing, jobs and transport, and federal department Services Australia. At least when they are not working from home, which has had a big negative impact in the past six months.

World.title: Killed on the Somme at 35, ‘Australia’s Chopin’ is finally getting his due
World.content:
NationalWorld War I Killed on the Somme at 35, ‘Australia’s Chopin’ is finally getting his due Rob Harris November 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A century after his death on the battlefields of France, the lost masterpieces of one of Australia’s most gifted composers will be brought back to life at Melbourne’s Shrine of Remembrance in a major effort to reclaim a forgotten figure in the nation’s musical history. Frederick Septimus Kelly, hailed as Australia’s answer to Chopin, was killed at the Battle of the Somme in November 1916, aged just 35, leaving behind a remarkable body of compositions and ambitious unfinished works that have remained largely unknown for generations. Australian composer, concert pianist and Olympic gold medallist Septimus Kelly, who was killed on the Western Front in 1916, is being celebrated as part of a campaign to revive his lost musical legacy 110 years after his death. Australian War Memorial A new biography of the Sydney-born composer will be launched at the Shrine on Sunday, alongside performances of his long-neglected piano music and a screening of an award-winning documentary examining his extraordinary life. The Australian War Memorial’s first musical artist-in-residence, Chris Latham, has spent almost two decades recovering Kelly’s compositions and believes his death represented one of the greatest cultural losses suffered by Australia during World War I.



“Sep, in order of his talents, was an Olympic gold medal-winning rower, a great pianist and an even greater composer,” Latham said. “It’s time for our long-lost son to come home.” Born in Sydney in 1881, Kelly grew up in a musical household before travelling to England, where he attended Eton College and subsequently studied piano and composition in Frankfurt alongside fellow Australian musician Percy Grainger. His talent was evident from childhood. At 14, he performed for Antoine Marmontel, one of Chopin’s last surviving pupils, who enthusiastically endorsed his musical ambitions. Kelly went on to perform with major orchestras and collaborate with some of Europe’s most accomplished musicians, including cellist Pablo Casals and violinist Jelly d’Aranyi. He was also an exceptional athlete, winning a rowing gold medal at the 1908 London Olympics before pursuing a professional music career that took him across Europe and Australia.



The grave of F.S Kelly at Martinsart, Somme, France. Australian War Memorial When war broke out in 1914, Kelly enlisted in Britain’s Royal Naval Division, serving alongside the celebrated English poet Rupert Brooke. Brooke died from an infected mosquito bite while moored of the Greek island of Skyros in the Aegean Sea, while on their way to the landings at Gallipoli. His death in 1915 inspired Kelly’s best-known composition, Elegy for Strings, which was written during the campaign and has since become the subject of an internationally award-winning documentary, Elegy. Despite the demands of military service, Kelly continued composing, completing two substantial collections of piano works inspired by Chopin’s études and preludes.



In May 1916, while on leave before deploying to France, he delivered corrected proofs of his 12 Studies and 24 Monographs to his London publisher. Six months later, on November 13, he was killed on the Somme. His wartime diaries reveal an artist acutely conscious that his creative ambitions might be cut short. Before leaving for the front, Kelly invoked the poet John Keats and his fear of dying before completing his work. Related Article Exclusive

Remembrance Day The war widow, the love story – and the Australian flag stitched from Japanese rags He listed a symphony, piano sonata, string quartet and numerous other compositions still forming in his imagination. Much of that music was never committed to paper. Latham believes Kelly’s decision to serve in a British military unit rather than an Australian battalion contributed to his subsequent neglect, leaving his musical achievements stranded between two countries.



“One can only speculate what would have happened if Kelly had lived,” Latham said. “Had he returned to Australia, he would have likely risen to be the head of music at the ABC or perhaps at the Sydney Conservatorium. The loss of Kelly and similar talents from his generation too often are stories we don’t know.” The new biography by Melbourne author Therese Radic and Olympic gold medallist Martin Cross forms part of a broader campaign to restore Kelly’s reputation, with his recovered compositions being made freely available to musicians and cultural institutions. Sunday’s event will feature performances by pianists Edward and Stephanie Neeman, alongside readings from Kelly’s diaries by Melbourne arts figure Carrillo Gantner. The concert, beginning at 2pm, will conclude a commemorative tour through Sydney, Canberra and Melbourne marking the 110th anniversary of Kelly’s death. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Nvidia scandal raises new concerns about scale of Chinese spying
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaChina relations Nvidia scandal raises new concerns about scale of Chinese spying Peter Martin and Philip J. Heijmans November 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Singapore: The Jensen Huang saga is the latest example of what governments around the world say is a broad push by China to steal commercial and technological secrets and gather intelligence on foreign leaders and military plans. The revelation that Nvidia’s now ex-CEO had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China has rocked the US artificial intelligence boom and thrust allegations that Beijing is seeking to infiltrate Western tech giants into public view. It fits into what foreign officials say is a globe-spanning project. In Germany, prosecutors allege a married couple posing as interpreters and car industry employees cultivated professors in AI, computer science and aerospace, drawing some to China for paid “civilian” lectures delivered to state arms companies. New Zealand intelligence says a Chinese observatory with close government ties tried to install space-tracking equipment through a local company – gear that could also collect military intelligence. Taiwan says Chinese operatives trawl social media for indebted soldiers, offer loans, then press them for secrets and introductions to colleagues. The revelation that Nvidia’s now ex-CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China has rocked the tech world. AP Security agencies around the world have raised the alarm. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) calls Chinese espionage “a grave threat to the economic well-being” of the US. Britain’s MI5 said it was running seven times as many China-related investigations in 2022 as four years earlier. Canadian intelligence calls China its “greatest counter-intelligence threat”, while Dutch intelligence says Chinese digital espionage against technology companies is happening on a “large scale”.



Beijing has dismissed the Huang espionage allegations as a smear, accusing Washington of fabricating “Chinese spy narratives” to justify restrictions on technology exports. Despite those denials, the suspected spy at the centre of the scandal that toppled Huang is now in China with the knowledge of the Chinese government. Related Article Analysis

Billionaires There has never been another scandal like this At stake is the balance of power between the world’s two largest economies. America has bet that its lead in AI and advanced semiconductors will underpin its continued economic strength and military superiority, while its ability to project force across the Pacific constrains Beijing’s ambitions over Taiwan. Espionage offers China a way to erode those advantages, accelerating its technological rise while gaining insight into Washington’s military plans and political decision-making. “There is a lack of appreciation for how professional the Chinese services have become,” said Holden Triplett, who ran the FBI’s office in Beijing and founded Trenchcoat Advisors, noting that parts of China’s intelligence service now rivalled the US Central Intelligence Agency and Russia’s Federal Security Service. “They’re hitting on human frailty and vulnerability and they’re spending all day thinking about how to do this,” he added. “Anyone can fall for it.”



China’s spying push is intensifying in its backyard as Beijing continues to expand its military footprint in the South China Sea. In the Philippines, suspected Chinese spies claimed to be using drones to carry fishing bait as they monitored warships around Subic Bay. Others posed as seafood buyers while flying drones near a naval base. In Manila, hired drivers cruised past the presidential palace, military camps and the US embassy in cars fitted with fake mobile phone towers capable of collecting data from nearby phones. Another vehicle, equipped with cameras and mapping technology, visited more than 120 locations, including bases used by American forces. Loading The alleged operations reached deep inside the Philippine government. Authorities say suspected Chinese agents also recruited people inside the country’s defence establishment, obtaining names of naval personnel and schedules for troop rotations and resupply missions to disputed South China Sea outposts. The cases offered a rare glimpse into the scale and sophistication of Beijing’s espionage operations – which an investigator said were carried out by a spy network that numbered in the hundreds. China has dismissed the allegations as baseless.



“It is extremely widespread because that is the modus operandi of the Chinese,” Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said in an interview. “It’s not only here – the United States. How many are being arrested? Within Australia, how many? In the UK, how many?” Related Article Technology & democracy Who is Alice Huang? The suspected Chinese spy at the centre of the Nvidia scandal China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) is at the centre of Beijing’s increasingly brazen espionage push. The country’s main civilian spy service combines the overseas remit of the CIA with a domestic remit like that of the FBI. Under Chinese President Xi Jinping, reforms have tightened Beijing’s control over provincial and municipal intelligence bureaus, allowing the MSS to co-ordinate operations across the country and pursue more ambitious missions overseas. “It’s become more aggressive,” said Randy Phillips, a former CIA Beijing station chief. “If you look at the kinds of targets they’ve gone after in the last 10 years, they’ve become a much more emboldened organisation.” The MSS is only one arm of what Britain’s parliamentary watchdog has called “the largest state intelligence apparatus in the world”: the People’s Liberation Army runs military, signals and cyber intelligence; the Ministry of Public Security operates at home and abroad; party bodies cultivate political, business and academic networks overseas.



Xi has also handed intelligence agencies broader powers and obliged citizens and institutions to help them. The 2017 National Intelligence Law says every organisation and citizen must “support, assist, and co-operate” with intelligence work. While the US and other countries spy on adversaries and allies, most argue that they don’t engage in industrial espionage the way that the MSS does and none has its scale. ‘They’re hitting on human frailty and vulnerability and they’re spending all day thinking about how to do this.’ Holden Triplett, who ran the FBI’s office in Beijing and founded Trenchcoat Advisors “The numbers in military and civilian intelligence and in the public security apparatus that feeds into intelligence are probably well into the millions,” Phillips said. As the AI revolution has taken off, the technology that underpins it has become a crucial target for Chinese spy agencies, including obtaining it through hacking and human sources, which has made people working at the cutting edge in government, industry and academia potential targets, according to Western officials familiar with the matter.



“The CCP considers itself as in pretty much an existential contest with the United States and other democracies. The hinge on which this contest will turn is scientific and technological power and central to that will be artificial intelligence,” said Peter Mattis, a former CIA counterintelligence analyst who is now president of the Jamestown Foundation. “Any C-suite in the AI industry is going to be an interesting target.” Related Article Analysis

China relations Downfall of world’s chipmaker-in-chief a potential headache for Beijing as well as US AI is also reshaping Chinese spycraft. The biggest gains come early in recruitment, helping services sift huge pools of potential targets and tailor approaches before a human officer steps in. In June, the FBI and Justice Department said suspected Chinese spies used fake consulting firms, lucrative job offers and AI-generated photographs to lure Americans with security clearances onto encrypted messaging apps. In October, US counterintelligence officials warned that Beijing was using AI tools, including DeepSeek, to profile American executives and government officials, identify their vulnerabilities and gain leverage over them. “With AI, you just set up the algorithm to go after targets. You save a tremendous amount of manpower and searching – it’s a force multiplier,” said Dennis Wilder, the CIA’s former deputy assistant director for East Asia and the Pacific. Then, once targets were identified, Chinese agents could meet them online instead of undertaking risky travel overseas, Wilder said. “Human espionage doesn’t any more have to be sneaking around back alleys.”



AI is also bolstering China’s already formidable cyber capabilities. Microsoft said last month that the China-linked group Storm-0940 used agentic AI to automate attacks against hundreds of organisations worldwide. In September, Britain’s MI5 warned that the China General Technology Research Institute was funding research in AI and cybersecurity primarily to strengthen the Ministry of State Security’s espionage capabilities. More than 100 UK-linked academics had contributed to projects ultimately funded by the MSS, MI5 said, sometimes without knowing who was paying. “This isn’t the only [alleged] operation against Nvidia. You should assume there are another 10 or more going on and, of course, it’s not the only operation going on against US tech,” said Triplett, the former FBI agent. “My guess is that they’ll be encouraged by how this worked out and they’ll do more and more of these operations.” Bloomberg Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: 111 'solid', 'fragile', 'effective' and a safety risk - all at the same time
World.content:
Police say the 111 emergency call system is "solid" and "effective", despite their own reports to the government calling it "increasingly fragile", and creating safety risks for the public and their own officers.

The system is built on 1990s technology and police are working to find a replacement, but were unable to give a timeline to RNZ for delivering one, after more than four years.

"It is complicated, but we are working on it with urgency," acting director for communications and dispatch Inspector Natasha Rodley said.

RNZ asked how 111 could be both effective and fragile at the same time.

"We actually think they both are true," said Rodley. "There's always opportunities to be better, to make improvements and that's what our new system would look to do, to build on what we've got, which is a solid system, and make it even better, more accessible, and more modern so that it's not reliant on voice calls."

Several times, she emphasised that people would get an effective response by calling 111.

Police reports to the government in 2023 detailed how that was not always the case - they described actual deaths and injury related to constraints or failures in the system, as RNZ revealed in 2024.

Another report on improving the whole of policing in April said: "The system has faced persistent reliability and performance issues, compounded by difficulties in integrating with other agencies, with some faults taking weeks to resolve.

"These outages and planned outages put pressure on call-takers and compromise public safety."

Maintaining 111 presented public safety risks, while its fragility and complicated structure presented a fundamental risk to emergency response, it said.

RNZ: "Does the system present a fundamental risk to emergency response?"

Rodley: "As of today, no."

RNZ: "Why does your report say it does?"

Rodley: "Because there are opportunities to be better always and it is an ageing system."

Police say people will get an effective response if they call 111. 123rf

Police, fire and ambulance share the system, but none is responsible for it all or developing it. To complicate things, the front end is privately run and owned by telecommunications company Spark.

Spark has said it wants that to change.

A police briefing to minister Mark Mitchell a year ago said the current system created safety risks for first responders - police, ambulance and fire staff.

RNZ: "Do you accept that?"

Rodley: "No."

RNZ: "Do you want to explain why you don't agree with the report that went to the minister?"

The inspector then asked RNZ to quote the report, which included outlining "seven key vulnerabilities" that the minister was told in 2025 created the risks.

RNZ: "Has something happened in the intervening year that we have not yet reported on that has changed that situation?"

Rodley: "No, I think I probably am interpreting it differently. I doubt whether that has changed.

"I guess then I have to change my answer to 'yes', because I would be consistent with the report."

The risk to responders was largely about the difficulty sharing information between the front-lines, she said.

"Maybe all three emergency services need to be involved and they are all not able to be contacted at the same time, which is a limitation of our current system."

She added: "It's an ageing system and IT moves quickly, and we want to make sure that we've got a robust system into the future."

When would that happen?

"That is what we are working through currently with the future of the emergency contact system working group to get the right information for the ministers for that decision to be made."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

The aim was to have the next briefing to ministers in February, nine months later than forecast in early 2026.

"As you know, this is complicated and getting all the information together is a lengthy process."

What happened after February would depend on the government, she said.

"It was never going to be a quick process. This is critical infrastructure - we've got to get this right."

The improvement plan in April 2026 said a new 111 system might be in place in the 2027/28 financial year.

Was that still the aim?

"That would be an aspirational date, absolutely," Rodley said.

Had they looked overseas for an idea of the possible cost?

"No, no, we're not at that stage yet, sorry... honestly, we're just not at that stage yet."

The April report called 111 "increasingly unfit for purpose", but Rodley said police's main message was the system "as it stands, is operating effectively".

World.title: Two men reportedly use crowbar to get in to Northland Woolworths
World.content:
Police are investigating a break in at a Northland Woolworths supermarket early on Saturday morning.

Officers were called to Dargaville's Woolworths on Victoria Street at about 5:30am.

"Reportedly two men used a crowbar to gain entry through the store's front entrance. An investigation is in progress," police said.

Woolworths spokesperson Robin Pinner said the store was working with police and had provided CCTV footage of the incident and those involved.

Pinner said the store was open and trading on Saturday with no impact on customers.

"Unfortunately, we continue to see retail crime have a very real impact in our stores, on our team, security guards and customers, and their whānau, despite extensive security measures and efforts individually and working across industry.

World.title: What we've learnt 10 years on from Kaikōura earthquake
World.content:
Audio player for " Ten Years Since the Kaikoura Earthquake " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/science-and-technology/2598860%2Fwhat-we-ve-learnt-10-years-on-from-kaikoura-earthquake

Ten Years Since the Kaikoura Earthquake Saturday Morning Download MP3 21m

Ten years have passed since the devastating Kaikōura earthquake, an event that took the lives of two people, demolished homes and led to changes in the country's seismic modelling.

Earth Sciences New Zealand volcanologist Graham Leonard told RNZ Saturday Mornings there was a lot to learn after the natural hazard struck.

"Global scientists learned a lot from this too. We realised that these large earthquakes can actually be across many faults at the same time."

He explained that earthquakes were typically the result of stress built up for hundreds of years across a plane and across a region.

Once the fault couldn't hold the stress, it began to unzip from a point that was the epicentre, then later transferred that stress onto other fault-lines.

"Our national seismic hazard model underwent a major revision and, globally, our understanding of the way earthquakes rupture and unzip changed with this event."

Immediately after the earthquake Leonard said there were "geological detectives in the air", taking photographs and assessing the damage for clues.

"Those fault cuts are 10-12 metres long. The uplift at the coast was up to eight metres."

Scientists also assessed satellite imagery and put drones in the air to utilise LiDar.

Road damage Kaikōura to Waiau Valley (file image) RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

Leanard said, along with land damage, offshore impacts were also significant.

"There was a massive sediment movement in the steep offshore bathymetry that dropped debris flows and sediment into the canyon that flows north from there, the Kaikōura Canyon, and right up through beyond Hawke's Bay off of the eastern North Island, 600-700 kilometres."

He said the earthquake took place on a steep coastal location, where many faults were part of the plate boundary action, bringing mountains out of the water.

"That means it's hard to get roads in and out, hard to have the connection of infrastructure. We saw tens of thousands of landslides in this event, really quite unprecedented."

Leonard said scientists could see it was a widespread earthquake right away from the geonet shake reports, but there were some blank spots.

"There was a dark spot in the middle, where people either didn't have connectivity or they were really busy dealing with something else, and we got no reports in the central area."

A damaged bridge on the road between Waiau and Mt Lyford following the earthquake in 2016. (file image) RNZ / Conan Young

"Throughout that area, there were widespread landslips and earthquake-shaking damage, and people were isolated for a long time."

The lessons learnt from the event were now part of the knowledge helping to prepare for future earthquakes, including a highly likely Alpine Fault quake.

Also known as the AF8, scientists estimate a 75 percent chance of a magnitude 8 or higher earthquake will happen at the southern fault in the next 50 years.

Leonard said, because the fault covered a larger location, the energy released was expected to be much more impactful, with far more landslides across the South Island.

"Directivity will be important. If it unzips again from south to north, that will send energy through to Wellington again.

"It will probably mostly be on land, but there is a chance of it rupturing offshore. In that case, more at the south end, so there's a chance of local tsunami."

He said scientists were coming together with emergency management to plan for the event.

"That's everything from thinking about the changes in engineering, and perhaps the opportunity to engineer buildings that might be more rapidly post-earthquake fixable or even usable.

World.title: Four rescued, one still missing at Kariotahi Beach
World.content:
Four people were rescued and one was still missing, after an incident at an Auckland beach.

Acting Inspector Kuhrt Wieneke said police responded to the "water-related incident" about 6.30pm Saturday.

He said four people were taken out of the water safely.

"One person is in a serious, but stable condition, while the three others are in a minor condition.

"At this stage, one person remains outstanding."

World.title: New Zealand reacts, as US progresses investigation into lamb imports
World.content:
New Zealand is "deeply disappointed" that the US International Trade Commission will move its safeguard investigation into lamb imports to the next stage, Minister for Trade and Investment Todd McClay says.

In May, McClay said he expected the United States government to launch a trade investigation into lamb imports, warning it could result in New Zealand lamb exports to the US facing increased tariffs.

On Saturday, McClay said the commission's vote was equally split, which meant it would now look at possible remedies.

"New Zealand lamb exports do not harm US producers," he said. "Our lamb complements US production and helps meet growing consumer demand.

"Our share of US lamb consumption has stayed stable for the past 20 years. We will keep working closely with industry and dealing directly with our US counterparts.

"I have instructed officials to travel to Washington DC for the commission's remedy hearing on 1 December.

"After the commission makes its recommendations, the US administration will decide whether to impose safeguard measures and what form they would take."

World.title: The 16 MPs (likely) voted out of Parliament
World.content:
Even as Parliament looks likely to grow to 131 MPs, several who have been there for the last term have been saying goodbye this week.

Because they were involuntarily ejected by voters, these 16 departing MPs probably won't get the chance to deliver valedictory speeches - so this will have to do for now.

National

Nicola Willis, the deputy leader and finance minister who also championed National's economic growth and social investment strategies, is the highest-profile exit, and one of National's hardest-working and most effective ministers.

She had worked as a staffer for both John Key and Bill English, and built a reputation as a fierce debater, going on to be a general manager at Fonterra and a director at the New Zealand Initiative, before returning to Parliament as an MP in 2018 on National's list, after the resignation of Steven Joyce.

After previously attempting campaigns in traditionally left-leaning Wellington electorates - against Grant Robertson in Wellington Central in 2017 and 2020, and Ōhāriu's Greg O'Connor in 2023 - she chose not to contest an electorate this time, ending up a victim of National's overhang.

Paul Goldsmith and Nicola Willis were key members of Christopher Luxon's cabinet. Fiona Goodall/Getty Images

At third on the list, Chris Bishop is another victim of National's electorate success, after conceding Hutt South to Labour's Ginny Andersen on election night and acknowledging his chances of returning in the final count were "extremely unlikely".

A former lobbyist for Philip Morris, and staffer for Gerry Brownlee and Steven Joyce, Bishop entered Parliament in 2014 on National's list, claimed Hutt South in 2017 after the departure of Labour's Trevor Mallard and lost it to Andersen in the 2020 'red wave' election, before winning it back in 2023.

Another of National's hard-working front bench, Bishop has led National's revision and replacement of Labour's Resource Management Act reforms, housing, infrastructure and transport, and became Attorney-General this year, while losing his role as National campaign chair in April, after rumours of an attempted leadership spill.

With National's low polling in 2026, Paul Goldsmith shifted from the one-tick strategy he'd run in Epsom against a succession of ACT leaders since 2011 to an explicit two-tick campaign against David Seymour, but appears to have fallen short, winning 30.5 percent of electorate votes on the night, compared to Seymour's 36.8.

A historian, biographer, pianist and taekwondo black belt, the trusted Luxon loyalist ended up with 10 portfolios (with GCSB and NZSIS being one combined role) - believed to be the most held by a minister this century - after Chris Penk's August attempt to topple the leader and sudden exit.

After being an Auckland councillor criticised for attempts to have homeless people removed from the CBD, he went on to become a National minister under John Key, had a stint as finance spokesperson under Judith Collins, and under Luxon, has led broadcasting, electoral and justice changes, including the move-on orders and removal of same-day voter enrolment.

Gerry Brownlee leaves Parliament as the father of the House - the longest continuously serving male MP - and Parliament's Speaker.

Gerry Brownlee leaves Parliament as father of the House. VNP / Phil Smith

He became MP for Ilam in the first MMP election of 1996, after unsuccessfully challenging Jim Anderton in '93, holding the seat until the red wave of 2020. He was deputy leader under both Don Brash and Judith Collins, and was a Leader of the House, defence minister, foreign minister, transport minister and led the response to the Canterbury earthquakes under Key.

His past life as a woodwork teacher stood him in good stead in the Speaker's chair, but whether his family's Olympic rowing history had much impact is unclear.

Nancy Lu was National's highest-ranked new MP in 2023, after Andrew Bayly's by-election win in Port Waikato saw him move to an electorate seat, freeing up a spot for a list seat.

Born in Guangzhou, China, she moved to Auckland at age 10 and became a chartered accountant, before becoming the party's only Chinese-heritage candidate in 2020.

Melissa Lee was the first Korean elected to Parliament - and the first Korean-born woman to enter a country's Parliament outside Korea - when she came in on National's list in 2008. She came close to unseating Labour's Helen White from Mt Albert in 2023, falling short by just 18 votes in a judicial recount.

After being a journalist for 23 years, including writing for the NZ Herald and the Listener, she was replaced as media and communications minister, and dumped out of Cabinet in Luxon's first reshuffle in 2024.

Carlos Cheung will hope special votes tip his way in Mt Roskill, with just 262 votes separating him and Michael Wood, who was dumped from cabinet in 2023 for repeatedly failing to declare shares and lost the previously safe Labour seat, as the red tide swept back out.

Cheung was born in Hong Kong and moved to New Zealand as a teenager, he has a PhD in diabetes and cardiac disease, and made it a point of pride to visit every junior, intermediate, secondary and special school in his electorate.

Vanessa Weenink had probably the most explosive comments of any departing MP, saying she would not miss the abuse from members of the public and expressing frustration at National's rightward shift.

A general practitioner for 20 years and an army medical officer for 22 - including deployments to Afghanistan and East Timor - Weenink was a Labour member, until the NZ Medical Association she chaired was disestablished in 2022, after which she joined National, narrowly taking Banks Peninsula in '23, before losing it again to Labour's Tracey McLellan.

Vanessa Weenink switched allegiances to National, after the Labour government disestablished her NZ Medical Association. VNP/Phil Smith

Labour

Deborah Russell was first elected in 2017, as MP for New Lynn, replacing former leader David Cunliffe, but after two terms, had to return on the list in 2023, after losing to Paulo Garcia.

An academic with a PhD in philosophy and co-writer of a book on tax fairness, she was minister of statistics and the Earthquake Commission under Chris Hipkins, and occasionally landed in hot water for expressing tax views out of line with the party's.

Rachel Boyack was an organiser for First Union, before reclaiming the Nelson electorate in the 2020 red wave from National's Nick Smith, who had held the seat since 1996, and narrowly held it in '23 by just 26 votes against National's Blair Cameron, before losing it to him by more than 1200 votes this election.

Her Plain Language Bill that aimed to make government documents easier to understand was reversed by the National-led coalition last term.

Dan Rosewarne was an army mechanic, who attained the rank of captain - with two deployments to Afghanistan, one to Solomon Islands and one responding to the Kaikōura earthquake - and survived leukaemia, before entering Parliament in 2022 on the list, after Kris Faafoi's retirement.

He was ejected again, after losing Waimakariri to National's Matt Doocey in '23, but returned to Parliament briefly this year, after the resignation of Peeni Henare in March.
